Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Together with the Preface
<Rhapsody on the Horse Archery in the Huálín Garden on the Third Day of the Third Month, with Preface>
Your servant has heard that Yáo, in the mid-spring month,
carved jade and traveled along the Hé River;
Shùn, on the morning of the Jiǎzǐ day,
unfurled maps and inspected the Luò River.
Atop the Jasper Terrace of the Xià Sovereign,
he sometimes rode two dragons;
before the Dark Orchard of the King of Zhōu,
he still harnessed the eight fine steeds.
When our Great Zhōu established its foundation,
the Nánzhèng governed the heavens,
and the Běizhèng governed the earth,
quelling the rebellion of the Jiǔlí,
and determining the crimes of the Sānwēi.
Cloud records governed the officials,
and bird-named officers followed their duties;
the August Sovereign possessed the tallies for holding the calendar,
and the Dark Scepter provided the auspicious sign of success.
Is it merely that Heaven and Earth joined their virtues,
or that the sun and moon shone with brilliance?
The Emperor, with the nature of a supreme sage,
has inherited the destiny of the "Following the Footsteps of Ancestors,"
communicating with the spirit of the celestial phenomena,
and manifesting the virtue of the divine.
Bó Yí directed the rites of the ancestral temple,
as seen in the "Three Rites";
Kuí served as the Director of Music,
as heard in the "Jiǔchéng."
He restrains himself and is perfected in ritual deportment,
while his majestic awe commands all military affairs.
Furthermore, he humbles himself and eats simple food,
using black curtains and plain silk robes,
taking the common people as his heart,
and the four seas as his concern.
If it does not rain in the western suburbs,
it immediately moves the Imperial sentiment;
if the spring farming in the east is not yet harvested,
the Heavenly concern is further extended.
Weapons and armor are not assembled,
without needing to wait for the Dānwū;
palaces and towers are not moved,
so there is no labor for the Báiyàn.
Silver jars and golden vessels,
mountain carriages and marsh horses.
Is it only that the bamboo and reeds, these two grasses,
both drip with sweet dew?
The three vapors of blue and red
together become the Auspicious Star.
The Diāotí and Záochǐ tribes
cross the seawater to come and pay homage;
the lands of Wūyì and Huángzhī
follow the eastern wind to receive their officials.
At this time, the Xuánniǎo governs the calendar,
and the Cānglóng directs the season;
lambs are offered as the ice melts,
paulownia flowers bloom and duckweed grows.
The Emperor visits the Huálín Garden,
the Jade Balance is aligned and the Tàijiē is level,
the Chānghé gates open and the Gōuchén constellation turns,
a thousand chariots move like thunder,
ten thousand riders gather like clouds.
Falling blossoms fly along with the fungus-shaped canopies,
willows share the same color as the spring banners.
He then commands the assembled ministers
to display the ritual of the Grand Archery.
Although the banquet of the Fúxì purification is held,
he employs the ceremony of the Chūnsōu hunt.
They stop to set up a temporary palace,
and briefly spread out the tent-hall.
The steps have no jade discs,
which is different from the stele of Héjiān;
the doors have no golden knockers,
quite unlike the rhapsody of Xǔchāng.
The Dòngtíng music having been played,
"Chéngyún" is then performed.
"Zōuyú" in nine stanzas,
"Líshǒu" in seven chapters.
The target is painted with five-colored clouds,
the jars hold wine of a hundred blessings.
Táng bows joined nine times,
with winter wood and spring glue;
Xià arrows in three finishes,
with green shafts and red feathers.
Thereupon, horses of sweating blood are selected,
and compared within the golden tracks.
Hóngyáng and Fēiquè,
Zǐyàn and Chénfēng,
the Sùshuāng of Táng Chéng Gōng,
the thousand-li steed of the Hǎixī Hóu.
None failed to bury the feathers in the target or strike the pole,
making the apes wail and the wild geese fall.
Bells and drums shake the earth,
dust and sand fill the sky.
Wine is served in jars,
food is presented in tripods.
As for silk, the entire brocade market is moved here;
as for coins, the entire copper mountain is transported.
The Tàishǐ listens to the drums to judge merit,
the Sīmǎ raises the banners to reward the successful.
Above, it is like the spreading of clouds and the falling of rain,
below, it is like the hiding of mountains and the receiving of the sea.
This is truly the ultimate joy of Heaven and Earth,
and the delight of great fortune.
As the Ruòmù tree is about to lower,
and the golden waves are about to rise,
the Heavenly gaze is solemn,
and the guests' songs are filled with drunken joy.
Although they have briefly left the Northern Gate
and hosted a banquet in the Western City,
it is just like the court at the Fēng River,
or the gathering at Mount Qí.
I, your humble servant, am not capable,
yet I have received the decree to compose this text.
Looking at the sky through a tube,
or measuring the sea with a gourd,
how can I describe such magnificent virtue,
or even present a rough outline?
The year is in the position of Zhāoyáng,
the month is in Dàliáng.
The day is the Shàngsì,
the season is Shǎoyáng.
The Spring Historian presides over his duties,
the Spirit of the East offers auspicious signs.
Ten thousand riders are summoned to Pínglè,
a thousand gates are opened at Jiànzhāng.
Following carriages pour the wine,
the covered walkways burn incense.
The Emperor assists the four enclosures at the Imperial stables,
turning his six-dragon carriage in the Heavenly Park,
facing the level woods of Xuānqǔ,
gazing at the long slopes of Gānquán.
The flowery canopies fly levelly,
the wind-vane birds turn subtly.
The road is straight and the city distant,
the woods are long and the riders are far.
The curtain palace was prepared overnight,
the tent-hall opens for the banquet,
adjacent to Xìliǔ,
diagonally bordering Qínián.
Deploying the stork-wing formation,
waving the fish-beard banners.
The portable clepsydra tracks the time,
the front banners carry the images of kites.
Grass is cleared on the riverbank,
the mouth of the Wèi River is refreshed by springs.
The target-mound is like five-colored clouds,
the center-ring is perfectly round.
The Yang pipes having been tuned,
the spring strings are indeed played.
The Zǒngzhāng harmonizes the melodies,
the Chéngjūn displays the feather-dances.
Soaring phoenixes form a forest,
numinous fungi form a garden.
Grass holds long ribbons,
paulownia trees hang with delicate blossoms.
Birds warble as songs approach,
blossoms are dense like gathered snow.
The jade pitch-pipes tune the bells,
the golden chimes pace the drums.
Thereupon, the steeds chew on bits and snap iron,
chasing the sun and pursuing the wind,
together testing the tracks lined with long catalpas,
together descending to the Lánchí Palace.
At the crack of the whip, their sweat turns red,
entering the track, the dust turns crimson.
Having observed the worthies in the Grand Archery,
he then issues administrative orders to the Master of Bows.
Changing the three-fold chase to a painted deer target,
and ascending a hundred feet to hang the bear target.
The Fánruò bow shakes the ground,
the iron-black steeds gallop through the air.
The ritual correctly arranges the six pairs of archers,
the poems are sung in nine stanzas.
All seven layers of armor are pierced,
five wild boars fall in the same pit.
Bows are like bright moons facing the target-mound,
horses are like floating clouds heading for the track.
Wild geese lose their flock and their lines are broken,
apes seek the forest but their paths are cut off.
Controlling the jade bits, they shake the stars,
straddling the golden saddles, they move the moon.
Thus there were the good families of the Liù Jùn,
and the elite chosen from the Wǔ Líng.
Having newly returned from the campaign at Mǎ Yì,
and recently ceased the battles at Lóng Chéng.
The generals, in their military attire,
came to attend the martial banquet.
Still carrying their Liú Xīng swords,
still riding their Bēn Diàn steeds.
They first heard the drums and announced the tallies,
then moved the poles and marked the arrows.
The spray from the horses dampened their clothes,
and the startled dust sprinkled their faces.
Stone weirs dammed the water to irrigate the gardens,
while flowers rode the wind to encircle the hall.
Cups were carved like Xióng Ěr,
and wine jars were painted with Fēi Yún.
The coins from the Shuǐ Héng were piled like mountains,
and the brocades from the Zhī Shì spread like clouds.
The Master of the Banquet granted rewards,
and the Supervisor of Wine brought the cups.
The supreme joy surpassed that of the *Qiū Shuǐ*,
and the cheer exceeded that on the Chūn Tái.
Soon the sun set over the Zé Gōng,
and the banquet concluded in the Xiàng Pǔ.
Regretfully watching the imperial clearance depart, leaving behind joy;
looking back at the returning carriage and the remaining dances.
Wishing to make Shí Liáng hold the arrows,
and Tóng Shān swallow the fletchings.
Drawing bows at the dragons of Chǔ Shuǐ,
and flying arrows at the tigers of Wú Tíng.
Moreover, practicing respectful non-action,
the *Nán Fēng* is here;
not having intent toward dragonfly wings,
how could there be feelings for halberd branches?
Only observing the etiquette of bowing and yielding,
taking the manner of majestic power.
○ *Wén Yuàn Yīng Huá*, 58.
*Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, 4.
*Chū Xué Jì*, 4.
*Xiǎo Yuán Fù*
As for atop a single branch,
Cháo Fù found a place for a secure nest;
inside a single gourd,
Hú Gōng had room for his body.
Moreover, Guǎn Níng’s bed of goosefoot stalks,
though worn through, could be sat upon;
Jī Kāng’s forge,
being warm, was fit for sleep.
Why must there be connected gates and inner chambers,
like the mansion of Fán Zhòng in Nán Yáng?
Green steps and blue lattice-work,
like the residence of Wáng Gēn in the Xī Hàn.
I have a dilapidated cottage of a few mǔ,
in solitude far from men;
just enough to pass the summer and winter festivals,
just enough to avoid the wind and frost.
Though like Yàn Yīng living near the market,
I do not seek profit morning or night;
like Pān Yuè facing the city wall,
I enjoy the pleasure of idle living.
Furthermore, the yellow crane is wary of dew,
having no desire for the carriages of lords;
the Yuán Jū bird avoids the wind,
originally having no feeling for bells and drums.
Lù Jī lived together with his brother,
and Hán Kāng did not separate from his nephew.
Snail horns and mosquito eyelashes
are also enough for mutual accommodation.
Then lingering in the cave-room,
just like tunneling into a mound.
Dew falls among the paulownias,
and wind comes from beneath the willows.
The zither is named Zhū Zhù,
and the book is titled *Yù Bēi*.
There are wild pears but no lodge,
plenty of sour jujubes but no terrace;
still reaching eight or nine zhàng on its side,
and dozens of steps in length and breadth.
Two or three rows of elms and willows,
and over a hundred pear and peach trees.
Pushing through the dense growth to see the window,
walking through the crookedness to find the path.
The cicada has cover and is not startled,
the pheasant has no net and what is there to fear?
Grasses and trees are intermingled,
and branches and twigs are interlaced.
Mountains are formed by baskets of earth,
and the ground has the hollows of a hall.
Hiding foxes share burrows,
and nesting magpies double their nests.
Strings of beads on fine mats,
and long-handled cold gourds;
they can satisfy hunger,
and they can provide rest.
Crooked and cramped is the narrow room,
pierced and leaking is the thatched roof.
The eaves are so low they strike the hat,
and the door is so level it brushes the eyebrows.
In the sitting tent there are no cranes,
and supporting the bed there are tortoises.
Birds have much leisure,
and flowers follow the four seasons.
My heart is like the withered wood of Lì Líng,
and my hair is like the tangled silk of Suī Yáng.
Not like a summer day yet fearsome,
unlike an autumn sky yet sorrowful.
Fish of one or two inches,
bamboo of two or three poles.
Cloud-vapors shade the clumps of milfoil; the essence of metal nurtures the autumn chrysanthemums. Jujubes are sour and pears are tart; peaches are small and plums are wild.
Fallen leaves cover half the bed,
and wild flowers fill the house.
It is named the House of the Rustic,
and it is called the Valley of Yú Gōng.
Testing a rest in the dense woods,
I have long envied the removing of the hairpin.
Although there is a gate, it is long closed;
truly without water, yet I am constantly submerged.
In the three spring months, I know those who carry hoes;
in the fifth month, I am sought by one wearing furs.
Asking after the medicinal properties of Gě Hóng,
and visiting the *Bǔ Lín* of Jīng Fáng.
The grass has no intent to forget sorrow,
and the flowers have no heart for Cháng Lè.
For what reason do birds chase wine?
With what feeling do fish listen to the zither?
Moreover, cold and heat change their commands,
violating one's inner nature.
Cuī Yīn shortened his years through unhappiness,
and Wú Zhì nurtured illness through long sorrow.
Quieting house spirits by burying stones,
and subduing mountain spirits by reflecting mirrors.
Often uttering the laments of Zhuāng Xì,
and nearly following the command of Wèi Kē.
In the quiet chambers at dusk,
the old and young lead each other.
Disheveled children like those of Wáng Bà,
and a wife with a mallet-shaped bun like that of Liáng Hóng.
Two jars of parched wheat,
and one plot of winter vegetables.
The wind soughs and the trees are restless,
the sky is dismal and the clouds are low.
Sparrows chatter in empty granaries,
and cicadas shrill, startling the Lǎn Fù.
Formerly, like common weeds, I was undeservedly puffed up by praise,
relying on the "surplus of blessings" from the *Wén Yán*.
My gate possessed Tōng Dé,
and my family inherited bestowed writings.
Sometimes accompanying guests at the Xuán Wǔ Guàn,
and occasionally visiting the ruins of Fèng Huáng.
Observing the reception of sacrificial meat in the Xuān Shì,
and composing the *Cháng Yáng* in the duty quarters.
Then the mountains collapsed and the rivers dried up;
ice shattered and tiles split.
The Great Thief secretly shifted power,
and the Cháng Lí was eternally extinguished.
Straight reins were broken at Sān Wēi,
and smooth paths were shattered at the Jiǔ Zhé.
Jīng Kē had the sorrow of the cold water,
and Sū Wǔ had the parting in the autumn wind.
At Guān Shān, the wind and moon are desolate,
and at Lǒng Shuǐ, the heart and bowels are severed.
Tortoises speak of the cold in this place,
and cranes are surprised by the snow this year.
A hundred years pass in a flash,
and the glory is already late.
Before clearing the grievance of Yàn Mén,
first thinking of the distance of the Hóng Lù.
It cannot be changed by the Huái Hǎi,
nor can it be transformed by the Golden Elixir.
Though my bones were not bleached at Lóng Mén,
I finally bow my head at Mǎ Bǎn.
Truly, the ways of Heaven are obscure,
alas, the lives of the people are turbulent.
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, 65.
*Wén Yuàn Yīng Huá*, 97.
*Zhú Zhàng Fù*
When Huán Xuān-wǔ pacified Jīng Zhōu,
an attendant reported:
"There is one called Chǔ Qiū Xiān-shēng
who has come to wait at the gate."
Huán Gōng said:
"That the son of such a famous father
should be wandering displaced through the Jiāng and Hàn rivers
is my own responsibility!"
When he ordered him to be introduced,
he then said:
"Alas,
Sir, you are old!
Crane-white hair and chicken-like skin,
a disheveled head and sparse teeth.
You are indeed the heroic spirit of the Jiāng and Hàn,
the fine timber of Héng and Jīng;
though your name is heard in every household,
fortunately you seek nothing from a thousand lǐ.
I have Líng-shòu wood staves with copper rings,
and peach-branch staves with silver horns.
They are like papaya blossoms that have opened but not fallen,
or nurtured lotus flowers that do not wither.
They welcome the immortal guest at Jǐn-shì,
and send off the swimming dragon at Gě-bēi.
Sir, you shall use this to sustain your old age,
and to support you in times of frailty."
Chǔ Qiū Xiān-shēng smiled and said:
"The Middle Kingdom is clear about rites and righteousness,
but dark regarding the understanding of people.
The sorrow of my heart
is only for our people.
Even with sparse branches of strong mulberry
or the tight nodes of upright bamboo,
with a bird carved at the staff tip
or a qílín depicted on the horn head,
how can they assist me in this illness,
or sustain this body of mine?
As for the world changing its marketplaces and courts,
and the years shifting the hills and valleys;
when apes howl and hawks cry shrilly,
and the wind and frost are miserable and dark;
when Chǔ and Hàn contend for the balance,
and Yuán and Cáo race in pursuit;
beasts find no grass to eat,
and birds find no trees to nest in.
At such times, one shivers without fear,
and trembles without being cold.
The Hú horses neigh mournfully,
and the Qiāng flutes trill sadly;
friends and relatives are separated and lost,
wives and children drift away.
Letters are sent from Yù-guān,
and bracelets are left behind at Zhāng-tái;
the cold passes are desolate,
and the traveler's life is full of sorrow.
Thin feathers meet with hunting arrows,
fragile bones are covered by wind and frost;
hair turns white and becomes shorter,
eyebrows grow bushy and longer.
Therefore, the sorrowful trunk spreads wide,
and the mournful branches are knotted;
once graceful, now frail and unseemly,
suddenly one is aged and elderly.
Tián Fèng was transformed at Chéng-gōng,
and Yáng-wén was changed at Zōng-miè.
Pān Yuè's autumnal stirrings,
Jī-shēng's weariness of wandering,
Huán Tán's unhappiness,
and Wú Zhì's constant sorrow—
all were not yet in the twilight of their years,
yet their appearance arrived at autumn early.
I have thus declined,
yet there is a reason;
it is neither a ghost nor a sand-spitting demon,
but the sorrow in my heart.
Before reaching the state of following the heart's desire,
I first seek the state of the compliant ear.
Why did Bó-yù sigh?
Qiū-míng only felt shame.
When tearing tigers and rending bears,
I was still like a young child;
observing my form and examining my appearance,
you truly pity the old man.
Separately, there are the bushy-browed high officials of the nine thorns,
and the aged counselors of the three pagoda-trees;
Kǒng Guāng resigned due to illness,
Yuán Féng retired from office,
Wú Bì ceased attending court,
and Yáng Biāo mourned his son.
This gift from you, Míng-gōng,
is perhaps not without reason."
Chǔ Qiū Xiān-shēng then sang:
"Autumn goosefoot with tight nodes,
white goosefoot with one heart.
In the end, it is fit to carry a hoe,
and is sufficient of itself to drive away beasts.
Once passed to Dà-xià,
it becomes the Dèng-lín forest in vain."
○ Yì-wén Lèi-jù, Scroll 69.
Wén-yuàn Yīng-huá, Scroll 109.
〈Qióng-zhú Zhàng Fù〉
Chén-míng-zǐ wandered to the summit of Bā-shān,
and took bamboo from its northern shade.
Graceful with high nodes,
solitary and hollow-hearted.
Its color made ancient by the frost and wind,
its mottling deepened by the staining of dew.
Always among the tribe of the infirm,
in deep and gloomy shadows.
Its pattern is not inherently distinct,
yet it is valued for its substance;
it contains the rhythm of the crying phoenix,
and is crafted into a staff that becomes a dragon.
Its branches are pulled strong and straight,
its luster and color are lush;
it matches the wheelwright's standard of lightness,
and waits for the feathered traveler to gift it.
Spring is about to fade,
and white clouds arrive late.
Consulting with an elder,
I take it up to follow him.
Holding the end, I present it,
having no way to support myself.
Sugarcane, though sweet,
cannot be leaned upon;
that goosefoot, though solid,
cannot be beautiful.
Nothing is like being among the 'useless' timber,
at the very beginning of being useful.
In Lǔ, it was granted by rank;
in Hàn, it was bestowed for age.
Formerly I valued your age,
now you favor my worth.
Books lie across the table,
the jade whisk is on the mat;
then it is encased from behind,
and brushed from the front.
You shall pluck fragrance in the woods and ponds,
and enjoy yourself on the porches;
moving amidst the hanging sashes of the high and low,
following the winding paths of the ascent and descent.
Its roots rest in Jiāng-nán,
by the vast and deep pools;
its nodes are passed to Dà-xià,
across the vast and distant wilds.
How can this compare to touching the shoes upon the lord's hall,
or serving as the motto by the lord's seat,
being able to join with silk sashes and jade pendants,
and exiting fragrant chambers into orchid courtyards.
○ Wén-yuàn Yīng-huá, Scroll 109.
With Preface
〈Āi Jiāng-nán Fù〉 with Preface
In the year of Wùchén,
in the month of Jiànhài,
a great rebel overthrew the state,
and Jīnlíng collapsed.
I then fled to the wild valleys;
public and private life were reduced to misery.
Fleeing for my life to Huáyáng,
I left with no return.
The path of restoration faded away,
ending in the year of Jiǎxū.
For three days I wailed at the Capital Pavilion;
for three years I was imprisoned in a guest house.
The way of Heaven completed its cycle,
but things reached their extreme without returning.
Fù Xiè only grieved for his own life,
having no place to seek survival;
Yuán Ān always thought of the royal house,
and naturally his tears flowed.
Formerly, the aspirations of Huán Jūnshān
and the life of Dù Yuánkǎi
were both recorded in books,
and both were able to write their own prefaces.
The literary elegance of Pān Yuè
first described his family traditions;
the poetic rhapsodies of Lù Jī
first set forth his family’s ancestral virtues.
Truly, just as my hair began to turn grey,
I immediately encountered mourning and chaos;
drifting and wandering in this small way,
until reaching my twilight years.
The "Yàngē" of distant parting
brings sorrow more than I can bear;
when elders of Chǔ meet,
what use is it to weep?
Fearing the rain of Nánshān,
I suddenly trod upon the court of Qín;
avoiding the shores of the Eastern Sea,
I eventually ate the grain of Zhōu.
Drifting at Xiàtíng,
a sojourner at Gāoqiáo.
The songs of Chǔ are not the means for seeking joy;
the wine of Lǔ has no use for forgetting sorrow.
Retrospectively composing this rhapsody
merely to record these words,
not without words of peril and bitterness,
with only sorrow as its theme.
The sun is setting and the road is long;
what world is this among men!
Once the General has departed,
the Great Tree withers and falls;
the brave warrior does not return,
and the cold wind soughs and sighs.
The jade of Jīng glared at the pillar,
accepting the "consecutive cities" only to be deceived;
the covenant documents lay across the steps,
holding the pearl tray with trembling hands.
Zhōng Yí, the gentleman,
entered as a prisoner wearing the southern cap;
Jì Sūn, the envoy,
remained at the guesthouse of Xīhé.
Shēn Bāoxū prostrated on the ground,
smashing his forehead;
Cài Wēigōng's tears were exhausted,
followed by blood.
The willows of the Fishing Terrace are moved,
and Yùguān is no longer in sight;
the cry of the crane at Huátíng,
how could it be heard at Héqiáo!
Sūn Cè divided the world into three
with troops of but a single battalion;
Xiàng Jí used the sons of Jiāngdōng,
though they were only eight thousand men.
Consequently, they split the mountains and rivers
and carved up the world.
How could there be a million righteous soldiers
who furled their armor in a single morning,
mown down and slaughtered
like grass and trees?
The Jiāng and Huái rivers offered no barrier of banks;
the pavilions and walls had no strength of fences.
Those who collected taxes by the head and winnowing basket
joined in alliances;
those with hoes, harrows, and thorn-staffs
took advantage of the opportunity.
Could it be that the royal aura of Jiāngbiǎo
has come to an end after three hundred years?
Thus we know that swallowing the six directions
could not avoid the disaster of Zhǐdào;
unifying the axles and scripts
could not save one from the calamity of Píngyáng.
Alas!
The mountains and peaks crumble,
having trodden upon the fate of ruin;
as the years pass in succession,
there must be the sorrow of leaving the old.
Divine will and human affairs
are enough to make one mournful and heartbroken!
Furthermore, the path for boats and oars is exhausted;
the Milky Way cannot be reached by a raft.
Gale winds block the way;
there is no date for reaching Pénglái.
The destitute wish to express their words;
the weary must sing of their deeds.
Lù Shìhéng might clap his hands upon hearing this,
and this I would willingly accept;
Zhāng Píngzǐ might see it and find it crude,
and that would indeed be appropriate.
Our family managed the granaries and served the Zhōu,
becoming a clan through generations of merit;
governing the state and assisting the Hàn,
holding office by discussing the Way.
Endowed with the jade and stone of Sōng and Huà,
moistened by the waves of the Hé and Luò.
Residing with the Luò at our back for generations,
our town faced the river in peaceful tranquility.
Until the hardships of Yǒngjiā,
when the Central Plains first lacked a master.
The people leaned against walls;
the roads were crisscrossed by jackals and tigers.

With Preface
〈Rhapsody on a Broken Heart〉 with Preface
Of the five blessings, I have no sign;
from the three spirits, I have received punishment.
As for my successors,
most died young.
Two sons and one daughter,
all had reached the age of wearing clothes.
During the chaos in Jīnlíng,
they stayed together but perished.
Wandering through passes and rivers,
suddenly my hair has turned white.
They sprouted but did not flower;
I frequently feel sorrow for them.
One daughter reached adulthood,
and one eldest grandson was an infant;
suddenly they returned to the dark earth—
what pain can compare to this!
Having been grieved by these events,
I mourn those who passed before.
Feeling only a broken heart,
I thus take "Broken Heart" as the title of this rhapsody.
As for entering the room and bringing light,
that is no longer attainable;
crossing the river to form a commandery,
the journey ahead grows even more distant.
Jiéyú wrote a rhapsody of self-lament;
Yáng Xióng wrote an essay of mourning and sacrifice.
Wáng Zhèngzhǎng had the sorrow of the northern outskirts;

how could I have expected this?

the rhinoceros horn hairpin was worn to no effect.
The wind lacks the Shàonǚ,
the grass is not the Yìnnán.
The crow's feathers covered in vain,
the beast's milk was held in the mouth for naught.
*Zhèn* is the palace of the eldest son,
*Xùn* is the position of the eldest daughter;
in the years of my life,
they first withered in this land.
How long is human life,
that a hundred sorrows should all arrive together?
The two Wáng brothers served the Buddha,
the two Xī brothers served the Dào;
though the end must come at a set time,
how could they protect one another?
Chilling is the fallen dew,
rustling are the autumn grasses.
Gone are the Límín,
alas for Zhòngrén!
Hoping for the prior knowledge of Yáng Yòu,
expecting the reincarnation of Zhāng Héng.
One morning like a candle in the wind,
for ten thousand ages, dust and soil.
Oh, hills and mounds, how can you endure?
How many people can remain?
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, 34.
*Wènyuán Yīnghuá*, 129.
〈*Kū Shù Fù*〉
Yīn Zhòngwén was elegant and refined,
his name known throughout the realm.
Times changed and the era shifted,
he went out to serve as the Tàishǒu of Dōngyáng.
Often melancholy and unhappy,
he looked at the pagoda tree in the courtyard and sighed, saying:
"This tree, once swaying and dancing,
its vitality is now exhausted!"
As for the Báilù upright pine,
the Qīngniú patterned catalpa,
their roots were coiled and vigorous,
inside and outside the mountain cliffs.
Why did the cassia waste away?
Why is the phoenix tree half-dead?
In the past, transplanted from the Sānhé,
roots moved from the Jiǔwǎn.
Blossoming at the Jiànshǐ Palace,
dropping fruit in the gardens of Suīyáng.
Their sound contained the Xiègǔ valley notes,
their melodies embraced the *Yúnmén*.
Leading their fledglings, phoenixes gathered;
wing-to-wing, mandarin ducks nested.
They heard the crying crane by the Fēngtíng,
and the howling gibbon by the Yuèxiá.
Then there are those twisted and swollen,
coiled and convoluted,
looking back like bears or tigers,
rising and falling like fish or dragons.
Knots standing like connected mountains,
patterns horizontal like rippling water.
Master Shí would look with astonishment,
Gōngshū would be dazzled.
Carving and engraving have just finished,
the chisels and knives are still applied;
leveling the scales and paring the armor,
shedding horns and breaking teeth;
layer upon layer of broken brocade,
petal after petal of true flowers;
scattered among the herbs and trees,
disordered amidst the mist and clouds.
As for the pine, catalpa, and Gǔdù,
the Píngzhòng and Jūnqiān,
towering for a hundred acres,
stumps and sprouts for a thousand years.
In the Qín, a tree received the rank of Dàfū,
in the Hàn, a general sat beneath one.
None are not buried by moss or weighed down by fungi,
stripped by birds or pierced by insects.
Some hang low in frost and dew,
some are shaken and battered by wind and smoke.
In Dōnghǎi, there is the Temple of the Báimù,
in Xīhé, there is the Altar of the Kūsāng,
in Běilù, willow leaves are used for the pass,
in Nánlíng, plum roots are used for the forge.
On the Xiǎoshān, clumps of cassia detain the traveler,
in Fǔfēng, tall pines tether the horse.
Is it only that the city overlooks the Xìliǔ,
and the frontier falls below the Táolín?
When mountains and rivers are obstructed and severed,
drifting and falling in separation.
Roots uprooted with falling tears,
damaged roots dripping blood.
Fire enters the hollow heart,
resin flows from broken joints.
Lying tilted across the cave mouth,
broken halfway down the mountainside.
Those with slanted grain break like a hundred spans of ice; those with straight texture crack like a thousand fathoms of tiles.
Bearing goiters and holding tumors,
hollowed out and harboring dens.
Mùmèi flash their eyes,
Shānjīng act as portents of evil.
Moreover, when wind and clouds no longer move the heart,
a traveler with no home to return to,
unable to gather gě,
instead returning to eat wēi.
Sinking into a dead-end alley,
overgrown by bramble gates,
already grieved by the falling of leaves,
even more lamenting the change and decay.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
"When the leaves of the trees fall,
the aged man is sorrowful."
This is what it means.
Then he sang:
"The fire of the third month at Jiànzhāng,
the thousand-mile rafts on the Huánghé.
If they are not the trees filling the garden of Jīngǔ,
then they are the flowers throughout the county of Héyáng."
Dàsīmǎ Huán heard this and sighed:
"In years past I planted willows,
swaying gently south of the Hàn;
now I see them withered and falling,
mournful by the banks of the river.
If even a tree is like this,
how can a man endure it?"
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, 88.
*Wènyuán Yīnghuá*, 143.
*Gǔwényuán*, 7.
〈*Chūn Fù*〉
In the Yíchūn Garden, spring has already returned,
in the Pīxiāng Hall, spring garments are being made.
In the new year, bird songs warble in a thousand kinds,
in the second month, willow down flies all over the road.
The whole county of Héyáng is filled with flowers,
Jīngǔ has always been full of trees in its garden.
A cluster of fragrant herbs is enough to hinder a person,
a few feet of drifting gossamer lies across the path.
Opening the Shànglín and racing to enter,
crowding the Héqiáo and competing to cross.
Emerging from the golden house of Lìhuá,
descending from the orchid palace of Fēiyàn.
Hairpins are so numerous they seem surprisingly heavy,
high-coiled hair makes one fear the wind.
Eyebrows compete with willows for greenness,
faces rival peaches in redness.
Shadows come into the pond,
petals fall onto the robes.
Moss begins to green and hides the fish; wheat is just turning blue-green and covers the pheasants.
The terrace where Nòngyù played the flute,
the waters of the waves where pendants ring.
Moving to Qìlǐ, the family is wealthy,
entering Xīnfēng, the wine is fine.
Pomegranate wine lightly floats,
grape wine is fermenting.
Lotus-patterned jade bowls,
lotus-seed golden cups.
New sprouts of bamboo shoots,
fine-pitted yángméi.
Lǜzhū arrives carrying a zither,
Wénjūn comes bringing wine.
The jade pipes are first tuned,
and the sounding strings are briefly caressed;
the melodies of *Yáng Chūn* and *Lù Shuǐ*,
and the dances of "Facing Phoenixes" and "Wheeling Luán-birds."
Warming again the reeds of the *shēng*,
and shifting once more the bridges of the *zhēng*.
The moon enters the singing fan;
flowers receive the rhythm of the drum.
The Xié Lǜ Dū Wèi
and the Shè Zhì Zhōng Láng
stop their carriages at the Xiǎo Yuàn
and ride their horses abreast through Cháng Yáng.
Golden saddles are first donned;
bows of cudrania wood are newly strung.
Brushing off dust, they look at the horse tracks;
dividing into groups, they enter the archery hall.
The horses are the dragon-breed of Tiān Chí;
the belts are jade bridges from Jīng Shān.
Splendid brocade is set with Tiān Lù;
new damask is woven with Fèng Huáng.
On the third day, the winding water flows toward the Hé Jīn;
at sunset, many offer sacrifices to the Jiě Shén by the riverside.
Guests floating cups beneath the trees;
people crossing the water at the sandy headland.
Finely carved thin sleeves of narrow robes;
strung pearls adorning the collars.
The sun begins to sink over the peak of Bǎi Zhàng Shān;
until the three afternoon hours pass and you are drunk, do not return home.
The reflection in the pond water hangs clearer than a mirror;
the fragrance of robes within the house is not as sweet as the flowers.
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, Scroll 3; *Chū Xué Jì*, Scroll 3.
〈Rhapsody on the Seventh Night〉
The rabbit moon rises first;
the sheep lamp is placed next.
One beholds the radiant light of Niú Xīng;
one observes the railing-like patterns of Zhī Nǚ.
Thereupon, the beautiful concubines of Qín É
and the lovely ladies of Zhào;
graceful ones named Yàn
and elegant ones surnamed Qín.
Disliking their morning makeup for being half-worn;
cherishing the evening's touch-up for being completely fresh.
At this time, they leave their rooms together
and go out together into the courtyard.
Threads are taut as they pass through the frames;
needle eyes are narrow as they pierce the air.
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, Scroll 4.
*Chū Xué Jì*, Scroll 4.
*Yù Lǎn*, Scroll 31.
〈Rhapsody on the Game of Xiangxi〉
Observe its creation and origin
at the very beginning of the August Kings.
It takes its law from the concentrated Yin in Thick Virtue;
it looks up to the Harmonious Qi in Clear Emptiness.
Thus, the green bamboo slips are opened,
and the vermilion board is set straight and true.
Its logic penetrates subtle depths;
its source exhausts the sagely works.
It is like striking a great bell;
it is like hanging a bright mirror.
White Phoenixes approach from afar;
yellow clouds reflect from on high.
It can change customs and shift traditions;
it can be used to govern officials and administer the state.
Thus, the board takes its form from Qián
and maps the Shàng Xuán above.
The moon's disk is newly full;
the sun's halo is freshly round.
It models the Huá Gài of the Yǔ Lín;
it depicts the Bì Quán of the Míng Táng.
Kūn is taken as the carriage;
hard and soft roll and unroll.
It is like a square mirror without a reflection;
it is like an empty city not yet inhabited.
It shortens the lines of the patterns;
it lacks the map of the Líng Guī.
The horses are as beautiful as thousand-gold steeds;
the tallies are as clear as the Liù Jiǎ tallies.
Thereupon, they tuck in their tablets and take their turns;
they take their seats according to the stars.
Revolving the geography on a square ritual jade;
turning the astronomy on a round jade disc.
Dividing the beautiful jade of Jīng Shān;
counting the alabaster stones of Lán Tián.
To the south, one moves the tallies of Chì Shuǐ;
to the north, one sends the strategies of Xuán Shān.
Occupying the Eastern Road, the dragon is green;
exiting the Xī Guān, the horse is white.
Having laid out the celestial images,
we briefly set the golden board.
It illuminates the light of the sun and moon;
it rides upon the spirit of wind and clouds.
It takes the primary colors of the four directions;
it employs the mutual generation of the Wǔ Dé.
Turning left following the Yuè Jiàn;
moving forward starting from the Huáng Zhōng.
When Yin flips, the Gù Tù emerges first;
when Yang transforms, the Líng Wū alone shines bright.
Moreover, wandering for pleasure in Rén Shòu
and seeking joy in Huī Yīn.
Water's reflection shakes the sun;
flower's light illuminates the forest.
Now spreading out the diagrams to enjoy them at length;
then opening the manuals to search them thoroughly.
Though it is executed by the hand,
in the end, it must be grasped by the heart.
Then there are dragon candles holding flowers;
golden braziers with floating vapors.
The moon sets and the cassia boughs droop;
stars tilt and the willows fall.
Hesitating at the pivotal moment;
doubting like the Jīng Wèi rivers.
Looking around in confusion;
the heart feeling fear.
One should face Kǎn but strikes Lí;
suddenly, when at Shēn, one takes Wèi.
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, Scroll 74.
〈Rhapsody on the Lamp〉
The Jiǔ Lóng is about to grow dark;
the Sān Jué are going to roost.
The jade hooks are half-raised;
the Ruò Mù tree is fully low.
The windows hide light against the white walls;
willows aid the darkness in the orchid chambers.
Kingfisher pearl quilts;
tasseled feather curtains.
Unfolding screens with folding hinges;
closing the portable barriers adorned with lotuses.
Rolling up clothes on the bed of the Queen of Qín;
sending pillows atop the Jīng Tái.
Then there are a hundred branches on a single tree;
four-way lights on connected trays.
Fragrance is added by burning honey;
the air is mixed with the scent of burning orchids.
The wick grows long as the night lingers;
the light is blue as the night grows cold.
Elegant blossoms are half-hidden;
salamander fat blazes bright.
Moving the scales of the whale lamps;
flaming with radiance on the crying cranes.
When moths flutter, broken flowers fall in disorder;
when the wind rises, shooting stars drop minutely.
Moreover, in the deep night of Shàng Lán;
the wine of Zhōng Shān is clear.
The Lady of Chǔ detains the guests;
Hán É harmonizes the voices.
Low songs follow the rhythm;
*Yóu Xián* rings out wonderfully.
Brilliant are the vermilion embers;
blazing are the red blossoms of fire.
Suddenly, nine lights join their colors;
or double wicks shine together.
Sending a word to Sū Jì Zǐ;
you should know the feeling of the lingering light.
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, Scroll 80.
*Chū Xué Jì*, Scroll 25.
〈Rhapsody on Facing the Candle〉
At Lóng Shā and Yàn Sài, the armor must be cold;
at Tiān 山, the moon has set and the traveler's clothes are thin.
Before the lamp, hanging clothes seem dimly lit;
beneath the moon, threading a needle is felt to be most difficult.
Picking off the lamp-flower to hold a cassia candle;
returning the lamp-stand and setting down the candle tray.
Cast phoenixes hold lotuses;
depicted dragons sleep side-by-side.
The wick is high, as if needing several snips;
the core is damp, making it briefly hard to light.
Bronze lotuses catch the weeping wax;
iron tongs are stained with floating smoke.
I already knew that the light of snow could illuminate paper;
I am further surprised that the lamp-flower now brings fortune.
By the lotus curtains and cold lamp-stand, dawn brushes the window;
in the bamboo cage, incense smoke fills the wadding.
From the sides hang thin trickles of wax;
above circle the flying moths.
The light is clear as cold seeps in;
the flame dims as the wind passes.
The tassels of the people of Chǔ are all torn off;
the letters for the Lord of Yàn are full of errors.
The night wind blows;
the fragrance follows.
Yù Jīn Yuàn;
Fú Róng Chí.
The "Evil-Expelling" incense of Qín Huáng is not worth mentioning;
what was so strange about the "Foreign Incense" of Hàn Wǔ?
The evening stars vanish;
the fragrant weeds wither.
One still holds it for a night stroll;
how could it be less than the moon over Xī Yuán?
○ *Yì Wén Lèi Jù*, Scroll 80.
*Chū Xué Jì*, Scroll 25.
Rhapsody on a Mirror
The Milky Way gradually fades,
the sun’s wheel is about to rise.
Swallows chirp to the King of Wú,
crows startle the Censor.
Upon the jade-flower mat,
inside the golden lotus curtains.
First folding the screens,
newly opening the door panels.
Morning light dazzles the eyes,
the early breeze blows against the face.
Facing the clothes rack, she pulls her robe;
approaching the chest, she puts on her bracelets.
Last night’s hair-coils are still wound,
residual makeup has already grown thin.
No more the vermilion pearl of the lips,
only the calyx-like brows remain.
Stars on the dimples are sparse,
the moon has set within the yellow forehead-makeup.
The mirror stand with silver bands
originally came from the Wèi palace.
It can lie across the "Retreating Moon,"
and deftly hang the "Whirling Wind."
Dragons dangle outside the case,
phoenixes lean among the flowers.
A mirror reflects the liver and heart;
it is difficult to encounter, difficult to find.
Engraved with five-colored coiled dragons,
inscribed with thousand-year-old ancient characters.
The golden pheasant sees it and dances alone,
the seabird beholds it and cries in solitude.
Facing the water, the moon emerges in the pond;
reflecting the sun, water caltrops appear on the wall.
Temporarily setting out the vanity case,
again drawing out the mirror drawer.
Competing to learn the ways of love,
vying for affection in this world.
The hair at the temples is level but lightly trimmed,
the brows are straight yet still shaved.
Flying-flower rouge cakes
must be applied in proper order.
Opening the vermilion in brocade wrappings,
eyebrow-black mixed with sandalwood oil.
Rouge blended with jiǎjiān fragrance,
hair gloss steeped in fragrant orchids.
Measuring the length of the bun and temples,
estimating the distance for placing hair-flowers.
Hanging charmer charms from the hairpin,
wiping the hairpin’s bridge with powdered cotton.
Having just finished combing her hair, she checks her reflection while dressing,
then returns to the vanity to retrieve it.
Briefly checking the garment ties,
knowing by heart the tie-dyed patterns.
The robe fits the body perfectly,
the skirt slants at the false loops.
Truly this mirror is exceptionally suitable;
it cannot be hidden in its case for even a moment.
Briefly going into the garden, it follows her along.
○ Yìwén Lèijù, Fascicle 70.
Rhapsody on Mandarin Ducks
Yú Jī from her youth served the King of Wèi,
possessing a voice enough to echo around the rafters.
When did she ever weave brocade?
She was unwilling to pick mulberry leaves.
In the end, she fell to a tragic fate,
remaining alone in an empty bed.
Seeing the mandarin ducks imitating each other,
she turns her eyes away as tears fall.
She no longer looks at the Nányáng soaked powder;
she has become too lazy to draw the new Jīngzhào brows.
Furthermore, they share hearts and wings,
tamed and familiar within the pond and cage,
floating on waves, playing with shadows,
preening feathers, riding the wind.
Flying together among the eaves and tiles,
throughout the Wèi palace;
perching together in the catalpa trees,
just like Hán Féng and his wife.
If Hán Shòu wished to wed,
or Wēn Qiào desired a wife,
the Jade Terrace was not sent,
and the Hú incense was not possessed.
Surely, seeing these two flying together,
she feels the empty bed is hard to keep.
○ Yìwén Lèijù, Fascicle 92.
Rhapsody on the Wandering Son
The wandering son toils on the campaign,
guarding the Great Wall, a thousand-mile wall.
The waters of Lǒng are eternally frozen over;
over the Pass and Mountains, only the moon is bright.
Moreover, resentment rises from the empty bed;
the lady of the house suffers the parting.
The gauze window is closed alone,
the silk curtains hang down long.
The new zither is not played,
she is ashamed to blow the long flute.
In the former years at the Cassia Garden,
in days past in the Orchid Chamber.
Luó Fū bound her hair when young;
Nòng Yù first pinned her hair.
Singing the new song "Zǐyè",
performing the old dance "Qiánxī".
After parting, the chamber’s passion is no more;
before the vanity, the bright mirror need not shine.
No letters sent through the "Joined Joy" messenger;
the palindrome brocade remains unwoven.
Floating dust fills the bed, no need to brush it away;
fine grass grows as it will across the steps.
The other day, the Hàn envoy arrived at Zhāngtái;
word was heard that the husband would certainly return.
The handkerchief is about to dry;
the sorrowful brows are about to unknit.
Thinking ahead to the traveler’s arrival,
she goes out to meet him with a smile.
○ Yìwén Lèijù, Fascicle 32.
Song
Song: Facing Wine
Spring waters gaze at peach blossoms,
spring islets are carpeted with fragrant pollia.
The zither was borrowed from Lǜ Zhū;
the wine was taken from Wén Jūn.
Leading the horse toward Wèi Bridge;
the sun dries the meat strips on the mountaintop.
Shān Jiǎn’s head-wrap is upside down;
Wáng Róng dances with his rúyì scepter.
Zithers sound in Jīngǔ Garden,
flutes resonate at Píngyáng Dock.
A human life lasts a hundred years;
laughter and joy only for a few.
Where can one find money-knives
to seek to be a merchant in Luòyáng?

Zhāo Jūn’s Departure, Written by Imperial Command
Zhāo Jūn’s Departure, Written by Imperial Command
Knitting her brows at the Guānglù Pass,
looking back toward the Lady's City.
Petal by petal, her rosy face fades;
pair by pair, tearful eyes arise.
Leading the horse across frozen rivers,
clutching the saddle along snowy roads.
The Hú winds are bone-chillingly cold;
the night moon shines bright on her heart.
Just as she tunes a song upon the zither,
it turns into the sound of the Hú reed pipe.

Wáng Zhāo Jūn
Wáng Zhāo Jūn
Wiping her tears, she leaves the Qī Quarters,
looking back, she gazes at Zhāoyáng.
The mirror has lost the water caltrop’s shadow;
the hairpin’s "Retreating Moon" bridge is removed.
Her waist measures less than a foot;
her falling tears number a thousand lines.
Her green robe catches the horse’s sweat;
her red sleeves brush away the autumn frost.
The song of parting is indeed full of regret;
the mournful strings must be tightened further.

Marching Out of the North Gate of Jì
From the Jì Gate, looking back north,
toiling and weary, her heart is utterly broken.
The passes and mountains meet the Hàn moon;
the waters of Lǒng flow toward the city of Qín.
The reed pipe is cold, the reed leaves are brittle;
the bow is frozen, the ramie string thrums.
A grove of plum trees can quench thirst;
a double surname can ward off soldiers.
The general challenges to battle in the morning;
the Protector-General patrols the camp at night.
Mount Yān still has its stone;
how many more names must be carved?

"Song of Meeting Guests at the Young Men's Gathering"
Meeting guests at the young men's gathering place,
The spring breeze fills the road with fragrance.
Songs provoke Military Commander Lǐ,
Fruit is thrown at Pān of Hé Yáng.
From behind flowers, wine is toasted from afar,
Beside the water, the couch is moved again.
This year, one rejoices for the husband,
Newly appointed as a Gentleman of the Feathered Forest.
Surely knowing that Liú Bì Yù
Secretly married the Prince of Rǔ Nán.

"Ten Pacing the Void Lyrics for Taoist Priests"
"Ten Pacing the Void Lyrics for Taoist Priests"
Primordial unity was formed before the void was established,
The Great Beginning is just unfolding its chart.
Red jade numinous texts descend,
The true qi of Zhū Líng arrives.
In the mid-sky stands the Nine Dragon Pavilion,
Reflecting upside down on the Eight Winds Terrace.
Clouds pass as the sound of strings and songs rings out,
Stars shift as the empty palace revolves.
The Green-clad Maiden ascends Shǎo Shì Mountain,
A young boy heads toward Péng Lái.
Wandering freely, they hear the Four Gatherings,
In a flash, they transcend the Three Calamities.

The Way is the origin of the hundred spirits.
In silent solitude, riding on cinnabar vapor,
In dark clarity, ascending to the Jade Void.

The Eight Sceneries pursue the returning carriage.
A vermilion phoenix comes holding a seal in its beak,

Resting the mind at the Sun-Bathing Pavilion,
Enjoying oneself at the Cloud Ruins.

Congealing the Truth beyond heaven and earth,
Cutting off thought before the silent vastness.
Forms remain empty and open,
Forgetting the self is fundamentally natural.
Opening the scriptures in the Rén Zǐ era,
Encountering the Way in the Jiǎ Shēn year.
Circling clouds follow the dance tunes,
Flowing water pursues the song's strings.
Stone marrow is as fragrant as rice,
Mushroom chambers are as crisp as lotus.
Resting the phoenix to banquet at the Jasper Waters,

The birth of the Way is the Great One,
Keeping to stillness is the Mysterious Root.
In the Middle Harmony, refining the Nine Vapors,
In the Jiǎ Zǐ year, bidding farewell to the Three Primes.
Keeping the mind like receptive water,
Teaching and learning give weight to the Fragrant Garden.
Wild ducks remain to report to the gate official,
Cranes depart, painting the city gate.
Even more delighted by being trackless,
Returning to lodge in the wordless.

The Spirit Grotto honors the Supreme Virtue,
At Yú Shí, meeting the Bright Truth.
Contemplating the subtle Mysterious Mother,
In emptiness, nourishing the Valley Spirit.
On Cinnabar Hill, riding a kingfisher phoenix,
At the Dark Garden, driving a dappled unicorn.

〈Respectfully Presented to the Minister of Justice, the Duke of Huáinán〉
〈Respectfully Presented to the Minister of Justice, the Duke of Huáinán〉
In the endangered state, virtue has long been in chaos,
The Heaven-appointed strategy finally seizes the opportunity.
At Jiǔhé, I hear the oath to the masses,
For a thousand miles, one sees the connected banners.
After the fall of Guó, the Chuíjí jade returned,
After the pacification of Qí, the precious tripod came back.
Long worn down by the customs of the world's dust,
Greatly toiled in the clothes of the border passes.
The fettered steed still covers a thousand miles,
The drooping Peng bird flies again ninefold.
Still pitying as the horse's age increases,
One should mind that the tassels of the staff have thinned.
Turning the carriage back to the old hometown,
The garden willows are just beginning to wave gently.
Old bamboos encroach upon the paths,
New paulownias have increased several girths.
In the cold valley, the pears must be heavy,
In the autumn woods, the chestnuts are even fatter.
Fine wine still partakes of the "Sages",
Carved writings essentially reach the subtle.
Quickening the song to welcome the Zhào zither,
Wandering strings summon the Lady of Chǔ.
As a minor official, I oversee surveillance and reporting,
In being promoted, I truly just padded the numbers.
In the southern region, I serve as a commandant,
Military strategy relies on the Jiànwēi title.
The recluses' stones of Shāngshān,
The Phoenix Ledge of the Dān Shuǐ.
At the rustic pavilion, horses are long saddled,
In the mountain town, gates are closed early.
The herald's call surrounds the crimson staff,
Crossed halberds reflect against the red palace doors.
Thus causing one to forget the melodies of Chǔ,
Why only eat the ferns of Zhōu?
The thirty-six waters have changed,
The forty-nine years were wrong.
The wind and smoke of the cinnabar furnace have ceased,
In age, like the rushes and willows, I decline.
How dare I not exhaust myself for my colleagues?
I fear the former days are hard to regain.

〈Zhèngdàn Presented to the Sīxiànfǔ〉
At early dawn, the gates are opened,
Elaborate words surge from the tip of the brush.
Like a Goshawk descending to the prison officials,
Or a Xièzhì beast adorning the judicial officers.
At court, they lead with jade tallies,
For covenants, they hold pearl platters.
The year ends as stars shift their positions,
In the remaining days, the musical pitch-pipes have not yet run out.
Snow is three feet high and thick,
Ice is ten feet deep and cold.
Short shoots are still buried among the bamboo,
The fragrant heart of the orchid has not yet risen.
At Mèngmén, I had long lost my way,
But suddenly, I am carried upward by the whirlwind.
The roosting crow returns to the government office,
The abandoned horse returns to the stable.
Honor and righteousness are weighty,
Being of little talent, it is hard to repay such kindness.
Méi Chéng rose again from his illness,
Gòng Yǔ finally flicked the dust from his cap.
Just now, the lotus-leaf sword is suspended,
There is no need for the bamboo-root elixir.
Once I know the law of the hanging signs,
Who would think of the fishing rod?

〈Assigned to Luòzhōu, Replying to Xuē Wénxué upon Departure〉
You live by the bend of the river,
Talented men have always followed in each other's footsteps.
Salt shapes may transform into tigers,
The vapor of the tripod suddenly becomes a dragon.
Such a man inherits and carries forth virtue,
The walls of his palace are surely several layers deep.
On the five thoroughfares, the path of debate opens,
To the four directions, the beacons of literature rise.
As for me, I was improperly recommended,
The people's wishes began to follow the will of Heaven.
Shàngluò is assigned a Dūwèi,
Hóngnóng opens a Fùyōng.
Sheep-gut paths connect nine slopes,
Xióng'ěr Mountain faces double peaks.
The white stone taro of the immortals,
The green forest pine of the recluse.
At Běiliáng, I see off Sūn Chǔ,
By Xīdī, I bid farewell to Gě Gōng.
If my old friend sends a letter,
The soil of Líyáng is enough to seal it.

〈Carrying Out a Mission to Yè, Replying to Zǔ Wáng Zhèngyuán〉
Our Emperor presides over the nine provinces,
His reputation and teachings reach where there are no borders.
He promotes literature and flourishes in rites and music,
He puts away weapons and allows the common people to rest.
Lacking talent, I drive the fine steeds,
With banners and flags, I attend to the jade scepters.
On ancient steles, the inscriptions are worn away,
In desolate cities, the ages are lost to time.
On the ridges, the patterned melons are ripe,
Across the fields, the fragrant ears of grain hang low.
Your gift of fine jade is truly a comfort,
To repay with a plum, there is no need for a path.

〈Carrying Out a Mission to Yè〉
The Great State practices the rites of diplomatic visits,
Kinship and neighborliness are strengthened from this.
Setting up banners to serve in the plains and marshes,
Facing the imperial screen to report the finished words.
Heading west, I encounter the wind and dew,
Pointing north, I cross over Huányuán.
For joyful friendship, I meet the Wángzǐ,
Observing the rites, I see the royal grandson.
How can I praise the fine trees?
I only take pleasure in reciting the "Cǎifán."
Four sacrificial meats fill the serving trays,

Xiāng Jūn formerly established the state here,

〈Following the Imperial Carriage to Observe Military Training〉
Military maneuvers take place at Chángyáng,
The soldiers enter the combat arena.
Formations are set, rising like horizontal clouds,
The camp opens, spreading like wild goose wings.
The gates are feared to be obstructed by magnetic stones,
The horses are afraid of being injured by iron caltrops.
Lóngyuān touches the constellations of Niú and Dǒu,
Fánruò startles Tiānláng.

A sudden wind blows the war drums,
High dust envelops the shell-adorned equipment.
Startled monkeys sometimes fall from the trees,
Alarmed geese frequently break their formation.
In the cold, the branches are even straighter,
On the withered mountains, the chrysanthemums become more fragrant.
The Leopard Tactics ensure complete victory,
The Dragon Chart honors what is superior.

The rain stops as the remnant of a rainbow breaks,

In dark caves, the morning stones are damp,

Across a low bridge, he crosses the bottom of the ravine,

This humble person has failed to maintain his health,
At the fork in the road, I was prevented from greeting you.
In how many months will the mushrooms in the fields ripen?
In what year will the golden furnace be completed?
The mournful reed-pipe plays tunes of the frontier passes,
The neighing of horses is the sound of parting.
Wángzǐ, your person is a treasure,

The five cities are adjacent to the Běijí,
a hundred wall-sections strengthen the western Kūnlún.
The Gōuchén constellation crosses the covered walkways,
the Chānghé gates reach the divine eaves.
A thousand pillars support the lotus-flower pagoda,
a yóuxún spans the purple citrus garden.
The Buddha’s shadow is recorded by the Húrén,
the scripture texts are translated into the Hàn language.
Stars peek through the Zhūniǎo window,
clouds lodge at the Fènghuáng gate.

drifting snow flows from the source of the Chánghé.

The wind flies, fanning the heavenly debate,

A stranded official follows the "scattered wood,"
having no way to participate in the center of heaven.

ultimately like looking up at the strings of a Kūn bird.

fireflies float like scattered sparks.
Finding joy in Heaven is to know one's fate;
when can I ever be without worry?

Confusedly, the Lord of Heaven dawns;
my spirit is truly lacking.
The whole commandery’s roosters urge the dawn;
birds are startled from sleep in several places.
When waking, I am carefree;
my sorrow is but silent.
Zhāng Yí was said to have poor conduct;
Guǎn Zhòng was said to have small capacity.
Those with feelings in this world
find their spirits withered after all.

Death can still be endured;
how can being shamed be considered lenient?
Ancient people held this character,
and thus were unable to find peace.
Though their faces could be warm,

Taking a bright mirror from the case,

Fortunately, I have not violated the principles of integrity;
I have somewhat crossed the military barriers.
Holding the tally, I drive the courier carriage;
staying at the station, I do not sit in the saddle.
In Dàijùn, the tumbleweeds first turn;
in Liáoyáng, the mulberries are about to dry.
Autumn clouds bunch like powder and floss;
white dew gathers like mercury.

it is useless to fight at Gāolán.

vast and hazy, human affairs are not as they were.
To avoid slander, one should pick kudzu;
forgetting feelings, one then eats vetch.
Harboring sorrow while things wither,
the center of my heart is pained by discord.
Alone I pity the end of life's vitality;
in vain, I am startled by the decay of the locust tree.

the scenery fills Shànglán.

the jujube tree of the eastern neighbor is whole.

facing the mirror, the solitary luan-bird's line is severed.
I say nothing of climbing the Lǒng crest;
I can only gaze toward Cháng'ān.

A fighting Qílín can eat the sun;
water battles certainly startle the dragon.

wind and dust disturb the nine-layered palace.
Departed to Dǐng Hú and never returned;
grieving at Cāngwú, unable to follow.

gaze afar at the pines of Xīlíng.

Harmonizing with Palace Attendant Zhāng's "Expression of Feelings"
When Yang is exhausted, there is regret and stinginess;
At the end of an era, truly it is like the hexagrams *Zhūn* and *Bō*.
The rushing river severs the earth's tether,
The broken pillar tilts the corner of heaven.
Gathering in groups, the sea waters fly,
Like rain, the heavenly stars fall.
Carrying shovels, they eventually move mountains;
Hiding the boat, it finally leaves the ravine.
Suddenly the common people have become fish,
The gentleman is a crane in vain.
Long ago, I met a kindred spirit,
Throughout my life, I have received deep favor.
The old official cords are eventually unheard of,
Chéng Yīng is left in lonely silence.
During the Yǒngjiā era, I lived in exile alone,
In the Zhōngyuán, only the sacrificial cauldrons remained.
On the dangerous road, I lie upon the windlass,
My life in peril is burdened by a simple shell.
Drifting along like a wooden stalk,
Swept by the wind like autumn husks.
Zhāng Hàn did not return to Wú,
Lù Jī is still in Luò.
At Hànyáng, the coins are finally exhausted,
In Cháng’ān, the rice is gone in vain.
Sometimes I consult the tortoise shells of Jìzhǔ,
Or briefly sell the medicine of Hán Kāng.
Tethered to the shafts, I finally enter the harness;
With drooping wings, I still fail to escape the arrow.
Vainly harboring a heart of fine jade,
Uselessly keeping a promise of gold.
In Guó or Kuài, there is ultimately no place to stay,
To Qí or Qín, what can one finally entrust?
The Grand Physician only grieves for Zhōu,
The gentleman always thinks of Bó.
In silence, we share our journey as strangers,
In desolation, we both lean against the city walls.
Farming talk stops at the grain harvest,
Wild meals consist only of pigweed and pulse.
Playing music, the Chǔ zither is sad;
To forget worries, the Lǔ wine is thin.
At the banks of the Wèi, I watch the seated fishing;
At Gǔkǒu, I see the autumn harvest.
I have only the shame of Qiūmíng,
No longer the joy of Róngqī.
In the month of Yízé, the Fire Star flows,
At Tiāngēn, the autumn waters dry up.
In the harsh winter, the sun does not warm;
Late in the year, the winds are mostly from the north.
Floating above, there are strange clouds;
In the fine frost, one hears of calamitous hail.
Tree bark is three inches thick,
The Jīng River mud is five dou turbid.
Though I delight in the curved-shaft tree,
I still fear the magpie of Diāolíng.
Life indeed has a beginning,
But the Way of Heaven is ultimately an empty bellows.
For now, I take pleasure in the company of good people,
And do not doubt the count of my friends.
When shall we obtain the clouds and rain
And once again see the soaring in the vast emptiness?

Blowing pipes on the Fènghuáng Tái.

Harmonizing with the Prince of Zhào on a Spring Day

Inside the garden is the Fènghuáng Chí.
Slender pipes tune the songs,

Dreaming of Entering the Inner Hall
Carved beams were formerly etched with apricots,
Fragrant walls were originally plastered with pepper.
Curtain ropes are like golden wheat ears,
Screen hooks are like silver garlic cloves.
Eyebrows are wiped a thousand times,
Hair is combed and arranged a hundred times.
Small shirts are cut to wrap the arms,
Winding strings are plucked while embracing the waist.
Sunlight moves upon the flame of the hairpin,
The shadow from the window shakes the mirror-flower.
Songs catch the rhythm of the wind,

We must go and play right now,

Harmonizing a Poem on Dance
Harmonizing a Poem on Dance
Festive candles shine in the bridal chamber,
after the swallows depart, the pair dances lightly.
Stamping shoes following the sparse rhythm,
lowering hair coils chasing the rising notes.
Steps turn as the movement begins to advance,
robes flutter before the melody is finished.
Like a turning luán bird, the mirror is nearly full;
like a crane looking back, the market should be overturned in admiration.
Having already studied in the heavens,
how could she be born of the common world!

〈Listening to Clothes-Beating at Night〉
The sound of beating clothes on an autumn night,
flies across the walls of Chángmén.
Tonight’s moon over Chángmén,
should be as bright as the day.
Small hair-coils suit the grain-shaped earrings,
a round waist moves with the woven silk.
The autumn pounding block tunes to a rapid beat,
disordered pestles change into new sounds.
When the stone is dry, the block rings louder;
when the paulownia is hollow, the pestle resonates perfectly.
Ringing stones come from Huàyīn,
hollow paulownia is gathered from Fènglín.
North Hall's slender-waisted pestle,
South Market's lady's pounding block.
Striking the rhythm requires no drum,
tuning the sound needs no qín.
Together tying the "linked branch" threads,
doubly threading "long life" needles.
In the singing towers, the resentment of parting is startled;
the traveler's heart is moved to sorrow.
Concentric "bamboo leaf" bowls,
going and coming in pairs, filled up.
Skirts and hems cannot bear to be long,
shirt sleeves are especially suited to be short.
Dragon-patterned engraved scissors,
phoenix-winged hairpins wrapped in tubes.
Elegant echoes harmonize in rhyme,
sorrowful sounds are mournfully broken.
New sounds wrap around the night wind,
graceful turns fill the empty air.
Should be heard in Chánglè Palace,
clearly penetrating Zhāoyáng Palace.
Flower-coils, eyes hazy as if drunk,
"dragon's son" fine red patterns.
Moistened folds through the night's dew,
wind blowing on clothes all night long.
On the jade steps, the wind turns gusty;
at the Great Wall, the snow must be dark.
New ribbons just about to be sewn,
fine brocade soon to be woven.
The sounds are as intricate as "Guǎnglíng Sàn,"
the pestles as rapid as "Yúyáng Càn."
The new moon stirs golden waves,
autumn clouds overflow and pass by.
Who pities the soldier on campaign,
tonight he is at Jiāohé.
Xǔyáng's Rhapsody on Parting,
Línjiāng's "Song of Sorrowful Thoughts."
Again causing sorrow with this tune,
how much is left of her youthful face?

〈Participating in the Book Collation at Línzhǐ Palace, Harmonizing with Associate Director Liú〉
〈Participating in the Book Collation at Línzhǐ Palace, Harmonizing with Associate Director Liú〉
Ceasing spears to raise rites and music,
cultivating literature, making grand the canons and plans.
Walls open to reveal seal scripts on metal and stone,
the River floats the diagram of clouds and mist.
Rue fragrance rises to Yángé,
stone tablets face Hóngdū.
Reciting books to summon Erudites,
understanding classics to appoint Grandees.
In the Bì Pool, the cold water falls;
in the School Market, the old locust trees are sparse.
Lofty talk transforms the "White Horse,"
grand eloquence blocks the Fēihú Pass.
The moon sets over the General's tree,
the wind startles the Censor's crows.
Zǐyún is still sweating over bamboo slips,
Wēnshū is currently scraping bulrushes.
Though there are pavilions touching the clouds,
ultimately one yearns for the rivers and lakes.

〈Harmonizing with Palace Secretary Yǔwén on Entering Chóngyáng Pavilion〉
On the Northern Plains, wind and rain disperse,
at the Southern Palace, the honor guards are sparse.
Attendants-in-waiting return to Jīnmǎ,
Confucian scholars go back to Shíqú.
In vain hangs the Mirror of Rénshòu,
emptily gather the books of Màolíng.
Bamboo tears hang from autumn shoots,
lotus garments fall from summer blossoms.
Gùchéng has just moved the ancestral temple,
Yánglíng is currently shifting its residence.
The old orchids grow withered and worn,
the remaining flowers unfold in brilliant profusion.
Separately, there is Zhāoyáng Palace,
long grieving for the former Jiéyú.

〈Humbly Serving in the Office of Water, Watching the Repair of the Wèi Bridge〉
A Grandee joining the lower ranks,
holding office on the sunny side of the Wèi.
Fùpíng moves the iron chains,
Gānquán transports the stone beams.
Striding like a rainbow, connecting the severed banks;
floating like giant turtles, continuing the broken bridge.
The spring islet has the color of parrots,
the flowing water has the fragrance of peach blossoms.
The Star Essence met the Hàn Emperor,
the fishing old man encountered the Zhōu King.
The level embankment's stone bank is straight,
the high weir's willow shade is long.
Enviously speaking of Dù Yuánkǎi,
at the river bridge, alone raising his cup.

〈On the Completion of the New Study in the North Garden, Composed at the Command of Prince Zhào〉
〈On the Completion of the New Study in the North Garden, Composed at the Command of Prince Zhào〉
Rainbow-colored roof-beams like bird wings in flight,
mountain-shaped brackets supporting orchid branches.
Around painted beams, clouds and mist coil;
through carved windows, jade maidens peek.
The moon hangs only in reflected light,
lotus blooms always hang upside down.
Coiled roots knot together broken stones,
passing rain suddenly drenches the pond.
Long vines move along with the trellises,
tall trees are moved carrying their nests.
Bird calls are but mixed melodies,
the flower-scented wind just blows in confusion.
Báihǔ inscriptions in the library pavilion,
black bear skins posted for archery practice.
Patterned strings enter the dance music,
moon-shaped fans hide the singing girls.
Jade rhythms tune the sheng pipes,
golden boats serve as wine cups.
If one speaks of Cáo Zǐjiàn,
heaven and man essentially both know him.

〈Joining the Gathering at Duke Héyáng's Newly Created Mountain Pond, Just Getting a Glimpse〉
Across the steps, a mountain stream is carved,
facing the door, continuous peaks appear.
In the dark stones, one suspects a hidden tiger;
coiled roots look like a crouching dragon.
On the sandbar, tangled reeds gather,
at the cave entrance, a horizontal pine obstructs.
Leading the spring water into several branches,
opening the crags reveals ten layers.
From the North Pavilion, one hears pipes blowing;
in the South Neighborhood, one hears bells striking.
In the chrysanthemum's cold, the flowers are just closing;
in the fragrant cup, the wine is exceedingly strong.
Since there was once the Prince of Wèi,
only today have we finally met.

〈Ascending the New Pavilion in the Midst of the Prefecture〉
Striding across the void and transcending the reflected light,
Reaching the clouds, it resists the Shǎoyáng sun.
Upon the dragon scales of the Xuánjí constellation,
On the carved rafters, the Péng bird's wings are spread.
A thousand fathoms of patterned apricot wood shine,
Ten miles of magnolia fragrance waft.
Opening the window, it faces the Gāozhǎng Peak,
Sitting level, one gazes at the river bridge.
The sound of songs is heard from the Chánglè Palace,
The toll of bells penetrates the Jiànzhāng Palace.
For the rhapsody, one employs Wáng Yánshòu;
For the calligraphy, one requires Wéi Zhòngjiāng.
Dragons arrive, following the painted walls;
Phoenixes rise, chasing the blown reed-pipes.
Stones create the shadows of lotus blossoms;
The pond is like the light of a bright mirror.
Floral beams inversely spread their leaves;
Lotus-patterned ceilings hang their pods upside down.
In vain I think of the swallows’ congratulations,
With no means to participate in the Kūn bird's flight.

〈Leaving the Héngmén Gate at Year's End〉
The season changes as the year-end shadows fall,
A traveler delights in ascending to look afar.
Leaning against the saddle, jade trappings hang down;
Across the waist, a brocade heart is girded.
The ice is weak, and the floating bridge has vanished;
The sand is loose, and the horse's tracks are deep.
Leaning a bow against the stone bank,
Turning a couch toward the willow shade.
Zhìqióng comes to urge the wine,
Wénjūn passes by to listen to the zither.
Tomorrow morning, clouds and rain will scatter;
Where then can we seek each other again?

〈The Newly Completed Archery Hall in the Northern Garden〉
〈The Newly Completed Archery Hall in the Northern Garden〉
The terrace and pavilion are suitable for practice,
The immortal target is not difficult to hit.
Turning the arrow, first adjusting the nock;
Drawing the bow, first eyeing the target-mound.
With a startling heart, a single wild goose falls;
With arms linked, two apes leap up.
I only knew of Wáng Jì’s skill;
Who realized Wèi Shū’s ability?
A hollow heart—the tree that does not die;
Without leaves—the vine that has not withered.
Only by choosing the worthy is this known;
Passing the goblet, I rejoice in gaining friends.

〈Garden Courtyard〉
Carrying the staff at sixty, following things beyond the world,
Nurturing my learning in the quiet outskirts.
In deep sorrow, I am just writing on bamboo slips;
Meeting no opportunity, I begin to observe the hexagrams.
The valley is cold, the pitch-pipes have already been blown;
The eaves are bare, the thatch is trimmed once more.
The woodcutter and the recluse always share the same path;
Humans and birds sometimes face each other's nests.
Water rushes blossom with late-season knots;
Wind-blown bamboos shed their cold husks.
On the old locust tree, the fire-wood changes with the season;
From the withered maple, the sap suddenly falls.
Putting on shoes backward to welcome a guest to the hanging couch,
Stopping the zither to listen to a "Dispelling Ridicule" speech.
From a fragrant conch, I pour fine wine;
On a dried clam shell, I lay out orchid-scented delicacies.
Flying fish occasionally touch the hook;
Hidden pheasants are frequently hung in the kitchen.
As long as our mutual understanding is deep,
We shall surely be able to form a friendship.

〈Returning to the Fields〉
Working diligently at the nine grains,
Returning home, I cherish my single plot.
Boring a canal to move the watermill,
Burning the thorns to establish mountain fields.
In the shade of trees, I encounter a resting horse;
By the fish pond, I see a boat being washed.
The bitter plums have no one to pick them;
Autumn melons are not worth a penny.
The village shrine chickens are about to brood;
The plateau silkworms begin to sleep again.
Today, Zhāng Píngzǐ
Has turned into someone to be pitied by others.

〈Sight from a Cold Garden〉
In the cold garden, dwellings are scattered like stars,
Shaking and falling over the small village ruins.
Traveling immortals fill half of the wall paintings;
A recluse possesses a single bed of books.
In the eleventh month, the heart of the spring stirs;
At the Yang hexagram line, the earth’s vapor expands.
Snowflakes are several feet deep;
The ice layer is more than a foot thick.
A gray hawk looks askance at a pheasant;
A white heron descends to watch the fish.
I think again of the outskirts of the Eastern Capital,
Where the various lords bid farewell to the two Shū.

〈Spring in a Secluded Dwelling〉
A man of the mountains has long been submerged in obscurity,
To this secluded path, spring suddenly arrives.
Opening the channel to move the watermill,
Clearing the garden to sweep the bamboo grove.
The slanted bridge has long been half-broken;
The crumbling bank has just begun to lean inward.
A short song is played on a slender flute;
In a low voice, an ancient zither is plucked.
Money and blades do not concern me;
Plowing and sowing must be deep for now.
For a single sheet of rhapsody at the Chángmén Palace,
Where can I seek the gold?

〈Sick in Bed and Beset by Sorrows〉
Perilous worries, wind and frost accumulate;
Deep distress, years and months encroach.
Fearing the snake, my head often aches;
Reflecting on the bow-string, my heart is frequently startled.
Seeking the records of medicine from Zhìchuān;
Asking the forest of divination from Jūnpíng.
An old man from the wilds visits from time to time;
A mountain monk occasionally seeks me out.
There are chrysanthemums, but alas, no wine;
No strings, yet there is a zither.
Who would know that I long hug my knees,
Alone chanting the "Liángfù Yín."

〈Mountain Study〉
In loneliness, I seek a quiet room;
In dense seclusion, I go to my mountain study.
Dripping springs water the path;
Vaulted stones lie upon the steps.
The shallow raft does not move at all;
The coiled roots are only half-buried.
Round pearls fall from the late chrysanthemums;
Tiny sparks drop from the empty locust tree.
Simply placed where wind and clouds are dismal,
I even more pity how my heart's desires have gone awry.

〈Gazing at the Wilderness〉
Testing my whip on a thousand-gold horse,
I come to ascend the Wǔzhàng Yuán.
There is a city that is still the old county seat;
There are no trees, so it is a new village.
Water pools toward the Lánchí;
The sun slants over the Xìliǔ Yuán.
Dry shoals connect to sandy paths;
Cold canals block the water gates.
If only one can enjoy the wind and clouds,
Why is there a need to discuss human affairs?

〈Bestowed with Wine〉
Golden elixir descends from the Emperor’s Terrace,
The jade calendar resides on Pénglái.
An immortal, once met, offers a drink,
Granting me two or three cups.
Suddenly I hear the mulberry leaves falling,
Just as the chrysanthemums bloom.
Ruǎn Jí throws on his robes and enters,
Wáng Róng comes with a smile.

〈Joy at the Clearing Sky, Written by Imperial Command, Following the Rhyme of the Imperial Decree〉
Driving the discourse, he truly receives the records,
As the Emperor, he is said to have established rule.
Formerly he fished at Léi Zé,
And at times engaged in trade at Fù Xià.
At Bǎi Liáng, he rides a carriage with four horses,
At Gāo Líng, he gallops with six relays.
Orderly succession belongs to the guests and retainers,
Impartiality manifests in balanced laws.
On the river dikes, the old willows collapse,
In the autumn waters, the new embankments rise high.
With a mind of fasting, he pities those submerged in the floods,
Removing the music, he feels for the commoners' complaints.
In the Chán River, he holds lofty discourses; the Wheel of Dharma begins superior debates.
At the King's City, the water battles cease,
At Luò Pǔ, the *River Map* is presented.
The hidden spring returns to the "Sinking" hexagram,
The returning wind has already reverted to the "Wind" hexagram.
The paulownia branches have grown to their former girth,
The rush joints sprout new inches.
The mountains and marshes rejoice in hiding ailments,
In secluded dwellings, one finds no distress.
Prosperity is shared by the millions of people,
May the Son of Heaven's years be ten thousand.

〈Harmonizing with Secretary Lǐ’s Poem on Joyful Rain〉
Pure Yang has indeed long been parched,

Approaching the river, jade discs are submerged,
Lining the road, dragon-steeds are painted.
The light of Li first entwines with lightning,
The breath of Zhen begins to ride the thunder.
The Sea Lad returns to Jié Shí,

〈Encountering Snow While Traveling in the Suburbs〉
Wind and clouds are both dismal and dark,
The wilderness and plains are together vast and hazy.
Snowflakes bloom with six petals,
Ice pearls reflect nine lights.
It is as if driving jade horses,
Or briefly like hunting silver roe deer.
The bank of clouds remains entirely motionless,
In the cold mountains, nothing is fragrant.
Lord Xué has a single white fox fur,
The Marquis of Táng has two Sùshuāng steeds.
At the cold pass, the sun is about to set,
Cloaked in snow, I cross the river bridge.

〈Respectfully Harmonizing with a Poem on a Summer Day Written by Imperial Command〉
The vermilion curtains roll up for the beautiful sun,
while the emerald screens block the overlapping light.
In the fifth month, the scorching, steamy air rises;
during the three watches, the water clock drips long.
Wheat ripens within the wind;
plums turn yellow following the rain.
Ice is cracked, brought along with well water,
and mixed with powder to blend fresh fragrances.
Robes hold the scent of plantain leaves;
fans stir the coolness of bamboo flowers.
Early water chestnuts grow soft horns;
first lotuses open their tiny pods.
I wish to accompany the immortal crane in its flight,
and at Luòpǔ, listen to the sheng and reed pipes.

〈In Harmony with Shào-bǎo Wáng Mourning Recluse Zhōu from Afar〉
In the dark vastness, you wander at Dài;
in desolation, I head toward Qín.
Though we say life and death are different,
we are both people who do not return.

waiting at the pass for the retired gentleman.

Melancholy like Zhāng Zhòngwèi;
