Wáng Sītú Bǎo
〈Mourning Wáng Sītú Bǎo〉
Once I heard of Wángzǐ Jìn,
who rose lightly to follow the immortals.
I say that you, Sir, accumulated goodness,
and were able to succeed the former sages.
In the four seas, all are displaced;
it is not you alone who was moved.
How could one expect the Middle Terrace to split?
You are like a candle before the wind.
Since you come from a family of bells and tripods,
in Jiāngdōng for three hundred years.
The precious sword was carried through generations;
the carved halberd was an old inheritance.
Green ribbons wind around the scholar-tree tassels;
gold ornaments grace the attendant’s cicada-hat.
The land established a country of loyal ministers;
the family opened the spring of filial sons.
Naturally able to make withered wood moist,
sufficient to make flowing water round.
With you following in the ancestors' footsteps,
the feudal lords had no room for criticism.
The blue collar already faced the sun;
even as a youth, you discussed the Heavens.
At Yǐngyīn, the pearls and jades are beautiful;
at Héyáng, the rouge and powder are lovely.
Your name is high among the six states;
your value is worth ten linked cities.
Eloquence sufficient to observe the Autumn Waters;
literary talent fit to write on a horsewhip.
Returning simurghs embrace the written characters;
parting cranes circle the zither strings.
Holding the banner, you governed the royal domain;
lowering the curtain, you were not at the border.
In the quiet pavilion, the horse is tied in vain;
from the idle beacon, smoke rises straight.
Not neglecting the book-reading desk,
without hindrance to sitting in a fishing boat.
In Màolíng, one suddenly fell ill;
in Huáiyáng, there has indeed been no recovery.
The attending physicians become more silent;
the spirit’s principle finally lingers on.
Everlasting farewell to Zhāng Píngzǐ;
forever burying Wáng Zhòngxuān.
At Bǎigǔ, the pine trees are moved;
at Yánglíng, burial plots are bought.
On the Shǎn road, the autumn wind rises;
the cold hall is already rustling.
The poplars on the mound shed their leaves;
the mountain fire burns instantly.
Once envied by others;
now pitied by others.
The world’s path goes from dawn to dawn;
human feelings are mystery upon mystery.
An old friend is grieved by this parting,
leaving resentment to fill the Qínchuán plains.
The final reputation is settled here;
the complete virtue is hereby perfected.
Only the flute of Shānyáng,
saddens me with the 〈Sījiù〉 chapter.

the protective walls belong to the flourishing relatives.
Noble positions connect to the Nándǒu,
high honors occupy the Běichén.
Welcoming the season, he calculates with the tally,
presiding over duties, he distributes the spirits.
Wherever the sun and moon shine,
wherever the frost and dew are equal.
Forever following the unified track of culture,
there will long be no one who needs to lock their outer doors.
○ Same as above.
Luxuriously layered buildings spread their ridgepoles,
towering and lofty, rivaling the *Dà Zhuàng*.
Great trees are decreed by the forest stewards,
and master carpenters are summoned for the complete model.
A thousand rafters float like patterned wings,
a hundred brackets are raised like long rainbows.
To the north departs the road to Hándān,
to the south comes the view of Yǎnshī.
Dragon heads carry the decorated eaves,
cloud lintels support the martial canopies.
Those who dwell there do not seek narrowness,
yet how could a humble palace be hard to honor?
Magnificence is for the world to behold,
thus following the example of Minister Xiāo.
○ Same as above.
〈Changed *Gōng* Mode Melodies, Two Songs〉
The sovereign travels where light emerges from Zhèn,
the bright lord holds power in Lí.
From the high halls, he offers only his caring gaze,
revering the ways of old, he values non-action.
The dragon’s cave is not difficult to approach,
the phoenix’s nest can be glimpsed.
Jùcí should not be far away,
why bother following to Fényáng?
The common people emphasize sowing and planting,
much toil is spent on the irrigation ditches.
Rain pours again upon Sānglín,
at Jīshí, the river was finally opened.
Clear signs meet the eternal mandate,
orderly regulation meets a year of harmony.
There is also the *Xūnfēng Qǔ*,
just now hearing the *Chénlù* song.
○ *Yǔ Zǐshān Jí*, Volume 7.
*Yuèfǔ Shī Jí*, Volume 15.
*Shī Jì*, Volume 119.
Changing customs broadens the Xuānyuán calendar,
exalting virtue flourishes in the years of Táng.
Elegant patterns arise in the *Dàyǎ*,
going out for pleasure moves the Jūntiān.
The Huángzhōng pitch and the six pipes are correct,
from the Chánghé gate, the eight winds are proclaimed.
Gūzhú bamboo tunes the yang-pipes,
Kōngsāng wood regulates the elegant strings.
In the forest of dance, the luán-bird descends again,
on the mountain of song, the phoenix is about to come forward.
Hearing the sounds, one can distinguish customs,
listening to the tunes, one then thinks of the worthy.
Moved by things, one observes order and chaos,
the heart always guards against what has not yet happened.
The gentleman attains the Way,
what more is needed for Tàipíng?
○ Same as above.
〈Four Songs in the Shāng Mode〉
The lord leads with the Gōng note,
magnanimous and wise in planning.
The minister responds with the Shāng note,
hearing what is right, he acts upon it.
Yǒuxióng governed,
seeking the Way from Róngchéng.
Yīn Tāng received the mandate,
entrusting matters to Āhéng.
Loyal in his respectful service,
having faults, he did not escape punishment.
Reciting his admonitions,
speaking without hidden feelings.
Firm and decisive,
the four quarters can be at peace.
Having both the *Sòng* and the *Yǎ*,
the world then reaches peace.
Concentrated and unified,
even metal and stone will open for it.
If two hearts are moved,
the affection of wife and children will be estranged.
If it benefits the state,
there is nothing he would not give.
August Heaven sends down blessings,
may the head of state be healthy!
○ *Yǔ Zǐshān Jí*, Volume 7.
*Yuèfǔ Shī Jí*, Volume 15.
*Shī Jì*, Volume 119.
All rivers meet together,
this is why the great sea is deep.
Since many materials have gathered,
therefore they can form Dènglín.
A fierce tiger is on the mountain,
the hundred beasts dare not invade.
A loyal minister resides in the state,
the world has no divided heart.
Formerly my refined ancestor,
held his heart with anxious concern,
driving out and cutting down wolves,
managing this heavenly path.
Now I have received the mandate,
also not daring to live in ease and pleasure.
Only you, the assisting ministers,
each should know to be cautious and fearful.
○ Same as above.
Rituals and music being corrected,
this is how spirits and men are in harmony.
Jades and silks are in order,
the will is to quiet the shields and spears.
Each distributed the tallies and omens,
together swearing to split mountains and rivers.
Today we enjoy each other's company,
facing the wine, we should sing.
Virtue is used as an allegory,
listen to the sound of the striking bell.
Spirits and monsters are not compliant,
observe the shapes of the cast tripods.
Having held court at Fènggōng,
the feudal lords are thus harmonious.
Hunting perhaps at Qíyáng,
the Huái Yí were henceforth pacified.
Like crossing a great river,
relying on boats and oars.
Like seasoning a tripod’s contents,
depending on salt and plum.
Ruler and minister are of one body,
they can quiet the dust of conflict.
Obtaining the right people leads to order,
in what age are there no exceptional talents?
○ Same as above.
The power of the wind is raised,
and the steps of the platform are ordered and level.
Zhònglí having ascended,
and the positions of Heaven and Earth are established.
Merit is not yielded to others,
engraved on the banners of Tàicháng.
Generations do not lose their offices,
receiving the covenant of the red-haired ox.
Collecting and distributing the auspicious jades,
solemn at the gate of Yáo.
Acting as the wings and the screen,
luxuriant on the plains of Zhōu.
Merit accomplished and order established,
rituals and music are thus preserved.
Returning the child to be the bright sovereign,
what more did Jī Dàn have to say?
○ Same as above.
〈Two Songs in the Jué Mode〉
Putting an end to war is seen in the fields of the loosened reins,
praising the conquest is heard in the campaign of Dānshuǐ.
Trust and righteousness both being preserved,
they first forget about food;
the five materials are used together,
who can dispense with weapons?
Though the great treasure of the sage is called the throne,
truly the great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called giving life.
The Jīng and Wèi rivers flow together,
clear and turbid have different capacities;
the qín and sè are played together,
elegant and Zhèng music have different sounds.
The restless common people,
their voices and teachings are not uniform;
the vast traces of Yǔ,
carriage tracks are not yet unified.
The will is set upon the four seas,
yet still respectful and frugal;
the heart encompasses the universe,
yet without pride or arrogance.
Speech without literary refinement
does not travel far;
righteousness without standing,
effort will result in no success.
A heart of compassion,
teaching with kindness and grace;
banishing and pardoning their faults,
sorrowfully pitying the standard punishments.
○ *Yǔ Zǐshān Jí*, Volume 7.
*Yuèfǔ Shī Jí*, Volume 15.
*Shī Jì*, Volume 119.
Scholars who assist and support
some follow fishing and angling;
talents of the clouds and rain
suddenly sighing in the deep valleys.
Those seeking fragrance pursue the orchids of deep paths,
those recognizing rhythm seek the bamboo of remote mountains.
Able to make his virtue bright,
contributing through the Three Tasks;
establishing the reputation of the wind,
spoken of in the Nine Provinces.
Harmoniously using the five regulators,
the wind is as if performing its task;
agriculture uses the eight governments,
gladly producing their grain.
Different customs on the same track,
seen in the *Zhōunán*;
different stalks with the same ear,
heard from Tángshū.
Severe cold and summer rain,
let there be no mutual resentment;
Heaven covers with oily clouds,
nourishing and soaking through.
Fortunate not to feel inferior to the pure people of high antiquity,
hoping they can be enfeoffed house by house.
○ Same as above.
〈Six Songs in the Zhǐ Mode〉
Heaven and Earth use containment and nourishment to cover and carry,
the sun and moon use constancy and brightness to shine upon.
The realized man takes the four seas as his concern,
the bright sovereign takes the common people as his heart.
If the water has waves, its source must be far,
if the tree is spreading, its roots must be deep.
Clouds and rain provide their gifts, and none are not moistened,
the court seeks talent, and many are given office.
○ *Yǔ Zǐshān Jí*, Volume 7.
*Yuèfǔ Shī Jí*, Volume 15.
*Shī Jì*, Volume 119.
Chún Fēng spreads governance, ever without desire;
the Great Way guards the people and can transform customs.
Seeking benevolence and righteousness more urgently than escaping water or fire;
practicing ritual and yielding more abundantly than beans and grain.
With the Qū Yì plant, there are no flatterers to point at;
with the Xiè Zhì beast, there are no excessive punishments to strike.
The King’s Way is vast, acting through non-action;
among the four classes of people in the world, who could be lacking?
○ Same as above.
A Sage is born only once in a thousand years;
the Huáng Hé runs clear only once in a thousand years.
Shè Tí is used to mark the records;
the Yù Zhú lamp thus brings cultural brilliance.
The Southeast can mend the gaps in the earth;
the Northwest can correct the tilt of the heavens.
Floating on a giant turtle, the Dōng Hǎi can be crossed;
wielding a spade, Nán Shān can be leveled.
All immortals pay court at the Yáo Shuǐ;
the various emperors receive offerings in the Bright Court.
Embracing harmony, the various instruments play together;
for great achievements, bells and tripods are both inscribed.
○ Same as above.
The three lights record things and show their forms;
the four seasons tailor and fix their positions.
Thunder and wind are the sounds of great mountains;
cold and heat communicate the breath of Yīn and Yáng.
Military merit unifies the six realms;
cultural education weaves the heavens and earth.
When the Way exists, all bathe in its virtue;
when life is cherished, each species flourishes.
The white sun crosses the sky and moves past the center;
the bright moon spans the Milky Way, waxing and then waning.
To be able to wane and be deficient is to act through non-action;
although full and overflowing, one is not in danger.
Opening trust and righteousness as parks and gardens;
establishing virtue and the Way as city walls and moats.
Zhōu observed the additions and subtractions of the two previous dynasties;
how grand and cultured its ways were!
Páo Xī personally attended to hunting and fishing;
Shén Nóng himself took up farming.
Tāng was diligent and worried about saving people from drought;
Yǔ had no time even to straighten his cap.
When the wind blows over the grass, it surely bends;
the people of a gentleman know how to be transformed.
Wishing to compare virtue with the Sān Huáng;
never following the tracks of the Wǔ Bà.
○ Same as above.
Thin threads unceasing form a thicket;
trickling streams unstopping create rivers.
Do not call a matter light because it is like a hair;
considering the distant and preventing the minute prevents falling.
The Yún Guān serve the sovereign who rules by letting his robes hang;
the Fèng Lì only respects the enlightened head.
Like the Sovereign on High, sacrifice to the Liù Zōng;
gaze at the mountains and rivers and hold court for the lords.
The Earth Mirror opens both mountains and marshes;
the River Map is borne by fish and dragons.
Our heavenly net covers everything;
the nine gates of Cháng Hé open to the celestial portal.
Ministers feel the profound resonance of wind and clouds;
assistants descend like the stars.
Having raised the Sān Shèng of the Zhōu house,
one appoints the Bā Cái of the Táng Cháo.
The minister from Shēn serves as counselor on the left;
Tiān Lǎo teaches governance in the central office.
One should take the wise as a model;
therefore, do not value or trust the treacherous.
○ Same as above.
The harmonious breath of Zhèng Yáng makes all species flourish;
the King’s Way matches the dignity of Heaven and Earth.
The common people farm in the Garden of Righteousness;
the gentlemen soar in the Garden of Ritual.
When eating the fruit, one thinks of the tree;
when drinking the water, one remembers the source.
Because Jiù Yáo was the counselor, the unrighteous stayed far away;
because Shì Huì governed, the thieves fled.
With leniency, even insects turn inward;
by manifesting trust, the hearts of distant customs are won.
At the floating bridge, the Yuè Zhī people hold horses;
in the imperial garden, the Wū Sūn learn the lute.
The Nán Hǎi sends tribute of red jade;
the Xī Shān offers treasures of white rings.
No need to labor in "boring through the void" to Dà Xià;
no need to wait for the "kneeling of horns" at Zhì Lín.
○ Same as above.
〈Five Songs of the Yǔ Mode〉
Establishing a ruler is to shepherd the people;
creating laws is to quiet disorder.
The chief evil was exiled to Nán Cháo;
the arch-criminal then fled to the north.
Living in auspicious breath, it fills the four borders;
in glory, it shines like two dawns.
Thus, as rain falls, the hexagram Jiě is made;
as the wind blows, only the hexagram Huàn is seen.
The great foundation of Zhōu's Wén and Wǔ;
the cultural brilliance dwelling in the world.
A thousand years bring the Sage and universal prosperity;
seven hundred years fall to me at the appointed time.
Truly, Hào Tiān has given the mandate;
only the four quarters shall be taught.
○ *Yǔ Zǐshān Jí*, Volume 7.
*Yuèfǔ Shījí*, Volume 15.
*Shījì*, Volume 119.
In peaceful times, favor the people;
in chaotic times, prioritize the heroic.
Crossing Guì Lín to drive elephants;
crossing the Ruò Shuǐ to receive the wild geese.
Having floated the spirit of a thousand measures;
returning to blow the winds of the eight pitches.
In the treasury, the strings of coins rot;
in the granaries, the red grain of the Cháng Píng is old.
Among the fires come the cold and heat;
the year is harmonious with one wind and one rain.
Listening to bells and chimes,
one thinks of the borders;
hearing flutes and pipes,
one thinks of accumulation.
When the Yáo Kūn jade and bamboo arrive,
the strange stones, lead, and pine follow in order.
Fine horses from Cháng Lè fill the stables;
the Shuǐ Héng office is a treasury for gold.
○ Same as above.
A hundred rivers follow the great sea;
all stars look up to the Běi Chén.
The Jiǔ Zhōu follow the tracks of Yǔ;
the four seas join in the virtue of the ministers of Yáo.
The morning sun rests upon the singing Phoenix;
the sacred altar grazes the spotted Qilin.
Clouds are like jade leaves in five colors;
the moon is like golden waves in two cycles.
The cool wind welcomes the season for the northern hunt;
the minor heat marks the time for the southern tour.
The mountains do not hide their purple jade;
the earth does not begrudge its yellow silver.
Though campaigning in the south, the north feels no resentment;
though expanding in the west, the east becomes a guest.
Having forever cleared the four seas,
there is finally a blessing for the One Man.
○ Same as above.
Setting the pitch with the jade pipes of Líng Líng;
adjusting the bells with the copper ruler of Shǐ Píng.
The lonely Paulownia below Lóng Mén;
the sounding stones by the banks of the Sì Shuǐ.
The spirit of the river thus offers the jade tablet;
the spirit of the mountain thus presents the jade disc.
Cleansing the Jiǔ Chuān to levy taxes;
ascending Sān Wēi to receive tribute.
The grain of Běi Lǐ has six ears;
the grass of Jiāng Huái has three ridges.
One may perform the Feng and Shan sacrifices with jade slips;
one may probe the records with gold cords.
Forever preserving a great name,
enough to spread light through the annals.
○ Same as above.
Highest of all is the establishment of virtue;
next is the establishment of speech.
Planting goodness flourishes by attending to the root;
removing evil is thorough by blocking the source.
When one's wisdom is deep and vast, it is thick;
when the Way is illuminated, it is honored.
The wealth of benevolence and righteousness is never exhausted;
the ritual of loyalty and trust is not burdensome.
When Heaven is moved, there is nowhere it does not reach;
in its time, there is no obscurity it does not penetrate.
In practicing virtue, the heart is at ease and daily grows more excellent;
in practicing deceit, the heart is labored and daily grows more clumsy.
Unless one uses hardness to cover righteousness,
there is no escape from total destruction.
○ Same as above.
〈Memorial Congratulating the Pacification of the Capital at Yè〉
〈Memorial Congratulating the Pacification of the Capital at Yè〉
Your servant [So-and-so] says:
I have heard that since the time of Tài Shān and Liáng Fǔ,
there have been seventy-two generations;
since the Lóng Tú and Guī Shū,
another three thousand years have passed.
Although they established laws and offices differently,
and their rituals and music were distinct,
when it came to the separation of patterns and the falling of military might,
or the carving of wood and the stringing of bows,
the way they swept up the hearts of the world
and encompassed the ambition of the eight wildernesses
was identical.
I prostrate myself before Your Imperial Majesty,
who holds the pivot of heaven
and grasps the axis of the earth,
who rides the winds and clouds
and drives the dragons and tigers.
With deep resolve and inner decisiveness,
you do not trouble yourself to consult Lì Mù;
with divine military strategy and courageous determination,
you do not wait to ask Róng Chéng.
Thus, where your majestic influence stirs,
it is like a fierce fire meeting a bird's down;
where your banners and drums approach,
it is like a rushing wind sweeping away autumn leaves.
I have heard that the Róng and Yí of Yī and Luò,
and the illegitimate pretenders of Yōu and Bìng,
have taken their maps and records
and already submitted to the Office of the Chancellor;
holding jade in their mouths and binding themselves with cords,
they have together gone to the camp of the Central Army.
Those who for a hundred years escaped execution
have finally seen their nests and dens exhausted;
the enmity of three generations
was suddenly swept away.
Long ago, the army of the King of Zhōu at the Wěishuǐ
still required a second expedition;
Xuānyuán’s battle at Shànggǔ
still needed nine campaigns.
Never has there been one who, with a single morning’s command,
solely determined by divine thought,
settled everything within the borders
and brought light to the entire world.
Of the twenty-eight constellations,
there remains only the single star of Wú and Yuè;
of the twelve hundred states,
only the small waters of Línzhōu have slipped through.
As for the years of Xiánkāng,
when the four directions were first settled;
or the era of Jiànwǔ,
when the feudal lords all came to court—
they cannot be spoken of in the same breath!
Even if the winds from the eight directions sang together,
it would not be enough to praise your heroic fame;
even if the six types of music were all displayed,
there would be no way to sing of your divine martial prowess.
Sitting on the fishing terrace to swear in the masses,
Sì Qǐ continued the achievements of Xià Yǔ;
entering the suburbs of Shāng to punish the guilty,
Jī Fā fulfilled the will of Zhōu Wén.
The way of making no changes—
is this not great filial piety?
Now Lùtái has been dispersed,
the detached palaces have been dismissed,
weapons are stored in the armory,
and horses are sent to Huà Shān.
Establishing the system of the Míngtáng,
and performing the music of the Dà Wǔ—
how magnificent!
Heaven has sent down blessings
such as have never been seen before.
There is only need for one commandant in the southeast,
stationed south of Bǐjǐng;
and one lookout in the northwest,
placed north of Jiāohé.
Then, command Dōnghòu,
proclaim to Cāngmíng,
carve the jade tablets at the crossroads altar,
and with silver cords and jasper seals,
announce the successful completion;
there will be no cause for shame in your virtue.
I, your humble servant, have unworthily received great honor
to govern the eastern marches;
being unable to personally attend the imperial court
to witness the great celebration,
I cannot overcome my extreme leaping joy, like a waterfowl bobbing on the water.
I respectfully send my subordinate official Cáo Mǐn to present this memorial for your consideration.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 566.
Also briefly seen in *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 59.
<Memorial Congratulating on the New Music for Zhōu Wǔdì>
Your servants say:
Your servants have heard that when Heaven and Earth move in accordance,
thunder comes forth as Yù;
when the Sage achieves success,
the wind moves with rhythm.
Therefore, when the Six Virtues reside in the office of Xiánchí,
the mountains and valleys can be harmonized;
when the Eight Winds enter the performance of Chéngyún,
humans and spirits do not intermingle in disorder.
Our Tài Zǔ, Wén Huángdì,
organized the state and managed the wilderness,
established offices and divided duties,
transformed Wèi into Zhōu,
and shifted customs to correct the Yǎ.
In ceremonial robes, he received the myriad states in court;
with jade tablets, he gathered the feudal lords.
As for organizing the maps and records,
and collating what remained from the ashes,
the Director of Music left no missing chapters,
and the Minister of Rites left no abandoned canons.
Was it only the ten chapters of the Shāng Sòng
that were obtained from the house of the Grand Master;
or the Yú Shū and the Five Rites
that were taken from the palace of Gōng Wáng?
We prostrate ourselves before the Emperor, who has risen through military succession
and continued the legacy of Zhòngyáng.
You wield the brightness of the sun and moon
and move with the deep considerations of a spring.
The laws of the calendar are made clear
without troubling the Tàishǐ;
the measurements of Yīn and Yáng and the sundial
are personally determined by the Tiānguān.
Thus you have been able to harmonize the Eight Tones
and refine the essence of the Six Generations.
You enfeoffed Jìn and Wèi as the Two Kings
and arranged Yīn and Zhōu as the Three Guests.
Although the red shields and jade axes
still recognize the old forms;
and the white knee-covers and vermilion skirts
still follow the heroic foundation.
They are not yet like the Shānyún rising uniquely,
where the Eight Trigrams take form;
or the phoenixes flying together,
where the Nine Provinces observe virtue.
You changed the metal music to the eight rows
and matched the Heavenly Origin to the six dances.
The sound contains the resonance of striking stones,
and enters again into the ascending songs;
the melody starts with the initial bell
and returns to join the jade pipes.
This is enough to move Heaven and Earth and communicate with the divine spirits,
to bring peace to the Imperial Virtue and bring light to the dark celestial signs.
In the past, while residing in seclusion at Xuánhù,
the composition was made at Yúnmén;
when the army crossed Méngjīn,
the practice of the dance returned to Shānlì.
Thus you have encompassed the Three Names
and harmonized an entire generation.
He who creates is called a Sage;
is this not what Heaven has inspired?
Is it only the large drums and divine hand-drums,
or the hollow mulberry and solitary bamboo?
How vast! How great!
How magnificent! How beautiful!
We know then that the filial and incorrupt one of Línglíng
passed down the jade pipes in vain;
and the Governor of Shǐpíng
falsely praised the bronze ruler.
Your servants all participated in the heavenly feast
and together observed the performance of music.
The porch and courtyard were vast and open,
and from the railings, we looked and listened.
The bell-frames were towering and grand,
and the fierce beast-shaped supports were majestic.
Kingfisher phoenixes flew on the banners,
and divine alligators stood by the drums.
Like distant clouds and mist,
surging over hills and mounds.
Sweet springs and sweet dew flew together,
while red geese and dappled qílín descended at once.
When one visits Lǔ to request to see the music,
it is only right to see such flourishing virtue;
when one goes to Qí and forgets the taste of food,
it is certainly from knowing such perfect beauty.
In the past, the fish in the deep listening to the music
could still raise their scales;
the horses in the stable hearing the strings
could still look up from their fodder.
Your servants are truly ashamed of our limited understanding of music,
yet how could we dare to forget this joy!
If we were asked to detail the tones and rhythms,
that would be far beyond us;
but being able to record its resounding sounds
is our great fortune.
We cannot overcome our sincerity of celebration and joy.
We respectfully go to the court hall
to present this memorial for your consideration.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 569.
<Memorial Written for General Yán Requesting Retirement>
<Memorial Written for General Yán Requesting Retirement>
Your servant [Name] says:
Your servant has heard that the *Lǐ* states:
"At seventy, a *Dàfū* retires from the court,
hands down the family affairs to his son,
receives double the delicacies for his meals,
and wears clothes according to the seasonal regulations."
Since your servant began his career to serve the state,
over forty years have passed.
I encountered the winds and clouds of change,
rising from obscurity to prominence.
*Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì* rescued the state from peril and brought relief to its hardships;
he completely possessed the *Guānhé* region.
Your servant truly had no great ability,
but served as a *Zhōngjuān* attendant.
Since the dust of war consumed *Luòyáng*,
and the flags and drums were at *Héliáng*,
there were *Bǎimǎ* troops at *Huáyīn*,
and the *Huángshā* battle at *Héqǔ*.
Although your servant followed orders,
I could not offer brilliant strategies.
My merits are slight, but the rewards have been generous;
I have achieved success through the efforts of others.
My inclusion in the annual tables of grace and favor
constantly fills my heart with shame.
Looking up, I encountered the *Zhōu* dynasty,
which rose to power through humble yielding and the appointment of the worthy;
it received the mandate amid songs of praise.
As the Lord became noble, the servants were promoted,
and I repeatedly received honors and favor.
As one of the *Sānhuái* who cast tripods to depict the nature of things,
one should know the divine and the evil;
as one of the *Wǔděng* who adorns the auspicious *Huánguī* jade,
one should guard the imperial household.
What virtue does your servant possess
to hold both these honors?
Furthermore, regarding the office of water and earth,
*Wáng Liáng* was summoned in response to omens;
regarding the generalship of soldiers and weapons,
*Hán Xìn* was uniquely appointed upon an altar.
Comparing myself to their kind,
what sort of person am I?
At present, the four seas are not yet tranquil,
and three powers stand like the legs of a tripod.
It is a time when Your Majesty labors in mind,
and a season for the various lords to display their effectiveness.
However, your servant's years are many,
and old age has arrived.
I cannot participate in the affairs of guests and visitors,
and I have wrongly reached the rank of the feudal lords.
Occupying a post without merit,
I have long disturbed the established laws;
like carrying a heavy load and inviting bandits,
I only trouble the officials in charge.
Furthermore, cold and heat have conflicted,
the regulation of my health has lost its order,
wind and water have invaded together,
and my vital essence is exhausted.
Even if *Lián Pō* could still eat heartily,
or *Mǎ Yuán* could still mount a saddle,
though they wished to repay the favor,
how could they still perform their service?
The joy of *Róng Qǐqī*
is just enough for oneself;
the words of *Zhú Zhīwǔ*
can no longer accomplish anything.
I specially beg to be relieved of my current office,
and to return to my original humble garments.
This matter accords with the request to "return my bones,"
not a plot to receive the gift of a stool and staff.
If your servant moves to *Běilíng* due to illness,
and returns to *Dōnggāo* in old age,
the fiefdoms of mountain and river,
shall once more be returned to the *Sīxùn*;
the jade tablets and disks of a duke or marquis,
shall be returned to the *Diǎnruì*.
Then the court will have no person overstepping his position,
and your servant will avoid the blame of obstructing the worthy.
In the *Yú* clan's system of caring for the elderly,
I dare to hope for the glory of the *Dōngxù*;
in the *Zhōu* dynasty, as numerous as rushes,
how could I expect the rites of the western suburbs?
But looking up at the celestial majesty,
I am about to depart from your presence;
lingering at the city towers,
my private sorrow and longing increase.
I cannot bear the feeling of knowing when to stop.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 603.
<Memorial on Behalf of Someone Requesting Retirement>
Your servant *Sù* says:
Your servant has heard that when a single leaf is about to fall,
it does not even wait for the wind and dew;
when the hundred rivers have all arrived,
the pools and puddles dry up on their own.
Your servant is suddenly moved by this,
with sadness and choking sobs.
Your servant [Name] bows and apologizes.
At the end of the second month of spring,
my old ailments gradually worsened.
My feet are quite lame,
and my four limbs are weak.
In my steps, I have the stumble of *Hàndān*,
and in my straining sight, I lack the clarity of *Lí Lóu*.
How can I lead and remain in these duties,
confusing these eternal laws?
Your Majesty's grace is pervasive and complete,
and you have not had the heart to cast me aside.
But your humble servant’s exhaustion has reached an extreme,
and I can no longer bear it.
This is why your servant blames and grieves for himself,
with tears followed by blood.
Your servant [Name] bows and apologizes.
Your servant has specially inherited the ancestral legacy,
and my advancement was not due to others.
Your Majesty pitied your servant's uselessness,
promoting the upright though I was blunt.
Since serving in the *Tàijí* Hall,
and proclaiming edicts in the *Zhōngshū*,
Your Majesty has accepted your servant with a single heart,
and entrusted your servant with sole responsibility.
For nine years, I hoped to serve as a *Zǎifǔ*,
and for eight years, I have occupied the position of *Zōngbó*.
Going out, I held the banners of authority;
coming in, I participated in the mirror of governance.
Sometimes atop the *Yúntái*,
your humble servant participated in the discussions of inquiry;
sometimes beneath the *Rìguàn*,
your servant was ordered to handle the texts for engraving.
To make them beautiful and expressive,
your servant truly felt excessive unworthiness.
Under the bright laws, I dare not have the slightest burden,
yet my contribution to the mysterious creation was less than a drop.
Time passes like ice and charcoal,
meeting together in my heart.
I recall previously attending to government affairs,
and personally receiving your virtuous words,
saying that because we had served in the imperial halls,
our descendants would still receive protection.
Your servant, as insignificant as an ant,
suddenly bore the weight of a mountain.
Your servant should spend his life and exhaust his fate,
and even in death offer his strength.
But secretly, I do not know when the end will come,
and I do not know when to stop.
Among the court ranks, there are several
who are of the same age as your servant.
Your servant is not yet sixty;
compared to them, I am young.
Yet I alone am increasingly withered and exhausted;
my illness does not wait for my years.
My capacity has reached its limit,
and fullness invites loss.
Often, as time passes, I fail to recover without medicine;
throughout the long days, I am still bound to the mulberry roots.
Observing my lot, it is inevitable;
coveting glory is what is forbidden.
I humbly beg to be relieved of my current office,
to retire and finish my remaining years.
To realize that your servant's honor cannot be sustained,
and to pity that my strength cannot be forced,
would be my good fortune.
How could I have realized that at the Gate of *Rénshòu*,
there would be this moment?
At the *Chéngmíng* Lodge,
I have no reason to visit again.
My mind and spirit are already worn out,
and every moment increases my sorrow.
Receiving the wise inspection, no scholar is ahead;
departing from the sagely countenance, how far will this minor servant go?
I only hope that when the three roads open the way,
and the imperial carriage tours the capital,
delighting the people who previously complained in the west,
and reaching those following in the east wind.
If my fragile soul should linger,
or if my withered bones still exist,
that would be my satisfaction,
but not what I expect.
Your servant has also heard:
In galloping to serve the carriage,
the weak and worn-out horses are removed first;
in soaring to celebrate success,
those with broken wings are left behind.
Even they know their twilight;
how much more so your servant!
Having heard this, I do not have time to wait to request;
such is your servant's earnest longing.
As for neglecting my duties,
your servant should record his guilt.
I cannot bear the utmost of trembling, longing, and attachment.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 603.
<Memorial of the Prince of *Qí* on Presenting a White Rabbit>
<Memorial of the Prince of *Qí* on Presenting a White Rabbit>
Your servant hears that when the territory is about to expand,
then the Yùhǔ cries at dawn;
when the paths of carriage tracks are just opening,
then the Yínzhāng is presented as tribute.
Humbly considering Your Majesty, who shines brightly above
and dwells in the high position with profound reverence,
Your virtue moves the Tiānguān,
and Your majesty shifts the Dìzhóu.
Therefore, the winds and mists are illuminated,
and feathered creatures bring auspicious signs;
the historians never cease their writing,
and the government offices have no idle days.
Your servant received the command of the great army
to pacify the borderlands.
Arriving at the camp gates,
we first halted at Xióngshān.
While the scouts were checking for threats,
they captured a white rabbit.
Its luster surpasses the pheasants of Yuè,
and its color is more beautiful than the foxes of Qín.
It corresponds to the signs of the Yuèdé,
and its Jīnjīng manifests an omen.
It presents an omen for popular praise
and displays a wonder that matches the maps.
Since the traces of reverence are clear,
the signs of responding to affairs are thus portended.
Your servant's respectful campaign
indeed follows the strategy at Shǎn.
The omen, with its white nature,
further strengthens the Xīqì.
I hope to receive the ancestral temple's plans again
as we are about to exert our majesty,
to eclipse Dài and subdue Qí,
to divide Hán and split Zhào.
I cannot contain my feelings of joyful leaping, like a duck among the weeds.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Vol. 612.
Also briefly seen in Yìwén Lèijù, Vol. 95.
<Memorial Presenting a Dark Crow by the Prince of Qí>
<Memorial Presenting a Dark Crow by the Prince of Qí>
Your servant (So-and-so) says:
Your servant hears that the flying pheasant of Nányáng
still explained the plan for hegemony;
the alighting swan of Jiànzhāng
still harmonized the vital energy.
How much more so when the court of Yú announces an omen,
and the shrine of Jī presents a sign,
all extolling the heart that knows how to feed its parents,
truly valuing the nature that can possess knowledge.
Humbly considering Your Majesty the Emperor,
whose virtue teaches the common people,
whose filial piety serves as a model for the four seas,
the Shètí stars follow their order,
and the world is civil and bright.
Therefore, the Dōnghǎi sends birds
that suddenly change their black nature;
the Xīshān deliver feathered ones
that perhaps transform into dark essences.
On the thirtieth day of last month,
Your servant arrived at Shǎnzhōu.
I received a report from the Dàdūdǔ Mòrén Huílè,
stating that within the archery hall of the prefecture,
he saw a dark crow
soaring around the thickets,
circling and not leaving,
resting as the essence of the wood element
and turning the wings that govern the wind.
He immediately summoned the Yítóng (So-and-so) and others
to witness it together.
This is truly the result of ritual reverence spreading
and the resonance of filial piety and compassion.
It is reasonable that this omen should be returned to the secret charts
and this sign recorded in the imperial annals,
to illuminate Your supreme virtue
and achieve an era of peace.
Let it not be that only the Chìfèng stays,
merely for the song of buried jade;
or that the Xuánhè lingers,
alone monopolizing the dance of holding a pearl in its beak.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Vol. 612.
<Memorial Presenting a Red Sparrow by the Prince of Qí>
<Memorial Presenting a Red Sparrow by the Prince of Qí>
Your servant (So-and-so) says:
Your servant hears that when the pheasant of Nányáng flew,
people still discussed the hegemony of Qín;
when the swan of Jiànzhāng alighted,
it still illustrated the virtue of Hàn.
At present, Heaven does not withhold its treasures,
and Earth must present its omens.
Naturally, one should observe signs at Chánglè
and initiate omens at Wénchāng.
Humbly considering the Emperor,
reverent, enlightened, accomplished, and thoughtful,
who only through diligent toil completes his duties.
He observes the movements of the sun and moon
and truly regulates the various officials.
The seawater has no waves,
and the stars in the sky do not shift.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month past,
I received a dispatch from the Lǒngyòu Tallies Office Cānjūn Lǐ Huī, stating:
a household belonging to Wéngǔlín in Bóyáng County, Qīngshuǐ Commandery, Qínchuān, captured a red sparrow in their courtyard.
Its brilliance is like the Zhūfèng,
and its color similar to the Dānwū.
This flying essence of descending fire
seems to have entered the Gōngchē office;
this manifestation of flowing gold
is as if it ascended the Língyúntái.
I respectfully note that a red sparrow once carried a scroll in its beak
and stopped at the gate of Fēng;
the Zhōu's reception of the Mandate
arose from this very omen.
Judging from what is observed now,
it matches and tallies with that event.
It truly can be illustrated in the register of omens
and recorded in the eulogies of the scholars.
This event is sufficient to build a tower,
and its name is worthy of being used as an era name.
Is it only that the Tàishǒu of Yúnzhōng
saw the red-hearted devotion to the lord,
or that the youth of Pénglái
knew the gratitude of the white ring?
We, your servants, have witnessed this auspicious sign;
our feelings are overwhelmed with constant celebration,
and we cannot contain our extreme joy like ducks among the weeds.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Vol. 612.
<Memorial Presenting Jade Pitch-pipes, Scales, Feet, Pecks, and Pints on behalf of the Jìnyáng Gōng>
<Memorial Presenting Jade Pitch-pipes, Scales, Feet, Pecks, and Pints on behalf of the Jìnyáng Gōng>
Your servant (So-and-so) says:
Your servant hears that once the Sāncái were established,
the way of lord and minister was displayed;
when the six positions were timely completed,
the merit of ritual and music was thus rectified.
Therefore, they are used to harmonize the sun and moon
and to measure Yīn and Yáng,
to bring joy and pleasure to the millions of people
and to serve as a model for the ten thousand states.
Humbly considering the Emperor,
who responds to the registers to govern Heaven
and opens the charts to receive the Mandate,
who relies on the Tàiyáng to hang the images
and treads upon Wénchāng to establish the ultimate pole.
The white ring manifests the sign of yielding virtue,
and the Xuánguī announces the omen of success.
The Tàijiē is already level,
and the ritual of Shēngzhōng can be practiced.
Surely the Water element shall be established for a thousand years,
and the Mountains shall cry out "Ten Thousand Years."
I have humbly seen the imperial decree
to correct the musical pitch-pipes
and to regulate the calendar and astronomical images.
Playing the Huángzhōng and singing the Dàlǚ,
transforming the Gūzhú flute and dancing the Yúnmén,
every instrument is made for clear communication,
and every sound follows peace and joy.
The Sìfēn are already clear,
and the Sānwēi are also fixed.
Therefore, hearing a bell at the shores of Luò,
one immediately distinguishes a discordant sound;
listening to a bell in Hándān,
one knows the resonance beforehand.
The two equinoxes and two solstices
are managed by the astronomical officials;
the nine transformations and nine completions
are assigned to the officials of Zhōnghé.
They are sufficient to move Heaven and Earth,
to resonate with ghosts and gods,
to influence customs, and to balance cold and heat.
Is it merely for chanting and whistling in the valleys
or for making phoenixes soar around?
Thus we know that before the temple at Línglíng,
searching for Shùn’s flutes was in vain;
below the city of Shǐpíng,
discussing the Zhōu foot-measure was to no avail.
Your servant has heard that those above establish the rites,
and those below practice their ceremonies;
the ruler determines the laws,
and the ministers carry out the tasks.
I have respectfully crafted a set of the Yùlǜ (Jade Pitch Pipes),
along with a Yùchèng (Jade Scale), Ruler, Bushel, Pint, Cup, and other measures,
and have finally achieved success.
As for calculating the grains and the broomcorn millets,
or measuring the silk threads and counting the *yuè* volumes,
I have truly relied on Your Majesty's sagely regulations
and consulted Your divine thoughts.
I hope that as the seasons shift within the *yīn* pipes,
there will be no need for the ashes of Hénèi;
as the *qì* moves the *yáng* bells,
there will be no need to wait for the bamboo of Jīnmén.
However, these Wǎnyǎn jade works are of little consequence,
and the considerations of a mere craftsman like Bān or Chuí are shallow;
they are insufficient to be displayed in the Chéngjūn Academy
or to add glory to the standard measures.
I present these vessels along with this memorial for Your awareness.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 613.
Also seen in *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 5,
with deletions.
〈Memorial on Presenting the *Xiàngjīng Fù*〉
Your servant [Name] says:
Your servant has prostratedly read the sagely composition, the *Xiàngjīng*,
and observed the *Xiàngxì* (Image Game);
in my private heart, I was filled with leap and joy,
unable to contain my delight.
I consider that nature and the Way of Heaven
are fundamentally beyond pursuit,
but because they are suspended like the sun and moon,
I was finally able to gaze upon them.
Once the Jiǔzhōu (Nine Provinces) were established,
one could closely face the *Hétú*;
when the four ruts follow the line,
one fully observes the Yùcè (Jade Slips).
Before the dark cranes fly,
one first hears the sound of metal and stone;
without ascending Chìchéng,
one alone sees the vapors of mist and clouds.
Measuring with a sighting tube,
the brilliance becomes even loftier;
observing through a submerged jade,
the source of the spring feels even more distant.
Unrestrained by my own limits,
I have gathered emptiness to compose a rhapsody;
the words are not clear and bright,
and my learning lacks refinement.
Thus I have dared to present it,
truly with a thick face.
Furthermore, the distance of the sun
was originally not a question for a child;
the theories of the Hún and Gài heavens,
how could they be a topic for a scholar?
Risking all to report this to Your Majesty,
I am prostrate and sweating profusely.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 610.
〈Memorial Congratulating the Abdication to the Crown Prince〉
〈Memorial Congratulating the Abdication to the Crown Prince〉
Your servant [Name] says:
I have prostratedly seen the edict of the nineteenth day of the second month,
passing the throne to the Huángtàizǐ.
In the past, those who descended to live by the Ruòshuǐ,
or rose to office had differences in merit;
those who came to court at Liyuáng
and succeeded the line had distinctions between ruler and subject.
One cannot compare them with the two suns in the sky,
or the sun being at its zenith again,
shining together in linked brilliance,
a double illumination of repeated light,
talking about them in the same year!
I prostrate before the Tiānyuán Huángdì,
only a sage can act as a sage,
only the kin can honor the kin.
He lowered his thoughts to entrust the capable,
and showed humility regarding the Great Instrument.
Wanting all officials to work in harmony,
one first hears the air of yielding and abdication;
for the world to have non-action,
one early recognizes the son of our ruler.
Therefore, employing the clarity of unique insight,
He performs an extraordinary act,
which is not in conflict with Heaven before its manifestation,
and follows Heaven after it has manifested.
The Huángtàizǐ upholds the ten thousand states,
his path illuminates the four gates.
He early received the tally of the second mandate,
and truly fulfills the destiny of the foundation of Heaven.
This is not about a son restoring a mandate,
and it differs from the succession from Yú to Xià.
Whether through decrease or increase,
there were still two Heavens;
being *Lí* and being Fire,
what harm is there in two suns?
Furthermore, in Píngyáng and Púbǎn,
there were twenty-five worthy ministers;
for Zhuānxū and Gāoxīn,
there were sixteen clans of talented sons.
With these taking part in affairs,
how could success not be swift!
Sound the drums!
Dance with high spirits!
Naturally, the Bāfēng (Eight Winds) will circulate,
the auspicious clouds will gather,
the Wǔlǎo (Five Elders) will travel together,
and the Sānxīng (Three Stars) will shine.
How could it merely be the double dragons bestowed again,
or the nine pheasants flying once more!
The Emperor remains distant like those on Mount Gūshè,
rightly riding the clouds and driving dragons,
seeking the Way at Kòngtóng;
how could he again be like the falling leaves before autumn?
Your servant was born to experience the years of Yáo,
and met the days of Shùn;
witnessing this celebration of renewal,
my feelings are ten thousand times greater than the norm.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 557.
Also seen in brief in *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 16.
〈Memorial on behalf of the Duke of Qǐ Declining the Positions of Zōngshī and Biàoqì〉
〈Memorial on behalf of the Duke of Qǐ Declining the Positions of Zōngshī and Biàoqì〉
Your servant [Name] says:
I have prostratedly seen the imperial edict,
appointing me as Shǐchíjié, Biàoqì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Zōngshī Zhōngdàfū.
Respectfully receiving these silken words,
my heart and soul are shaken with awe.
Your servant has heard that Yáo divided the Sìyuè,
thus ranking the mountains and rivers by prestige;
Shùn appointed the Jiǔguān,
thus bringing glory to the sun and moon.
One must model oneself with virtue
and be clearly tested by merit,
only then can one harmonize the ten thousand states
and bring success to all tasks.
Your servant lacked learning and cultivation in youth,
and was deficient in refinement as an adult.
At the gates of Hóngdū,
I cannot determine the chapters and sentences;
at the pass of Jīlù,
I have no way to name the stone tablets.
Relying on the waters of the Tiānhuáng stream,
clinging to the branches of the Ruòmù tree,
at the Dōngyuè, my name is registered for morning attendance;
at the Nángōng, I am listed at the gates.
Given my mediocre and inferior nature,
I have long known I have reached my limit.
Wǔyáng, with the gravity of a meritorious official,
was specially appointed as Zōngshī;
Dōngpíng, with the dignity of a maternal younger brother,
was promoted beyond others to become a supreme general.
What virtue does your servant have
to be able to double these honors?
Your servant early lost the shade of the parental courtyard,
before I could even lean against a wall.
My mother’s kind instructions
were filled with sorrow and bitter toil.
Just as I reached adulthood,
she again passed away.
As if she were still present at the offering table,
I cannot bear to leave the grace of her nurturing.
This lifelong debt cannot be repaid,
and striking the ground in grief is hard to endure.
I wish to remain by the earthen mound
and stay at the grave site for the rest of my life,
expressing the feelings of the changing seasons and frost and dew,
like a swallow or sparrow showing the heart of hovering and returning.
Unexpectedly, the Heavenly Grace flowed abundantly,
mistakenly granting me this promotion.
At present, the Yùzhú is in harmony,
it is not an age of war;
while the Xuánjī regulates the government,
how could one forget the remains among the pines and catalpas?
Furthermore, a single crooked branch
will eventually endanger a nine-story tower;
a single leg in a puddle
will surely injure a carriage traveling a thousand miles.
The Emperor is profoundly enlightened, cultured, and wise,
magnificently illuminating the entire realm.
His rituals reach the four directions,
and he would not tolerate depriving this subject of his ambition;
he governs the world with filial piety,
and naturally should pity this subject's sentiments.
Taking the *Dà Zōng* as a teacher,
seek further among states of the same surname;
for the chariot-companion of the *Yuán Róng*,
separately select capable and worthy officials.
I prostrate and hope you will look upon this memorial from the *Qīngpú*,
and kindly grant my humble sincerity;
issuing a decree from the *Fènghuáng Zhī Chí*,
specially withdrawing the strict summons.
Then the Heavenly Mercy will not be excessive,
my private wish will be granted,
and as for this subject's physical presence,
there will then be a place for it.
Unable to endure my sincerity of frantic fear and trembling,
I respectfully go to the court hall
and offer this memorial for your hearing.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, 578.
〈Memorial Requesting That Families of Meritorious Officials Who Did Not Die in Royal Service Be Allowed to Inherit Titles〉
〈Memorial Requesting That Families of Meritorious Officials Who Did Not Die in Royal Service Be Allowed to Inherit Titles〉
Your subject has heard that when laws are applied to the people,
sacrificial rites must be passed down;
when the state is settled through labor,
there must be a family to inherit.
That the sacrifices to *Sūnshū Áo* were unheard of
was a harm to the memory of a fine minister;
that *Nǚ Shūqí*’s descendants were cut off
was truly a slight to a worthy official.
I respectfully note the regulations of the sixteenth year of *Dàtǒng*:
those who previously held titles but died in royal service without heirs
were permitted to have a younger son succeed them;
if they did not die in royal service,
they were not allowed to inherit according to the former records.
The meritorious officials of the five ranks
are all those who worked diligently for the royal house,
personally facing hardships,
warding off disasters,
and assisting in the great plan.
If one day they encounter illness
and pass away in their guest house,
and unfortunately have no direct heir,
their sacrifices are then cut off;
this is insufficient according to ritual
and harmful to righteousness.
Before they could seek a hunt in *Shànglín*,
their marquisate has already been stripped;
before they could wear the *chānyú* robes,
their state has first been abolished.
I prostrate and consider that the Emperor exalts virtue and honors merit,
raising up what has fallen and continuing what has been cut off.
Hearing the drums, he thinks of generals;
painting the *Yún Tái*, he remembers old ministers.
How can there be merit preserved for the state
but no descendant to maintain it?
Deeds performed with full loyalty and integrity,
but no shrine for sacrifice?
*Zhōu* made covenants for the protective states,
the matter lying in generational merit;
*Hàn* swore by mountains and rivers,
the meaning residing in permanence.
Your subject has heard that preserving a person's state
is greater than saving a person from disaster;
establishing a person's heir
is more significant than sealing a person's tomb.
I humbly note that in the *Yīn* dynasty, succession reached the collateral branches,
without abandoning the lesser lineages;
in the *Zhōu* house's rise and fall,
importance was placed on preservation after death.
Those who succeeded the Marquis of *Gāomì* lasted for many generations;
was it exclusively for *Dèng Yǔ*’s direct heir?
Those who inherited the Marquis of *Píngyáng* lasted for many ages;
why must it have been *Cáo Cān*’s legitimate grandson?
My humble opinion is that if one had merit in life
but did not die in royal service,
even if they are of the branch families,
they should all be allowed to succeed the title.
May it cause the soul of *Bó Yǒu*
to be unable to become a vengeful ghost;
and the ghosts of *Ruò Áo*
to not go hungry.
The dark and the manifest respond to each other;
humans and gods are but a foot apart.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, 51.
〈Letter of Thanks for the Preface to the Collected Works of the *Téng Wáng*〉
From so-and-so:
I prostrate and read the writing
you have graciously bestowed as a preface to my collection.
The *Zǐ Wēi* star reflects from afar,
like the passing down of books from *Quèlǐ*;
the *Qīng Niǎo* flies from the distance,
like sending a jade disk from the *Céng Chéng*.
As for in the *Gānquán* Palace,
a cluster of jade trees,
or before the *Xuánwǔ* Gate,
a six-inch bright pearl,
they cannot be compared to this radiance
or match this illumination.
Possessing rhythm and measure,
it can indeed calm the eight winds;
the more it is sung, the higher it goes,
almost coming within three feet of heaven.
Your Highness (*Diànxià*) possesses heroic talent that surpasses the age,
and an extraordinary spirit that traverses the clouds;
you are the *Yán Yuán* of *Jìběi*,
the *Kǒngzǐ* of *Guānxī*.
Comparing your brush and ink,
then wind and rain compete in flight;
discussing your literary patterns,
then fish and dragons undergo a hundred transformations.
Grapes surround the lodge,
newly opening the Palace of *Jiéshí*;
tall bamboos line the pond,
where the Garden of *Suīyáng* was first made.
Lapis lazuli overflows with wine,
and parrot cups hold the brew.
Songs from the *Fèng Xué*,
and dance tunes from the *Luán Lín*.
Moreover, moving clouds chase the rain,
and swirling snow follows the wind.
The Commandant of *Húyáng*
has already become the cause of joy;
the Marquis of *Chōnglíng*
is then the place for dispelling sorrow.
I originally lacked talent and utility,
and have not written much.
Additionally, during the calamities of *Jiànyè*,
I barely escaped the scholar's grindstone;
during the disasters of *Jiānglíng*,
I nearly followed the gentry to the grave.
As for the tattered volumes and fallen slips,
they have all entered the dust;
red scrolls and blue boxes
have mostly turned to ashes.
In recent years, my illnesses have lingered,
my time is spent merely breathing,
the shadows of the mulberry and elm press upon me,
and like the reed and willow, I am withering.
I cannot help but feel the sadness of the autumn air,
and truly have the regret of reaching the end of the road.
Therefore, my spirit is dazed and confused,
much like *Sòng Yù*;
my words are hesitant and stuttering,
even more than *Yáng Xióng*.
From a single chant or poem,
its quality can be known.
Those who love curiosities do not seek me out,
and those who understand music do not employ me.
Lacking the ambition of *Bān Chāo*,
I have already cast aside my brush;
not yet seeing the writings of *Lù Jī*,
I have long since burned my inkstone.
As for what remained after the fading away,
the remnants of the fragmented pieces
have also been mixed in to patch robes
or used at times to cover sauce jars.
Your Sacred Mercy took pity
and thus deigned to record and preserve them.
I only now realize that the praise is excessive,
a gentleman's error in words;
the comparisons are so wide-ranging
that a petty man is bewildered.
Using the jade of *Jīng* to pelt a magpie,
I only fear the light use of a heavy treasure;
using the *Lóngyuān* sword to carve jade,
does it not waste your divine thoughts in vain?
When *Jiàng Shí* looks back,
rotten wood is transformed into carved beams;
with one word from *Sūn Yáng*,
a galloping hoof is recognized as a fine steed.
Thus I know that receiving praise through others
is more valuable than a city-linking jade;
borrowing others' feathers and fur
is more honorable than a foot of jade.
The *Míng Chí* is ninety thousand *lǐ*,
yet none exceeds the depth of this favor;
Mount *Huá* is five thousand *rèn*,
yet I am ultimately ashamed of the weight of this kindness.
On this day at the Jīnmén,
the spring ashes have not yet stirred;
the light thunder at the stone walls
still hides in winter hibernation.
I humbly pray that your Sagely Person
may find ease and health in accordance with the season.
The precious pheasants of Nányáng
are fortunately sufficient for viewing;
the chrysanthemum springs of Lì Xiàn
can somewhat extend one’s life.
I humbly look forward to the expected date of reaching Yè
and the day of following to Liáng.
Like the alliance meeting of the Son of Qǐ,
I must desire to behold your style and presence;
coming to court together with the Marquis of Xuē,
I shall respectfully welcome your carriage and canopy.
A silk letter like the fish-gut,
a few lines on phoenix-foot paper,
I write these words of thanks,
knowing they are ultimately insufficient.
Respectfully submitted.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 656.
<Letter in Reply to the Prince of Zhào>
I submit:
I respectfully acknowledge your command throughout all of Hán,
and your continuous camps in the Shàng Dì.
Setting up formations at Miǎnchí,
you relieved the siege of Dèng Yǔ;
opening the pass at Hángǔ,
you cast away the seal of Wáng Yuán.
Bee flags rise in the morning,
and night-watch bells sound at night,
greatly emboldening the hearts of brave men,
and sufficient to stir the ambition of heroic deeds.
Moreover, when a person of talent is betrothed,
she again finds a worthy husband.
Beyond the frontier, there is the "City of the Lady";
within the army, there is the "spirit of women."
The green flags of the Commandant
are the colors of spring in an instant;
the great tree of the General
has once again blossomed.
Cloud vapors float over the ramparts;
shooting stars drift past the pillows.
Slender dances and long songs,
horizontal pipes and vertical flutes.
At this very time,
above the blue clouds.
Truly, I am unlearned and without skill,
my lot is to be submerged in mud.
Suddenly I encountered the work of Heaven,
which sought out and promoted the lowly.
Now I have finally been appointed to the Censorate,
participating in the inscribed vessels.
The penal codes of the New Year
should already be hung as law;
the wooden clappers of early spring
are about to signal the people.
But the hair of my years is already autumnal,
and my spiritual nature has long been exhausted.
The Fine Stone and the Lung Stone,
I have no way to measure;
at the tip of my tongue and the tip of my brush,
I only know confusion and congestion.
One month of separation
has thus crossed into two years.
Tilting my head to gaze eastward,
mountains and rivers stretch a thousand *lǐ*.
The dust of the world has not settled,
and frost and dew moisten my clothes.
I humbly pray that you treasure yourself
and regard your person as a jewel.
Respectfully submitted.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 665.
<Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Showing New Poems>
I submit:
Zhèng Ruì arrived,
presenting several pages of your handwritten teachings,
along with the new poems shown.
The "eight styles and six scripts"
are enough to startle the brush;
the "four beginnings and six principles"
truly move the spiritual nature.
The words are lofty and distinctive,
the meaning is airy and far-reaching.
The writing differs from water yet gushes like a spring;
the brush is not autumn yet hangs like dew.
If stored in mountain crags,
it could cause clouds and mists to rise thick;
if cast into river banks,
dragons would surely coil around the boat.
Early summer is clear and mild,
and your Sagely Person is joyful and at ease.
With lapis lazuli and red pipes,
the magpies look back and the phoenixes return;
gracefully winding with dark green,
apes are startled and geese fall.
From a lower position, I tilt my head toward you,
counting the days as years.
The Attendant of Jiànwéi
truly has a sincere wish;
the Registrar of Bìjī
has no way to fulfill his heart.
My brush-gate is lonely,
my orchid path is overgrown.
To drive my carriage to Liáng,
the day has not yet been divined;
to send a rider to Yè,
I hope you will deign to go out of your way.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 856.
<Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing Silk, Cloth, etc.>
I submit:
Zhèng Ruì arrived,
and I received the gift of ten pieces of silk, cloth, and damask.
Wáng Bāo arrived,
and I further received the promise of a gift of money.
Grace beyond expectations
truly corresponds to a great bounty;
an extraordinary gift
thus overflows my life.
Pulling the silk and observing it,
I need not labor in the expectation of white horses;
the flowing springs of coins about to be entrusted,
I wait to see the flight of green mallards.
Digging lotuses in Yáng Shì's pond,
moving trees in Lǐ's garden,
I already rejoice in the profit of the grain,
and even more think of the green wood.
Bestowing grain in Chénliú,
I feel ashamed of such deep kindness;
raining gold in Lìyáng,
I am conversely humbled by such specific favor.
Having been a guest at the Língtái for long,
from now on I can cook many times;
the Shǔ Gǔ has long been cold,
but now it is warmer.
Following the fields of Yúnmèng,
could not exceed this joy;
obtaining the sword of Fēngchéng,
could not equal this happiness.
Respectfully submitted.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 655.
<Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing Silk and Cloth>
I submit:
I have received your command and the gift of thirty pieces of miscellaneous colored silk and cloth.
Last winter was frozen and closed,
and this spring is harsh and severe.
Sleet is like fields of jasper,
and ice is like the salt shores.
The walls of Zhāng Chāo
were not enough to block the wind;
the gate of Yuán Ān
had no one to clear the snow.
Covering myself with bird feathers brought no warmth;
burning animal charcoal only made it colder.
From afar your Sagely Compassion descended,
and you deigned to show pity and relief.
Speaking of the silkworm months,
the mulberry carts were almost exhausted;
truly holding the shuttle,
the weaving rooms were nearly empty.
It thus causes one to count coins at the new market,
suddenly suspecting the sale of colorful silks;
on a moonlit night in Pínglíng,
one is startled to hear the pounding of clothes.
When a concubine encounters new fine silk,
she naturally submits in heart;
when a wife hears the tearing of silk,
she should then wear a smile.
In the carriage ruts of Zhuāng Zhōu,
there was indeed a parched fish;
before the whip of the Lord of Xìnlíng,
I was originally not a bird in distress.
I have humbly received your relief,
and I prostrate myself in gratitude for your deep compassion.
Respectfully submitted.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 655.
<Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing Silk and Cloth>
I state:
My son Gǒu Niáng,
yesterday received the favor of an introduction,
and was specially bestowed five pieces of silk and cloth.
A captive from the south has obtained pardon,
and is already included in the ritual invitations;
my young child is now old enough to wear clothes,
and has also been granted an audience.
Like the weaving of the bridge at Guān Yǐn,
or the double-threaded silk of the land of Yè;
the loom of colorful patterns from Fú fēng,
or the single cocoon from the Immortal Garden.
It is fitting to wear the blue collar,
as the scholar does not neglect the poems of learning;
since the spring clothes are finished,
the youth may join the dance at the Yú and Yí rivers.
Furthermore, like a perching crow clutching its chick,
we together know the grace of the cassia tree;
like a marsh pheasant leading its young,
we together rejoice in the command of the traveling spring.
Once the roots and trunk are moistened,
the branches and leaves all flourish.
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing White Gauze Robes and Trousers〉
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing White Gauze Robes and Trousers〉
I state:
You have condescended to bestow a set of white gauze robes and trousers.
Chéng Jù submitted a memorial,
fruitlessly discussing pheasant heads;
Wáng Gōng walked into the snow,
vainly praised for his crane-feather cloak.
Never before has there been such a loom with skillful heddles,
changing the treadles to produce wondrous patterns:
phenixes do not depart but constantly fly,
flowers, though cold, do not fall.
Donning this thousand-gold warmth for a moment,
I discard the long-lasting cold of a hundred patches,
forever without the sighs of the yellow creeper,
now seeing the importance of the blue silk.
Facing the accumulated snow of Tiān Shān,
I can still open my lapel;
braving the long winds of Guǎng Lè,
I would still wipe away sweat.
For the white turtle to repay its master,
there is ultimately no set time;
for the yellow sparrow to return the favor,
on what day will it finally be?
○ *Yì wén lèi jù*, Scroll 85.
*Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Téng for Bestowing a Kerchief〉
I state:
I have received your command,
bestowing one fawn-patterned kerchief.
Like a new embryo shedding its horns,
or the first pregnancy within the vines.
Falling stars reflect each other,
connecting pearls in sparse dots.
The Coiled Dragon knife has already cut it,
and the long-life threads are still being sewn.
The kingfisher feathers are set aside,
and the lotus flowers yield their high place.
A wandering recluse like this
can well laugh at drum skins;
entering those spring woods,
I shall boast of my bamboo-shoot sheath.
My disheveled hair is loose and fluttering,
my withered face is aged and decaying;
having not washed for three autumns,
I truly carry this current favor;
donning a cap once in ten years,
I rejoice all the more in this gift.
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Emperor Míng for Silk and Cloth〉
〈Letter of Thanks to the Emperor Míng for Silk and Cloth〉
Your servant states:
I have received an edict bestowing thirty pieces of various-colored silk, cloth, cotton, and fine silk, along with two hundred silver coins.
In recent years, I
have had great lack and deficiency.
Within Bái Shè,
I brush aside grass to see ice;
inside Líng Tái,
I blow away dust to look at the steaming pot.
Resented by my wife and hated by my concubine,
I am both sighed over and loathed;
my emaciated sons and weak grandsons
offer empty respect but harbor real resentment.
The royal messenger suddenly arrived,
and the great gift first descended.
If the Heavenly Emperor granted more years,
it could not exceed this joy;
if an immortal youth gifted medicine,
it would not equal this happiness.
Stretching my sleeves to dance,
the black cranes are about to come;
tapping the rhythm to sing,
the passing clouds are almost severed.
It is what is called: when a boat has no shore,
Hǎi Ruò reverses the wind for it;
when the shepherd's purse and wheat are about to wither,
the mountain spirits bring forth rain for them.
Furthermore, completely drawn from white cocoons,
like a snowy slope seemingly tilting;
together falling like green ducks,
as if a mountain of silver were moving.
Thus I know the Daoist of the Qīng niú
can further extend a life about to end;
the Perfected One of the Bái lù
can bring life back to dried-up bones.
Even if one could pull up mountains or leap across seas,
one's strength could not surpass this debt of gratitude;
even with "hanging dew" and "suspended needle" calligraphy styles,
I could not write of your grace to the end.
Like the sparrow of Péng lái returning thanks
with four white jade rings;
or the snake of the Hàn River repaying virtue
with a one-inch luminous pearl.
Looking upon this,
how could I not feel ashamed in my heart?
It is simply that living things receive their life,
and do not thank Heaven.
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing a Rhinoceros-Horn Belt and Other Items〉
I state:
I have received your command,
bestowing a rhinoceros-adorned belt and ten strings of coins.
The precious belt of the Lord of Wèi
was specially given to Liú Zhēn;
the state taxes of the Prince of Zhào
particularly supported Péi Kǎi.
The strings of coins hide patterned horses,
like the smelting of silver from Ān xī;
the belt is inlaid with communicating rhino,
as if hunting the beasts of Yún nán.
The long-standing poverty of Běi guō sāo
is what I have been content with;
carrying treasures like Nán gōng jìng
was truly beyond my expectations.
When flowers bloom with Fourfold Brilliance,
I see only their glory;
when the giant turtle bears the three mountains,
I deeply know their weight.
Formerly, when Shěn Xī was near the end,
he met the Arbiter of Fate and returned to life;
when Shì Xiè was about to be buried,
he encountered an immortal and lived again.
Today's compassionate pity
is exactly what this means!
The horse gallops ahead to lead the way,
perhaps as if recognizing grace;
the cock crows before dawn to open the pass,
likely able to repay its master.
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing Rice〉
I state:
I have received your command, bestowing ten dàn of rice.
The cinnabar crow carries an ear of grain,
already gathered in Xī Zhōu;
the yellow sparrows follow the carriage,
returning to fly to the Dōng Shì.
Soaking them to be seeds,
they are not without the essence of frost and snow;
taking them to discuss military strategy,
they immediately take on the form of mountains and rivers.
In my humble alley with but a single gourd,
combed by the wind and bathed by the rain,
I peeled elm bark at the autumn frontier,
and dug up hibernating swallows in the cold mountains.
Relying on the expenditure of state taxes,
I finally open my dusty steaming pot;
it is not a cinnabar furnace flowing with pearls,
but it is different from the Jīng Tái where jade was cooked.
Dōng fāng Shuò's holding of the rice
has already ceased his long hunger;
Xī mén Bào's reclamation of fields
is now put to shame by this gift.
○ *Yì wén lèi jù*, Scroll 72.
*Wén yuàn yīng huá*, Scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to the Prince of Zhào for Bestowing Dried Fish〉
I state:
I have received your gift of ten dried fish.
In the morning they float on the waters of Lǐshuǐ,
their brilliance resembling red tortoises;
at night they encounter the Wényáo fish,
their wings like those of the green phoenix (Qīngluán).
Moreover, like the fresh crucian carp of Dòngtíng
or the fine carp of Wēnhú,
the waves turn to rain
and their scales protect against the cold.
I am originally a man of Wú,
and often think of the flavors of the rivers and lakes;
when hungry,
I relied only on the leftovers of goosefoot and pulse.
Your compassionate gift is a bountiful grace;
fat and richness flow into the stove.
There is no need for the Pavilion of the Lion;
this surpasses the Chief of Léichí.
It would even surprise the God of the River (Hébó),
who alone does not receive such gifts from men.
It is enough to laugh at Rèn Gōng,
who spent the whole year fishing.
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to Téng Wáng for the Gift of a Horse〉
I state:
I have received your instruction bestowing one black-and-white horse (Wūliú).
Though the Liǔgǔ valley has not yet opened,
I have unexpectedly encountered a purple swallow (Zǐyàn);
though the Língyuán spring is still far away,
I suddenly see peach blossoms.
Its speed competes with flowing lightning;
its shadow connects with the floating clouds.
In the leisure time when Zhāng Chǎng paints eyebrows,
he gallops straight to Zhāngtái;
in the joy of Wáng Jì drinking wine,
he drives long through the Golden Track (Jīnliè).
Respectfully stated.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 93.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to Téng Wáng for the Gift of a Pig〉
I state:
I have received your instruction bestowing one carcass of a fat pig.
White-headed ones are seen as treasures
when crossing the waters of Liáodōng;
red railings are held in high regard
when facing the city of Xiāngyáng.
Suddenly, full grace has descended,
to be used for roasting and searing.
Sūn Hóng herded them by the Zīshuǐ,
only to seek money;
Bǔ Shì raised them in Shànglín,
but how could he know their flavor?
Respectfully stated.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to Zhào Wáng for the Gift of a Horse and an Umbrella〉
I state:
I have received your instruction bestowing a purple-and-black horse (Zǐliú),
along with silver-studded riding equipment and one purple silk umbrella.
From high heaven falls the rain,
especially bestowing deep favor;
like the Ruòshuǐ flowing with light,
I particularly receive your private illumination.
Returning with this emerald canopy,
the matter is as heavy as the grace shown to Liú Jī;
bestowing this black steed,
the honor is as deep as the gift given to Lǐ Zhōng.
The crimson curtain of the northern regions
must now be rolled up high;
the bamboo horse of Xīhé
is already being welcomed in the outskirts.
As for the lightness of my life,
it is like a swan feather floating on the Weak Water (Ruòshuǐ);
knowing the weight of your grace,
it is like a tortoise back carrying the Spiritual Mountain (Língshān).
Furthermore, like a startled swan leaving the water,
one only sees it lingering;
like a yellow crane leaving the pass,
it only knows to look back.
The heart of longing and attachment
is just like this.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 655.
〈Letter of Thanks to Zhào Wáng for the Gift of Pheasants〉
The summer pheasants (Xiàzhái) fly in autumn;
the river pheasants (Jiānghuī) are in the spring mountain stream.
The guest of Zhōngmóu Xiàn
is thus able to sit and observe;
the wife of Grandee Jiǎ (Jiǎ Dàfū)
should already be smiling.
Raising expenses from the central kitchen
to provide for an inferior guest.
Mountains and rivers make the road long,
but my appetite knows your grace.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, scroll 90.
〈Forty-four Stanzas in Imitation of Liánzhū〉
I have heard that talent which weaves heaven and earth,
and strength which pulls up mountains and surpasses oceans,
with bravery in battle like wind and gale,
and strategies emerging from the mind,
can cut the scales of the long whale
and sever the wings of the flying tiger.
Therefore, with one anger the feudal lords are afraid,
and when they dwell in peace, the world is at rest.
I have heard that Xiāo and Cáo assisted the government,
providing the heroic strategy;
Lǔ and Wèi served as the vanguard,
providing the majestic air.
Therefore, at the meeting of Huángchí,
one could contend for leadership among the feudal lords;
at the covenant of Hónggōu,
one could divide the world in half.
I have heard that to untie the knot of the great pig
and block the source of the long snake,
one must prepare garments for a thousand li
and smear blood at the gate of the camp.
Therefore, to break a siege of a hundred li,
one uses a single strategy of Chén Píng;
to form a covenant for a country of a thousand chariots,
one requires a single word from Jì Lù.
I have heard that when the worthy are present,
there is no need to brandish a blade;
if the ministers are excellent,
there is no need to mention responding to changes.
Therefore, with Qū Ní as a chariot attendant,
the feudal lords lifted the siege of Fāngchéng;
with Gàn Mù as a minister,
the world had no battles at Xīhé.
I have heard that when Hándān was already in danger,
they vainly thought of the Lord of Mǎfú;
when the city of Jì was gone,
they uselessly employed Jīng Kē.
Therefore, a bamboo staff supporting the endangered
cannot straighten the stone of Wǔdān;
reed ashes to shrink water
cannot save the river at Xuánfáng.
I have heard that when ants in a hole rush at a spring,
they do not know far-reaching worries;
when mysterious birds nest in a curtain,
how can they endure for long?
Therefore, when a great mansion is already burning,
it cannot be sprinkled with tears;
once a long river bursts its banks,
it cannot be blocked with a hand.
I have heard of glib tongues chattering,
and the marketplace bustling with activity,
some using reed-like eloquence to promote themselves,
some using trickery and deceit to overthrow others.
Therefore, when Zǐgòng was sent as an envoy,
the five capitals fell into chaos;
when Zhāng Yí was employed,
the six states were joined and separated.
I have heard that strategies and plans must be practiced,
and adaptability must be long-lasting,
sometimes increasing the stoves of Qí,
or lying by the walls of Yān.
Therefore, the soldiers at Jǐngxíng
were like swan feathers meeting fire;
the troops at Chángpíng
were like autumn grass in the midst of frost.
I have heard that when those broomcorn millets grew thick,
the grandee felt the grief of loss and disorder;
when the wheat ears grew tall,
the gentleman felt the sorrow of leaving his country.
Therefore, when the Jiànzhāng Palace rose and fell,
one could no longer gaze at the banks of the Bà River;
when the Déyáng Hall was submerged,
one could no longer visit Yǎnshī.
I have heard that marketplaces and courts change and shift,
and mountains and rivers are distant.
Therefore, where foxes and rabbits dwell
was originally the Jiànshǐ Palace;
where thorns and brambles reach the sky
was formerly the Chángzhōu Garden.
