I have heard that Heaven is sending down plagues,
and loss and disorder are widespread,
vainly thinking of discussing swords,
uselessly hearing of pillowing on weapons.
Therefore, with the heroic strategy of Liú Kūn,
he did not know how to save himself;
with the high spirits of Zǔ Tì,
he was barely able to cross the river.
I have heard that Gǔlín is long and far,
and Cāngwú does not follow,
there are only paulownia and kudzu,
there are no trees and no burial mounds.
Therefore, the pearls of Suí like the sun and moon
were of no benefit against the fires of Líshān;
the strings and pipes of the Sparrow Tower (Quètái)
vainly look toward the pines of Xīlíng.
It is heard that thunder startles beasts and
lightning drives the wind;
they cross through mountain passes and fortresses,
and span across rivers and lakes.
Thus, city shapes are like the waning moon,
and the aura of battle formations spreads like clouds;
these are either scattered soldiers from *Lǜlín*,
or rebels from *Líshān*.
It is heard that there is the parting of death at the *Chángchéng*,
and the parting of life at *Hángǔ*;
the sorrow of the widow in *Liáodōng*,
and the weeping of the bereaved wife in *Dàijùn*.
Thus, moved by flowing grief,
the walls of *Qǐ Liáng* collapsed;
dampened by shed tears,
the bamboo of *Xiānglíng* finally changed.
It is heard that if three generations take up arms,
it is not a legacy to bequeath;
if secret schemes span generations,
they must end in disaster.
Thus, amidst the wind and frost of Commandant *Lǐ*,
arrows were exhausted on Mount *Lán*;
with the high spirits of *Lù Píngyuán*,
the path ended at the *Hé* Bridge.
It is heard that the souls in camp do not return,
and phosphorescent fires fly at night;
sometimes they encounter soldiers hunting in the night,
or ghosts perishing in empty pavilions.
Thus, in the wind and rain of the *Shèshēng* Camp,
there are often wronged souls;
in the dark cold of *Guǎnghàn* Commandery,
there is much nocturnal weeping.
It is heard that at the borders of war-horses in *Jiāng* and *Huáng*,
and the violent winds of *Yān* and *Yǐng*,
some depart and never return,
or become distant travelers with no set date.
Thus, below *Zhānghuá*,
there must be a Terrace for Thinking of One's Son;
beside *Yúnmèng*,
there should be many Rocks of the Longing Wife.
It is heard that one does not resent the parting of life,
though affection is severed midway;
in vain one thinks of the lotus emerging from water,
no longer seeing the snow in the whirling wind.
Thus, facing wine in the tower,
*Lǜzhū* departs;
singing sadly within the tent,
*Yú Jī* bids eternal farewell.
It is heard that the appointment of a shepherd of the people
hangs the lives of the commoners upon him;
when he grows weary of the world and passes,
it again overturns the hearts of all under heaven.
Thus, when a single horse bolts,
not a single hair remains still;
when a single boat capsizes,
not a single thing does not sink.
It is heard that when the severe frost falls,
there is nothing that is not solemnized;
when the great forest perishes,
there is nothing that does not wither.
Thus, when the moats of *Chǔ* are filled,
the wandering fish have no sanctuary;
when the palaces of *Wú* have burned,
where can the returning swallows nest?
It is heard that those whose names were as high as the Eight Talents (*Bā Jùn*)
were harmed by the faction of eunuchs;
those whose wisdom encompassed the Three Heroes (*Sān Jié*)
perished by the schemes of women.
Thus, a dragon of the *Hóngzé* marsh
may be thwarted by a long-starved tiger;
an ant of *Pínggāo*
can overcome a dragon out of water.
It is heard that the vessels of *Wú* and the boats of *Shǔ*
cannot float without water;
with a bow decorated in red and green,
one cannot shoot without a string.
Thus, for a crane in a cage or a pen,
how could there be a time for its six primary feathers to soar?
For a horse that is stubborn and unyielding,
it no longer possesses the value of a thousand gold pieces.
It is heard that when the spirit is bent and broken,
suppressed and unable to rise,
it may suddenly be moved by the heartless,
or be saddened by those of a different kind.
Thus, the waters of lamentation and resentment
especially form springs of indignation;
the clouds of sorrow and grief
particularly contain an air of melancholy.
It is heard that migrating to *Báiyǔ*
or being exiled to *Fánglíng*,
leaving home and splitting from one's village,
one beats their breast in bitter regret.
Thus, when *Wú Qǐ* left *Xīhé*,
he shed tears in streams;
when *Jīng Kē* bid farewell at the *Yàn* market,
his grief was unbearable.
It is heard that at the guest house of General *Lián*,
and the high gate of Commandant *Zhái*,
fullness and emptiness change in an instant;
how can nobility and lowliness be discussed?
Thus, of his lifelong old friends,
*Guàn Fū* did not leave;
of the guests at his gate,
*Rèn Ān* alone remained.
It is heard that one may hold the jade tablet to serve *Chǔ*,
or remain in *Qín* as a court academician;
like the traveler in *Jìnyáng* longing to return,
or the official in *Línzī* living as a sojourner.
Thus, when friends and relatives gather,
it does not prevent the heart from feeling sorrow;
though mountains and rivers separate them,
it does not stop the wind and moon from affecting a person.
It is heard that at the age of fifty,
heroic passions have long since ceased;
worry can harm a person,
hence the lamentation.
Thus, it is like the *jiāoràng* tree,
which is truly half-dead yet spoken of as living;
like the *wútóng* tree,
though it has a remnant of life, it is as if dead.
It is heard that the atmosphere of autumn
brings disappointment and self-pity;
*Gěng Gōng*'s sorrow at *Shūlè*,
and *Bān Chāo*'s thoughts of *Jiǔquán*.
Thus, when *Hán Fēi* stayed in *Qín*,
there was no way to avoid slander;
while *Xìnlíng* was in *Zhào*,
he longed to return for many years.
It is heard that one with a hundred patches on his rags
knows his fate and does not worry;
even cooking once in ten days,
what shame is there at any time?
Thus, the legacy of the *Sùwáng*
lay with the poor man of the *Dōngmén*;
the lords of *Gūzhú*
were in truth the starving scholars of the *Xīshān*.
It is heard that to have no learning in one's heart
is like having no money in one's hand;
as for today's learning,
I have yet to see it produce the virtuous.
Thus, *Gāo Fèng* of *Fúfēng*
abandoned his wheat for no reason;
*Nìng Yuè* of *Zhōngmóu*
toiled in vain without sleep.
It is heard that in a town of ten households,
loyalty and trustworthiness must exist;
within five paces,
fragrance may be found.
Thus, a dried clam from *Rìnán*
still contains a pearl of the bright moon;
a dead tree from *Lóngmén*
still holds the melody of the *Xiánchí*.
It is heard that a height of a hundred feet
is built upon nine layers of chess pieces;
a weight of a thousand *jūn*
is suspended from a single wooden branch.
Thus, stepping on a tiger's tail is not necessarily perilous,
and hurting a dragon's scale is not yet a crisis.
It is heard that dwelling among orchids or dried fish
depends on what one is accustomed to;
white feathers or plain silk
follow whatever dye they are dipped in.
Thus, though the nature of metal is pure,
it becomes auspicious or calamitous when made into a sword;
though the virtue of water is level,
it becomes dangerous when passed by wind.
It is heard that a *yùzhāng* tree after seven years
may perish among the lush grass;
fragrant orchids across nine fields
may be lost in a deep valley.
Thus, if one seeks the truth,
there is the self-buried mugwort of *Jìnyáng*;
if one appreciates the sound,
there is the withered bamboo of the *Wú* pavilion.
It is heard that using a bright mirror to steam food
is not its proper use;
using the *Gānjiàng* sword to mend shoes
is especially lamentable.
Thus, one whose spirit is enough to reach the clouds
should not stop at being a mere cavalryman;
one whose talent is fit for a royal advisor
should not be simply exiled to *Chángshā*.
It is heard that where power converges
and where authority is borrowed,
one can certainly tie the wind and catch shadows,
or wrestle tigers and cross rivers by foot.
Thus, when light, a swan's feather will sink in water;
when heavy, a massive rock will glide over the waves.
I have heard that spirit is difficult to suppress,
and does not rely on lifting tripods;
presence is naturally brave,
and does not wait for the lifting of gate bars.
Therefore, when Cáo Guì ascended the altar,
the lands of Wènyáng were suddenly returned;
when Xiàngrú glared at the pillar,
the jade disk worth several cities was returned once more.
I have heard that the Juǎnshī plant does not die,
for who must possess a heart?
The sweet plantain grows of its own accord,
thus we know it has no nodes.
Therefore, if spiral shells and mussels find a path,
I fear it is different from the abyss of the black dragon;
if sparrows and rats share the same destination,
it must surely not be the Cinnabar Cave.
I have heard that the height of Běimáng
cannot be leveled by the Lords of Wèi;
the clash between the Gǔ and Luò rivers
cannot be altered by the Kings of Zhōu.
Therefore, what virtue did Yúgōng possess
that he could shoulder a shovel and move mountains?
What kind of bird was Jīngwèi
that she wished to carry stones in her beak to fill the sea?
I have heard that if a gentleman lacks the Way,
then he cannot possess wealth;
if he forgets his poverty,
then he cannot feel shame for his food.
Therefore, Yán Huí drinking from a gourd
was more worthy than the jade cup of Qìng Fēng;
Zǐsī’s silver pendant
was more beautiful than the Chuíjí jade of the Duke of Yú.
I have heard that when water is churned,
its source actually becomes turbid;
when a tree is infested with worms,
its roots will eventually be pulled up.
Therefore, the family of Yánnián
discussed sweeping the graves in advance;
the clan of Yángshé
knew beforehand of their family's destruction.
I have heard of sharpening the lips and mouth,
and greasing the teeth and jaws;
fanning poison into the wind,
and blowing sand at shadows.
Therefore, respect them but keep them at a distance;
the jackal has five cubs;
alas, it is fearsome indeed;
the ghost has a whole cartload.
I have heard that an empty boat causes no resentment,
and excellent virtue has no worries;
loyalty and trustworthiness serve as the zither and lute,
while benevolence and righteousness serve as the kitchen.
Therefore, if one follows Zhuāng Shēng,
then all things naturally become minute;
if one returns to Lǎo Shì,
then all that exists becomes nothingness.
I have heard of pausing one's steps at the Three Passes,
and drooping one's wings at the Great Wall;
being both a captive and a traveler,
possessing neither talent nor wisdom.
Therefore, mooring the oars at Wūjiāng,
one knows there is no road by which to return;
when the white goose clutches a letter,
it is certain there is no home to which it can be delivered.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 771.
<Letter Written on Behalf of the Heir Apparent of the Marquis of Shànghuáng to His Wife>
<Letter Written on Behalf of the Heir Apparent of the Marquis of Shànghuáng to His Wife>
In the past, when immortals practiced breath-guiding,
they still carved out three autumns;
when the Goddess prepared to comb her hair,
she still set a date in nine days.
Whenever a dragon flies from its sword-box,
or a crane departs from its zither-terrace,
there is none who does not harbor resentment and feel sorrow in their heart,
or shed tears upon hearing the cry of the gibbon.
Since I am not in Xīnshì,
where shall I find my home?
Separated from Hándān,
how could I know the way?
I imagine you looking at your reflection in the mirror,
surely not containing tears;
holding a flower outside the railing,
you must be smiling along with it.
Sharing the cup within the curtains,
and moving the fan aside before the bed;
if you do not think of these things as of old,
when will you ever remember them?
You should learn from the God of the Sea,
coming and going by following the tide and wind;
do not be like the Weaving Maiden,
waiting for the river to be filled before meeting.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, Scroll 32.
<Preface to the Collected Works of the Duke of Zhàoguó>
I have heard that when stones were struck at Píngyáng,
the mountains and valleys harmonized with them;
when Great Yǔ played the bamboo flute,
the wind and clouds were moved by it.
Compared with expressing one's spiritual nature
and modulating the tone of one's words,
where the melody changes into "Yángchūn",
and the radiance turns back the bright sun—
how could they be mentioned in the same breath?
When the Pillar of State, the Duke of Zhàoguó, speaks to form an argument,
his brush creates a masterpiece;
elegant postures overflow,
and fresh sentiments are stirred up;
wind and clouds vie to fly,
and fish and dragons each undergo transformations.
Comparing his works to jade sceptres and disks,
they are as numerous as those at the assembly of Mount Tú;
likening them to clouds and mist,
they are like the thousand-fathom cliffs of Chìchéng.
His writings correlate with the celestial phenomena,
entering the *Records of the Celestial Offices*;
his rhythms involve the strings and paulownia wood,
all returning to the Observation of the Zǒngzhāng.
Discussing their grandeur,
it is like a Péng bird rising to the middle of the sky;
speaking of their delicacy,
it is like a wren nesting on a mosquito's eyelash.
Not only do they rise brightly like the morning sun,
with the Layered City embracing the light of the sun and moon;
but they also fly flaming through the night,
with the Southern Dipper touching the aura of the flood-dragons!
In the past, Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù
began with the depths of lamentation and resentment;
Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng
lived in an age of parting and separation.
Since the end of the Jiàn'ān era of Wèi and the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
the fine literary craftsmanship
has seen its style change three times.
Everyone claims to hold the pearl of the spirit-serpent
and to embrace the jade of Mount Jīng.
The Duke weighs the *Yǎ* and *Sòng*,
and harmonizes the pitch-pipes.
If his words were at odds with the musical rhythm,
then the Terrace of Songs would not look upon them;
if his sounds were limited to mere practice melodies,
then the Imperial Academy would find nothing to take from them.
Thus he has become a pillar of the literary garden
and a crown of the forest of lyrics;
the *Dàyǎ* supports his wheels,
and the Xiǎoshān support his canopy.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, Scroll 55.
*Chūxué Jì*, Scroll 21.
<Biography of Qiūnǎidūn Chóng, Grand General with Imperial Scepter and Founding Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery of Zhōu>
<Biography of Qiūnǎidūn Chóng, Grand General with Imperial Scepter and Founding Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery of Zhōu>
Chóng,
was a native of Xiàoràng Village, Guǎngyì Township, Gǔchéng County, Dài Commandery, Héngzhōu.
Long ago, when the state was established at Shòuqiū,
twelve people were granted surnames;
when the worthy were raised at Píngyáng,
sixteen clans entered the court.
How much more so when the great lightning circled the pivot
and the shooting star entered the Pleiades—
the branches branched out and the sources diverged,
and their descendants rose in succession?
Emperor Dàowǔ of Wèi, with his world-commanding heroic plans,
watered his horses at the Hé and Luò rivers;
of ten brothers,
they were divided into ten surnames.
Distinguishing the winds and blowing the pitch-pipes,
the Qiū clan was indeed one of them.
His ancestor of five generations prior was Miǎo,
General of Agile Cavalry, Opener of Office with the same Three Dignities, and Founding Duke of Yíngqiū Commandery.
At that time, when the Way of Heaven was in the northwest,
he already received strategic plans;
when the horses' heads turned southeast,
he truly provided assistance and support.
He was granted a surname based on his enfeoffment name,
and thus it became his conferred surname.
With Nángōng Bó,
he shares a common lineage.
As for the clan being Yuèzhèng,
it was not without a standard.
His great-grandfather was Shuāngguǐ,
Grand General with Imperial Scepter, Minister over the Masses, Governor of Qīng and Yǎn Provinces, and Duke Wénzhāo of Fànyáng.
At the beginning of the reign at Luòyáng,
he mounted his horse to govern the state;
at the start of his official appointment,
he ascended to the scholar-trees to discuss the Way.
In life, he held the highest seat in the Martial Palace;
in death, his tablet was enshrined in the Clear Chamber.
His wife was of the Wáng clan of Tàiyuán;
for three generations they were generals,
and for four generations they were dukes;
they were a great clan of the state,
a noble family of the bell and tripod.
When she was wed to him,
it was a match like that of Qín and Jìn.
Zǔ Tí,
Commissioner with Ritual Staff, General of the Guard, Commandant-Fùmǎ, Governor of Hé and Jiāo Provinces, and Founding Duke of Língshòu County.
His sons and grandsons
possessed distinguished reputations;
adding luster and glory,
they entered the court in their youth.
His wife, the Grand Princess of Qīnglián Commandery,
was the second daughter of Emperor Xiàowén.
When the royal lady was married,
she did not rely on her carriages and finery;
thus she obtained a great general like Wèi Qīng
and a worthy husband like Zhāng Ěr.
His father, Yuàn,
was Commissioner with Ritual Staff, Grand Commander of Military Affairs for Xú Province, Governor of Xú Province, and Founding Duke of Píngyáng County,
with a fief of four thousand households.
In his youth he studied military tactics,
and saw many books on war.
Camps formed by pouring sand and piling stones,
and battle arrays that pushed back the sun and spanned the clouds;
drawing his bow, his arrow split the small branch of a halberd,
and drawing his sword, spring water flew from a dry well.
His wife, Lady Yǔwén,
was the third younger sister of Emperor Wén of Zhōu.
A model of motherly conduct and a fine example,
a virtuous and wise teacher for women,
her virtue surpassed that of the Princess of Lónglǜ,
and her righteousness was as significant as the Princess of Héyáng.
As Wèi reached its end
and Zhōu renewed its mandate,
the tombs were ceremonially built and mounds were raised
to posthumously honor his great virtue;
he was then posthumously granted the titles of Commissioner with Ritual Staff, Great General, and Founding Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery,
with a fief of one thousand households.
His wife was posthumously named Grand Princess of Āndé Commandery.
For wandering souls and pent-up grievances,
there is no lack of the city of Guǎnghàn;
for a long-time guest longing for home,
there are only the trees of Dōngpíng.
Since the Yǒng'ān era,
the House of Wèi suffered great decay.
The sea waters surged everywhere,
and the celestial stars moved in disorder.
Rituals, music, and military expeditions
did not originate from the sovereign;
promoting the worthy and punishing the violent
were debated among powerful ministers.
Grand Chancellor Gāo drove the winds and clouds
and overran Qí and Jìn;
our maternal uncle, Emperor Wén,
commanded dragons and tigers
and occupied Zhōu and Qín.
South and North broke their treaties,
while East and West were hostile enemies.
Thereafter, each received the mandates of Heaven
and both held the ritual jades.
Among the people, fathers were in the south and sons in the north,
while elder brothers were in the east and younger brothers in the west.
Serving a master, they worried for their kin;
seeking to live, they feared disaster.
The relatives of the Great Zhōu
all met with suffering and hardship,
being sent to hard labor
or cast into the weaving chambers.
The passes and rivers were strictly barred
for over thirty years.
Heaven grew weary of the chaos and ruin,
and people longed for a return to virtue.
The dust of war over there
has been quieted at Hángǔ;
the official carriages here
have frequently crossed the banks of the Zhāng River.
The remnants of those wronged in Zhōngshān
and those withered in Dàijùn
all encountered the news of reform
and were all honored with ritual send-offs.
The two brothers Chóng and Bīn
looked at each other’s countenances;
with loved ones withered away,
their hearts had long been in turmoil.
Like the broken wings at Mount Héng,
how could they hope to fly together?
Yet among the captives like Ānguó,
he rose to become a high minister;
like Bān Chāo in the far-off regions,
he finally returned alive.
In the fourth year of Tiānhé,
they arrived at the new capital.
Because the state was connected through maternal uncles and nephews
and the kinship of inner and outer relations,

the court then granted Bīn the titles of Commissioner with Ritual Staff, General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry, Specially Advanced with the Same Dignity as the Three Ducal Ministers, Grand Commander, and Founding Duke of Ānlè County,
with a fief of one thousand households.
Bīn escaped the tiger's mouth
and ascended the Dragon Gate;
his reputation was already high,
and his spirit reached far.
Just as he intended to discuss the national humiliation
and avenge the family grievances,
such that leaving his corpse on the plains
was his heart's desire,
time was not on his side,
and he preceded the morning dew
at the age of so many years.
The State of Wèi raised the lament for Wénzǐ;
Cháng'ān issued an edict of mourning for the burial.
Thus he was posthumously granted his original titles,
with the addition of Junior Tutor, Commander of Military Affairs for the Three Provinces of Pú, Yú, and Xùn, and Governor of Púzhōu.
On a certain day of a certain month in the sixth year of Tiānhé, he was buried at Hóngdù Plain in Cháng'ān.
His wife, Lady Shí of Qīngzhōu,
was the Lady of Chángchéng Commandery.
His heir is a lonely orphan,
and his living wife remains in a widowed room;
yet she can maintain her chastity
and uphold her righteousness.

Chóng was granted the titles of Commissioner with Ritual Staff, Grand Commander, General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry, Specially Advanced with the Same Dignity as the Three Ducal Ministers, and Founding Duke of Guǎnghuà County,
with a fief of one thousand households.
The two brothers
became great generals in the same year;
their glory reflected upon the vermilion court,
and their ceremonial halberds stood side by side.
In the past, the two Féngs shared virtue
and held office in succession;
the two Dùs shared fame
and governed commanderies across the river.
Compared to this honor and favor,
they would feel ashamed.
Suddenly Bīn fell ill,
and unexpectedly passed away.
When Chóng and his brothers were just of age,
they suffered this cruel tragedy;
born of the same spirit and raised together,
they had reached adulthood.
Now that they have returned,
they have again met with misfortune;
every time he grieves and laments,
travelers are moved to sorrow.
In nurturing the beloved child,
his affection is as deep as the kindness of Mǎ Yuán;
in respectfully serving his widowed sister-in-law,
his righteousness is like the filial piety of Yán Hán.
In the sixth year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Great General,
with other titles as before.
The Dragon Court rewarded the merit of leaving the passes;
the Jade Gate honored the grace of the returning army.
Different generations sharing the same harmony
is seen today.
In the second year of Jiàndé,
he was appointed Commissioner with Ritual Staff, Commander of Military Affairs for Yízhōu, and Governor of Yízhōu.
Within the quiet and spacious halls,
there was only the sound of reading;
behind the heavy curtains,
only reports of good governance were heard.
His purity was such that he did not even need to settle water,
and his clarity was such that he did not need to raise a candle;
it was truly a case of changing the customs upon entering the territory,
and more than just stopping the carriage to wait for rain.
There was an imperial decree to Great General, Governor of Yízhōu, and Duke of Guǎnghuà Commandery, Chóng:
"Since the summer there has been no rain
until now;
although every god has been prayed to,
no response has yet been felt.
I have learned that within your province,
you alone have received heavy rain,
which is surely due to the Great General's perfect sincerity.
You care for the people of the commandery,
and a bountiful harvest is to be expected;
this truly brings me comfort."
Another decree to Duke of Guǎnghuà, Chóng:
"I know you set your mind on the methods of governance
and work hard for the people;
entrusted with responsibilities, you have proven worthy of the post,
and my praise for you is unending.
The ancients had a saying:
'It is not the action that is difficult.'
Continue to exert yourself
to achieve perfection.
My instructions have been delivered,
and the gifts have been granted;
the items are as listed separately.
You should understand my sentiments.
Of old, the Governor of Yángpíng
was granted the special favor of red millet;
the Governor of Jīngzhōu
was uniquely given the gift of ceremonial robes.
Exceptional administrative merit—
is this not what it means?"
He esteemed purity and stillness in governance,
and integrity and clarity as the law.
The people could not bear to betray him,
and the officials could not bear to deceive him.
By nature, he did not drink wine
and had no addictions or desires.
Deep and profound as a high wall,
joy and anger did not show on his face.
His writings necessarily used correct words,
and his strings played only elegant tunes.
Benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and moderation
were where he applied his mind.
Red cases and yellow silks,
he loved and appreciated them without end.
Now, the four suburbs are filled with fortifications,
and there is still the humiliation of the high officials;
the war drums do not cease,
and the strategies of the generals are still labored.
Speaking of the enemy and the shame,
he only wishes to stride across the land of death;
thinking of repaying the state,
he does not begrudge his own body’s fat fertilizing the plains.
If only Heaven grants him years
and the fortune of a peaceful time,
the matters of loyalty and integrity
shall surely be achieved by his lordship.
Briefly writing the outline,
I present it to the honest historian.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 792.
〈Reply to the Notice of Moving the Market〉
In the past, the great scholar Zhāng Kǎi
still moved the market of Hóngnóng;
Yì Guān’s wondrous seal script
still drew guests to the wine stalls.
How much more so for one whose virtue combines that of Xún and Zhōu,
and whose reputation is high in Liáng and Chǔ.
Men who admire his style and follow his righteousness
raise their sleeves to form a canopy;
those who lie in the ruts to stop the carriage
follow shoulder to shoulder.
Consequently, the place where Wáng Chōng browsed the market
has moved far out to the wild suburbs;
the spot where Shí Bāo sold iron
has instead approached the cliff banks.
Sagely virtue is humble and modest,
and has not forgotten the noise and the low-lying areas.
Wishing to make the flutes play and the cranes dance,
and return to the old marketplace;
selling divination and butchering sheep,
they request to take leave of the new market area.
Yet the parties of trade and exchange love to stay,
and the crowds of Bīn and Qí are difficult to send away.
○ *Yìwén Lèijù*, volume 65.
*Chùxué Jì*, volume 24.
〈Official Document Sent to the Qí Héyáng Authorities〉
On the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month of the fourth year of Zhōu Tiānhé,
the Envoy Holding the Tally, Great General of Chariots and Cavalry, Equal to the Three Commandaries, Grand Commander, and Regional Governor of Shǎnxī sent this document to the Qí Héyáng authorities:
Since the war drums were laid down at the border
and the beacon fires were retracted from the frontiers,
the practice of righteous yielding
has not yet lasted a full month.
Kǒng Chéng’s instruction to thieves
immediately encountered concealment.
Therefore, the army of the board-carriers
must move according to the time.
Self-securing our own territory,
it is not for the sake of seeking a confrontation.
Although wind and dust briefly met,
flags and drums did not infringe.
The five generals immediately returned,
and the double Xiáo peaks are already quiet.
Just as we received the imperial decree,
we obtained your letter
ordering the acceptance of the rebel city
and the return of the military supplies.
We expect that your border officials
have already received the instructions.
Since there is this return,
it must be received and accepted.
It is not known on what day
the garrison troops can be sent?
Directly entrust it to the traveler,
so that he can report quickly.
The alliance is not yet violated,
and neighboring lands are friendly to each other.
Looking out over the plains,
there is indeed much good fortune.
Thus, this document is sent.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 650.
On the tenth day of the eleventh month of the fourth year of Zhōu Tiānhé,
Liáng Xīn, Chief Secretary to the Regional Governor of Shǎnzhōu, sent this document to the Qí Héyáng authorities:
Since the jade was wiped and letters were continued,
and the passes were opened and messengers sent,
it was truly thought that the higher-ups would melt down the swords
and Shānyáng would rest the horses.
Therefore, in hosting guests,
some were negligent of the heavy gates.
It happened that the former border officials
secretly practiced clever theft.
One lord and two ministers,
harmony above and discord below.
The state, because the hearts at the frontiers were shaken,
must solidify the defense.
The Grand Minister of War, the Qíguógōng,
is the Son of Heaven’s younger brother
and the Grand Marshal of the Central Army.
He commands like Sūn and Wú,
and drives the brave like pǐxiū.
Taking advantage of the agricultural break,
the righteousness is different from the city wall boy.
The army patrols our territory;
it was not at all like the rebellion in Yùn.
Just as the loading was finished,
the front flags had already returned.
Your country’s soldiers and horses were not prepared,
and the remaining dust at the rear
consequently came into contact.
Banners were set up upon the ramparts,
and before five orders were issued,
beside the city of Ānyè,
seven ambushes were first startled.
At that time, the blades
might have fertilized the plains.
The captured general of yours,
Liáng Lǎo, the leader and Regional Governor of Xiàzhōu,
is now being returned.
His hometown is not far;
do not let him be a guest for long.
Horses, donkeys, armor, and weapons,
are listed and restricted accordingly;
the border guards should receive and accept them.
We had no intention of fighting,
and did not manage to exchange greetings peacefully.
Who is responsible for
causing this dust and chaos?
Thus, this document is sent.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 650.
〈Official Document Sent to the Retained Barbarian Envoy〉
On [Date] of [Year],
[Official Title] announces to the [Prefecture/Commandery]:
Previously, it was intended to send back the envoy,
but since [Name] entered the borders,
the national auspicious event was near.
From autumn to winter,
we have not yet extended a sincere reception.
Moreover, the Wolf Star marks the state,
and severe frost has already given warning.
Crossing the rivers and fording the waters,
the long road is bitterly cold.
As it is now the beginning of the new year,
the Three Origins announce celebrations.
Jade tablets and gifts fill the court;
Chinese and barbarians join their carriages.
To witness the grand ceremony
and partake in this joyous celebration,
once the Yang harmony begins to move
and the moisture reaches the ten thousand nations,
we shall then send an envoy to accompany you,
to forever strengthen neighborly harmony.
Thus, this document is sent.

〈Encomium on Cranes〉
〈Encomium on Cranes〉
In the second month of spring in the second year of Wǔchéng,
A pair of white cranes flew and gathered in the Shànglín Yuán.
The Great General Zhèng Wěi spread nets and set snares,
And both were captured.
Their six wing feathers were already broken,
Their two hearts were both filled with resentment;
They looked at each other with mournful cries.
The solitary male died first,
The widowed mate faced her own shadow;
The Emperor pitied them.
An official reported this at the court steps,
And was immediately ordered to compose an encomium:
Gathering from the remote Jiǔgāo,
Returning from the three mountains.
A parting cry from Huátíng,
An immortal flight from the banks of the Luòpǔ.
They did not guard against the arrow with string,
And were first to suffer restraint.
In the cage, their moon-colored feathers were crushed,
By the snare, their frost-white robes were shattered.
The passes transmit their remaining title,
The gates bear their former name.
Roaming south to the Xiāng Shuǐ,
Entering east into Liáochéng.
Flying through clouds, they wished to dance,
As the dew fell, they were the first to cry.
Their six wing feathers are broken and snapped,
The nine gates are strictly closed.
They look at each other with mournful cries,
Their livers and hearts are severed in grief.
A long sorrow atop the pines,
A final parting within the qin.

With Preface
〈Inscription for the Buddhist Niche at Màijī Yá in Tiānshuǐ Jùn, Qínzhōu, with Preface〉
As for Màijī Yá,
It is a famous mountain of the Lǒngdǐ region,
And a spiritual peak of Héxī.
Its high peaks reach for the clouds,
Its deep valleys are immeasurable.
Comparing it to the Jiùdǎo,
Its traces elude the Sān Chán;
Likening it to the crane's cry,
It flies through the void of the Liùjiǎ.
The bird's path suddenly comes to an end,
The winding sheep's intestine path is sometimes broken.
Clouds are like the wings of the Péng bird,
Suddenly hanging from the heavens;
Trees are like osmanthus blossoms,
Able to brush against the sun.
For this reason, flying staffs have come from afar,
And floating cups have arrived from a distance;
Clearing the mountain and carving caves,
They have densely formed a Pure Land.
To bow to the Dēng Wáng in the stone chamber,
One must borrow the power of riding the wind;
To pay respects to the Huāshǒu in the mountain niche,
One relies upon controlling the crane.
The Grand Commander Lǐ Yǔnxìn,
With roots planted in past merit,
Has deeply awakened to the Dharma gates.
Thus, upon the southern cliff wall,
Scaling the clouds and carving a path,
He respectfully made a niche for the Seven Buddhas on behalf of his late father.
It is as if carved from sandalwood,
As if crafted from rock crystal.
Serene as the full moon,
It shines like the blue lotus.
Its shadow appears on Mount Xūmí,
Its fragrance is smelled in the Dāolì heaven.
In this dusty world,
He has opened anew a hall for preaching the Dharma;
Just like that Fragrant Mountain,
It faces the Buddha in tranquil retreat.
In the past, when the Tathāgata sought merit,
There was the Sutra on Repaying Kindness;
When the Bodhisattva left home,
There were offerings out of longing for parents.
Venturing to draw upon this meaning,
I have composed the inscription, which says:
The town land is densely coiled,
its celestial foundation is high and steep.
Ten ascents to *Shí Guān*,
nine rests at *Tóng Liáng*.
A hundred-fathom cliff lies horizontal,
a thousand-seek pine stands straight.
The Lunar Rabbit borrows a path,
the Solar Crow turns back its wings.
Dredging the mountains with baskets,
carving niches and framing the ridges.
Entwining with the *Xīnghàn*,
circling the light of the sun and moon.
Walls are layered with scriptures,
niches are doubled with Buddha shadows.
Carved wheels in the Moon Palace,
engraved mirrors in the Flower Hall.
Horizontally chiseling the stone walls,
darkly boring through the mountain beams.
Thunder rides the Dharma drum,
trees accumulate heavenly fragrance.
Rinsing at the springs in the *Mín* Valley,
blowing dust from the stone couch.
Gathering spirits at the True Abode,
hiding immortals in the Record Bureau.
Lingzhi caves in autumn rooms,
sandalwood forests with spring sap.
Water valleys with silver sand,
mountain towers with stone pillars.
Different ridges share the clouds,
the same peak has separate rains.
Remaining customs of *Jìchéng*,
old winds of *Héxī*.
The sound of water is faint and sobbing,
the mountain's form is like *Kōngtóng*.
The Dharma cloud dwells forever,
the Sun of Wisdom is inexhaustible.
Though the realms turn to mustard seeds,
the Heavenly Palace remains unchanged.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 785.
〈Inscription on *Zhōngnán Shān Yì Gǔ*〉 with Preface
〈Inscription on *Zhōngnán Shān Yì Gǔ*〉 with Preface
In the second year of *Bǎodìng* of the *Zhōu*,
the year being *Rényǔ*,
on the first day *Jǐsì* of the seventh month,
the Grand Chancellor, the Duke of *Jìnguó*, ordered the carving of the valley of *Shí Guān*,
to bring down timber from *Nán Shān*.
As the Duke rectifies and assists the social order,
and grandly spreads the various achievements,
in his spare time from harmonious governance,
he perused the mountain classics,
considering that *Zhōngnán* and *Dūnwù*
obscure the sun and moon,
and that *chūn*, *gàn*, *guà*, *bǎi*, *yǐ*, *tóng*, *zǐ*, and *qī* trees
have accumulated there for generations,
what could not be found there?
He thus consulted the officials of mountains and marshes,
and also brought in craftsmen of the forests.
Going east from *Lántián*,
they control the *Bà* and ride the *Chǎn*;
going west connecting to *Zǐwǔ*,
they occupy the *Jīng* and float on the *Wèi*.
Branches divide into eight streams,
currents split into nine valleys.
*Tóng Liáng* has four pillars,
*Shí Guān* opens in a pair.
The green-patterned Spring Gate,
ditches and canals reflect each other.
The green locust trees in the autumn market,
boats and oars communicate with each other.
When stored, they become gathering clouds;
when released, they become falling rain.
Patterned catalpa like green oxen,
upright pines like white cranes,
transported to build the palace,
exalting these cloud-like houses.
A thousand brackets support the hall,
dragon heads reach the clouds.
Ten thousand acres of sparse sprouts,
where the cicadas chirp, they ripen again.
The Lord of the River yields in virtue,
the spirits of the mountain follow in admiration.
How could it be like transporting stones to *Gānquán*,
which only reached the hall of *Yuèyáng*?
Or dredging the *Gǔshuǐ* canal,
which only circles the city of *Jīnyōng*?
The work was not yet laborious,
yet the merit achieved is truly great;
the state is wealthy and the people are numerous,
this shall be passed down for a thousand years.
Because of this achievement, the matter is established,
and I venture to carve it on the mountain slope.
The inscription says:
The vastness floats above,
the loftiness settles below.
Walls stand a thousand fathoms high, peaks lie ten thousand fathoms wide.
The cinnamon moon hangs precariously,
the wind and springs echo in the void.
Riding the chariot over the mountain slopes,
raising shovels at the roots of clouds.
Eight streams pour separately,
nine valleys communicate with the source.
To the north it contains the *Tóng* Well,
to the south it floats by *Shímén*.
Patterned after the *Dàzhuàng*,
measuring with ropes for a hundred walls.
Intertwined in nine layers,
wandering among a thousand pillars.
Cinnamon rafters over the waves,
*Bǎiliáng* hall dripping with rain.
Dredging the rivers and establishing the valleys,
falling fruits and breaking branches.
The task is equal to the felling of trees,
the merit is comparable to the chiseling of the River.
○ *Chūxué Jì* 5.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 787.
〈Inscription on *Yùzhàng Shān*〉
〈Inscription on *Yùzhàng Shān*〉
*Yùzhàng* is vast,
*Kūnshān* hits the magpie.
Gathering leaves to make a curtain,
connecting clouds to raise a tent.
The jade slips are hard to move,
the golden flowers do not fall.
Hermits play the zither,
immortals watch the game.
The cliff retains the old tripod,
the stove gathers new thorns.
Stones are first boiled until soft,
cinnabar is about to be refined.
Mulberry fields have changed repeatedly,
the ocean water has frequently filled.
Long hearing the phoenix melody,
forever listening to the flute's sound.

〈Inscription on *Chuītái Shān*〉
At the blowing ridge of *Jiāngníng*,
although the mountain produces bamboo.
The *Qín* flute brings down the phoenix,
this peak is the true one.
Green locust trees avoid the sun,
vermilion grass announces the morning.
A stone is named "New Wife,"
a tower learns from the immortals.
In *Wúzhōng* her name is *Yù*, south of the city her surname is *Qín*.
Comparing flowers by the tree,
climbing the terrace to welcome spring.
Dancing can detain the guests,
the voice then conveys new songs.
Carved beams shake several times,
no more light dust.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 787.
〈Inscription on *Wàng Měirén Shān*〉
〈Inscription on *Wàng Měirén Shān*〉
*Gāotáng* is obstructed by stones,
*Luòpǔ* has no boats.
Where can we gaze at each other?
A tower on the side of the mountain.
The peak is because of the five wives,
the stones are the three marquises.
More dangerous than *Dìfèi*,
high above *Tiānzhù*.
The Forbidden Garden connects obliquely,
people of spring often gather.
Singing is heard within the trees,
dancing is seen among the branches.
Exactly facing the dressing table,
all windows are open during the day.
Glancing sideways, she is already recognized,
calling directly, she turns back.
How could she be like the Weaver Girl,
who does not come except in autumn?
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 787.
*Yìwén Lèijù* 7 ascribes it to *Xú Líng*.
〈Inscription on *Zhìrén Shān*〉
Peaks lie across *Hèlǐng*,
waters imitate *Lóngjīn*.
A single piece of auspicious cloud,
two immortal boys.
Clouds are thin in the three months of autumn,
the cold is new on the ninth day.
Real flowers fall for a moment,
painted trees are always in spring.
Horizontal stones overlook the steps,
flying eaves pillow on the ridge.
Walls are entwined with rattan sprouts,
windows hold the bamboo shadows.
Chrysanthemums fall into the autumn pond,
paulownias are sparse by the cold well.
The benevolent find joy,
surely because they love tranquility.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* 787.
Inscription for Míngyuè Shān
Bamboo pavilions mark the mountain peak,
facing the void on four sides.
The mountain is steep and the eaves are distant,
leaves fall and windows are sparse.
Looking at the rafters, there are flutes;
facing the trees, there is no wind.
Wind rises from the stone cavern;
clouds emerge from the mountain’s root.
On frosty mornings, a crane cries;
on autumn nights, an ape howls.
Embankments and bridges resemble weirs;
wild paths are mistaken for a village.
A boat lies across below the dam;
trees flank the ferry gate.
Is this any different from Huágài Shān?
How could one recognize Táoyuán?
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 787.
Inscription for Xíngyǔ Shān
Inscription for Xíngyǔ Shān
The mountain's name is Xíngyǔ;
the land is different from Yángtái.
Countless beauties are here;
even the Divine Woman is ashamed to come.
Emerald curtains open in the morning;
they rise at dawn with fresh makeup.
Trees enter by the bedside;
flowers appear within the mirror.
The green of the grass is like their robes;
the red of the flowers is like their faces.
The year begins and the cold ends;
in the first month, they wander in spring.
They all remove their brocade capes
and take off their red ribbons together.
Gossamer is more tangled than lotus fibers;
butterfly powder turns to dust.
Transverse vines obstruct the path;
weak willows droop over the people.
Who says the banks of the Luò Shuǐ
have only one river goddess?
○ Yìwén Lèijù, 7.
Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 787.
Three Inscriptions for Blades
Fēngbó blows the furnace;
Yúnshī refines the smelting.
Iron flames flow in the morning;
metallic essence descends at night.
Its price is as heavy as ten cities;
its name is as high as a thousand horses.
For a thousand gold, the point is joined;
after a hundred refinings, the edge is formed.
Its light connects with the aura of the Dǒu constellation;
its flame stirs the mountain spirits.
The patterns on its body move like water;
the ancient blade produces pearls.
The essence of the Dǒu constellation descends from afar;
mountain spirits follow from below.
Water patterns with a thousand curves;
snake scales in a hundred layers.
With a whetstone from Yàn, the blade is honed;
with water from Shǔ, the edge is sharpened.
Its aura brings forth the Fēnjǐng sword;
its ring forms a crouching dragon.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 789.
Inscription Remembering Old Friends, with Preface
In the year of Shètí,
when the star resided in Jiāndé,
the late Marquis of Guānníng of Liáng, Xiāo Yǒng, passed away.
Alas, how tragic!
When a person perishes,
it is not something that metal or stone can avert;
when a scholar grieves,
how can there be a difference between spring and autumn?
The high terrace has already collapsed;
at Jìxià, there are tears upon hearing the zither.
Once the brave warrior has departed,
south of Yàn, there is the sorrow of striking the zhù.
Xiàng Yǔ rising in his tent at dawn,
Lǐ Líng lingering at the fork in the road,
the grandson of the King of Hán as a hostage in Zhào,
or the Prince of Chǔ staying in Qín—
no need for the depth of autumn
to be sorrowful at such times!
Furthermore, fish flying in the Wǔkù armory
was an advance sign of abandoning armor;
birds lurking in Díquán
were a prior omen of the coming chaos.
In the cycle of the Star Chronicle, Wú perished;
in the Gēngchén year, Chǔ was destroyed.
The Marquis of Jǐ departed forever;
the Viscount of Yǔ had no home to return to.
Galloping through the plains and marshes,
a long parting at Huànyuán.
Armor and robes are lost;
the Yúhuáng ship is abandoned.
The river pours into Suānzǎo;
fine woods like the qǐ and zǐ flow away with the bitter and oak trees.
The sea becomes shallow at Pénglái;
fish and turtles perish together with dragons.
Burning incense on the covered walkway,
how could it summon the wandering soul?
Carrying wine for the attendant carriage,
how could it dispel the air of sorrow?
In the autumn of orchids and mugwort,
though their forms differ, they wither together;
in the resentment of creatures of feather, fur, scale, and shell,
though their voices differ, they all mourn.
What is called "Heaven"?
It is but the vast azure mist.
What is called "Earth"?
It is truly just the clumped soil.
As for those who are full of resentment,
how can they be moved?
To have one's feathers broken and destroyed
does not depend on the violent winds;
to wither and die in spring
need not trouble the frost and dew.
When the headquarters were first opened,
the talented and worthy raised their heads;
remaining as guests for the whole year,
the disciples expressed their thanks.
As for facing east to say farewell,
and departing forever to Xīlíng.
The carriages and horses of Shānyáng
gazed at the parting at the suburban gate;
the guests of Yǐngchuān
grieved from afar along the pine-lined path.
In the mountain garden of Jī Shūyè,
there are still many willows;
along the old path of Wáng Zǐyóu,
only the bamboo grove remains.
The burial ground of the descendant
becomes the Chánglè Palace;
the place where the hero's soul is buried
is the tomb of the general.
Formerly, we often enjoyed joyous banquets,
lingering amidst the wind and moon;
recalling our lives,
it is vividly before my mind and eyes.
When wings drooped over Qínchuān,
sojourning among the passes and rivers,
descending into the scenery of the valley of sorrow,
there truly is a feeling of anxiety over life.
Pouring fine wine,
one still thinks of the waters of Jiànyè;
with the sounding zither in hand,
one ultimately thinks of the cranes of Huátíng.
Adding weight to this parting,
alas, how extreme it is!
The unicorn dies and the star falls;
the moon dies and the pearl is damaged.
When the pitcher is empty, the wine-jar is ashamed;
when the orchid is burned, the clover sighs.
It is hoped that as the bell sinks into the Déshuǐ,
its sound will emerge from the wind and clouds;
as the sword is buried in Fēngchéng,
its aura remains between the Niú and Dǒu constellations.
Tearfully remembering old friends,
I thus compose this inscription, which says:
The wind and clouds above are gloomy,
the boat in the ravine secretly moves.
Rapidly come the frost and dew,
the gentleman is the first to face peril.
Jì Hóu has departed forever,
Huái Wáng will not return.
The jade tree is buried for long,
and his elegant style is thus far away.
The old county of Xún Bó,
the remaining town of Qìng Fēng.
A returning soul from ten thousand lǐ,
how can he enter the Xiū Mén?
The tomb lies across from the Wǔ Kù,
the mountain pillows Lú Lóng.
Thinking of return, the road is far;
returning for burial, there is no way.
In vain remain the departing geese,
empty sways the tall pine.
To the east of Píng Líng,
no longer are there wútóng trees.
The sound of pines is soughing,
as the autumn wind rises long.
In the past of high nobility,
hand in hand, in speech and silence.
Entrusting feelings like Jī and Ruǎn,
meeting like wind and clouds.
There was wine like the Miǎn,
always gentle and controlled.
At Cháo Yáng fell the phoenix,
at Dà Yě grieved the qílín.
Jiā Chéng is lush and gloomy,
he lived as a refugee in Qín.
Sending him off at Shān Yáng,
only old friends remain.
The widow at the loom, the bereaved wife at the shuttle,
a solitary phoenix, a lonely luan.
The inner chamber is deep, the night is quiet;
the wind is high, the moon is cold.
His life is already over,
when can we cherish old memories?
In the case, the strings are broken;
the neighbor's flute is sorrowful.
Formerly at the Mù Fǔ,
now he has become a Suì Wéi.
— Yìwén Lèijù, volume 34.
— Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 790.
〈Stele for the Sūtra Repository of Wǔ Zhāng Temple in Hóng Nóng Commandery, Shǎn Zhōu〉
I have heard that when the Rú Lái preached the Dharma,
it was like ten million Ganges sands;
when the Pú Sà turned the wheel,
it was in life after life, world after world.
How could it be just Yōu Bō Tí Shè,
Qí Yè, and Xiū Duō alone?
Therefore, at the Xī Lián Chán River,
under the Zhì Duō Luó tree,
in the seven places and eight assemblies,
the three purities and four preachings,
using skin as paper and bone as a brush,
tree leaves and mountain flowers,
even what elephants carry cannot outweigh it,
and the Lóng Zàng cannot exhaust it.
Although silver cases were brought to the east,
and Jīn Dié were turned to the south,
Qín Jǐng was transmitted from afar,
and Zhú Lán's private records were kept,
it is like obtaining one pearl from the sea,
or a piece of jade from Mount Kūnlún.
As for the deep treasury of the Fǎ Yún,
the Shī Zi Léi Yīn,
the Fàn Zhì’s rebirth,
and the Shēng Wén’s preaching of the precepts,
the treatises of the Luó Hàn of the Xuě Shān,
and the Dharma of Pú Tí on Jiù Lǐng,
they were originally without limit,
how can they be fully told?
As for the Wǔ Zhāng Temple in Hóng Nóng:
Zhāng Yuán Gāo of Nányáng resided in this land.
In the past, families of a thousand gold
were moved to the Wǔ Líng;
people of great surnames
moved their homes to the Liù Jùn;
he was of such a lineage.
Yuán Gāo had five sons,
who carried on the ancestral teachings.
Analyzing the classics and discerning their will,
they all achieved fame;
entering the room they brought light,
and all were able to manifest virtue.
Moreover, they reverently upheld the Huì Yè,
and respectfully received the Fǎ Mén.
The brothers lived together,
and together gave up their residence to be a temple.
When the Qié Lán was first established,
it was named after the Wǔ Zhāng.
Thus we know that when Zhào Xìn dwelt in a city,
it was still named the City of Zhào Xìn;
when Xiāo Hé entered a hall,
it was called the Hall of Xiāo Hé.
Furthermore, they were not stingy with elephants or horses,
and gave away their clothes.
The willow paths of the spring gardens
were transformed into the Chán Lín;
the mulberry fords of the silkworm months
were turned into the Dìng Shuǐ.
Although Píng Yú was prosperous,
how could it alone possess the Èr Lóng?
Fù Fēng was most excellent,
yet it could not exclusively claim the title of the Wǔ Mǎ.
The Temple Master and Great Dharma Master of the Sān Zàng, Fǎ Yìng, and the Head of the Region, the Governor of Luò Zhōu, Zhāng Lóng, and others,
practiced the charity of Fǎ Tán,
exhausting their bodies and minds.
They also transformed the townships and counties,
with thousands of monastics and laypeople,
reverently creating the Yī Qiè Dé Lún,
which resulted in over three hundred volumes.
Thunder-seal and cloud-script,
golden cords and jade tags,
tablets of carved Shēng Lì,
ornaments of Suān Zǎo pearls,
all entered the Xiāng Chéng,
and all were sealed in the Chán Gé.
Sitting in the hall and leaning on the railings,
these are certainly not the spirits of the Xiāng Shuǐ;
with green chambers and purple seeds,
it is enough to rival the palace of Gòng Wáng.
Gāozhǎng Peak is seen to the west,
and the Cháng Hé is approached to the north.
The tripod-vapor always floats,
and the censer smoke all rises.
The doors and windows are vast and open,
blowing the ten thousand winds of Lóng Mén;
the beams and pillars are towering,
made from the solid trees of the Hé Yuán.
Monks gather like clouds,
not far from the city of Dùnhuáng;
fellow students rush together,
further joining the market of Huáyīn.
The two Shǎn regions were formerly divided,
truly the foundation of the King's transformation;
the Èr Líng are now obstructed,
and Yǔ Jì are sent in haste.
Yú Gōng's Qū Chǎn horses
are entangled in the dust of war;
Zhào Bó's Gān Táng
withers in the frost and dew.
Although they are capable of governing together,
the beasts that cross the river have not yet been sent away;
beacons and clappers give warning,
truly disturbing the people moving through the pass.
Thus, the Fǎ Wáng governs the world,
heavenly beings discuss the Dào,
drawing in the four currents,
and encompassing the five fears.
Therefore, he can subdue resentment and hatred,
and eliminate the bonds of attachment.
On the bridge of the Dharma-water,
there is no longer the difficulty of the Dǐzhù Rock;
on the tracks of the Xiāng Shān,
it is no longer the danger of Zhōngnán.
The Tiān Zǐ commanded me
to temporarily govern this state.
My stove has not yet turned black from soot,
and my seat has no warmth;
just as I arrived at the border of the Dū Wèi,
there was the service of the Lóu Chuán.
After the southern wind was not strong enough,
I spoke of returning by the northern road.
Since the Mù Fǔ has been opened,
the lord of the state shall stay.
The elders of the village
still remember this parting;
pertaining to this Buddhist ceremony,
they required me to compose a text.
I casually put forth my humble effort,
to make an inscription as follows:
The kingdom of Shèwèi,
the garden of Qǐhuán.
At the ultimate stage of the Sānmíng,
and the deepest source of the Bāhuì.
Along the river, they vie to preach;
with superior eloquence, they contend in debate.
Bōtí crossed to the East;
Qǐyè was translated in the South.
Not emptiness, it is form;
apart from existence and non-existence, it is beyond words.
The man of realization stops here;
he alone awakens within the heavy darkness.
Though the body is like a tethered horse,
the heart avoids the leaping monkey.
The Dhyāna tower retreats from the moon;
the Hall of Doctrine hosts the soaring Kūn bird.
Whirlwinds stir the fragrant canopy;
returning dew falls on the pearl banners.
To the west it faces Dǐzhù;
to the east it backs onto Huányuán.
The river roars at Yángxiá;
the mountains echo at Sūmén.
Soaring birds warble their songs;
flowing streams sound their strings.
The remaining beasts have crossed the river;
the old village has moved beyond the pass.
Formerly it was the imperial domain;
now it has become the frontier wall.
The city is like Guǎngwǔ;
the land resembles Lóufán.
Beacons and signal fires shine together;
elephants and horses gallop alone.
Without bells, attacking Jǔ;
with rain, surrounding Yuán.
Without relying on the Ten Directions,
who could resolve the Three Grievances?
Winds topple the earth's pillars;
fire reaches the heavenly origin.
The silver hooks are forever firm;
the golden tablets exist eternally.
Enfeoffed as a lord at the horse’s head,
he was just then attending to the southern frontiers.
Following the words of Yáng Pǔ,
he declined the request of Liú Kūn.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 850.
〈Spirit Way Stele of King Xiàn of Qí, Pillar of the State of Zhōu〉
In the past, the Xuānhuáng bestowed surnames
upon fourteen people;
the Zhōu house first enfeoffed
fifteen states.
Since then, they have inherited foundations and continued lineages,
preserving surnames and receiving clan names;
though a sage appears but once in a thousand years,
they are ultimately of the same clan for a hundred generations.
Thus we know that the former Dōngjīng
was called the second reception of the Fiery Yánhàn;
the current Zhōu calendar
is the restoration of Fèngdū.
The Duke’s taboo name was Xiàn,
his courtesy name was Pǐhètū,
a man of Wǔchuān in Héngzhōu.
During the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
his ancestors occupied Huánglóng;
at the beginning of the Xiàochāng era of Wèi,
they took control of Xuántù.
Tàizǔ, with one hundred and two marquises,
divided the world into three parts;
Hángǔ Pass was first ascended,
and at Hònggōu great peace was settled;
with achievements such as these,
a subject reached his end.
The Duke possessed natural brilliance and heavenly endowment;
he was born as a man of his age.
He descended from the spirit of Tàiyī
and came down from the constellation of Wénchāng.
With pearl-like horns showing his rarity
and a mountain-like forehead manifesting his virtue,
his bearing was clear and cool,
his spirit high and soaring.
He moved the courtly halls
and brightened the city gates.
Before he had even lost his milk teeth,
he already discussed the affairs of the world.
Someone said:
"This is what is called a single branch of the Ruò tree
shading several countries;
a single straight stretch of the Long River
naturally reaching a thousand lǐ."
"The wind and storm intend to go far;
the light and shadow are about to rise."
In the second year of Later Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as the Founding Duke of Fúchéng County;
at that time he was five years old.
Rainbows filled the fields,
signifying the removal of those high on the road;
the Yuèzhuó birds sang at Qí,
truly starting the mandate of renewal.
The state's radiant residence received the charts
and reverently held the calendar;
the great wind first rolled,
and Chángshā was first enfeoffed.
In the first year of Zhōu,
he was promoted to Duke of Ānchéng District,
with a fief of two thousand households,
and was still appointed Commissioner with Special Lictor, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Grand Marshal of the Opening Office with Equal Three Tiers.
His opening of the office was like that of Mǎ Jùn;
his rank was comparable to the Six Ministers.
His chariot and cavalry were equal to those of Liú Cāng;
his position was higher than the Three Excellencies.
As a scion of the imperial house protecting the city,
many others felt ashamed in comparison.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
he was appointed Commissioner with Special Lictor, Great General, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for twenty-four prefectures including Yì, Shòu, and Níng, and Governor of Yìzhōu;
his title was changed to Duke of Qí,
with a fief of ten thousand households;
at that time the Duke was sixteen years old.
Wáng Wǔzǐ became a top general and opened an office
before he reached thirty;
Xún Zhōngláng was commander of ten prefectures
just after passing twenty.
Compared to the Duke,
they were already old.
Furthermore, Yíngqiū faces the sea,
the city where Duke Huán of Qí received the sacrificial meat;
Mount Mín directs the river,
the place where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sought immortality.
If not for the solitude of Zháolíng and Gūzhú,
his fame shaking the people of the frontier,
how could he have reached Mùlíng in the south
or climbed Jīshí in the west?
Fortunate to have no trouble with the White Tiger,
why wait for the covenant of the Yellow Dragon?
The Qióng and Zuó tribes feared his majesty;
the Wēi and Lú looked up to his virtue;
during his life, they built temples for him,
and carved stones to praise his merit.
Chéngdū has the sacrifice for Wén Wēng,
but it was not established during his life;
Hànyáng has the stele for Zhūgé,
which only discusses him after his death.
Comparing them to today,
how can they be mentioned in the same breath!
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng,
he together with the Dà Sīmǎ, the Duke of the State of Shǔ, besieged Jīnyōng City.
When the army approached Luòpǔ,
the Guǎngwǔ camp fled;
when the soldiers ascended Mángshān,
the road to Héqiáo was cut off.
The customs of the eight rivers,
the fame and profit of the five directions,
the iron markets and copper streets,
wind blew and dust rose.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
he was summoned back
to serve as the Shepherd of Yōng Zhōu.
With the brilliance of the sun and moon,
the Duke governed with majestic divinity;
the Qī and Jǔ rivers were made to follow their course,
and Jīng and Qí were soon pacified.
When Shàoyáng held sway,
oxen did not pant on the roads;
by mid-autumn when harvests were abundant,
the people were not alarmed by the waters.
In the second year,
he was appointed Dà Sīmǎ,
while still managing the duties of Xiǎo Zhǒngzǎi and Director of Military Equipment of the Yíngshì Palace.
The Heavenly Official takes the state as its foundation,
thus administering the Six Canons;
the Summer Official takes weaponry as its priority,
specializing in planning the Seven Virtues.
Consequently, military equipment was piled high,
encompassing the merits of Wú Hàn;
the palaces rose majestic,
further strengthening the laws of Xiāo Hé.
At the time of white dew and cool winds,
taking advantage of the slack season in farming,
he commanded thirty thousand troops,
departing from Yíyáng,
to capture the city of Fúlóng
and level the ramparts of Yáo Cháng.
As trees were barked at Mǎlíng,
the Wèi general reached the end of his road;
as crows were heard at Píngyīn,
the Qí army took to flight.
As the younger brother of the Son of Heaven,
his etiquette was superior to all the other dukes,
and wherever benevolence and righteousness were directed,
matters relied upon his virtue.
In the first year of Jiàndé,
he was promoted to the rank of King,
and further appointed Dà Zhǒngzǎi.
Jī Dàn was enfeoffed at Qūfù,
yet did not cease residing in the center;
Liú Jiāo had his state at Péngyáng,
yet it did not hinder his constant attendance at court.
How could it be that only the Zhōu and Shào of the Èr Nán
both held the positions of tutors;
or that the two states of Jìn and Zhèng
were merely ministers?
The Xiōngnú burst forth at Wǔchuān,
and beacon fires reached Bàshàng.
The Duke performed his duties of inspection and defense,
training troops in Shuòfāng.
At Mǎyì, stars flew;
at Lóngchéng, the moon moved.
Having stirred the liúlí wine of the barbarians,
their strategic plans could not advance;
having lost the Yānzhī Mountains,
they dismounted and departed.
The eastern neighbor rebelled against the imperial command,
turning against the Way and failing in virtue,
imprisoning Jīzi in the granary
and detaining Wén Wáng at Yùmén.
The Son of Heaven was about to send the army to Mèngjīn,
and the Duke of Shào alone deliberated.
The Duke responded by grandly answering the Mandate of Heaven,
successfully achieving those merits.
Formerly, Qín Zhāo raised an army in Shǔ
and directly consulted Zhāng Yí;
Jìn Wǔ used troops against Wú
and only planned with Yáng Hù.
Thus, when the central army lacked a commander,
everyone said it should be him.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Shàng Zhùguó.
The Grand Army marched east to punish the rebels,
providing the King with twenty thousand armored cavalry
to first surprise Tàiyuán.
As the Dǒujiàn waved the troops,
and the Tiānlí shifted the battle,
he was like a roaring tiger and rising wind,
like flying clouds and striking lightning.
Could the dates and chestnuts of the Línhú
possibly satisfy hunger?
Could the reeds and mugwort of Jìnyáng
possibly provide defense?
Furthermore, the King was given sixty thousand elite troops
to conduct a long siege of Jìn Zhōu.
Then the Six Armies were arrayed like stars,
and ten thousand cavalry moved like thunder;
when the central force first arrived,
the vanguard had already engaged.
From then on, he served as the vanguard,
marching irresistibly into Yè.
Observing them, chariots were snagged on locust tree roots,
and horses were startled into the mud;
stacked armor was higher than the city of Kūnyáng,
and corpses blocked the waters of Fùpíng.
Everything was like tipping a water jar from a height,
or like the splitting of bamboo;
with one morning's command,
the six directions were grandly settled.
Thus he brought glory to the ancestors through Xiàwǔ,
and assisted the central capital;
it was enough to vent the long-held resentment of the ancestors
and relieve the grievances of the common people.
He was just about to wait at that Shílǘ,
and arrange those jade drums,
regulating Heaven and Earth
and making the sun and moon shine.
But then a red bird flanked the sun,
and a yellow bear entered the bedroom;
Shíchén was without sacrifice,
and the Sānglín was not worshipped.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month in the first year of Xuānzhèng, he passed away
at the age of thirty-four.
With the death of Jìyǒu,
the fate of Lǔ can be known;
when Qí lost Zǐyǎ,
how perilous must the House of Jiāng be!
The Duke's temperament was deep and broad,
his spirit was transcendent and far-reaching.
His insight was like a clear mirror illuminating the forest,
his magnanimity was like mountains and rivers accommodating all.
Like a flagon set out and waiting to be poured,
or a bell hung and waiting to be struck,
his renown shook the world,
and his brilliance shone upon the neighboring lands.
Wǔ Huángdì, because the Duke was his younger brother and close kin,
showed him special affection and friendship;
moreover, for his secret plans and extraordinary strategies,
the Emperor added further respect.
The Emperor often said to those around him:
"Kǒngzǐ said:
'Since I have had Yán Huí,
my disciples have grown closer daily.'
This truly describes the Qí Wáng."
When employed as a minister,
the ten thousand directions achieved harmony;
when employed to pacify the army,
the four borders were awed into submission.
Was it merely that when Gāo Yáo served as the judge,
the state had no one who was not benevolent;
or that when Suí Huì served as a minister,
the people had no gangs of thieves!
He loved and cherished books,
and esteemed the rites and music.
When the sounds of pipes and strings reached his ears,
the streams and valleys seemed to harmonize;
when refined elegance permeated his heart,
the mist and clouds moved in rhythm.
Like Yǎng Yóu hitting the target a hundred times,
bringing down geese and making apes cry;
like Yìng Fèng reading five lines at once,
through the silk and scrolls of the library.
In his dignified carriage and behavior,
and in his rising and falling discourse,
the current age took him as a model,
and the gentry took him as a standard.
Since his youth, he had great ambitions,
and thoroughly studied military texts.
The spirits of the Xuánshuǐ descended,
and the strategies of Gǔchéng were bestowed;
the flying winds of Chángliǔ,
the lunar forehead and starry brows—
there were none he did not recite in his heart
or compile with his hand.
The military methods he composed
totaled five volumes.
Regarding the *Liùtāo* and *Jiǔfǎ*,
he did not use the old books of Wú Qǐ;
regarding the "three orders and five warnings,"
he had no need for the prior admonitions of Sūn Wǔ.
It can be said he possessed loyalty and filial piety,
and possessed martial prowess.
He was not arrogant or boastful,
but humbled his light to treat others with respect.
Like the man of Sòng offering jade,
he did not consider greed a treasure;
like Bóchèng Zǐgāo,
he considered maintaining benevolence as true wealth.
He did not believe that trustworthiness would lead to deception,
or that doing good was not a joy.
His heavenly years were not fulfilled—
alas, how sorrowful!
On a certain day of a certain month and year, he was buried in the village of Hóngdúchuān in Shí'ān Xiàn.
The plains and marshes are desolate and sad,
where his great virtue has been buried for several years;
the hills and mounds are withering,
where his talent and goodness are hidden forever.
Thus, the inscription says:
Vast is the northern region,
distant is the extreme darkness.
Mountains connect like bird paths,
the land ends at Guìlín.
Zhònglí's legacy was great,
Bóyì's merit was deep.
Their descendants accumulated virtue,
surely a ruler would arise.
Tàizǔ quelled the chaos;
though the lord was lost, a new lord appeared.
His merit turned the axis of the earth,
his strategies moved the patterns of heaven.
Still approaching the Chìshuǐ,
yet returning to the yellow clouds.
The eight hundred feudal lords,
the world divided in three.
The Duke's extraordinary birth
was truly granted by Heaven.
A deity descended from Cuìwēi,
a star fell from Wénchāng.
He shone upon the four states
and filled the two altars.
A boat and oar for the rivers,
a pillar and beam for Huàxià.
Eloquence flowing like water,
elegance flying like the wind.
His nature was pure and deep,
his righteousness reached the heavenly principles.
His path of loyalty and integrity
moved the hundred spirits.
Serving the sovereign and parents as one,
the subject and son were at peace.
The spring of loyalty gushed from the well,
the bamboo shoots of filial piety grew in the courtyard.
He served as the Minister of Heaven,
acting as the assistant to the state.
He held the position of Supreme General,
acting as a pillar of heaven.
Sagely and divine,
both civil and martial.
His strategies were as high as the creation of the world,
his majesty moved the clouds and rain.
Divine strategies of the nine palaces,
brilliant plans of the three arts.
The Tiānlí turned the battle formations,
the lunar virtue redirected the troops.
At Líyáng, the waters were startled;
at Guāndù, the mountains were alarmed.
Jìzhōu was already recorded,
and Dōngyuán was finally pacified.
The waves of the dark sea were about to stir,
the weak wood was about to be endangered.
The central peak of the mountain was severed,
the wings of the rukh hung halfway over the sea.
The phoenix sank into the Dānxué,
the dragon perished at the black bank.
The markets of Línzī were abandoned,
the mountains of Dōngwǔ moved.
For a thousand ages and ten thousand years,
his heroic name shall remain here.
Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Fascicle 890.
Stele of the Junior Guardian to the Crown Prince of Zhōu, Bùlù.
Stele of the Junior Guardian to the Crown Prince of Zhōu, Bùlù.
The Duke’s taboo name was Chěng,
his style name was Jìmíng;
his original surname was Lù,
a man of Wú Jùn.
When the gentleman arrived,
he succeeded as the guest of Yú;
as the phoenixes flew,
the state of Qí truly rose.
The envoy of Nányuè
took off the robes of the Hàn Emperor;
the general of Xīlíng
covered the canopy of the King of Wú.
His great-grandfather was Lù Zài,
who served as the Sīmǎ for the Sòng Wáng
and remained to garrison Guānzhōng.
During the chaos of Hèlián,
he wielded his sword for the Wèi House.
At the Yellow River and the tomb,
some lost the path of pursuit;
at the Wū Jiāng where boats were moored,
there were no more traces of return.
He is now a man of Luòyáng in Hénán.
His great-great-grandfather
was General of the Brave Cavalry and Governor of Yíngzhōu.
Those of the Wú people who surrendered and attached themselves
were all led as a separate army.
From then on, the officials and teachers held the bells,
changing them into the soldiers of Wú and Yuè;
the gentlemen were accustomed to the currents,
having separate formations of tower ships.
His father was Lù Zhèng,
General of Agile Cavalry, Grandee of Equal Dignity with the Three Offices, Governor of Héngzhōu, and the Dedicated Duke of Zhōngdū.
Tàizǔ supported the endangered and saved the fallen,
managing the barbarians and obstacles;
to avenge the disgrace of his lord,
he went on a distant expedition to Píngyuán.
Because Gāopíng was the foundation of the hegemonic enterprise,
he entrusted Lù Zhèng to stay and handle affairs.
Food was provided from within the passes,
not just by the army of Xíngyáng;
supplies for the military came from Hénèi,
not just from the bamboo of Qíyuán.
The Duke shone with the spirit of Jìn,
and descended with the virtue of the bright gods.
When the fierce tiger shook the cage,
he was not startled at seven years old;
when the ram butted the fence,
he could answer at nine years of age.
His elder brothers, considering the Duke the beloved son of the late lord,
praised him for his benevolence,
and stepped aside so he could inherit the title.
Even though it was late in the era,
his heart for great achievement maintained its integrity;
having encountered the smoking of the cave,
he turned to follow the pressing of the seal-knob.
When Tài Zǔ was first enfeoffed at Hángǔ,
and began to gather the feudal lords,
he used the Duke's diplomatic rhetoric
to deliberate on secret matters,
so that military policies could be proclaimed
and army secrets were not leaked,
and he was bestowed the surname Bùlùgū.
Leaving the deer carriage to discuss the capital,
entering Hóngmén to dance with the sword,
comparing this to the tuning of the pitch-pipes,
there was plenty of surplus glory.
He began his career as Yǔlínjiān and Qīngchējāngjūn,
and was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
His official duties were linked to accounting,
and his tasks were concentrated on the price-stabilization office;
in the office of the Water Equilibrator, the strings rotted,
and in the Constant Level Granary, the grain turned red.
He was granted the titles of Shǐchíjié, Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, and Yítóng Sānsī,
and his household allotment was increased by one thousand households.
Soon he was promoted to Jiàbù Zhōngdàfū,
and also served as Lìbù Zhōngdàfū,
having held the posts of Fánbù and Yùbó Zhōngdàfū.
Like the cauldrons of Dōngjīng,
he was first added to the merits of Dèng Zhì;
in selecting officials for the Western Jìn,
many used the recommendations of Shān Tāo.
How could it be otherwise when the five kings ascend the court,
they must preside over the rites of host and guest;
when the six dragons drive the reins,
they take the rhythm from the Luan bells.
Because the office of Yùzhèng conflicted with his father's name,
he did not accept it.
In Kuìjī, there was the name of Wáng Huì;
his son would not become the Governor;
in Bólíng, there was the fief of Wáng Chén;
his son would not become the Inspector.
He was promoted to Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ.
He entered to manage the Nàyán,
and governed the Sīzōngbó.
He also served as Jūnsīmǎ.
Occupying the position of Chángbó,
he diligently inquired at the Nángōng;
his position controlled the royal words,
linking his office to the Běidǒu.
Not only for the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
with the sounds of Lóngmén and Xiègǔ;
but also praising the drums and distributing the flags,
in the months of white dew and cool winds.
In the dark of night, someone offered him several dozen rolls of silk,
but the Duke closed his door and would not receive them.
When a traveler offended him,
he reported it all to the throne,
and the court and commoners praised him.
Grand Marshal Yáng Zhèn
straightforwardly rejected the gold from his former subordinate;
Zhāng Huàn of Liángzhōu
bowed deeply and rejected the horses of the Qiāng people.
With a purity that fears people knowing,
I have no shameful virtue.
When the State of Qí made peace,
the border guards received the envoy.
Because the Duke had the talent for going beyond the borders,
he was ordered to perform the rites of Zhāng Zhān.
Having smeared blood on the jade plate,
he established the joint alliance with the State of Chǔ;
with a dagger, he ascended the altar,
and regained the occupied lands of the people of Qí.
Is this what is called an envoy?
He surely brought glory to the nation.
Among the lords of the Sānfǔ,
and the noble families of the Wǔlíng,
in the streets of paulownia and the markets of willow,
where dust rises and wind flies,
he was then appointed Jīngzhàoyǐn,
with his household allotment increased to a total of one thousand six hundred households,
and his other offices remaining as before.
Soldiers at Shànglín rested,
and bandits at Lánchí were quiet;
he did not learn Wáng Yáng's lifelong art of casting gold,
nor did he join Zhāng Chǎng in his daily excursions to Zhāngtái.
When his house servant returned from a night walk,
he found lost money on the road,
along with ten bolts of white coarse silk;
the Duke sought out the owner
and immediately returned them.
Seeing gold on the road,
he pointed to show others;
finding money on the path,
he held it and hung it on a tree.
Compared to today,
different eras share the same spirit.
Soon he was promoted to Sīkuài,
and served as Xiǎosīmǎ.
Again he commanded the six armies,
and twice he wielded the eight powers.
His performance evaluation was recorded in the annual results,
and his merits were written in the Niánbiǎo.
Soon he was appointed Dūdū of the various military affairs of Yízhōu and Cìshǐ of Yízhōu.
He exposed his carriage to observe the local customs,
and stopped his carriage to wait for rain.
Officials of a hundred cities resigned their seals,
fearing the majesty of Zhū Mù;
people from a thousand miles came to welcome him,
loving the virtue of Wáng Jī.
Before a full year had passed,
he was recalled by imperial decree.
The devoted officials and people
made requests like those in Hénài;
the lingering elders
truly felt the sorrow of the parting at Líyáng.
The Shǎoyáng cultivates virtue,
and the Front Star guards the ritual vessels;
respecting the teacher and yielding to age,
one must wait for a man of talent and ability.
Thus he was appointed Tàizǐ Tàibǎo.
Comparing him to Liú Shí,
his Way was higher than that of the Great State;
likening him to Shān Tāo,
his glory was deeper than that in the small carriage.
Originally he had the illness of thirst-extinguishing,
and often took minerals and stones to treat himself.
His old illness slightly increased,
and he suddenly passed away in his residence.
Below Mùlíng,
he left no writings on the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices;
in the camp of the Colonel,
only the vessels for diet and medicine remained.
Alas, how sorrowful!
His age was forty-seven,
on the eleventh day of the fifth month of the second year of Jiàndé.
The Emperor, because of the death of a great minister,
personally suspended the hearing of litigations;
the Eastern Court, because of the honor of the teacher and tutor,
personally attended the funeral rites.
A decree posthumously granted him certain offices,
and the posthumous title of Duke So-and-so,
according to the rites.
On the tenth day of the first month of the third year of his era,
he was buried at Gāoyáng Yuán in Jīngzhào.
His wife, Lady Yùjiǔlǘ,
met the royal princess in the west.
Receiving respect with solemnity and reverence,
her words and appearance were fair and virtuous;
she was known for her adherence to the rules of conduct and washing,
and never neglected her work with hat strings and silk threads.
While in her prime years,
she first entered the long night.
Now the tomb of the chaste woman is opened,
and the pines and cypresses have already grown large;
as Jì Sūn completed his resting place,
the mounds are now joined together.
Furthermore, the portrait of the virtuous consort
is now in the chamber of Gānquán;
the burial of the talented gentleman
takes place at Gāoyáng Yuán.
The Duke’s appearance was bright on the outside,
and his spirit shone within;
his capacity was deep and profound,
and his foundations were unfathomable.
In serving his sovereign he was loyal,
and in serving his parents he was filial;
his words were a model for the world,
and his actions were a rule for scholars.
He lingered over the *Fén* and the *Suǒ*,
and was moved by literary compositions.
The Censorate was recorded in the *Shàngshū*,
and the *Tiānguān* was summarized in the *Sīhuì*.
Coming and going, he assisted and supported,
regularly holding several concurrent posts;
