his person possessed six jade tablets,
and his waist always bore four ribbons.
The secret plots of Chén Píng
were not seen by the Son of Heaven;
the superior strategies of Xún Yù
were not heard by the feudal lords.
When he governed a commandery,
he only took red clay to seal his letters;
when he governed a province,
he only used blue salt to exchange for grain.
Leaving his home, a thousand trees provided no wealth;
leaving his sons, there was only one classic.
His legitimate son Cāo
possessed a nature that exceeded ritual requirements,
and his pure filial piety was unwavering.
Among the trees before the grave,
those stained with tears withered first;
among the birds by the courtyard,
those who heard the grief descended.
The inscription says:
The mountains connect to Rìguān,
the waters pillow the Diānjī.
At Fùchūn the sands rose,
at Kāiyáng the pillars flew.
The Grandee bent his integrity,
the General shook with majesty.
Nányuè received the official,
Xīlíng was relieved of its siege.
Formerly our illustrious ancestor
drooped his wings in Qínzhōng.
At Báimǎ there was no road,
at Wūjiāng there was no passage.
Flutes chanted in the home village,
the zither mourned the local customs.
Yíngzhōu and Héngzhōu
held the banners for generations.
Grand integrity and felt-clad pride,
a hero of the passes and fortresses.
Straight rivers pierced Zhào,
level clouds looked over Dài.
In life he established merit,
in death he left behind love.
Descending from these mountains and rivers,
this upright and bright one was born.
Auspicious omens in the clouds,
blessings joined with the essence of stars.
Deciding strategies within the palace curtains,
writing his name upon the palace pillars.
The spring of loyalty leaked secretly,
filial bamboo shoots grew in the cold.
The world belonged to Yīn and Zhōu,
the times met with Chǔ and Hàn.
The world was divided into three,
the Hónggōu canal split it in half.
Using my brilliant strategies,
he came to participate in assistance.
The sun reached its zenith again,
the heavens became double dawns.
Successively participating in the Three Excellencies,
serving as deputy to the Six Ministers.
The Heavenly Preceptor’s radiant dwelling,
the Earth's Support was wise and bright.
The Spring Official established rituals,
the Summer Official governed the troops.
Prophetic words were silently noted,
the warm trees remained nameless.
Humble, respectful, and meticulous,
his words and deeds never went astray.
Faithful and public-spirited as the rhinoceros killed,
with hidden virtue like the snake buried.
Military and state affairs were numerous,
leading departments on the ornate steps.
Horses did not enter his stable,
gold did not enter his bosom.
All looked up only to his virtue,
as one gazes up at a high mountain.
When first entering the crown prince's palace,
when first ascending the Dragon Tower.
Huán Róng in the eastern state,
Shū Guǎng in the Western Capital.
His lifespan was but a moment,
wind and lightning destroyed each other.
The funerary banners both disappeared,
the pond willows both turned back.
The solitary descendant,
suffered illness and harbored grief.
His body displayed the wild fire,
his heart feared the heavenly thunder.
As the days and months passed away,
glory ended and grief began.
The horses returned to the *Sīlì*,
the records returned to the *Tàishǐ*.
The calendar corresponds to the stars,
the tomb connects to the earthly market.
The mountain terrain connects with flight,
the pine shapes rise like canopies.
The sound of his virtue shall not end,
though the plain has suddenly vanished.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Fascicle 900.
Spirit Way Stele of the Zhōu Grand General Cuī Shuō.
The Duke’s taboo name was Shuō,
his courtesy name was [blank],
a man of Ānpíng County, Bólíng Commandery.
Formerly, in the fields of Huáyáng,
descended the spirit with a dragon’s head;
in the capital of Lièshān,
began the omen of tortoise shell patterns.
Assisting Zhōu, there was a meeting at Méngjīn;
aiding Xià, Lóngmén was first carved.
Traveling west, he rose from his family to be a Minister of Qín;
entering the east, he was a Minister of Qí for generations.
All this is fully recorded in the historical records
and can be told.
Grandfather Biàn,
General of Píngyuǎn and Governor of Wǔyì Commandery.
Father Kǎi,
Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary,
Grandee of Guānglù and Inspector of Yīnzhōu.
Both braved wind and frost,
both displayed sharp edges;
their mansion records followed one another,
and their offices were awe-inspiring.
This was like Bǎo Huī of the *Dūguān*,
at whom a hundred cities trembled with fear;
or Gě Fēng holding the tally,
at whom the capital stayed its hands.
The Duke especially received a heroic spirit
concentrated from the mountains and peaks;
he had a majestic appearance and handsome looks,
with brows and eyes clear and bright.
Observing the tiger in the cage,
he was not startled even as a child;
weighing the elephant on the boat,
he could answer as soon as he could wear adult clothes.
As for wrestling tigers and tethering bears,
crushing stripes and smashing paws,
forgetting to return with the *Fánruò* bow,
bringing down geese and making apes wail,
thus his spirit covered Guānzhōng,
and his majesty extended beyond the River.
He began his career as a Clerk in the Headquarters of the General of the Guards,
then transferred to Consultant.
At the time the Dāngtú lost control
and the government was in the hands of powerful families,
it began with discussions of troops at Hángǔ,
and immediately the Battle of Hánlíng arose.
When the Grand Preceptor Hèbá Shèng acted as the Governor of Xījīng,
the Duke served as Acting Tally-holder, Champion General, and Area Commander of Fángchéng.
When Nányáng was lost,
he rolled up his armor and fled to Liáng.
Lè Yì was a traveler,
yet still thought of the road to Yàn;
Chén Zhěn was sorrowful,
ultimately longing for the sounds of Qín.
Fortunately, meeting with peaceful neighbors,
he returned to his former state;
he was appointed General of the Guards and Area Commander,
and was enfeoffed as the Founding Viscount of Āncháng County,
with a fief of three hundred households.
Hóngnóng was recovered,
and at Shāyuàn he brandished his blade;
he was promoted in rank to Marquis,
and his fief was increased to a total of one thousand one hundred households.
The jade tally of trust was then received by the *Sīxùn*,
and the grain-patterned jade disc was returned to the *Diǎnruì*.
With armored horses there was the Battle of Héqiáo,
and with halberd ships there were troops at Fénshuǐ;
he was appointed Governor of Jīngzhào.
Moving the people to the lower towns,
he did not emulate Biān Sháo;
riding horses at Zhāngtái,
he was not like Zhāng Chǎng.
He was promoted to Commandery Commander, Tally-holder, General of the Supporting Army, Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary, and Grand Area Commander.

Soon after, he was promoted to Commissioner with Special Powers, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Great General rank, Equal in Status to the Three Ceremonies, Minister of the Bureau of Officials, and Grand Rectifier of Dìngzhōu.
When reporting matters in the Five Sections,
he possessed the loyalty of Zhū Mù;
when evaluating people in the Nine Ranks,
he showed the integrity of Yáng Qiáo.
His title was changed to Marquis of Ānguó County,
with an increase in his fief to a total of one thousand four hundred households including the previous.
He was bestowed the surname Yǔwén
and his name was changed to Yuè.
The King of Hàn changed the clan of Lóu Jìng,
an act of great weight regarding the debate on the capital;
the Empress of Wèi changed the name of Chéng Yù,
a deep grace like upholding the sun.
He was promoted to Great General of Chariots and Cavalry with the opening of an office and Equal in Status to the Three Ceremonies,
with the additional rank of Palace Attendant.
Like Dòu Xiàn holding successive offices,
the precious tripod of the Shányú could be obtained;
like Zhāng Kuān securing his position,
the falling star of Wèi Qiáo could be recognized.
Controlling the seven woodworkers,
he managed the taxes of the hills and mounds;
as Controller of the Six Statutes,
he possessed the talent to balance the state’s administration.
Choosing the right people for office,
it reached its peak with him.
He was elevated to the rank of Duke
and enfeoffed in Wànnián County,
with a total of two thousand four hundred households including the previous.
He was appointed Regional Inspector of Lǒngzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Lǒngzhōu.
The roads of the Lǒng hills were distant,
and the Qín plains stretched far away;
like Dèng Zhònghuá who would not leave,
or Mǎ Wényuān who wished to return.
Soon he was appointed Regional Inspector of Liángzhōu and Governor-General of all military affairs in Héxī, Gān, and Guā.
The land was like a crouching dragon;
the city was like a flying bird.
The true records of Dùnhuáng
were clearly held in his heart;
the watchtowers and barriers of Yùmén
needed no labor of maps or drawings.
There were horses like sheep,
yet he did not bring them into his stable;
there was gold like grain,
yet he did not take it into his bosom.
The Pillar of State, Prince of Qí,
was the younger brother of the current Emperor.
Respectfully carrying out the military campaign
to punish the crimes at Héyáng,
he appointed the Duke as the Chief Administrator of the marching army,
to join the strategic planning within the headquarters.
For the management of the central army,
Wèi Jiàng had already been recommended;
as the assistant to the high minister,
Xún Lín was truly employed.
Comparing the Duke to them,
he had no shameful lack of virtue.

He was appointed Commissioner with Special Powers, Great General, and Grand Commander-in-Chief of the thirteen defense commands of Chóngdé, Ānyì, Jiànzhōng, Jiǔqū, Ānlè, Sānquán, Fúliú, Zhōuzhāng, Píngquán, Gù'ān, Mán, Tōng, and Gǔ; of the three prefectures of Xióng, Hé, and Zhōng; and of the ten garrisons of Huánglú, Qǐgǔ, Wángyàn, Gōngchāo, Qiānyáng, Wēnhú, Jiāohé, Dàlǐng, Bìyǔ, and Mùzhàsì, as well as the Defense Commander of Chóngdé.
In the superior lands of Yíyáng,
there were still troops of Qín;
before Mount Xióng'ěr,
he again encountered hidden ambushes.
Because of this, he linked camps at Hángǔ
and hunted on horseback at Líyáng;
his awe shook the lands between the two rivers,
and his fame surpassed the Three Jìn.
His title was changed to Duke of Ānpíng County.
The entire state of Huáiyīn
was the old home of Hán Xìn;
the ten thousand households of Hùyǒu
were the village of Chén Píng.
When the Duke returned in such fine clothing,
it was sufficient to be likened to them.
On the tenth day of the first month in the fourth year of Jiàndé,
he passed away at his private residence in Yǒngguì Lane, Cháng'ān,
at the age of sixty-four.
By imperial decree, he was posthumously awarded the military command of the five prefectures of Fū, Yán, Dān, Suí, and Héng, and the title of Regional Inspector of Fūzhōu.
He was given the posthumous name Duke Zhuāng,
which was according to ritual.
On the twenty-fourth day of the second month of that same year,
he was buried in Jíqiān Lane, Píngyuán Village, Jīngzhào.
Looking back with longing at the Northern Tombs,
the Grand Minister of War bestowed the grace of the seal ribbon;
at the funeral gift in the Western Capital,
the Marquis of Guànjūn received the ritual of an imperially decreed burial.
Alas, how sorrowful!
His heir, the Equal in Status to the Three Ceremonies, Yǎn,
served him in life according to ritual
and buried him in death according to ritual;
in loving his parents, he had the filial piety of Wáng Xiáng,
and with his siblings, he had the harmony of Jiāng Gōng.
The roots of all conduct
were complete in him.
Moreover, the pines and catalpas are deep and still,
and the blue stone tomb has already been sealed;
to signal the mound and hill,
a golden stone monument must be inscribed.
The inscription says:
The spirit of Huáyáng,
the ancestor from Lìshān.
In the phoenix fields, he assisted Zhōu;
at the Dragon Gate, he aided Yǔ.
The sun bathes in the deep pool;
the mountains float upon the sea shore.
Fǔ and Mù made the state a hegemon;
Yíngqiū was a joyous land.
Descended from this ancestral city,
inheriting from this king of the soil.
The fief was moved to Dōngwǔ,
following the lord to Ānyáng.
The principles of the central army,
the sharp edge of the General Who Guards the North.
The autumn wind hunts through the grass;
the lightning fire drives away the frost.
The Duke's magnificence,
a successor of upright character.
His appearance was like a towering hill;
his spirit was like a lofty wall.
His filial piety was of the highest virtue;
his loyalty could rectify and assist.
He did not neglect the horizontal zither,
nor did it interfere with his leaning over the desk.
Having been ranked among the Three Excellencies,
he also served as an assistant in the Six Offices.
Like Wèi Qīng receiving the decree,
or Hán Xìn ascending the platform.
The horse caves of the Great Wall,
the military enclosures of Guǎngwǔ.
The military officers committed no offenses;
the people in the camps did not suffer from cold.
He then employed the six strategies,
and then discussed the three plans.
The orientation of fortresses and ramparts,
the guest and host stars.
The sword rose like a submerged rhinoceros;
the bow opened like a hidden stone.
The ruler of Chǔ yielded in the alliance;
the lord of Qín returned the jade disc.
A hundred years of life are fragile;
a thousand fathoms of height are brought low.
The land of the feudal lords cracks;
the star of the frontier general falls.
Light chariots and cavalrymen,
dark armor and yellow-cypress coffins.
His altar is like the land of Qí;
his temple is like Tóngxiāng.
Inscribing his merit and praising his virtue,
the stele and gate-towers face each other.
— From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 904.
<Stele of the Great General of Zhōu, Sīmǎ Yì>
<Stele of the Great General of Zhōu, Sīmǎ Yì>
The Duke’s taboo name was Yì,
and his courtesy name was Zūnyìn;
he was a man from Wēn in Hénèi.
Long ago, by the command of Zhuānxū,
it began with the Southern Regulator managing the heavens;
among the descendants of Zhòng and Lí,
Xī and Hé were again appointed to manage the calendar.
When Xiàyáng went to Jìn,
he fled together with Suí Huì;
avoiding Qín at the Eastern Sea,
he went into seclusion with Lord Máo.
Later, when the metal element received the mandate,
the jade coffers moved south;
the imperial lineage reached the limits of the maps,
and the central court extended to the lands of the Yangtze River.
His great-grandfather was Chǔzhī,
the Jìn Tài fù, Lù shàng shū, and Yáng zhōu mù,
who was the second son of Kuàijī Wénxiào Wáng
and the younger brother of Yuánxiǎn.
After Yuánxiǎn was harmed
and at the beginning of Huán Xuán’s usurpation,
from the time he was a young child,
he lived as an exile, fishing and butchering.
By the roadside of Hénèi,
he held his sword and wailed aloud;
before the city of Dàijùn,
he offered mournful sacrifices to the spirits.
Men of integrity and ambition from the Jiāng and Huái regions,
and travelers in the wind and dust of the Rǔ and Yǐng rivers,
were moved by a single word from him,
and many came to rely on him.
Soon, clouds arose over Fùguī,
and stars appeared over Jīngyú;
Tàibái crossed the heavens,
and Chīyóu reflected across the fields.
The Gōng then gathered the remaining forces,
weeping tears of blood as he mounted the ramparts;
overlooking the pass of Wǔláo
and occupying the slopes of Chénggāo,
he led ten thousand households
to submit to the House of Wèi.
Wèi Míngyuán Huángdì
remotely appointed him Píng nán dà jiāng jūn and Jīng zhōu cì shǐ.
He inherited the title of Lángyá jùn wáng,
married the Hénèi Gōngzhǔ,
and was authorized to Chéngzhì,
following the protocol for honored guest states.
At that time, the Sòng troops were aggressive,
their banners and drums encroaching;
Hǔláo was not fortified,
and Jīnyōng had no reinforcements.
Wèi Tàiwǔ Huángdì appointed the Wáng as Shǐ chí jié, Shì zhōng, Ān nán dà jiāng jūn, and Kāi fǔ yí tóng sān sī,
granting him front and rear ceremonial music.
The great army set out,
determined to avenge the humiliation and shame;
he ascended the altar with a stirring heart,
and the three armies wept together.
Grain transported via the Huánghé
had already passed through Shímén;
with continuous banners at Báimǎ,
they were about to reach Yěbǎn.
Soon, signals rose in Yúnzhōng,
and beacon fires burned in Dàijùn;
he turned his banners south,
as the northern path was blocked.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Zhēng xī dà jiāng jūn, Dū dū of the ten provinces of Liáng, Yì, Qín, Níng, Jīng, Yǎn, Qīng, Yù, Yǐng, and Luò, Yáng zhōu mù, and Sī tú.
His posthumous name was Zhēn Wáng.
His grandfather was Jīnlóng,
enfeoffed as Lángyá Zhèn xī dà jiāng jūn, Yí tóng sān sī, and Lì bù shàng shū;
he was posthumously granted the title of Sī kōng
and the posthumous name Kāng Wáng.
His father was Yuè,
Zhèn nán jiāng jūn, Yù zhōu cì shǐ, and Yúyáng Zhuāng hóu.
While serving as Cì shǐ of Jīng and Hé,
he encountered a time of chaos and displacement;
conflict arose within the Xiāoqiáng,
and he met an untimely death.
The Gōng was born posthumously,
drifting through the midst of banditry and rebellion;
he was carried in swaddling clothes behind double walls,
and sheltered among the trees of deep mountains.
Just as Chéng Yīng hid Zhào Wǔ,
he served among the household retainers;
like Wáng Chéng hiding Lǐ Xiè,
he worked as a laborer in a wine market.
He suffered the loss of the Tài fū rén,
mourning on straw at the tomb
until the mourning period ended;
his body became emaciated,
exceeding the requirements of the mourning rites.
At the age of fifteen,
he began to manage the family affairs.
He carved into the pillars before the eaves
to retrieve the hidden books;
he cleared the pines from the stones
to find the old sword.
He began his career in the Sī tú fǔ as a Cān jūn,
and was appointed Zhōng jiān jiāng jūn and Yuán wài sǎn jì cháng shì.
During the many troubles of the Wèi House,
uprisings broke out everywhere;
north of Mèngjīn,
the royal domain was no more;
south of Sōngshān,
all was the front line of battle.
The Gōng proposed the Xiūwǔ,
establishing palisades in Wēnchéng;
Hángǔ Pass was sealed to the west,
and the Héqiáo was cut to the north.
Horses from the post stations
were all brought into Wǔchéng;
tax carts from a hundred miles around
were all delivered to Wēn xiàn.
Tàizǔ Wéndì established the capital in the Guān region,
managing affairs through smooth and difficult times;
he recruited the talented with ritual
and cherished those from afar with virtue.
Like Mǎ Wényuán choosing a lord,
he left Lǒngdǐ to submit himself;
like Dòu Zhōugōng entering the court,
he was in Héxī and received the imperial decree.
In the seventh year of Dàtǒng,
he was granted the titles of Píng dōng jiāng jūn and Běi Xúzhōu cì shǐ.
In the tenth year,
more than four thousand families of old loyalists from Hénèi
wished to demonstrate their loyalty
and waited for the Gōng to return in glory;
he was then appointed Shǐ chí jié and Hénèi tài shǒu,
with the added title of Qián jiāng jūn.
Expanding the borders of Huáizhōu,
two garrisons fled in haste;
fighting across Liǔquán,
three cities surrendered.
In the thirteenth year,
Tàizǔ summoned the generals from Shāndōng who had raised loyalist armies,
declaring that those who could lead their people into the Guān
would receive heavy rewards.
The Gōng was the first to arrive,
leading a thousand households;
though these were intended as his fief,
he firmly declined them.
Regarding the gifts of grain,
some he used to point to the granary for others;
for rewards of horses and cattle,
he shared them as if measuring out grain.
The Cháotíng considered Huáyáng to be the western limit
and the Hàn Shuǐ to flow east;
they lamented Mèng Dá’s desertion
and wondered at Liú Fēng’s failure of strategy.
In the first year of the Wèi Era,
he moved his garrison to Hànzhōng,
being appointed Lord of Báimǎ City
and Huáyáng jùn shǒu.
Formerly called Yàng,
now known as Shàngzhū;
mist settled on Bīngjǐng,
and rain ceased at Yúnmén.
In that year,
he was appointed Dà dū dū
with the added title of Sǎn jì cháng shì.
The Zhù guó and Shǔ guó gōng
opened the Jīnniú Road
and cleared the Mùmǎ Pass.
The Gōng rolled up his armor and set out for the northern frontier,
traveling through difficult terrain where carriages are suspended and horses bound;
thus his strategies were involved in Jiāméng,
and his merit reached Miánzhú.
He was enfeoffed as Lóngmén xiàn kāi guó zǐ and Púzhōu cì shǐ,
while also overseeing Xīnzhōu.
Soon he was appointed Shǐ chí jié, Jū qí dà jiāng jūn, Yí tóng sān sī, and Dà zhōng zhèng.
When the Great Zhōu received the Mandate
and Tiānbǎo was established,
because of the Gōng’s talent and reputation,
he remained a veteran official.
Thus, with a deep sense of righteousness in honoring his ancestors
and profound grace in continuing the broken lineage,
he was re-enfeoffed as Lángyá xiàn gōng,
with five hundred households.
He was then promoted to Piào qí dà jiāng jūn, Kāi fǔ yí tóng sān sī, Dū dū of Bāzhōu, and Bāzhōu cì shǐ.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
he was decreed to provide aid to Xìnzhōu.
The road to Yúfù was obstructed,
and he repeatedly repelled Cén Péng;
the waters of Jīngmén were swift,
nearly drowning Wú Hàn.
The Gōng was the first to ascend the Yuèxiá,
going straight up the Qútáng.
The Tiānzǐ, because the Gōng’s conduct was loyal and diligent
and his bearing upright and honest,
summoned him to be the Dà yù bó,
and soon transferred him to be the Dà yù zhèng,
with a fief of one thousand one hundred households.
As a close attendant in the pivotal organ,
he announced the Imperial edicts;
he was well-versed in the old regulations,
without peer in the palace.
In the fourth year,
the great army campaigned to the east.
The righteous troops led by His Lordship
first defended Zhǐguān.
He was appointed Area Commander of Huáizhōu Military Affairs and Regional Inspector of Huáizhōu.
He pitched tents at Yǎnshī
and pastured horses at Héyáng.
Though he engaged in battle at Fùpíng,
he had already linked camps at Guāndù.
In the fifth year,
an imperial decree recalled him,
and he was appointed Regional Inspector of Shǐzhōu.
Further campaigning against Xìnzhōu,
the rebels Shān Zhāng and Xún Bǎo-Yú relied on the precipitous terrain.
The gorge paths were only five feet wide,
and only passable by using ropes and cables.
At the hanging waters of Sānmén,
flying bridges were used for the crossing.
Soon after, like the wind bending the grass,
the valleys became quiet and the mountains empty.
In total, he subjugated eleven cities
and captured over nine thousand individuals.
The horses returned to Pínglè,
and the gold was delivered to the Shuǐhéng treasury.
In the second year of Tiānbǎo,
he was appointed Regional Inspector of Xìnzhōu and Area Commander of Xìnzhōu Military Affairs.
Departing Báidì in the morning,
he rested in Jiānglíng by evening.
His spirit stirred the troops of Bāqiū,
and his majesty alerted the garrison of Jiànpíng.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to Regional Inspector of Tóngzhōu.
The Pillar of State Duke of Yìzhōu,
who held the great importance of an Emperor’s son,
guarded the star of Tiānjǐng.
His pavilions were like those of Cóngtái,
and Mínshān was compared to Dàijùn.
His Lordship relied on heroic schemes
and consulted on far-reaching strategies;
thus he was personally involved in the merit of Wǔyáng
and achieved the height of favor like Chángpíng.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Ritual Aspect, Grand General, Grand Area Commander of Xīníngzhōu Military Affairs, and Regional Inspector of Xīníngzhōu.
Just as he was about to secure the Mò and Ruò rivers,
patrol Zāngkē,
meet the Marquis of Yèláng,
and practice the warfare of Kūnmí,
the flying kite fell into the water.
Mǎ Yuán left and did not return;
the Golden Horse galloped in light,
and Wáng Bāo went and did not come back.
Alas, how tragic!
He passed away on the tenth day of the first month of the seventh year
at the age of sixty-five.

An imperial decree posthumously awarded him the titles of Commissioner with Ritual Aspect, Grand General, Commander of Military Affairs for the Four Prefectures of Huái, Shào, Fén, and Jìn, and Regional Inspector of Huáizhōu.
His lady, the Princess of Xiāngchéng,
was the great-granddaughter of Emperor Xiàn of Wèi
and the youngest daughter of King Mù of Zhào.
The royal lady was solemn and respectful,
her pheasant-feathered robes following the ritual codes.
She was diligent in the Four Instructions
and as virtuous as the Three Stars,
shining with the virtue of Lónglǜ
and manifesting the prosperity of Píngyáng.
In life, she followed her husband’s rank;
in death, she was buried in the same tomb according to ritual.
On the twelfth day of the eighth month of the first year of Jiàndé,
they were buried together at Sānzhìyuán in Wǔgōng.
For a Grandee, the tomb is planted with cypresses;
for a Lord, the tumulus is higher than a parapet.
Oh, Lord Téng!
You have come to reside in this neighborhood.
An imperial decree posthumously titled him Duke Dìng,
as is the ritual.
His Lordship was naturally loyal and practiced filial piety,
possessing righteousness and harboring benevolence.
He was like a straight trunk of a thousand fathoms,
or clear waves over ten thousand acres.
He mastered the archery of Féng Méng
and the military texts of Lì Mù.
Through divination of the stars’ positions
and interpreting the auras of wind and rain,
he ensured his armies marched with discipline;
he was truly a general favored by Heaven.
As for official files and documents,
they were never cluttered or blocked.
While war horses galloped,
it did not hinder his ease.
He was enough to make the Four Peaks loftier
and the Three Terraces brighter.
He served in court for forty-one years
and personally experienced over a hundred battles.
In total, he served in four commanderies
and passed through eight provinces.
He never concerned himself with the accumulation of wealth;
he departed just as he first arrived.
With a thousand acres of bamboo in Wèinán,
he feared even more the state of being full.
With two hectares of fields in Chíyáng,
he always thought of contentment.
On the day of his death,
his family had no surplus wealth.
With plain carriages and white horses,
his rooms were narrow and the paths rugged.
Between the yellow-wood coffin and black armor,
his courtyards were cramped and humble.
An imperial decree ordered the Ministry of Works
to build his final resting chamber.
Zhū Yì had no place for sacrificial offerings,
so the Hàn Emperor granted gold.
Chén Biǎo’s wife and children stood exposed,
so the King of Wú opened a residence for them.
Alas, how tragic!
His heir, Kǎn,
is filial to the family and loyal to the state,
spreading his name and honoring his parents.
Therefore, this great stele is inscribed,
fearing the change of mountains into valleys.
Planting pines and cypresses,
he cannot bear to see them wither.
The inscription reads:
Revering the celestial phenomena,
balancing the order and respectfully receiving the guests.
*Shǎoliáng* rushed toward splendor,
the land entered *Xiánqín*.
The clan was exterminated like *Xīngmǎ*,
writings reached their end at the capture of the *Lín*.
The jade mirror marked the beginning,
and the Metal Element was established.
*Xiàngpǔ* opened the pass,
*Lóngshā* established the watch.
*Shàngsǎn Shí* arose,
the waters of *Héyáng* battled.
Five horses floated south,
three stars lodged in the east.
The *Tàifù* acted as governor,
possessing the lands of the *Jiāng* and *Tuó*.
The *Sītú* fled the chaos,
receiving mandates by the *Jīng* and *Hé*.
In the south, laboring at the chariot wheel,
yet still thinking of pillowing on a spear.
Dragon steeds covered the fields,
azure rhinoceroses braved the waves.
In the final years of *Zhuānghóu*,
the mechanisms of disaster met.
The descendants left by Lord *Dàn*,
were carried through rugged paths.
Hidden in the mountains like *Zhào Wǔ*,
sheltered in a house like *Lǐ Xiè*.
*Wǔ Yuán*'s path was obstructed,
*Yàn Dān*'s road was far.
Fleeing south to the *Chǔ* fortress,
avoiding the north at the *Qín* bridge.
Waters flowed up the mounds,
cold winds crossed the *Liáo*.
Having the merit of a *Dūhù*,
more esteemed than a *Piáoyáo*.
Carrying books and mounting a horse,
practicing rituals while joining the military.
Battle formations of the Six *Jiǎ*,
military divinations of the Eight Winds.
A precious sword hidden in the pines,
a carved bow for shooting willows.
Sincere like *Jiǎ Fù*,
yielding like Lord *Lián*.
Eight wings frequently flew,
six cycles repeatedly held.
Brave in this benevolence and righteousness,
practicing this leniency and severity.
Holding the seal as the mountains opened,
the *Chénlí* bandits became silent.
Taking armor without mounds,
equalizing fields without well-systems.
Splendid merit was rewarded with a title,
a supreme general was granted office.
Receiving decrees in the army,
ascending the altar beyond the borders.
Just as they slaughtered at *Cānhé*,
they further battled at *Gāolán*.
Poisonous waters of the *Yú* River,
disastrous vapors of the *Bódào*.
The land lost its *Dūwèi*,
the shoals grieved for the *Shǐjūn*.
The valleys are cold without the sun,
the mountains are empty, filled with clouds.
The northern wind blows the funeral banners,
autumn rains weep for the army.
Sacrificial offerings set in pairs,
inscription banners displayed twice.
Sharing a grave by the *Qìn* water,
a joint tomb at *Píngyáng*.
The grieving heir,
wailing with nowhere to appeal.
Grief greater than the wind-blown branches,
sorrow deeper than the frost and dew.
What era is it since then?
How many years have passed from this?
The *Qílín* desire to fight,
the *Huábiǎo* burn within.
The terrain rises like a tower,
the heart of the pine is a round canopy.
Vast are the mounds and graves,
of generations of heroes and sages.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 904.
<Spirit Road Stele of the *Zhōu* Pillar of State General *Tuòbá Jiǎn*>
<Spirit Road Stele of the *Zhōu* Pillar of State General *Tuòbá Jiǎn*>
It is heard that when *Fàngxūn* was established, *Xīhé* rose;
when *Chónghuá* ascended, the *Yuánkǎi* were employed.
Thinking of the many august gentlemen,
they completed the merit of the *Xībó*;
when eminent virtue is brilliantly illustrated,
then the conquest of *Náncháo* is settled.
Thus it is known that unless there is a sage, the ruler is not sustained;
unless there is a ruler, the sage cannot govern.
As for a lord and minister of one virtue,
opening and enriching the heart,
this was seen in Lord *Wén* of *Chāngníng*.
The Duke’s taboo name was *Jiǎn*,
his style name was *Qìngmíng*,
a man of *Gāolù* in *Héngzhōu*.
The star of the Heavenly Grandson of the Northern Peak,
the state of the Imperial Son of the *Yàn* River,
hence he possessed many extraordinary qualities,
and was very abundant in refined spirit.
At *Gāoquè*, he looked toward the south,
two kings rode side by side;
at the Great Wall, the roots were pulled,
ten clans divided the source.
His great-great-grandfather
was the *Tàiwèi* and King of *Běipíng*.
He illustriously assisted five rulers,
and harmoniously regulated the hundred offices;
*Héng* and *Wèi* followed him,
*Huái* and *Yí* were governed by him.
His grandfather *Bào*
was the *Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn* and *Cìshǐ* of *Héngzhōu*.
Serving as the governor of *Chángshān*,
he was not without the tokens of succession;
as the *Lóngxiāng* commanding the army,
it was like the title for pacifying *Wú*.
His father *Yù*
was only twenty years old
when his glory ended and he resigned his seal.
The Duke stored wisdom through the Five Constants,
and derived virtue from the Six Energies.
Following Heaven, he spurred his horse and held the spirit;
descending like a deity, *Qiān* and *Láng* corresponded to the signs.
With a heart straightforward toward all things,
he was tranquil in water or fire;
having no debt to Heaven,
he did not fear thunder or lightning.
Wealth and honor were achieved by himself,
not relying on the words of *Táng Jǔ*;
his fame and reputation were known,
requiring no effort from the recognition of *Lǐ Yīng*.
At the age of eighteen,
he entered service as a *Yuánwài Sànqì Shìláng*.
Soon he was appointed *Qīngchē Jiāngjūn* and *Yǔlín Jiān*.
*Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì* drove the heavenly net,
encompassing heroes and outstanding men.
Selecting the Duke's talent and virtue,
he illustriously assisted in the Central Secretariat.
When *Zhūgé Liàng* returned to the west,
the Jade Rampart achieved the enterprise of the Three Kingdoms;
when *Guǎn Yíwú* entered service,
*Kuíqiū* saw the merit of unifying the realm.
For the cunning *Qiāng* of *Tiānshuǐ*
and the many bandits of *Yúyáng*,
he was moved to be the *Chángshǐ* and *Fángchéng Dàdūdū* of *Qínzhōu*,
and enfeoffed as the Founding Count of *Xìndōu Xiàn*.
In the third year,
when the masses swarmed like ants in *Huázhōu*,
and lives were lost at the fortresses,
with flags scattered and chariots in chaos,
he crossed the river on ice.
The Chancellor and the Grand Minister of the Mobile Administration granted him the Title of *Jiǎjié Fǔjūn*,
and he served as the *Cìshǐ* of *Huázhōu*.
In the first year of *Dàtǒng*,
he was appointed *Chíjié* and *Cìshǐ* of Western *Xiàzhōu*,
with the additional title of *Sànqì Chángshì*.
*Zhìzhī* clutching his horse,
was like hearing of the battle of *Gěng Bǐng*;
the *Chányú* wishing to know him,
was like fearing the awe of *Wáng Shāng*.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to *Shǐchíjié*, *Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn*, *Dūdū* of All Military Affairs in Northeast Three *Xiàzhōu*, and *Cìshǐ* of Western *Xiàzhōu*,
increasing his fief by a thousand households,
and changing his title from Count to Duke.
Subsequently, the *Jiāng* and *Hàn* were far away,
and there was silence in administrative unity.
The Dilu horse of the Lord of *Shǔ*,
had not yet emerged from the waters of *Tánxī*;
the flying pheasant of the King of *Qín*,
still faced the city of *Nányáng*.
In the sixth year,

the Duke was appointed Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Twelve Prefectures including the three Jīng, two Xiāng, Nán Yōng, Píng, Xìn, Jiāng, Suí, Yǐng, and Zhè, Inspector of Jīngzhōu, and Vice President of the Branch Department of State Affairs for the Southeast Route.
In the neighborhood of Chǔchéng,
there were indeed instances of yielding land;
when facing the camps of the Wú people,
there was no harm in gifting medicine.
Within the subordinate cities of his jurisdiction,
there was a legal dispute among the people;
the Duke then gathered the civil and military officials,
and bared his torso to punish himself.
When brothers would not yield to each other,
Yánshòu blamed himself;
when officials or citizens committed errors,
Wēngguī took the culpability upon himself.
The Emperor marveled at this,
sending a sealed letter of commendation,
and bestowing gifts and currency;
royal envoys arrived in close succession.
The Grand Chancellor wrote in a letter:
“Such beautiful deeds
have never before been witnessed or heard of.
My admiration and praise are boundless,
and thus I have sent a special envoy.”
The Duke was skilled at governing and leading,
and excelled in receiving and guiding others;
no talent was wasted in the mountains or marshes,
and bribery was not practiced.
He showed people a sincere heart,
and met them with a kind countenance;
thieves did not dare to arise,
and the people could not bear to deceive him.
Thereupon, the officers and elders at the south of the provincial city
built the Pavilion of Pure Virtue
and inscribed the Eulogy of the Worthy Minister.
When Dù Zhènnán served as governor,
a stele was erected in his era;
when General of Chariots and Cavalry Dòu led the troops,
a stone was carved during his lifetime.
Comparing them to today,
who were they to stand alone!
At that time, the population increased daily,
and the wilderness was entirely cultivated;
flowers and fruits spread in abundance,
and the common people were prosperous and joyful.
However, there was a fear that the robes of state had deficiencies
waiting for the Duke to mend,
and the seasoning of the tripod was not yet harmonized,
requiring the Duke to correct it.
Thus, the hopeful people of Hànyīn
and the fine talents of Jīngnán
all submitted petitions to the palace,
signing their names in unison to beg him to stay.
Just as Hénèi begged for Kòu Xún,
they felt even more ashamed to have the Duke leave to meet the Emperor;
as Jiāozhōu requested Shì Xiè,
they again composed a memorial.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Specially Advanced with the Three Revisions.
In the twelfth year,
he was appointed Minister of the Grand Branch Department of State Affairs
and continued to serve as Marshal to the Grand Chancellor.
Because the Duke’s discernment and judgment were strict and clear,
and his integrity was pure and frugal,
the Duke’s name was changed to Jiǎn,
and his courtesy name to Qìngmíng.
It did not concern the writing of the moon,
nor did it wait for the reading of a stele;
fortunately, the thousand acres were no different,
and the two mountains were not abandoned.
In the thirteenth year,
he was granted the title Opening the Office,
with other offices remaining as before.
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Vice President of the Right of the Department of State Affairs,
added the title of Palace Attendant,
and promoted to General of Agile Cavalry.
Occupying the position of the upper stars in enforcing the law,
and holding the rank of Wénchāng,
with the Duke’s talent and reputation,
he possessed both.
In the fifteenth year,

he was re-appointed Vice President of the Branch Department of State Affairs for the Southeast Route, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Fifteen Prefectures, and Acting Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In the sixteenth year,
the Grand Chancellor gathered sixteen armies
to pacify Héluò.
The Duke again took command of his division
and participated in the planning within the command tent.
High-ranking staff for the hegemon were selected,
and the Duke was appointed Chief Secretary.
In that year,
he was added as Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Thirty-Six Prefectures of the Southern Route,
with other offices as before.
The scholars of Nányáng
again encountered Wáng Jī;
the ceremonial robes of Zhānghuá
once more welcomed Guō Hè.
In the past, regarding the plan to attack Shǔ,
Zhāng Yí and Qín Zhāo reached an agreement;
regarding the benefit of pacifying Wú,
Yáng Hù and Jìn Wǔ shared the same intent.
When Tàizǔ first pacified Chéngdū,
he immediately had the ambition to take Jiānglíng;
the Duke secretly presented his strategy,
which coincided with the profound intentions.
Provisions had long been accumulated,
and siege ladders and rams were prepared.
In one battle, they captured Yān and Yǐng;
in a second battle, they burned Yīlíng,
and subsequently swept through the three Jīng regions.
This was also the Duke’s achievement.
A decree rewarded him with three hundred slaves.
Tàizǔ wrote to the Duke:
“Because of the plan you established,
the result was exactly as planned.”
The Duke then personally garrisoned Jiānglíng
to bring peace to the Shǔ region.
In the second year of Later Wèi,
his title was changed to Founding Duke of Chāngníng Commandery in Wǔchuān.
The residents of Yuèyáng
were not only for the enfeoffment of Jǐng Dān;
the households of Qūnì
were not only for the state of Chén Píng.
In that year,
he was appointed Grand General.
During the Tàihé period,
Cáo Zhēn received the patent within the office;
at the end of Yuánfēng,
Wèi Qīng was appointed within the army.
Comparing the Duke to these examples,
he has more than enough honor.
The decree said:
“The Wú people have not yet submitted,
and your assistance in planning is required;
now let the troops of the King of Liáng
be under your command.”
In the third year,
he was added as Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Fifty-Three Prefectures of the Southeast Route,
and his fief was increased by ten thousand households.
When the Zhōu revolution occurred,
the bright residence of the mandate was established;
he served as the assistant to the Celestial Official,
and harmonized the governance of the state.
In the first year,
he was appointed Junior Minister of State.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
he served as Inspector of Pǔzhōu and Overseer of the Military of the Six Defenses.
In the fourth year,
he governed Xiāngzhōu,
and was appointed Grand General Pillar of State,
with other offices as before.
His rank rose to that of the Four Peaks,
and his status leveled the Six Treasuries.
Is his merit not weightier than Zhāoyáng,
and his name higher than Cài Cì?
Governing fifty prefectures,
his influence spread for thousands of miles;
he uprooted the garden mallows to discourage competition with the people,
remained free of the three delusions, and refused bribes in awareness of the “four knowings.”
Within a single room,
it was not without pure emptiness;
his daily sustenance
was but three cups.
The decree bestowed one thousand segments of silk
and two thousand bushels of grain and wheat.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
he served as Inspector of Shànzhōu and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Eight Prefectures and Twenty Defenses,
was relieved of his post as Jīngzhōu General-in-Chief,
with all other offices as before.
The road passed through Wángguān,
and the city overlooked the river bend;
the garrison cleared the area west of Shàn,
and he looked with respect at the shade of the pear tree.
The fatigue of leading the region was great,
and overwork led to illness.
In the fourth year of Tiānhé,
he resigned due to illness and returned to the old capital,
passing away at his private residence
at the age of seventy-eight.
The Imperial Carriage visited in mourning,
the bells were stilled and music ceased;
he was bestowed with the dragon banner of nine tassels
and escorted by the cavalry of the Three Rivers.

A decree posthumously appointed him as Grand Guardian and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Ten Prefectures—Liáng, Xià, Líng, Yín, Cháng, Yuán, Hé, Shàn, Gān, and Guā—and Inspector of Liángzhōu.
His posthumous name was Wén.
The Duke's appearance was as imposing as a towering peak,
his spirit open and noble,
standing elegantly like a jade mountain,
rising straight like a tall pine.
The boundaries of his misty depths were undiscoverable,
and the surges of his river-like character were immeasurable.
In his youth, he suffered the bitterness of mourning;
he completed his mourning period in the mountains.
The cypress trees withered as he clung to them;
the beasts died as they neared the pines.
He served the state with full loyalty
and devoted his utmost effort to governance;
though his gate was as busy as a market,
his heart remained as calm as water.
With his brilliant strategies and secret plans,
the hundred officials looked up to him;
through his loyalty and integrity,
the enlightened sovereign held him in high esteem.
As for the divination of Yīnyáng of Fēng Hòu,
the measurements of the stars of Lì Mù,
the military treatises of Wèi Gōngzǐ,
and the archery methods of Lǐ Jiàngjūn,
there were none he did not memorize in his heart
and apply for the needs of the time.
In his daily life and personal effects,
he sometimes used cloth blankets and a pine bed;
upon his dining table,
there were nothing more than mulberry cups and stone vessels.
In his final instructions regarding his burial,
he desired nothing lavish;
gifts and shrouds from both public and private sources
were not to be accepted.
He requested only to be laid by the side of Tàizǔ’s mausoleum,
never forgetting his service to the lord.
Dūn and his brothers were all of the highest nature;
they observed the mourning period with excellence,
crying in longing by the tomb
and following his last instructions.
Thus, the tomb of Wèi Qīng
still accompanies the mausoleum of Hàn Wǔ;
the grave of Guǎn Zhòng
joins the tomb of Qí Huán.
In the sixth year of Tiānhé,
the Emperor, seeing that the world was not yet at peace
and the three regions stood like the legs of a tripod,
cherished the ambition of employing generals
and thought of the officials at the borders.
Having already had his portrait painted in the Yún Tái,
he then inscribed his name in the Lín Gé,
and further posthumously honored the Duke as the Duke of the State of Guài,
with a fief of five thousand households.
Honoring him among the deceased lords,
the ritual reached the very spirit and soul;
twice the funeral banners were altered,
and grace was abundantly bestowed upon his tomb.
While the Duke lived, the people held him in affection;
after his death, he is remembered with longing.
On auspicious days and fine hours,
sacrifices are made in the suburbs and fields.
Six hundred and ninety-seven people, including the Yí tóng Zhào Chāo,
submitted a petition to establish a temple
and requested to display his achievements at the Xiàng Wèi gates;
an imperial decree granted this.
With cinnamon pillars and apricot beams,
green steps and azure lattice windows,
songs are performed and dances gathered,
with phoenix canopies and rainbow garments.
The clouds depart as he is escorted from the southern bank;
the rain falls as the east wind blows.
Thus we know that in front of Hànyáng Commandery,
it is not only the temple of Wǔ Hòu that stands;
and beneath the walls of Línzī,
it is not only the shrine of Luán Gōng that remains.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus the inscription says:
The Way encountered the hexagrams of Zhūn and Bō;
the era belonged to clouds and thunder.
The axis of the earth turned to the left;
the gate of heaven opened in the north.
Accommodating carriages in the Zhōu court,
tethering horses at the Qín terrace.
Regulating the seven celestial bodies,
he responded to the three powers of heaven, earth, and man.
His illustrious ancestors harmonized the world;
for nine generations they were the pillars and beams.
Talent was found during a hunt;
the worthy was sought in a dream.
Assisting in the administration of the "cloud officials";
planning and recording under the "phoenix offices."
Laws were set for the imperial clan;
jade tablets were assigned for the duties and tributes.
It was only through his inherited virtue
that he truly possessed a heroic spirit.
His stature was mapped to the Big Dipper;
his countenance was surrounded by the Pivot Star.
In his youth, he was dedicated to his studies;
as a child, he mastered the classics.
Like Xìnlíng leaving the seat on the left vacant;
like Duàn Gànmù sharing the courtyard.
His loyalty and filial piety were pure and deep;
his pivotal actions were thorough and discreet.
Like Kǒng Guāng who remained silent;
like Cáo Shān who made no errors.
Warming the mat and fanning the pillow;
attending to his parents' countenances and pleasing them at their knees.
Fish were startled in the frozen pond;
bamboo shoots emerged in the cold forest.
Solemn were his wind-like policies;
profound was the capacity of his character.
Upright like the enduring bamboo;
warm like the auspicious jade.
His purity needed no water to be seen;
his clarity needed no candle to be raised.
He wished for his horses to be like sheep;
his gold was regarded as no more than grain.
As a top general, he achieved promotion;
as the commander-in-chief, he brought order.
Three victories at Xiàyáng;
a single action at Yílíng.
Leaning on the carriage rail to pacify Qí;
crossing the river to enter Chǔ.
The tripod returned to the rightful house;
the bells returned to the Dà lǚ pitch.
The six ministers all attended to their duties;
he presided over the Ministry of Heaven.
Serving as a regional chief in the manner of the Two Nán;
his governance was truly like the shade of the pear tree.
The pure wind has its odes;
the green bamboo is heard in poetry.
With the scroll of posthumous honors,
he surpassed all as the teacher of the Emperor.
Formerly he served in the orchid garden;
now he rests in the apricot forest.
In life and death, through distance and closeness,
his single-mindedness never wavered.
The wind and clouds gather in sorrow;
the mountain barriers are cloaked in continuous gloom.
The fields around the mausoleum are silent;
the path through the pines is deeply cold.
The mound of Xià Yīng;
the grave of Qiáo Xuán.
A horse is seen after a thousand years;
a carriage turns back after three steps.
To the left, there is no Chánglè Palace;
in front, it is not the armory.
Looking directly at the tall stele,
the grief of the traveler increases.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 905.
〈Spirit Way Stele of the Zhōu Pillar of State Grand General Hégān Hóng〉
〈Spirit Way Stele of the Zhōu Pillar of State Grand General Hégān Hóng〉
The Duke’s taboo name was Hóng,
and his courtesy name was Guǎnglüè.
He was a native of Chángchéng County, Yuánzhōu.
His original surname was Tián.
When the guest of Yú was in his position,
it was based on the custom of yielding;
when the phoenixes flew together,
it continued in the state of the kin and the worthy.
Discussing the achievements of successive generations,
there is a temple in Díchéng;
recording the beginning of the family’s relocation,
there is a stele in Chánglíng.
Furthermore, in submitting a memorial at the Gāo Temple,
he faced the Hàn Wáng in a small carriage;
sacrificing to the birds at Liáochéng,
he drove away the Yàn general at the great mountain.
During the Duke’s month of prenatal education,
the virtue of the year was in Yín;
at the time of his birth,
the star essence emerged from the Pleiades.
Thus, a tree grew in the moon;
as a child, he knew how to speak wisely.
Melons floated upon the water,
yet in his youth, he did not engage in play.
Receiving the book from Huángshí,
his intent was on the plans of a king;
brandishing a sword like the white ape,
his heart was set on the utility of a hegemonic state.
During the *Yǒng'ān* era of *Wèi*,
serving as a Commander of Cadets,
he returned to the city of *Yuánzhōu*
and received authority from the Prince of *Lóngxī*.
At that time, *Luòyì* was in a state of chaos and displacement,
and those in power were under perilous pressure;
rites, music, and military expeditions
did not originate from the Son of Heaven;
raising the worthy and punishing the violent
truly rested with powerful ministers.
*Tàizǔ*, Emperor *Wén*, first founded his hegemonic achievements,
initially laboring for the royal house,
feeding horses and reviewing chariots,
and vowing to the troops at *Tàiyuán*.
The Duke grasped his sword at the camp gate,
planning roughly for the contemporary world.
As *Suí Hé* arrived from afar,
it truly relieved the worries of the *Hàn* Emperor;
as *Xǔ Yōu* came by night,
it immediately secured the legacy of the King of *Cáo*.
In the *Yǒngxī* era,
he first welcomed Emperor *Wǔ* of *Wèi* into the Pass
and was enfeoffed as the Founding Viscount of *Chúnyīn Xiàn*,
with a fief of five hundred households.
*Tàizǔ* bestowed his own iron armor upon the Duke,
saying:
"If the world is settled,
bring this armor back to show me."
A fine sword of *Báishuǐ*
was given to *Chén Chǒng* upon leaving the court;
a good black horse
was given to *Lǐ Zhōng* upon the army's return.
Both are gifts of carriages and robes,
sufficient to be considered of the same class.
In the third year of *Dàtǒng*,
he was transferred to Commander-in-Chief
and promoted to the rank of Duke.
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs in *Yuánzhōu*, and Governor of *Yuánzhōu*.
An immortal returning again,
re-entering the city of *Guìyáng*;
the dragon-seed returning home,
seeking the road to *Báishā* once more.
The Duke thus wore brocade,
and his home village honored him.
Attending *Tàizǔ*,
he fought at *Héqiáo*,
recovered *Hóngnóng*,
broke the siege of *Huàshān*,
and leveled the formation at *Shāyuàn*;
he surely achieved great merit
and often received special rewards.
When *Tàizǔ* was in *Tóngzhōu*,
civil and military officials gathered,
and he issued an order, saying:
"If everyone put forth their heart as *Hégān Hóng* does,
how could the world not be settled early?"
He was then appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and *Yǐtóng Sānsī*.
In the first year of Former *Wèi*,
he was transferred to General of Agile Cavalry and opened an office.
*Qílián* was still far away,
yet he immediately received the title of Marquis of *Guànjūn*;
the sandy desert was not yet opened,
yet he was granted the office of *Chángpíng*.
*Xiāo Sháo*, the Governor of *Xìnzhōu* of *Liáng*, and *Qiáo Yān*, the Governor of *Níngzhōu*,
still resided in *Yǒng'ān*
and raised troops at *Yúyáng*.
The Duke received orders for the central army
and sped down the rapids,
consequently setting out from *Báidì* in the morning
and lodging at *Jiānglíng* in the evening;
the apes' cries were not startled,
and the cock's crow signaled the pacification.
The *Qiāng* rebels in *Xīpíng*
originally had the courage of *Yúyáng*;
the *Dī* rebels in *Fèngzhōu*
again practiced the spirit of *Qiúchí*.
The Duke pushed his vanguard straight ahead,
white blades crossing before him;
deciding a thousand deaths in one,
the fierce bandits mostly collapsed.
His body was struck by over a hundred arrows,
with nine wounds that pierced flesh and broke bone;
his horse was struck by ten spears;
the victory report was placed on his armor,
and the court considered him valiant.
Tight are the hemp shoes,
*Wèi* has the song of leaving the old;
the fallen dew is heavy,
*Zhōu* received the mandate of renewal.
He was then promoted to the rank of Duke of *Yànmén Jùn*,
with his total household fief reaching two thousand seven hundred.
In the first year of *Bǎodìng*,
he was appointed Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs in *Mǐnzhōu*, and Governor of *Mǐnzhōu*.
The flowing water at *Lóngtóu*
stretching one's gaze toward *Qín* Pass;
the *Éméi* Mountains above the river
still connecting to the *Shǔ* Road.
The Duke did not send personal letters
nor did he burn official candles.
Beasts carried one another across the river;
insects held each other in their mouths to leave the border.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Grand General,
his other offices remaining as before.
*Wèi Qīng* received his edict
before entering *Yùmén* Pass;
*Dòu Xiàn* was at his post
still below *Yānshān*.
As for this appointment of the Duke,
he had no cause for shame in his virtue.
The *Hún* king rebelled
and obstructed our western frontier;
the *Dàngqiāng* chiefs fled
and the buffer states wavered in loyalty.
The Duke received the sacrificial meat at the altar,
his auxiliary army raided from afar,
raising banners at *Lónghù*
and tethering horses at *Gānsōng*.
Twenty-five kings
saw their flags fall and their wheel-tracks in chaos;
seventy-six palisades
fled like quails and scurried like pheasants.
Having received rewards for carrying out orders,
he then enjoyed the music of the returning army.
In the second year of *Tiānhé*,
he was sent on a southern expedition
with a million armored troops,
vessels stretching for a thousand *lǐ*;
the water rose at the source of the river,
and *Hǎiruò* rode the current.
In the city of *Chuánguān*,
they nested in high places and hung cooking pots;
the *Wú* soldiers were skilled on the water
and drove warships for a long distance;
with wind-borne ash and fire arrows,
they suddenly overran the city.
The Duke commanded the army with a white feather
and crossed the water with red silk;
for over seventy days,
he only then was able to undress.
Because the court of *Zhōu* took *Xiàyáng* like *Jìn*,
it first practiced the policy of destroying *Guó*;
as *Qín* opened *Wǔsuì*,
it began the strategy of swallowing *Hàn*.
Therefore, messengers were sent to summon the Duke
to make him the Lord of *Rénshòu* City.
The *Qí* generals *Duàn Xiàoxiān* and *Hǔlǜ Míngyuè*
led armies to settle *Lóng*
as support for *Yíyáng*.
The Duke stood with his back to the *Luò* River and faced Mount *Xióng*,
arraying the central army and spacing out the vanguard;
taking the opportunity in a single battle,
*Yíyáng* surrendered.
His fief was increased by five hundred households
and he was promoted to Pillar State Grand General,
according to the records of the Minister of Merit.
In the first year of *Jiàndé*,
he was appointed Grand Minister of Works.
In the second year,
he was transferred to Junior Guardian.
Among the three ranks of the *Jī* court,
the Junior Guardian was in front;
among the five officials of the *Yánzhèng*,
the Winter Official was to the north.
Receiving honored appointments repeatedly,
this is what is called being worthy and capable.
In the third year,
he was appointed Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs in the six provinces of *Xiāng*, *Yǐng*, *Chāng*, *Fēng*, *Táng*, and *Cài*, and Governor of *Xiāngzhōu*.
Between the *Jiāng* and *Hàn* rivers,
the chickens and dogs were not startled;
below *Fán* and *Xiāng*,
there were even more officials' hats and carriages.
Soon, the Three *Xiāng* were distant,
and occasionally a *fú* bird entered;
the Five Creeks were low and damp,
and sometimes a kite was seen flying.
His old illness increased,
and he died in the provincial garrison.
The Son of Heaven painted the Hall of *Língyān*,
remembering the old ministers;
he left the *Pínglè* Palace,
truly thinking of the worthy tutor.
There was an edict to posthumously award him certain titles,
as is the ritual.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month of the fourth year, he was returned for burial at *Zhànshān* in *Gāopíng* of *Yuánzhōu*.
The black armor of the tributary states,
light carriages and armored soldiers,
all followed the ritual for *Huò* the Agile Cavalry General
and the burial of General *Wèi*.
Oh, how grand!
The Duke entered government service forty-five years ago,
and personally experienced one hundred and six battles.
His body was pierced and wounded by blades,
more severely than Cáo Cān;
scraping the bone to apply medicine,
his experiences were as numerous as those of Guān Yǔ.
Yet his spirit was resolute and brave,
and his appearance was profound and heroic.
In serving his parents, he had no secrets and committed no offenses.
In learning, he did not specialize in the Classics,
but skimmed through various books;
in military matters, he did not merely follow the ancients,
but naturally attained mastery of strategy.
The *Qīngwū* divinations of the *jiǎ* and *yǐ* cycles,
the *Báimǎ* changes of the stars and constellations,
the calculations of the Nine Palaces,
the risings and fallings of the Three Gates,
the archery methods of the Heavenly Arc,
and the encampment diagrams of the Supreme One—
all were recited and held in his heart,
as clear as pointing to his own palm.
In capturing the troops of the Qīngdù,
he had many secret plans;
in burning the grain at Wūcháo,
he originally lacked no stratagem.
The retreat of the Xīlíng rebels
could be known by counting on his fingers;
the return of the Nánjùn troops
was awaited by marking the spot with a pole.
He often wished to strike the golden drum to question the King of Wú,
and to carry the carved halberd to return to the land of Qí;
having ambitions unfulfilled,
he died with loyalty and integrity.
His heir-son Gōng and others,
whose filial piety is pure and deep,
observed mourning beyond the requirements of ritual.
Facing his straw-mat sleeping quarters,
the catalpa trees felt a chill;
hearing their sorrowful weeping,
the nesting birds descended at night.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus the inscription says:
Where the Tiānqí waters meet,
and the Rìguān mountains connect.
With strong troops in Eastern Chǔ,
and land far into Western Yàn.
The five ministers were all upright,
and the three kings were equally virtuous.
The spiritual dragon rose again,
and the fire-elephants burned once more.
From the virtue of Heaven,
down to the ancestors and the father.
The Great Peak sent down its spirit,
giving birth to Shēn and Fǔ.
A pillar and beam of the Northern Gate,
clouds and rain of the Western Province.
His bravery awed the city of Yàn,
and his name was inscribed on the columns of Hàn.
When the Duke first wore the blue collar of youth,
his spirit was praised by the world.
He was not startled by fierce beasts,
and could answer domestic birds.
In swordplay, he studied a thousand schools;
in books, he observed six generations.
He exhausted his loyalty and integrity,
and never strayed from respect and love.
Then he counted the military resources,
and held the military tallies.
Pouring sand to form ramparts,
gathering stones to create diagrams.
Wind and clouds, favorable and contrary;
camp formations, solitary and empty.
Spiritual rain and the sounding of gongs,
signal fires at Fēihú.
Huáiyīn received the commission,
the General of Chariots and Cavalry ascended the platform.
The Duke served as a High General,
having such colleagues.
Going down the river to burn Chǔ,
ascending the land to swallow Hán.
Presenting merits at the jade table,
deciding strategies at the pearl tray.
Heaven has three tiers,
and the Duke received its mandate.
The state has six ministers,
and the Duke followed its administration.
The stars of the Terrace shone together,
and the Courtyard of Sophora reflected again.
Assisting in the Seven Virtues,
and planning with the Eight Authorities.
His belly was full of spirit,
and his heart opened like a bright mirror.
Like Fùbō receiving the sacrificial meat,
and the Tower Ships being pushed by the wheel.
The eastern road was not followed,
and from the southern expedition, he did not return.
For drinking cinnabar, there is a well;
for pouring at the spring, there are no chrysanthemums.
His achievements remain in the Willow Forest,
but his body lies in the fir wood coffin.
Moving the mat for reburial,
carrying the coffin through the mountains.
Straw effigies by the Lǒng Waters,
sorrowful dirges by the Long Wall.
The mountains are like Běimáng,
the trees are like those of Dōngpíng.
Stones rise at the Pine Gate,
and gold is born in the words of the stele.
Vague and distant are the mountains and rivers,
lonely and desolate is the heir-son.
Weeping blood and walking on foot,
rushing over a thousand miles.
The River of Filial Piety dried up first,
and the Clouds of Sorrow immediately rose.
The numbers of the generations mark life and death,
sorrow and honor from beginning to end.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Volume 905.
Also briefly seen in *Yìwén Lèijù*, Volume 46.
Spirit Way Stele of Ěrmián Yǒng, Pillar State Grand General, Great Commander, and Governor of Tóngzhōu of Zhōu.
Spirit Way Stele of Ěrmián Yǒng, Pillar State Grand General, Great Commander, and Governor of Tóngzhōu of Zhōu.
The Duke's taboo name was Yǒng,
his courtesy name was Yǒngbīn,
a man from Língquán Neighborhood, Shíchéng County, Liáodōng Commandery, Eastern Yàn.
His original surname was Duàn.
Long ago, Chāngyì lived in the highlands,
first dividing the surname of Ruòshuǐ;
Gòngshū fled,
and thus began the clan of Jīngchéng.
The scholar of Xīhé
protected Wèi and repelled Qín;
the general of Běiyuè
overawed the Hú and served the Jìn.
Later they resided in Běidài,
and were first enfeoffed at Liáoshuǐ;
this is recorded in the historical records,
and can be briefly stated.
His grandfather Yuán
was General of the Guard of the West and Governor of Féngyì.
His father Rú
was General of the Guard of the East, holding the tally, overseeing military affairs of the three provinces of Héng, Yàn, and Shuò, and Governor of Héngzhōu.
When the Duke had just reached the age of twenty,
he encountered chaos and separation;
galloping between the passes and borders,
he early on had the ambition of strategic mastery.
For the square and round formations of the military,
there was no need to pile rice;
for the terrain of mountains and rivers,
he did not wait to consult a map.
In the fifth year of Zhèngguāng of Wèi, he entered service,
beginning his career as General of the Palace.
In the third year of Xiàochāng,
he was promoted to Dragon-Prancing General.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
he was appointed General of the Guard of the East and Commander.
During the righteous uprising in the central plains,
his merit and planning were foremost;
he received the title of Founding Male of Cāngquán County,
with a fief of one hundred households.
In that year, the Huái and Féi regions were invaded,
and troops were levied from the southern borders;
the Duke received the sacrificial meat for a subsidiary army,
winning three victories in one month.
Formerly, Zhāng Liáo arrived suddenly.
... Founding Count of ... County,
with a fief of five hundred households,
and was promoted to the rank of Marquis.
In the first year of Yǒngxī,
he was appointed Commissioner with Retaining Tally, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Grand Army, and Left Senior Bright Luxuriant.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi issued a special decree for him to enter service as Grand Commander of the Inner Bureau.
Mǎ Wǔ was cautious,
serving the Prince of Xiāo within the bedchamber;
Diǎn Wéi was loyal and brave,
accompanying the Empress of Wèi in the palace.
At that time, the rebel leader Yuán Bó
plundered and looted cities,
stretching from Tóng and Hán in the west
to Gǒng and Luò in the east.
The Grand Commander of the Capital Region requested seven thousand horses,
but the Duke said:
"This rebel has no other strategy;
he will soon scatter like birds.
I request only five hundred cavalry
to capture him by hand."
The court praised his strategy,
and the common people rejoiced at his removal of the harm.
Subsequently, disturbances were numerous,
and the people were displaced;
the imperial carriage traveled west,
and the ancestral shrines moved north.
The Duke skillfully perceived the celestial omens
and deeply understood the mandate of heaven.
He then conspired with his brothers for self-preservation,
beheaded the West Palace Gentleman-of-the-Household,
and sent the head within the Passes.
He was rewarded as the Founding Viscount of Chāngpíng Xiàn,
with a fief of three hundred households.
In the first year of Dàtǒng,
he was appointed Commissioner with Retaining Tally, Commander, and Inspector of Běixú Zhōu.
He suppressed the Dòu army,
recovered Hóngnóng,
and fought at Shāyuàn and Héqiáo.
The Duke was always among those who first scaled the walls,
personally facing the spearhead.
His strategies adapted to every change,
and all were recorded in the Bureau of Merit.
His fief was increased by eight hundred households,
totaling two thousand households including the previous ones.
He was promoted in rank to Founding Duke of Wòyáng Xiàn
and appointed Commander of Military Affairs of Nánfén Zhōu and Inspector of Nánfén Zhōu.
In the fourteenth year,
his fief was increased by three hundred households,
and he was transferred to Grand Commander.
In that year, he was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Grand Army, Unequalled in Honor,
with the added rank of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed General of the Agile Cavalry of the Grand Army with the right to open a headquarters,
and additionally appointed Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was appointed Commander of Military Affairs of Héng Zhōu and Inspector of Héng Zhōu.
He was further transferred to Inspector of Yún Zhōu.
Anciently, when the clans split at Xuānqiū,
there were fourteen people with different surnames;
when marquises were established at Fèngyì,
there were forty states in the ancestral alliance.
Tàizǔ, Emperor Wén, swept through the Guānhé region
and divided the world into three.
Those from Yǐngchuān followed him,
all sharing the closeness of fellow villagers;
old friends from Xīnfēng
were not without the ties of commoners.
He re-established ninety-nine surnames
and restored thirty-six states;
the old lineage returned to the surname Ěrmián.
His fief was increased by one thousand households,
and he was promoted to Founding Duke of Guǎngchéng Jùn.
Soon after, he was appointed Commander of Military Affairs of Wén Zhōu and Inspector of Wén Zhōu.
Because the state resisted to the west of Yùmén,
the watchtowers had long been toiled;
herding to the north of Yángguān,
there was much turmoil.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
a decree promoted the Duke to Commander of Military Affairs of Guā Zhōu and Inspector of Guā Zhōu.
Thus his name sped to Zǐlǐng
and his reputation shook Yúguān;
Wúléi feared his might,
and Guìshuāng cherished his kindness.
In the third year of Bǎodìng,
he returned to court
and was appointed Grandee of the Ministry of Works,
soon transferring to Marshal of the Army.
As the Summer Official in charge of military affairs,
he waited for the "White Dew" to train the troops;
as the Winter Official examining the works,
he recorded the "Dark Clouds" to assign duties.
In the fourth year,
his fief was increased by three hundred households,
totaling three thousand nine hundred households including the previous ones.
In that year, he was appointed Commissioner with Retaining Tally, Grand General, and Commander,
managing the Left Eight Armies
as Commandant-in-Chief of Military Affairs.
In the morning he would rise as a high general,
and in the evening he would meet with the common soldiers;
when matters involved engagement,
he would watch for an opening and return.
In the second year of Tiānhé,
while holding his original office, he concurrently served as Lesser Minister of Justice.
Among the Three Degrees, there is a star named Heavenly Prison;
among the Eight Trigrams, there is the Kǎn hexagram representing penal law.
The Duke’s cases were not as dense as autumn reeds,
and his severity was not like the summer sun.
The people knew the simple laws
and would not hold the jailers in high regard;
the officials understood the legal definitions
and none dared to use "dead ashes" to frighten others.
He also served as Commandant-in-Chief of the Third Army of the Left Wing
and was further ordered to lead troops
for training on the Northern Route.
Hán Xìn entered the Pass
and immediately enforced military orders;
Chén Nóng received the decree
and still edited military texts.
Not merely the good families of the Six Commanderies
or the knights of the Five Camps,
but even from afar they knew his orderly flags
and recognized his upright aura.
Braving frost and dew,
he galloped with flags and drums.
Suddenly he contracted an illness,
and the sickness became critical.
On the sixteenth day of the sixth month of the fifth year,
he passed away at Hègě Chéng
at the age of sixty-eight.
The general died at his post,
and the three armies wept as they marched;
the Protector General’s funeral returned,
and memorials were held along the borders.
On the twenty-third day of the ninth month,
the coffin reached the Capital;
the Emperor attended the funeral,
and the hundred officials offered condolences.
A decree sent Commissioner with Retaining Tally, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Grand Army, and Unequalled in Honor Hèbá Guǐ to oversee the funeral.

It also sent Commissioner with Retaining Tally, General of Chariots and Cavalry of the Grand Army, and Unequalled in Honor Hédòulíng Liàng to posthumously confer the titles of Commissioner with Retaining Tally, Pillar of State Grand General, Commander of Military Affairs of the five provinces of Tóng, Huá, Yí, Fū, and Dān, and Inspector of Tóng Zhōu.
His posthumous title was Duke Gōng.
On the fifth day of the eleventh month of that year,
he was buried at Gāosī Lǐ on Gāoyáng Plain, south of the Capital.
His wife was Madam Hèlián,
daughter of Yuè, the Inspector of Yǎn Zhōu.
At age fourteen,
she married into the Ěrmián clan.
She was appointed Lady of Lǔchéng Xiàn,
transferred to Lady of Qīngyīn Jùn,
and then transferred to Madam of the State of Guǎngchéng.
Respectful and virtuous,
she was a model of talent;
her Four Virtues shone,
and the Three Stars added to her radiance.
A wife of the Three Excellencies
was seen in her.
She died in the twelfth month of the first year of Jiàndé
at the age of fifty-eight.
In the first month of the second year,
she was returned to the tomb at Gāosī.
Like the tomb of Liú Jīngzhōu
buried together on the north bank of the Xiāng River,
or the mausoleum of General Wèi
sharing the same cave below Mount Lú.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The heir, Jí,
is a Commissioner with Retaining Tally and Unequalled Grand General,
acting as Grandee of the Ministry of War.
He serves his parents with pure filial piety
and the state with loyalty;
he established himself with ritual and righteousness
and possesses a fine reputation.
The inscription says:
The clan name was received at Xuāntái;
they descended and resided by the Ruòshuǐ.
The second son's lineage was at Xīchéng;
the remaining branches were placed in Běilù.
The mountains and rivers are majestic and fierce;
the customs are widespread and flourishing.
Formerly at our mountain passes and barriers,
there was a succession of shields and spears.
The times suffered the uprooting of foundations;
the generations encountered turbulent waves.
To the north, they enfeoffed Dàijùn;
to the east, they occupied the Liáohé.
The land was not yet unified;
Heaven continued to send down calamities.
Our Lord restored the light of glory,
continuing the literary refinement and following the martial footsteps.
He took general charge of the three frontier regions
and concurrently governed the six auxiliary capitals.
He observed the customs with elegance
and waited for the rain at the capital pavilions.
No corrupt officials were questioned;
no war drums were heard.
The Lord, through successive generations,
upheld this excellent reputation.
In filial piety, there are three virtues;
in loyalty, there is but one sovereign.
At Mǎlíng, he released distress;
at Liáochéng, he resolved disputes.
The military defenses were as full as the moon;
in battle, they avoided the welcoming clouds.
Like the Commandant of Chángsōng,
or the General of Xìliǔ.
Having governed Huáihǎi,
he also served as a bulwark for Héng and Dài.
High walls backed the passes;
long pavilions pierced the barriers.
Blood-smeared drums presided over alliances,
Subordinates could not deceive him;
soldiers dared not turn their backs.
He left his regulations at Yùguān
and left his love at Fénhǎi.
The Great General received the patents of office;
the Lord ascended the altar.
The six ministers all attended to their duties;
the Lord was second in rank among the officials.
Like the burning of Chǔ at Yīlíng,
or the partitioning of Hán at Shàngdǎng.
He encamped the army at Cānhé
and engaged in battle at Gāolán.
As the years deepened, illness arose;
when blessings were exceeded, disaster was born.
The upper star of the tripod fell, and the peak split;
the secondary general's star declined.
The parched earth wept tears of sorrow;
the white tiger let out a mournful cry.
His bow was hung in the spirit tent;
his horse was tied at the border pasture.
The mist congealed and did not move;
the springs froze and made no sound.
The Son of Heaven was grieved
and pursued him with a posthumous title.
The ritual officials presented the patent;
he was granted land to accompany the imperial tomb.
The seal and ribbons were called the patent;
the clothes and quilts were called the funeral shroud.
The dark coffin was placed in the row;
the yellow cedar lining was in its position.
Since then, how many eras have passed?
From this, how many springs?
The trees have become the shrine of the oak;
the tomb has become the spirit of the valley.
How could one know that in the Cloud Pavilion,
his name is among the meritorious officials.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 905.
〈Spirit-way Stele of Lord Hèlóu, Cavalry Grand General of Zhōu〉
〈Spirit-way Stele of Lord Hèlóu, Cavalry Grand General of Zhōu〉
In the past, the clan name was bestowed at Xuānqiū,
first distinguishing the surnames of brothers;
descending to reside at Ruòshuǐ,
they first established the states of the feudal lords.
Since then, they took their offices as their surnames
and their lands as their ancestral houses;
the branches diverged like river currents,
as can be known.
The Lord’s taboo name was Cí,
his courtesy name was Yuándá;
his original surname was Zhāng,
a man of Wǔchéng in Qīnghé.
Serving in the Zhōu,
Zhāng Zhòng was known for filial piety and friendship;
planning for the Jìn,
Zhāng Yàn was a worthy minister.
Hán had Kāidì,
and thus for five generations it was a strong state;
Zhào had Mèngtán,
and thus the three ministers did not have to fight.
His grandfather, Qìng,
practiced as a frontier general from his youth,
relying on wisdom and courage.
Although he had five carts of bamboo slips,
he did not seek the title of an Erudite;
with a single scroll of military strategy,
he immediately considered himself a general.
With the bow in his hand,
there was surely no invasion from Qí or Lǔ;
with the lotus-patterned sword at his waist,
he possessed the spirit of the flood dragon.
He served as Cavalry Grand General, Pillar of State with Three Dignities, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Founding Baron of Bàchéng County;
he was posthumously promoted to Governor of Hézhōu.
His father, Càn,
was a son and grandson of lords,
possessing the foundation for the world;
like a skilled bow-maker or metal-caster,
he maintained the family tradition of hereditary profession.
In books, he could know the hundred schools;
in swordsmanship, he was a match for a thousand men.
Like the three locust trees and the tripod vessels depicting all things,
he could recognize the divine and the treacherous;
with the five ranks of nobility and the jade tablets and banners of auspiciousness,
he guarded his palatial house.
The Lord, with talent and reputation,
possessed both of these.
He ended his career as Commissioner with Imperial Scepter, Cavalry Grand General, Pillar of State with Three Dignities, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and Founding Duke of Wǔdìng County;
he was posthumously promoted to Governor of Hézhōu.
The Lord held the spirit of the mountains and peaks
and received the essence of the stars and constellations.
When he was but a child,
just beginning to wear formal robes,
he was welcomed with bamboo horses,
already having his name known to Guō Jí;
with his sheep-drawn carriage on the road,
he was immediately appreciated by Wáng Chéng.
It was not merely a child understanding the classics
or a scholar explaining the hexagrams.
As for the pure discourses on the Chánhé
and the lofty talks on the *Autumn Waters*,
he was thus able to debate and analyze in the forest of scholars,
his fame galloping through the Deer Park.
Among the official clans of the state,
the Lord belonged to the leading family.
He began his career as Cavalry Grand General and Pillar of State with Three Dignities,
inheriting the title of Duke,
with a fief of one thousand six hundred households.
Attaining court office at twenty,
his heralds called out with great favor.
Among the high offices of Hán and Wèi,
there was truly no comparison;
among the regional governors of the Central Court,
few were of his age.
The Grand Minister held the general responsibility of the state's machinery,
diligently managing the royal affairs;
cherishing the Lord’s loyalty and bravery,
he entrusted him as his claws and teeth.
He served as the trusted commander of the Left Wing
and went out as the Defense Commander of Liángzhōu.
To the west reached Huáyáng,
while the Hàn River flowed to the east;
once the Bā and Pú regions were pacified,
the people of Chén and Lí became quiet.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng,
the Royal Army campaigned to the north;
because of the Lord’s bravery,
he was summoned to lead the troops.
The army descended upon Yíyáng
and he personally ascended Hángǔ;
they were about to burn the city of Bǎimǎ
to overturn the ramparts of Wūcháo.
Shortly after, heavy rain fell mid-journey,
and they did not manage to besiege Yuán;
the army heard of the mourning
and did not complete the invasion of Sòng.
The Pillar of State (Zhùguó) and Prince of Zhào (Zhào Wáng)
was the ninth younger brother of the current Emperor.
