In literary talent, he was like the memorial from Héjiān;
in martial skill, he was like the battle formation of Rènchéng.
Acting as a guardian of the Mín hills,
he raised his banners by the Jǐn water.
The customs of the Bǎihǔ were difficult to pacify,
and the alliance of Huánglóng was unsettled.
With the Duke's wisdom and strategy,
he entered to assist the central command.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Commissioner with a Tally, Grand Commander (Dà Dūdǔ), and Director of the Grand Secretariat of the Pillar of State General Office (Zhì Zhùguó Zǒngfǔ Sīlù),
then transferred to the post of Marshal (Sīmǎ),
with his other offices and fiefs remaining as before.
Like Xiàngrú persuading the west,
engraving stones at Língshān;
like Wǔhóu campaigning to the south,
floating boats on the Lú river.
Comparing those to today,
how were they unique?
In the merit evaluations of the nine ranks,
he was graded as the Superior of the Inferior.
In the fourth year,
he entered the court
and returned to serve among the ministerial ranks.
He then received the post of Grand Master of Land Management (Zàishī Dàfū),
and took a mission to the state of Qí.
Seeking an alliance across the border,
he employed the etiquette of neighboring harmony;
hearing of a funeral upon entering the state,
he followed the rites of attending the burial.
"He can be made to face south,"
is this not what it refers to?
Soon, with his original office,
he entered to manage military justice.
As for the military books of the Wèi River,
he kept them in his heart as his goal;
and the battle formations of Xuānqiū,
he gathered stones to form enclosures.
Since the army he led did not become fatigued,
and the soldiers had no resentment or slander,
he entered to attend the inner forbidden palace
and further held the rank of Yítóng.
Guest residences and city walls,
gates, doorways, and household registers,
all relied on his patrols and guards,
and were all managed by his office.
To the close officials of the Imperial City
and the intimate relatives of the Ducal House,
he was like encountering the Sīlì
or fearing the Dūguān.
However, the old woman of Zhèng in the lonely city
could not divine his age;
the old man of Fù by the Bā river
could not cure his illness.
At thirty-three years of age,
he suddenly passed away in his official residence.
When Lǚ Zǐmíng's illness was severe,
it caused the King of Wú to sigh in grief;
when Ruǎn Yuányú passed away forever,
it caused the Lord of Wèi's sorrow to be deep.
An edict posthumously granted him a certain office,
as is the rite.
On a day in the third month of the fourth year of Jiàndé, he was returned for burial at Jìnshān in Yuànchuān Commandery, Hézhōu.
The Duke came from a fine family of the Six Commanderies,
and a prominent clan of Xīhé.
His land was strong with the element of metal,
and his character was heroic with the spirit of the frontier.
The "Military Books" in seven volumes
floated down from the Hé river;
the "Archery Methods" in three chapters
saw the Heavenly Bow star descend at night.
Blades and banners never rested,
the watch-gongs were constantly sounding,
yet he could still read books on horseback
and practice rites within the army.
Tàishǐ Zǐyì was good at strategy,
and Zhūgé Gōngxiū was skilled at commanding.
For four generations, they were Yítóng Sānsī,
and for seven generations, Provincial Governors (Cìshǐ) of Hézhōu.
Ritual vessels were arranged in rows,
hats and carriage covers cast continuous shade;
so it is said he was a noble official in life
and a noble spirit in death.
But because his wandering soul had been a guest for so long,
the path to return for burial was distant.
The road was obstructed and the mountains long,
his wife was widowed and his children young.
Sounds of mourning filled the fields,
and the air of sorrow reached the clouds.
Moreover, the pine and catalpa trees sway,
as they face the garrison of Wǔwēi;
the hills are far and winding,
directly facing the city of Líntáo.
Mǎ Yuán died at Wǔxī,
and his coffin returned to Huáilǐ;
Liáng Hóng died at Kuàijī,
and his wife and children returned to Pínglíng.
Alas, how tragic!
The rugged path is far indeed.
Formerly, in front of the Fánchāng Shrine,
there was a golden tablet;
below the Déyáng tomb,
a blue stone stele is still passed down.
This is called recording merit,
thus the inscription says:
For seven generations assisting Hàn,
for five generations as ministers to Hán.
A loyal minister entering service,
a filial and friendly person holding office.
The immortal cave of Qīngchéng,
the shrine altar of Huángshí.
The terrace was fit for galloping horses,
his calligraphy was enough to make a swan turn.
Military might calmed the storms,
the frosty city was solemn and stern.
Driving double chariots together,
dividing the two bamboo tallies.
Generations of holding high provincial office,
following horses in ceremonial robes.
Grass bending at Qīngqiū,
wind rushing through Chìgǔ.
The generations never lacked worthies,
and produced this superior heir.
Filial piety has three virtues,
loyalty has no divided mind.
His sword was sufficient, his body upright,
his writing fit for an imperial exam.
Having held the banners and tallies,
and wearing the high cicada hat-ornament.
The turtle turning on the seal box,
the snake coiling in the ribbon case.
Left and Right Generals,
Front and Rear Attendants.
Following in the footsteps of the Five Marquises,
following the precedents of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Banners at the Nine Slopes,
ships in the double currents.
Returning to drive the wooden horses,
further leading the golden cows.
River waves and Jǐn flowers falling,
fire wells and stars floating.
Offering wine to Wàngdì,
singing peacefully to the Marquis of Shǔ.
Receiving the sacrificial meat at Héyáng,
a detached force at the banks of the Luò.
Setting battle formations at Chénggāo,
connecting banners at Guǎngwǔ.
In the morning, the army reduced its stoves;
in the night camp, many drums were sounded.
Arrows rose like six elks,
blades crushed nine tigers.
Suddenly the world of men changes,
in an instant, present becomes past.
Misfortune arose from the two stars,
the physician was startled by the two demons.
The wandering soul communicates in dreams,
saying he will return to the old graves.
Purple mud sealing the vermilion edict,
yellow-gutted wood granted for the burial.
The journey ascends Shíniǔ,
the road enters Jīnchéng.
Trees stand straight at the cold pass,
clouds hang level at the autumn frontier.
The sword is buried at Hézhù,
books are hidden in the carved pillars.
Wǔhóu has his temple,
Lord Luán has his shrine.
Cloud canopies descend low,
rainbow garments flutter down.
The stele rests on a golden tortoise,
pines lie across stone horses.
Eternal is his life and legacy,
leaving a name in Huàxià.
—Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Fascicle 906.
〈Stele Inscription of the Spirit Way of Pǔtún Wēi, Pillar of State, Duke of Sù State, and Commander-in-Chief of Hézhōu of the Zhōu Dynasty〉 with Preface
〈Stele Inscription of the Spirit Way of Pǔtún Wēi, Pillar of State, Duke of Sù State, and Commander-in-Chief of Hézhōu of the Zhōu Dynasty〉 with Preface
The Duke, whose taboo name was Wēi,
and whose zì was Mǒu,
was a man of Luòyáng in Hénán.
His original surname was Xīn,
and he was from Lǒngxī.
His foundation was at the source of the Ruòshuǐ,
and he continued the lineage of Shāngqiū.
He was enfeoffed at Dàbó,
which truly became his residence;
he was enfeoffed at Xiǎoxīn,
thus establishing his surname.
Therefore, at Sānchuān, with hair unbound,
Xīn Yǒu perceived the hidden signs of events;
in the divination of the hexagrams and lines,
Xīn Liào possessed the insight to judge men.
Assisting the administration as a Shàngjiāng of Dōngdū,
the Emperor of Wèi removed his own robe to gift him;
as Wǔxián was a meritorious official of the Western State,
the King of Hàn pushed the wheel of his chariot in honor.
His grandfather was Dàhàn,
the Cìshǐ of Wèizhōu.
His father was Shēng,
the Sìmian Zǒngguǎn and Dà Dūdū of Hézhōu.
He was a noble minister of Lǒngyòu
and from a prominent clan of Héxī,
where Gōng and Hóu followed in each other's footsteps,
and Yuèmù rode side by side.
Their collective reputation shook Chángyú,
and their names were formidable at Gāoliǔ.
The Duke embodied the spirit of the mountains and peaks,
being born under the influence of the stars.
From the time he tied his hair, he was exceptionally upright,
and his virtue was established in his early youth.
His character was like clear waves spanning ten thousand qǐng,
and he stood like a landmark of a thousand rèn.
His sharp brilliance was high,
and his radiance reached far.
Wearing the blue collar of a student, he studied the sword,
and was praised by the sovereign;
as a lad discussing military affairs,
he assisted in the strategies of the central army.
In the first year of Yǒngxī,
he entered official service
and was granted the position of Zhídàng Dūdū.
Tàizǔ Wén Dì washed away the shame of the former ruler
and established the merit of Xībó.
He first split the Hónggōu
and first ascended Hángǔ.
The Duke tidied his clothes and washed his hair,
leaning on his sword at the camp gate.
The Emperor stopped washing his feet to welcome him,
and descended the guest steps to consult him.
From then on, he resided within the inner tent
and served as a Zhíqǐng.
He was appointed Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Yǔlín Jiān, and Kāiguó Bó of Báitǔ County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the first year of Dàtǒng,
he followed to welcome the Imperial Carriage.
He was promoted in rank to Hóu,
his fief increased by three hundred households,
and he was granted the additional titles of Guànjūn Jiāngjūn and Sànqì Chángshì,
before being transferred to Dà Dūdū.
The Duke was skilled in deploying troops
and excelled in pacifying and governing.
From the attack on Luòyáng,
the pacification of Hóngnóng,
the battle of Héqiáo,
and the leveling of Shāyuàn,
he braved blades and charged the front,
and no enemy formation could stand before him.
Moreover, with a bow of six jūn,
and armor of seven layers of rhinoceros hide,
many captured helmets hung at his gate,
and his arrows unfailingly struck the horse-saddles.
Military equipment was piled high as mountains,
and cattle and horses were as numerous as the valleys.
Military officers calculated his merits,
and the Bureau of Honors rewarded his strategies.
He was appointed Commissioner with a Tally and Silver-Blue Guānglù Dàfū,
promoted to the rank of Gōng,
and his fief increased by eight hundred households.
In the past, receiving the mandate of the Red Charm,
Hán Xìn was a match for a thousand lǐ;
leading troops from Báidì,
Zhāng Fēi was a match for ten thousand men.
Comparing their paths to the present,
it refers to the Duke.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of the various military affairs of Yángzhōu, and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
He sailed upon the rivers and seas
and reached the Huái and Sì.
Small and large bamboo were widely distributed,
and precious tributes were put in order.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Chēqí Dà Jiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
Soon after, he was promoted to Piàoqí Dà Jiāngjūn with the right to open an office,
and was further bestowed the surname Pǔtún,
thereby joining the official clan.
Internally, he attended the Emperor's military council,
and externally, he oversaw military strategy.
He established his office at Yángguān
and unfurled his banners at the Hànhǎi.
Thus, when submitting memorials to the Hàn court,
he was treated as one of the same clan;
when contending for seniority in Zhōu,
he was still regarded as having no different surname from the royal house.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed Dūdū of the various military affairs of Fùzhōu and Cìshǐ of Fùzhōu.
The Duke twice served as the governor of these two provinces;
his governance was divinely inspired.
Tigers left Xīhé,
and owls moved away from Dōngjùn.
The auspicious vapors at the riverbank
specifically manifested his integrity and fairness;
the divine light at the Fù sacrifices
everywhere illuminated his uprightness and honesty.
When the Wèi dynasty reached the end of its heaven-sent mandate
and Zhōu received the new one,
the bright decree had already shifted,
and the cardinal rules were reformed.
In the first year of Zhōu,
he was reappointed Dà Jiāngjūn and Kāiguó Gōng of Bāohǎn Commandery,
with his fief increased by one thousand households.
Receiving edicts while in the army,
it was not merely to discuss the merits of the northern expedition.
When the Dà Jiāngjūn ascended the altar,
he did not need to wait for the strategy of returning to the east.
He set up battle formations at Tàipíng,
and opened the path to Yīnjìn;
he connected his troops at Guǎngwǔ,
and took the city of Xíngyáng.
Fighting battles at Dānshān
and moving his camp to Báibì,
he was always the bravest of the three armies,
and his fame surpassed that of the Five Generals.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng,
he was appointed Zǒngguǎn of Níngzhōu.
Guarding its northern gate,
he was entrusted like the lords of the State of Zhèng;
defending its western borders,
he did not fear the pressure of Qíntíng.
Thus he built the city of Pínggāng,
at which the people of Wèi folded their hands in submission;
he garrisoned the marsh of Xíngbō,
making the Liáng clan tremble with fear.
The court shared close familial ties with the Duke,
allowing him the nobility of the imperial relatives' quarter.
Thus, the daughter of Wèi Wén Dì was made the Duke's wife.
Consequently, to the left of Chángmén,
a separate garden for the Princess was opened;
beside the Zhuólóng pond,
there was the residence for the Imperial Lady.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to the capital
and appointed Shào Sīmǎ.
Entrusting him with military administration,
they regarded the Duke as another Wèi Jiàng;
assisting in the central army,
they regarded the Duke as another Xún Shǒu.
How could he merely be called the Chúnhuǒ,
or just be known as Jìnyún!
In that year,
he was sent leading troops out of West Liángzhōu
to welcome the Tūjué Empress.
As when Jì Lièxū came,
the minister met her on behalf of the lord;
he traveled under the clan name
to honor the sovereign's command.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Zhùguó
and served as Dàsīkòu.
Like the Zhùguó of Chǔ,
he corresponded to the Fire of the South;
like the Sīkòu of Xuān,
he was compared to the Clouds of the West.
These duties were all entrusted to the Duke,
as he was capable of managing officials.
In the second year of Jiàndé,
he was appointed Shàofù.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Commandant of Hézhōu and Dūdǔ of the military affairs of seven prefectures,
and served as the Dàzhōngzhèng of Hézhōu.
The Duke’s ancestral home
was originally in this land;
serving as a regional governor for a second time,
he frequently returned in embroidered robes.
The dragon seed of Xiāngchéng
returned again to the ponds and terraces;
the immortal of Guìyáng
returned to his home village.
Old friends and relatives
celebrated together with feast and song;
with a comfortable carriage and four horses,
the world honored him.
In the first year of Xuánzhèng,
he was appointed Shàngzhùguó,
and further appointed Shàofù.
Ranked among the high ministers,
he assisted with the plans of Xuánhù;
residing in the capital,
he possessed the strategies of Yǐqiáo.
His title was changed to Duke of Sùguó,
with a fief including the previous ones of five thousand five hundred households.
By the old park for shooting geese
and the remaining city of dancing cranes,
he floated on the river of Suānzǎo
and looked upon the bamboo of Qìyuán.
When he came to court at Jiànzhāng,
the Son of Heaven would descend from his seat;
when he went out to visit the imperial relatives' district,
the various dukes would descend the steps.
Thus his conduct filled heaven and earth,
and his name was known within the four seas.
Just as he was to assist five emperors
and participate in the seven policies of governance,
a sudden illness was not avoided,
and he passed away at his residence
at the age of sixty-nine.
Liǔ Zhuāng announced the funeral,
mourning a minister of the state;
Zhèng Qiáo passed away,
receiving the rites of the feudal lords.
An edict posthumously granted him certain offices
and the posthumous title of Duke [Blank],
according to the rites.
In the first year of Kāihuáng, on a certain day of the seventh month,
he was reburied in Yuànchuān Village, Jīnchéng Commandery, Hézhōu.
The mountains run along the base of Lǒng,
the land enters the frontier plains;
gazing at Jīshí along the river,
overlooking Kòngtóng down the slope.
With black armor and yellow cypresses,
through the rugged outposts,
when the offerings were cleared,
then came the labor of the elm-seed burial.
As for raising the burial mound
and building the grand tomb,
one eventually needs a stele like that of Yǐngchuán
to see a monument like that of Huáyīn.
His heir, the Yítóng Yǒngdá,
is known for his filial nature
and observed the rites during mourning.
Lamenting that the sea changes and fields form,
fearing the mountains fly and the earth ends,
he carved a stone in the tomb field,
and the inscription says:
Descendant of Shǎodiǎn,
son of Xuánwáng.
A rainbow pierces the moon,
Gold succeeds Water.
Descending to the Zhōu dynasty,
dukes and marquises began anew.
Customs and climate,
mountains and rivers inside and out.
The river connects to Jīshí,
the mountains belt Kòngtóng.
Qín Pavilion goes north,
Hàn envoys connect to the west.
The Metal element is strong in spirit,
the terrain produces heroic men.
Towering high integrity,
awe-inspiring sparse wind.
Ancestors were the shields of the border,
between the muddy River and clear Wèi.
Brilliant plans in both lands,
magnificent glory in both streams.
The water has no distinct color,
the clouds have no different aura.
Serving as officials or as people,
they were cherished and feared.
The Duke's succession
truly held a heroic spirit.
Spirit descended from the Central Peak,
patterns returned from the ranked stars.
Like a soaring luan and a looking phoenix,
pearl-like brow and mountain-like forehead.
As a subject, profound in the root of righteousness;
as a son, reaching the peak of heavenly constants.
Battle lines at Luòchéng,
flags and drums at Héqiáo.
Arrows drank at Shíliáng,
swords blazed at Tóngzhù.
Both as beautiful as six elms,
both pulling two tigers.
Yùmén opened as a commandery,
Yángguān established as a prefecture.
Twice served as a high minister,
twice served as Shàofù.
A model as the Emperor's teacher,
managing the steps of the state.
Truly inheriting lofty virtue,
reverent, bright, and careful in instruction.
Not grudging the carriage mat,
who speaks of the warm tree?
The Way of Heaven is vast and obscure,
age is fleeting.
The general's star falls,
the meritorious official's tripod sinks.
Jiǔyuán becomes mounds and hills,
mountains and rivers filled with soldiers.
Dangerous terrain at Guīlín,
perilous camp at Mǎkù.
Eternal parting from Xīzhōu,
long farewell to the Běiquè.
Mountains spread an empty canopy,
the wilderness offers sacrifices to empty curtains.
The tomb plain is vast and distant,
the wind is sorrowful on the pine-lined path.
Inscribed on the Jiéshí stone,
carved for the faithful tortoise.
Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 911.
Spirit Road Stele of Duke Mùróng, Zhùguó of Zhōu, Duke of Chǔguó, and Cìshǐ of Qízhōu.
Spirit Road Stele of Duke Mùróng, Zhùguó of Zhōu, Duke of Chǔguó, and Cìshǐ of Qízhōu.
Formerly in the Books of Yīn, rewards were encouraged,
and in the Rites of Zhōu, merit was discussed;
feudal lords calculated their achievements,
and grandees declared their deeds.
Only for Grand Master Shàngfù
did Kūnwú carry the inscription of the precious tripod;
the King commanded the officer Shī
at Xúnyì to pass down the gift of the carved halberd.
Thus we know that the highest standard is establishing virtue,
then testing clearly with merit;
in life, there is the glory of noble rank,
and in death, there is the dignity of a great name.
Since Great Heaven shows no pity,
is it not for the Duke of Chǔguó?
One may record his virtue on the great bell
and carve his merit on the sacrificial vessels,
so as to manifest his grand beauty
and spread his great achievements.
The Duke’s taboo name was Níng,
his courtesy name was Yǒng’ān,
and he was a man of Túhé, Chānglí.
The Commandant commanded the officials of six counties;
the famous mountain is called the assistant to the Five Peaks.
Yàn Tàizǔ, Emperor Wén, Mùróng Huàng,
as a hero of his age,
possessed the lands of Héshuò.
In the southern borders of Zhào,
he built a royal city;
in the northern lands of Jì,
he founded a prosperous state.
The Duke was a descendant of Huàng,
whose family had lived on the borders of Yàn for generations.
The Gāozǔ was `
` the Shìzhōng, Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì, Tàibǎo, and Lù Shàngshū. `
` During the generation of Mùróng Chāo, the King of Běidì, `
` he served as a protective screen for the royal house; `
` this is detailed in the *Yàn Lù* `
` and is worthy of praise. `
` The Great-Grandfather was `
` the Shàngshū Fǔjūn, `
` who, due to the difficulties of the Wèi house, `
` changed his surname to Dòulú, `
` yet remained of a family of officials. `
` The Grandfather served Wèi Wénchéng Huángdì. `
` The father died early, `
` but as the imperial court recognized his merit and service, `
` it bestowed deep grace in remembrance of the past. `
` In the third year of Bǎodìng, `
` an edict posthumously granted him the titles of Zhùguó Jiāngjūn, Shàoshī, and Fúlíng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng, `
` with a fief of two thousand households. `
` The Duke was endowed with a balanced and harmonious nature; `
` his birth was a blessing from the rivers and mountains. `
` His extraordinary intelligence was evident in his childhood, `
` and his mastery of rituals was acclaimed in his youth. `
` From an early age, he exhibited exceptional character, `
` and in his youth, he showed great potential. `
` When the brothers divided fruit, `
` he fully understood how to yield; `
` when guests unfastened their bells, `
` he never showed a hint of stinginess. `
` In the first year of Yǒng'ān, `
` Tàizǎi Ěrzhū Tiānguāng, `
` the chief minister of the Wèi house, `
` held troops at Huáiyòu `
` and countered power in Jiāngnán; `
` the Duke then served as a Biéjiàng `
` and followed the expeditions. `
` From then on, at Chángchéng and Xiáshí, `
` he was always in the front ranks; `
` at Qínnán and Lǒngxī, `
` he frequently faced arrows and stones. `
` Breaking through strongholds and riding on victory, `
` he was always the vanguard; `
` when recording merit and awarding honors, `
` he always ranked first. `
` In the first year of Yǒngxī, `
` he was appointed as a Zǐdūdū, `
` with the addition of military honors including drums and banners, `
` and was made the Sānggān Tàishǒu, `
` later transferring to be a Dūdū. `
` In that year, `
` because the Wèi King traveled west, `
` he welcomed the imperial carriage, `
` and was enfeoffed as Héyáng Xiàn Kāiguó Bó, `
` with an increase of three hundred households. `
` Shortly after, he was promoted to Dàzhōng Dàfū, `
` and his rank was changed from Count to Marquess, `
` with a total fief of nine hundred households. `
` He was then appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Xiǎnzhōu Zhūjūnshì, and Xiǎnzhōu Cìshǐ. `
` In the fourth year, `
` he was promoted to Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū. `
` In the autumn of that year, `
` during the battle of Héqiáo, `
` he was the first to scale and break the formation, `
` and was promoted to Chēqì Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī. `
` In the fifth year, `
` for his merit at Shāyuàn, `
` his fief was increased, `
` totaling two thousand households including previous grants. `
` Shortly after, he was appointed Fūzhōu Cìshǐ, `
` with the additional title of Sànjì Chángshì; `
` externally, he was deeply trusted with military command, `
` and internally, he served in the Jíshū. `
` In the fifteenth year, `
` he was appointed Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn. `
` In the sixteenth year, `
` he was appointed Dàjiāngjūn. `
` In the first year of Hòuwèi, `
` he was re-appointed Fūzhōu Cìshǐ. `
` Because the Duke had previously held this governorship, `
` he firmly declined and did not take the post. `
` In the third year, `
` his title was changed to Wǔyáng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng, `
` and he was appointed Shàngshū Púshè. `
` His duty was solely to assist with memorials, `
` and his responsibility lay in administrative oversight; `
` he managed the divisions of the Left and Right `
` and also oversaw the selection of officials. `
` It happened that Jiāngnán was blocking the army, `
` and Zhǔgōng faced enemies on the border; `
` military matters were urgent, `
` and arrows and spearheads flew in all directions. `
` The Duke received his orders and set out by night, `
` the great army clearing the way; `
` he gathered the elite soldiers of Qín `
` and integrated the vast troops of Jīnghù. `
` Naval vessels vied in the formation of double swords, `
` and infantry and cavalry displayed the power of four divisions; `
` once Yílíng was burned, `
` Qiánzhōng was then pacified. `
` He turned the army and returned the banners, `
` unarmored his men and rested the troops. `
` Later, Fèngzhōu rebelled within, `
` and Chéngdū was cut off from without; `
` the Duke again commanded the various armies, `
` mobilizing against the rebels. `
` Without the weapons being bloodied, `
` they were all captured; `
` he relocated their chieftains `
` and accepted those who surrendered. `
` When the Imperial Dynasty received the mandate, `
` and Wénzǔ changed the decree, `
` Shénzōng selected the virtuous and capable, `
` reforming the laws and creating new systems. `
` A patent was then issued, `
` appointing the Duke as Zhùguó, `
` with an additional four thousand households. `
` In the second year, `
` he was appointed Tóngzhōu Cìshǐ. `
` This region was the strategic belt of Guānfǔ, `
` and served as the lips and teeth of Qín and Jìn. `
` The registered households were dense and numerous, `
` and the granaries were well-stocked. `
` This was a defensive responsibility; `
` no one but the virtuous and close relatives should hold it. `
` The Duke set up his banners as the Shepherd, `
` lifted the curtains of his carriage to inspect the districts; `
` the Six Articles were thus implemented, `
` and the hundred cities were all encouraged. `
` In the third year, `
` he was appointed Dàsīkòu. `
` Also, because the Duke's merits were exceptionally prominent, `
` he was enfeoffed as Chǔguó Gōng, `
` with a fief of ten thousand households; `
` this was because he had defeated Hóu Fāngrén and others in Jīng and Shǎn, `
` and was enfeoffed in those lands. `
` He strictly punished the king's enemies `
` and moderated the penal administration. `
` To suppress banditry and cruelty, `
` he governed with a blend of leniency and severity; `
` to soothe those afar and manage those nearby, `
` he then pacified them with moderation and harmony. `
` When Shùn employed Gāoyáo, `
` the unkind were kept at a distance; `
` when Jìn promoted Suíhuì, `
` the bands of thieves all fled. `
` In the fourth year of Bǎodìng, `
` he was appointed Dūdū Qízhōu Zhūjūnshì and Qízhōu Cìshǐ. `
` A chronic illness lingered, `
` and on the fourth day of the third month of the fifth year of Bǎodìng, `
` he passed away at his private residence `
` at the age of sixty-two. `
` An edict posthumously granted him [certain offices], `
` and the posthumous name Duke [Certain], `
` according to the rites. `
` In the tenth month, on the Gēngshēn day, `
` he was buried in the valley of Hóngdù. `
` Ropes were pulled and the clan mourned, `
` guest carriages filled the roads; `
` dark armor covered the soldiers of the tributary states, `
` and mailed warriors lined the chariots and cavalry. `
` He achieved a virtuous end, `
` with honor in life and lamentation in death. `
` Alas, how sorrowful!
The Duke went through virtue and held wisdom,
embodied the Way and dwelt in integrity,
practiced humility despite his noble status,
and thought of loss when in fullness.
Like a vast expanse of calm waves,
his clarity or turbidity could not be changed;
like a high wall of a hundred fathoms,
his depth or height could not be measured.
In his conduct and self-regulation,
he lived in security as if on the edge of a precipice;
sacrificing himself for righteousness,
he viewed danger as level ground.
As for military strategy and responding to changes,
launching surprises and setting ambushes,
the divination of *Tàiyī* and *fēngjiǎo*,
the constant observation of the stars,
the records of tower-ship battle formations,
and the manuals of powerful crossbows and mounted archery,
there was nothing that did not align with his divine intuition,
acting as swiftly as lightning and thunder.
Wherever his siege engines were directed,
the ground would be cleared of cities with a hundred towers;
wherever his long halberds reached,
the fields were cleared of the "three-gate" formations.
Thus he slew generals and captured banners
in forty-three battles;
he held honorable positions and high salaries
for thirty-seven years.
His martial prowess manifested the righteousness of the Seven Virtues,
his achievements were sung in the Nine Merits,
his traces were recorded in the inscriptions of ceremonial vessels,
and his conduct was illuminated by the rites of posthumous naming.
Formerly, after Zāng Wén died,
Mù Shū praised his "establishment of words";
when Zhèng Qiáo passed away,
Xuān Ní wept for his "bequeathed love."
The tomb of the green stone at Déyáng
will not be leveled in a thousand years;
his stele of the white tiger at Zhījiāng
will not be destroyed for a hundred generations.
Daring to follow this principle,
I thus compose an inscription:
East of the Liáo River,
north of Jìzhōu.
He was called the Commandant,
and also known for the Dependent State.
Gathering his spirit and remaining brave,
he left a model for the heroic frontier.
Filial piety is truly the constant of heaven,
and loyalty is the excellent virtue.
Official caps and hereditary salaries,
a model and glory for his descendants.
Customs were influenced by Yàn Dān,
but his character put Yīng and Lìn to shame.
Toiling in labor and expeditions,
suffering hardship in battle arrays.
Bravery exceeding the drowning steed,
spirit surpassing the shaking of tiles.
The kingdom produced such a man,
thinking of the august and numerous scholars.
Gentle and respectful was the man,
a modest and humble gentleman.
Holding the yak-tail banner and the tally of authority,
serving in the frontiers and entering the civil service.
Serving through five reigns,
raising banners over a thousand *lǐ*.
When the times met with change,
his name was recorded for meritorious service.
Summoned and appointed like Huái Yīn,
breaking the army at Zhāoyáng.
Holding office in the administration of justice,
the prisons were handled with care for the law.
The sheep of Shěn did not drink,
and the bandits of Huán were unheard of.
Briefly campaigning against Bā and Yōng,
leading the expedition to the Jiāng and Hàn.
Commanding six divisions of the army,
the troops encompassed seven camps.
Using length to strike weakness,
the reality followed the fame.
Increasing fortifications to awe the enemy,
reducing stoves to hide the troops.
The bell sounds and the night water-clock drips,
the dew dries in the morning sun.
The villages are desolate,
the residence and curtains are forlorn.
The great stele follows the coffin,
the wooden burial vault moves for the funeral.
The palace is near Chǔlǐ,
the terrace leans towards Mèng Cháng.
Divining the site and setting the date,
the distant celestial signs announce the divination.
Virtue remains after his life,
fame shines after his death.
The guesthouse is forever abandoned,
the gates of the underworld are eternally closed.
Yàn Yīng mourned for Qí,
Liǔ Zhuāng grieved for Wèi.
The autumn wind on the northern plain,
the sun sets and the river flows away.
The burial field is an old plot,
the guest soil is a new mound.
Tears fall upon the stone,
a sword hangs on the solitary pine.
Pure aura and fine example,
traces remaining for a thousand years.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Volume 919.
<Spirit Road Stele of Duke Yǔwén, the Duke of Guǎngráo and Governor of Yǎn Prefecture of the Zhōu Dynasty>
<Spirit Road Stele of Duke Yǔwén, the Duke of Guǎngráo and Governor of Yǎn Prefecture of the Zhōu Dynasty>
The Táng dynasty saw Yuán and Kǎi advanced together,
sixteen people in total;
the Zhōu house saw Zhāomù enfeoffed first,
fifteen states in total.
Originating from the lineage,
branches and leaves divided;
founding states and inheriting families,
like a string of pearls or a combination of jade.
Thus he was able to illuminate great virtue,
thinking of the august and numerous scholars,
great virtue has descendants,
and the Duke was truly abundant!
The Duke’s taboo name was Cháng,
his courtesy name was Zǐyuán,
and he was a man of Xíngyáng in Yùzhōu.
After Zhōu Xuān's restoration,
the worthy were established and relatives were enfeoffed;
after Zhèng Wǔ held the state,
the surname was preserved and the clan name received.
The tribute of Jīng and Héng reached a thousand chariots,
and none dared to attack;
the fiefs of Guó and Kuài were ten cities,
which were instead presented as cities.
Furthermore, at the gates of the suburbs, cavalry arrived
to first welcome the guests of the Palace Secretary;
at the morning audience in the Nángōng,
the shoes of the Shàngshū were uniquely recognized.
His grandfather was Sīqìng,
General of Establishing Prowess and Governor of Shānyáng.
"Establishing Prowess" took the title of Cáo Rén,
by which the name was fixed;
Shānyáng had the worthiness of Wáng Chàng,
sufficient to observe the local customs.
His father was Xù,
wearing Silver-Blue and Golden-Purple ribbons,
comparable to Wēn Xiàn and Fù Zhī;
General of Guarding the South and General of Conquering the East,
equal to Liú Hóng and Xún Yǐ.
In the records of rewarding merit,
he was a model for the Three Ducal Ministers;
in the rites of posthumous honors,
he was the shepherd of Jīng and Hé.
The Duke was intelligent from a young age,
and his youthful ambitions were early formed.
His posture was always upright,
and his words were never stolen or repetitive.
With the wisdom and courage of a young student,
he once buried the snake of Yúnmèng;
with a child's benevolent heart,
he already loved the pheasants of Zhōngmóu.
He first attended the local schools,
not without the glory of a scholar;
or when seeing military books,
he then had the ambition for the "wind and clouds."
Filial at home and loyal abroad,
he served with all his heart;
cultivating himself and establishing a name,
he exhausted the principles of human nature.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
he raised an army in Huáyáng,
first ascended Guǎngwǔ,
sailed across the Miǎn,
entered the Wèi, and crossed the Hé,
and was granted the title of Founding Baron of Yǒng'ān County and General of Assisting the State.
From then on, he constantly followed Tàizǔ
and entered the court as a Palace Commander.
In the battle at Héqiáo,
the autumn waters did not flow for three months;
at the city of Luòyáng, he brandished his blade,
and the road to Jīnyōng was cut off for a month.
The Western Capital was not submissive,
and the Qiāng and Róng tribes invaded.
The city was like a flying bird,
and the ground had hidden dragons.
The Duke drew his golden arrows
and momentarily raised the divine halberd;
those with bee-like eyes fled,
and those with wolf-like hearts were transformed.
He was promoted to General of Leveling the East and Commander-in-Chief.
In the fifteenth year,
he inherited his father's title as Founding Count of Wèichāng County,
and was transferred to Great Commander.
In the second year of the latter Wèi,
he was appointed Commissioner with General Power, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Ceremonial Equal to the Three Officers.
Huáng Quán received the imperial edict,
which commended his merit in entering Wèi;
Dòu Xiàn held office,
and was rewarded for his strategy in pacifying the Róng.
Regarding this appointment of the Lord,
his achievements and service are illustrious.
He was promoted to the noble title of State-Founding Duke of Guǎngráo County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the third year of Bǎodìng,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Luózhōu and Governor of Luózhōu,
while still leading the troops and horses of Jīnzhōu,
to receive the Duke of Shàngyōng at the Wéngǔ Road.
The mountain streams were steep and lofty,
the cliffs were gaping and perilous;
the mountains were exhausted and the waters cut off;
horses were reined in as if crossing flying bridges.
Once the central fortifications were opened,
the twin cities immediately submitted.
In the past, Shēn and Xī were entirely obscured,
and Jiāng and Huáng had no aid.
The distant shores of Cényáng
were frequently troubled by the dust of war;
at the head of the Xià River, ships floated westward,
frequently encountering spearheads and arrows.
Like Fúbō receiving the sacrificial meat of commission,
the Lord swore to his troops on a tower ship,
entering the Héngjiāng formation
and advancing the Xiàlài soldiers.
The tattooed guests of Yuè
saw the Zhànlú sword finally depart;
the long-whiskered people of Wú
watched the Yúhuáng ship sail into the distance.
In the fourth year of Jiàndé,
he was appointed Commissioner with General Power and Superior General who Opens the Office and is Ceremonial Equal.
Gōngsūn Áo descended the Guānglù fortress,
and Zhūgě Dàn inscribed the Wándū mountains;
in the Lord's occupation of these positions,
he truly had no shameful virtue.
Regarding the various customs of the four directions
and the differing winds of the world,
because the Lord was incorruptible and capable,
he was sent as an observer.
He galloped on the postal relay holding the staff of authority,
raising the banners and wielding the axe.
Having ridden the dapple-grey horse
and worn the embroidered robes,
the bandits stood in fear
and the noble relatives withdrew their hands.
Staying overnight in local villages,
fortunately, there was no suspicion of the "return taboo";
reporting matters at the chariot office,
how could there be a day of "reversed support"?
This caused Yáng Qiú, the Director of Retainers,
to have nowhere to exert his power,
and Bào Huī, the City Official,
to achieve his tasks only through others.
Emperor Wǔ of Gāozǔ swore to the masses in mid-spring
and on the jiǎzǐ day he crossed the river;
the Lord grasped his sword among the six armies,
unfolding the maps of the eight formations.
Like Zhāng Liáo
serving as the vanguard to repay the Lord of Wèi,
or compared to Gěng Yǎn
fighting first to await King Xiāo.
When the Nine Provinces were unified
and the four regions were settled,
he eventually achieved merit to share in the ranks of the brave,
and his name was entered into the Bureau of Merit;
he was appointed Superior General who Opens the Office,
and his fief was increased by five hundred households.
Additionally, merit was cited and rewards were bestowed,
grace was extended and fiefs were divided.
Returning with double carriages,
he brought glory to the city of Qiáojùn;
laden with treasures he returned,
illuminating the waters of Línzhāng.
That same day, he was granted the surname Yǔwén,
becoming of the same clan as the State.
Lóu Jìng submitted a memorial at the deer carriage,
and Xiàng Bó danced with his sword at Hóngmén;
the Lord's honor in this
is sufficient to be ranked with them.
Because the Lord's achievements were prominent in times of difficulty
and his sincerity endured through wind and frost,
in that year he was appointed Commissioner with General Power, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Dōngxúzhōu, and Governor of Xúzhōu.
In the first year of Xuānzhèng,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu and Governor of Nányǎnzhōu.
Serving as a shepherd by the Jì River,
his influence moved like the wind over Léizé;
setting up his banners in Hǎidài,
his transformation reached the Huái and Yí rivers.
When his carriage curtain entered the borders,
the greedy and cruel resigned their seals;
as he governed in ceremonial robes,
the benevolent and righteous welcomed him in the suburbs.
Was it only the digging of canals at Báishí,
the exchange of green salt for grain,
the auspicious clouds entering the border,
or the rain following his carriage?
While in office, he fell ill
and died at his regional post.
Huángfǔ Sōng was an overseer of such governors,
a virtuous and capable Governor;
Palace Attendant Xún led such examples,
a regional leader of the restoration.
Illustrious reputation and abundant substance,
the Lord possessed these.
An edict posthumously granted him a certain office
and titled him a certain Duke,
in accordance with the rituals.
On the tenth day of the eleventh month of the second year of Dàxiàng,
he was returned for burial at the old tomb in a certain mountain in Xíngyáng.
Jiǔyuán is sorrowful,
what would Zhào Wénzǐ say?
The four horses neigh in sadness,
Duke Chéng of Téng is already far away.
As for engraving tripods and carving stelae,
inscribing merit and praising virtue,
and setting forth his excellent example,
these must be rooted in his life.
Alas!
The erection of this stele
is different from the waters of the Zhū and Sì;
this carving of stone
is different from the mountains of Yànrán.
How tragic!
Thus follows the inscription:
Son of Gāoyáng,
grandson of Shǎodiǎn.
Distant encounter at Cānglín,
remote source at Ruòshuǐ.
Dukes and marquises renewed their lineage,
bells and tripods became more numerous.
Inheriting the foundation and succeeding the line,
establishing the state and opening the frontier.
Strong and martial,
both duke and marquis.
The black robes departed from Zhèng,
the high officials returned to Zhōu.
Yúlíng to the north,
Xíngzé flowing east.
The River moved to Suānzǎo,
rain of grain at Chénliú.
Ancestors guarded the southern state,
fathers governed the eastern region.
Two turtles for the seal,
two snakes for the ribbon.
Daily observing the dark winds,
stars divining by the tall willows.
This is called generations of record,
the name is immortal.
The way of serving parents,
establish oneself through filial piety.
The way of serving the lord,
establish benevolence through loyalty.
Now the Lord inherits virtue,
unifying this for lord and parents.
Flourishing like the pine,
lustrous like the bamboo skin.
Merit among thorns and brambles,
duties over weapons and shields.
Northward facing the Qīnglǐng,
southward reaching the Báibō.
Straight clouds across the frontier,
long stars crossing the River.
Battle formations opening across the sands,
the army moves with many stoves.
Merits raised and rewards given,
borders sealed and positions received.
Palace chambers carved with jade tablets,
mountains and rivers divided as land.
Deciding victory from a thousand lǐ away,
deep schemes and secret plans.
Martial success achieved in Jiànwǔ,
name connected to the stellar order.
Raising banners between the Jì and Tà,
holding the tally at Guī and Méng.
Cultivating silkworms in the mulberry lands,
truly soothing the Wútóng trees.
No strange vessels in the fields,
no divergent winds on the river.
At the pavilions of Wú and barriers of Chǔ,
none dared to bend a bow.
Suddenly, a lifetime passes,
in an instant, the pines and catalpas.
The road turns by the bronze fish,
the mountain winds around the stone horses.
The temple of Wǔhóu,
the shrine of Luán Gōng.
Looking upon this high stele,
tears fall in sorrow.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, scroll 919.
Spirit Way Stele of Lord Dòulú, Zhōu Chief Administrator of Lǒngyòu General, Posthumously Granted Prince's Junior Protector.
Spirit Way Stele of Lord Dòulú, Zhōu Chief Administrator of Lǒngyòu General, Posthumously Granted Prince's Junior Protector.
The Lord’s taboo name was Yǒng’ēn, courtesy name [X],
a man of Túhé in Chánglí.
His original surname was Mùróng,
a descendant of Emperor Wénmíng Huàng of Yàn.
The fief of Jīzǐ in Cháoxiǎn,
the state of Bóyí in Gūzhú,
the four cities of Hàn,
the one marquis of Qín.
His ancestors preserved the surname and received the clan name,
first establishing merit at Liǔchéng;
opening the state and succeeding the family,
first quieting the chaos of Liáoyáng.
Since the evil star in the Tiānshì market,
and the military defeat at Lián and Jīn,
the Lord of the Secretariat changed the surname to Dòulú,
and began his official career in Wèi.
His grandfather Dài was General of the Left and Right and Imperial Chamberlain to Emperor Wén of Wèi.
His father Zhǎng,
known for his grand strategies since youth,
unfortunately passed away early.
The Zhōu dynasty, because the Lord and his brothers assisted the Mandate,
wished to extend righteousness to their ancestors.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
an edict posthumously granted him the titles of Pillar of the State Great General and Duke of Fúlíng Commandery.
Thus it is known that spring rain moistens the trees,
flowing from the leaves to the roots;
Xībó practiced benevolence,
extending it from the living to the deceased.
The Lord possessed the essence of mountains and peaks,
the outstanding spirit of the stars and constellations,
his qi matched the sacrificial bells and tripods,
his reputation resonated with the wind and clouds.
When observing the Qín soldiers, he was still called a youth; when facing the Chǔ battles, he was still in his student robes.
Tàizǔ, Emperor Wén, took advantage of the times to quell chaos,
and possessed the hegemony.
Those from Yǐngchuān followed him,
old affections were not forgotten;
old friends from Chōnglíng,
their mutual understanding was profound.
In the second year of Pǔtài,
the Guānxī uprising was established,
and he was appointed General for Exterminating Bandits.
He welcomed the Imperial Carriage,
and was granted the title of Count of Xīnxīng County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
Opening the township of Xīn'ān,
returning to move the pass of Yáng Pǔ;
lifting the siege of Hóngnóng,
further entering the commandery of Liú Kūn.
Grasping the drumsticks and riding side-by-side,
he was among the vanguard.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
there was the Battle of Shǎyuàn.
In the fourth year,
there was the campaign at Héqiáo.
Lice grew in the armor and helmets,
warhorses were born in the wild,
the Lord’s ability to adapt grew even greater,
his fierce bravery like a whirlwind increased,
steady as if facing a rival state,
his performance was most satisfactory,
he was appointed General of Dragon Gallop and Grandee of Chóngsàn.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed Imperial Chamberlain and Commander of the Right Trusted Guards.
Soon he was transferred to Grand Commander,
and added the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the sixteenth year,
he was appointed Commissioner with Trident, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Equal to the Three Offices.
In the first year of Wèi,
he was appointed General of Agile Cavalry and Opening Office Equal to the Three Offices.
Dèng Zhì, as a relative of the Hàn court,
was first appointed to the central platform;
Huáng Quán, as a meritorious official of the Wèi state,
first ascended to the rank of supreme general.
The Lord received frequent and favor-filled appointments,
honored by both the court and the commoners.
In the third year,
he became Regional Commander of Military Affairs of Chéngzhōu and Governor of Chéngzhōu.
Soon he was added as Palace Attendant.
Externally he led the regional commanders,
his prestige shaking a hundred cities;
internally he participated as a Palace Attendant,
his honor surpassing the eight residences.
At that time, the cunning Qiāng of Lǒngdǐ
occasionally pierced through Shànggǔ;
groups of bandits from Yúzhōng
sometimes gathered at Yúyáng.
The Lord donned his armor and sped like a star,
driving a thousand cavalry over long distances.
The fierce followers at Huílù
collapsed like grass before the wind;
the heroes of Guāzhōu
surrendered to the army with bound hands.
In the first year of Later Wèi,
his title was changed to Marquis of Lóngzhī County.
In the third year,
the court sent Great General Ān Zhènggōng to accompany the Tūjué and Tǔyùhún on their return to their countries.
The two provinces of Hézhōu and Shànzhōu
were located at the main road's head,
the Lord led five thousand cavalry
to serve as a military defense.
Reaching Dānsù in the south,
looking toward Báilán in the west,
the passes and barriers were without worry,
this was the Lord's achievement.
In the first year of the Zhōu dynasty,
he was appointed Commander-in-chief of Military Affairs of Shànzhōu and Governor of Shànzhōu.
In that year,
his title was changed to Duke of Wòyě County,
and his fief was increased by one thousand households.
In the second year,
he was appointed Chief Secretary of the Lǒngyòu General Administration.
In the first year of Wǔchéng,
he was appointed Commander-in-chief of Military Affairs of Lì, Shè, and Wèn Prefectures, and Governor of Lìzhōu.
In the fifth year,
his troops defeated the Yángzhèn Mán of Wènzhōu,
and subsequently pacified the Lúshuǐ region.
In the first year of Bǎodìng, he led troops to defeat the Héngmàn Liáo of Bāzhōu.
Crossing the Lú in the fifth month,
he had the deep-penetrating troops of Gè Liàng;
traversing the nine bends of Chángbǎn,
he had the path of the loyal official Wáng Zūn.
Frost and hail did not alarm them,
water and grass were never lacking;
"Heaven favored the General,"
as the saying goes.
In that year,
he was appointed Sīkuài.
Managing the Eight Laws,
equalizing the Nine Taxes,
affairs were summarized at the year's end,
and merit was recorded in the monthly essentials.
In the third year,
he returned and
was appointed Chief Secretary of the Lǒngyòu General Administration.
The Duke repeatedly assisted heroic princes
and frequently served in major administrations.
When the Prince of Běihǎi entered the court,
he looked up to provide responses;
when the Prince of Dōngpíng had an audience with the Emperor,
he consequently established the rites.
He caused the horse's head to yearn for Yàn,
not unlike Yuè Yì;
and as a regional official modeling himself after Hàn,
he was much like Tián Shū.
His elder brother, the Duke of Chǔ State,
through humility and yielding,
and through dignified praise and joyful promotion,
established a state and opened a capital,
ruling over the southern regions.
He requested to take his previous fief of three thousand households in Wǔyáng Commandery
to increase the Duke’s fief in Wòyě.
The court, considering that brothers yielding to each other
is not absent from former histories,
extended grace and divided the households;
an imperial decree permitted it,
increasing his fief to a total of four thousand seven hundred households including the previous amount.
Soon after, the six disharmonious breaths encroached upon him,
and the five sounds clashed;
the staff of longevity did not reach its end,
and the wandering soul was about to transform.
He passed away in his official residence
at the age of fifty-eight.
A decree posthumously promoted him to Junior Protector, Commander-in-chief of Military Affairs of five prefectures including Yōu, Jì, Dìng, Xiāng, and others, and Governor of Yōuzhōu.
His posthumous title was Jìng Gōng,
as prescribed by the rites.
On the sixth day of the second month of the first year of Tiānhé,
he was buried at Hóngdùchuān in Xiányáng.
The tomb of a Grand Master is planted with cypresses;
the mound of a feudal lord is higher than a rampart.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The Duke possessed loyalty and practiced filial piety,
embodied righteousness and harbored benevolence.
A straight trunk of a hundred fathoms,
clear waves of a thousand acres.
He applied his mind to official duties
and took pleasure in maps and books.
The documents and records of the bureaus
never became a burden;
even when warhorses galloped to and fro,
it did not disturb his composure.
With brothers as Dukes and Marquises,
and as relatives of the imperial court,
he had the prosperity of the bathing fiefs at Yíchūn,
yet lacked the ostentatious flow of the water at Zhuólóng.
Like the thousand acres of bamboo in Wèinán,
he still feared becoming overfilled;
like the two hundred acres of fields in Xiányáng,
he always thought of knowing when to stop.
In establishing himself, ten generations could be granted clemency;
in leaving a legacy to his sons, it was but a single classic.
The stele of Governor Jiǎ Kuí
has already produced golden grain;
the tomb of General Wèi Qīng
now retains its stone qilin.
Thus the inscription says:
Cháoxiǎn established the state,
and Gūzhú was its ruler.
The land is called Gāoliǔ,
and the mountain is named Mìyún.
Liáoyáng was split by Zhào,
and Wǔsuì was divided by Qín.
A descendant of a lineage of precious scepters,
with the old merit of carved halberds.
His reputation matched the reality,
and his words were the refinement of his character.
Displaying this inner brilliance,
he was born with this precocious talent.
Upright in dissent without concealment,
the King's Way is straight.
With only love and respect,
he forever maintained a joyful countenance.
Resting within the gates of rites,
he lingered in the cultivation of learning.
Strategizing within the curtains,
his merit cleared the brambles.
Wielding the halberd in the Hán ranks,
leaning on the carriage rail in the Qí city.
The Leopard Strategy was established,
and the Dragon Secret was opened.
Verifying battle at Qíyáng,
extending majesty to the Lǒng hills.
Drawing fortresses upon the ground,
gathering rice to model mountains.
Mounting a horse to explain books,
facing the army while practicing rites.
Jiǎ Fù opened his camp,
and Lián Gōng humbled himself.
Calmly associating and gathering,
responding to inquiries and making visits.
Utilizing this incorruptibility and fairness,
he balanced leniency and severity to the end.
The Lǜlín troops rested,
and the Huángchí bandits were quieted.
His name shook Chìshān,
and his majesty towered over Qīnglǐng.
Black beasts floated in the river,
and flying locusts departed the borders.
The calamitous aura left Lǒng,
and the poisonous waters invaded the Jìng.
The court laments the tilting of a terrestrial pillar,
and at night falls a star of the Three Ducal Ministers.
A stone altar receives the sacrifices,
and a grand stele praises his spirit.
The cypresses before Wèichéng,
the courtyard below Chānglíng.
One must know the marketplace of the underworld
to read the mountain inscription.
— *Yìwén Lèijù*, Volume 50.
— *Wènyuán Yīnghuá*, Volume 925.
<Stele of the Warm Springs>
<Stele of the Warm Springs>
When the sun bathes in the Xiánchí pool,
it first responds to the omen of the Green Armor.
When the Pillar Rock floats in the sky,
it first receives the mandate of the Black Barbarians.
Benevolence cleanses the dust and haze;
righteousness stirs the clear and the turbid.
Courage has the leftover strength to carry a mountain;
weakness cannot even overcome a goose feather.
In mid-spring, the elm seeds flow together;
in the third month, the peach blossoms descend together.
Those whose color changes
flow as the nectar of the five clouds.
Those whose taste is sweet
congeal as the dew of Sānwēi.
The steam is greener than at Tóngpǔ;
the color is whiter than at Qiánxī.
It is not a divine tripod, yet it boils long;
it is different from the Dragon Pond, yet it surges alone.
It washes the stomach and cleanses the intestines,
reviving the weak and raising the emaciated.
The remaining stones of the Qín Emperor
still serve as the "goose-tooth" steps.
The old ceramics of Hàn Wǔdì
are used as the "fish-scale" tiles.
Water surging among the mountains
truly manifests loyal sincerity.
A river flowing within the chamber
further illustrates pure filial piety.
How could it be only like the Sweet Spring curing illness,
as heard of in the Jiànwǔ era?
Or divine water removing ailments,
as in the Xiánkāng era?
The hall of the three immortals of Sōngshān
does not alone hold sway over the Celestial Pool.
The hundred-fathom spring of Huàyīn
is not alone superior to the Lotus Well.
— *Yìwén Lèijù*, Volume 9.
— *Chūxué Jì*, Volume 7.
<Epitaph Inscription of Zhèng Wěi, Grand General of Zhōu and Duke of Xiāngchéng>
The Duke, whose taboo name was Wěi,
and whose courtesy name was Zǐzhí,
was a man of Kāifēng in Yíngyáng.
A younger brother of King Xuān of Zhōu,
he was enfeoffed in Zhèng.
In the lands of the Hé and Luò rivers,
there were people;
the lords of Guó and Kuài
were not without commanderies and cities.
Later, snakes fought at the gate,
and a soft-shelled turtle was tasted in the tripod.
Hán invaded Fùshǔ,
and Jìn destroyed Yángchéng.
Their sacrifices were suddenly extinguished,
and they took their state's name as their surname.
His grandfather, Chè,
was General Stabilizing the Army
and was posthumously granted the title of Governor of Jìzhōu.
His father, Xiānhù,
was Great General of Agile Cavalry, Equal to the Three Senior Vice Presidents, Duke of Xiāngchéng Commandery, and Governor of Qīngzhōu.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
the gates of Luòchéng were closed by day,
and the Huáng Hé froze over.
At the place of the Zháiquán covenant,
a dark bird suddenly flew;
within the weapon racks of the armory,
scaly fish ascended.
Three commanders were bound in the north,
and five horses floated to the south.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng exerted great influence in the Central Plains,
establishing a ruler between the Yī and Luò rivers.
The Duke leaned on the crossbar of his carriage,
speaking of returning to his ancestral lands,
and was appointed as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Heaven grew weary of the virtue of Wèi,
and government fell into the hands of powerful ministers.
The Duke was ashamed to enter the steps of chaos
and thus raised a righteous army in Chénliú.
Tàizǔ sealed Hángǔ Pass to await the feudal lords,
and sat in the Fèng Palace to receive the various lords in audience.
Majesty and kindness were thus met,
and he swept westward like a rolling mat.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
he entered the court
and was granted the title of Founding Baron of Wǔyáng County,
with a fief of six hundred households.
Soon after, he was appointed General of Dragon Soaring and Governor of Běixúzhōu.
He opened the battle at the Hé Bridge,
and relieved the siege of Yùbì.
He unfurled banners at Fùpíng,
and donned armor at Yīquè.
He probed the tiger's den while brandishing his halberd,
and ascended the Yú Gate to hang his helmet.
Thus his name was recorded in the Ministry of Merits,
his achievements surpassing the mere granting of wine.
The Wèi general Hóu Jǐng
looked back like a wolf toward the Jīng and Hé rivers.
The Son of Heaven commanded me
to lead a partial force to assist.
Dangling bait in the tiger's mouth,
but halfway through, the covenant was betrayed.
Matters were settled by a mutual withdrawal,
which was due to the Duke's strength.
He was appointed General of the Central Army, Cavalier Constant Attendant, and Grand Commander,
and inherited the title of Duke of Xiāngchéng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
He was also appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Great General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Equal to the Three Senior Vice Presidents.
Other titles remained as before.
He was promoted to Great General of Agile Cavalry and Opener of Office,
with the added title of Attendant Gentleman.
The position of Constant Attendant was weighty,
like Huò Qùbìng ascending to court;
the rank of High General was honorable,
like Gōngsūn Áo going out beyond the frontier.
Comparing the present to the past,
different eras shared the same glory.
In the second year of the Later Wèi,
he was granted the rank of Great General, Defense Commander of Jiānglíng, and Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for fifteen provinces.
The soldiers of Wú were trained,
and the fleets practiced on the currents.
Islands were encroached upon,
and waves surged with force.
The Duke briefly approached the river boundary
and already knew the troops of Nányuè;
just as he began to sail the multi-decked ships,
he excelled at the battle of Kūnmí.
Thus he could sing peacefully at the Lǐ Shore,
and rest his whip at Cènyáng.
He detained the Marquis of Lǔ for a banquet at Zhāngtái,
and faced the men of Qí to hunt at Yúnmèng.
In the first year of Bǎodìng of Zhōu,
he was appointed Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for Yízhōu, and Governor of Yízhōu.
In the sixth year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Commander-in-Chief and Governor of Huàzhōu.
Other titles remained as before.
The Xiáo and Hán passes have layered peaks,
and the Qiān and Wèi rivers branch out.
The overflow of Yánglíng had already rushed forth,
and the scholars of Huàyīn gathered once more.
However, he suffered from wasting thirst for consecutive years,
repeatedly having the ailment of Xiāngrú.
When it reached the final stages of illness,
it was like the malady of Fàn Zēng.
Tóngjūn's remedies
lacked divine efficacy;
Lǐ Zhù's attending physicians
had no further means.
He passed away on the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the sixth year of Tiānhé,
at the age of fifty-seven.
An imperial decree posthumously granted him his original offices,
with the addition of Junior Tutor, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for the five provinces of Sī, Yù, Luò, Xiāng, and Jì, and Governor of Sīzhōu.
His posthumous name was Duke Sù,
as per ritual.
The Son of Heaven suspended court,
deepening the bond with his high official;
the various dukes gathered for the funeral,
all following the rituals of a sworn alliance.
His wife, Lady Lǐ,
was from the noble clan of Dùnqiū.
From a house of ministers
and a family of virtuous talents,
frost and dew first encroached upon her.
Her enfeoffment was decreed at the suburbs.
On the sixth day of the eleventh month of that year,
they were buried together at a certain plain in Cháng'ān County, Xiányáng.
Joint burial was not the ancient way,
being different from the time before the Three Kings;
yet "in death, sharing the same hole"
was the same as the beginning of the sixth year.
Although two cranes carrying pearls
return together to the pines of the purple canopy,
and a pair of dragons emerging from their case
sink together into the waters of Yánpíng.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus is the inscription offered:
The state has rocky cities,
the court has many gentlemen.
Duke Wǔ and Duke Zhuāng
were ministers to King Píng.
The wheat of Wēn violated the covenant,
and sacrifices at the fields of Bàng were abandoned.
The attendant stopped the carriage,
and those coming to court recognized the shoes.
Both grandfather and father
were marquises and dukes.
Their mechanisms were meticulous,
their administrative dealings clear and thorough.
Managing complexity with simple governance,
facing chaos with a heroic heart.
Legacy of kindness at the Jì and Hé rivers,
remaining fiefs at Hǎi and Dài.
Generations continued this beauty,
and this vessel of talent was born.
In loyalty, there was nothing he would not do;
in filial piety, he was never lacking.
Yōuzhōu and Jìzhōu were in turmoil,
the passes and rivers were boiling like a cauldron.
From north to south,
his fame was heard in Liáng and Wèi.
Raising banners in Rǔ and Yǐng,
his majesty shook the three rivers.
Holding the banner at the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
he swept up the multi-decked ships.
Dust rose at Chénggāo,
and beacon fires burned at Guǎngwǔ.
The elk rose at the deer-arrow,
and the wild geese fell at the startling string.
Commanding the armory guards,
he displayed majesty beyond the river.
Mountains were like drum towers,
trees were like carriage canopies.
Protector-General of two routes,
the general was uniquely honored.
Firmiana trees in the lush garden,
willows by the singing girl's house.
A thousand pieces of gold for swirling snow,
a hundred days of flowing rosy clouds.
Suddenly they withered and fell,
the glory was mournful.
Ancient trees of Héyáng,
remaining flowers of Jīngǔ.
The burial mound is dark with dim clouds,
the mountains are deep and the road is late.
The wind's air has just risen,
and the sound of pines grows distant.
Friends of former days,
bonded in joy.
Not for the sake of an ordinary life,
but should be for this parting.
Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 947.
Epitaph of the Zhōu Great General of Agile Cavalry and Opener of Office, Hóumòchén Dàoshēng.
The lord’s taboo name was Dàoshēng,
his courtesy name was [omitted],
he was a man of Wǔchuān in Shuòzhōu.
His lineage originated from Yīnshān
and emerged from the state clan.
Descending to the Wèi dynasty,
he resided in Qín and took the surname Liú.
His father, Shǎoxìng,
was the Garrison General of Wǔchuān.
Mountains and rivers stood in resistance;
the passes and fortresses were on the border.
They early on commanded a prestigious reputation,
and most were of heroic valor.
The gentleman read books while on horseback
and engaged in pure conversation at the tip of a sword;
he uniquely wielded the "Six Wonders"
and was expert in the "Three Strategies."
Although he held the rank of a minor officer,
his bravery was foremost at the gates of the army;
though his position was in a branch unit,
his counsel reached the commanding tent.
In the fifth year of the Zhèngguāng era of Wèi,
he served as a Commanding Officer,
subordinated to the Pillar of Heaven, Ěrzhū Róng,
to campaign against the King of Běihǎi.
In the third year of the Yǒng'ān era,
he followed Grand Preceptor Hèbá Shèng into the Pass.
Soon he was transferred to become a Separate General.
Rolling up armor at Huáyuán,
and tying up horses at the Pass city,
all were victories,
and the lord contributed his strength to them.
In the third year of the Yǒngxī era,
he was appointed as a Commander.
When Tàizǔ Emperor Wén held the lands of the Yellow River and the Pass,
and his commands were carried out throughout the world,
because of the lord’s administrative and strategic talents,
he was entrusted as a protector.
His name was well-known among the attendants,
and his merits were ranked with the high achievers.
When the army approached Héqǔ,
he was the first to ascend the Bǎimǎ Ford;
when the rebels emerged from Púchéng,
he fought first at the Huángshā Garden.
At Línjìn, he crossed with boats
and captured the General of Zhào;
at Mǎlíng, he peeled the trees
and again defeated the troops of Qí.
He was distributed the auspicious tallies by the Ministry of Merits,
and granted a fief according to the maps,
being appointed as Piàoqì Dàjiāngjūn, Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū, and the Founding Duke of Hù Xiàn,
with a fief of five hundred households.
When Zhào Yǎn became a Piàoqì General,
he only rode a single carriage;
when Zhāng Zhàn was appointed as Guānglù,
he always rode a white horse.
By comparing these types,
the court and the commoners honored him.
In the ninth year of the Dàtǒng era,
his surname was changed to Hóumòchén.
Following General Tuòbá Yuǎn to manage Shǐyáng,
the two waters fought for a long time,
and the three rivers had no market;
he fell ill while clad in armor
and died at the camp gate,
at the age of fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Envoy with a Tally, Commander, and Governor of Shuòzhōu.
When the lord was in Wǔchuān,
he was a fellow townsman of Emperor Wén.
Once the hegemonic achievements were established
and the royal enterprise was completed,
the Emperor did not forget the times they set aside lectures,
and still discussed their past gambling.
Now that the successor’s virtue is renewed,
the meritorious officials are remembered from afar.
At the Eastern Capital, the horse neighs,
not without the lament of seeing the day;
as the carriage passes the Northern Tomb,
one finally recalls the words of his lifetime.

There was an edict to further grant him posthumously the titles of Envoy with a Tally, Piàoqì Dàjiāngjūn, Opener of Office with the Same Ceremonies as the Three Ducal Ministers, Commander of the military affairs of Yí, Fū, and Jiàng provinces, and Governor of Fūzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title of Duke [Name Omitted],
in accordance with ritual.
His wife, Lady Tuòbá,
was the Lady of Ānyì Commandery.
The courtyard had bells and drums,
and the family inherited admonitions and warnings;
she taught appearance and virtue,
announcing her departure and returning to her home.
She passed away in the sixth month of the fifth year of the Tiānhé era,
and in the tenth month of that same year, she was buried together with him in Hóngyuán Township, [Name Omitted] County, Jīngzhào.
Wǔzǐ completed the burial chamber
and requested the western steps for a joint burial;
Píngyáng was married off
and shared a tomb at Lúshān.
The inscription says:
The congealed shade is distant and silent,
the vast desert is level and cold.
The sands exhaust the Hānhǎi,
the land ends at Gāolán.
The frontier geese depart in autumn,
the Hu mulberry withers in summer.
The local customs have a robust spirit,
the mountains and rivers are awe-inspiring.
The armies were at Shànggǔ,
their majestic power was at Wǔchuān.
The lord then followed in their footsteps;
the generations never lacked worthies.
The scabbard held a loyal sword,
the courtyard flowed with a fountain of filial piety.
The House of Wèi had many troubles,
and the remaining winds were not yet extinguished.
The Tiānbǎo era yielded its virtue,
and the established laws of the ruling path fell into disuse.
The high general pointed the way,
and the attendant exerted his strength.
Victory was achieved at Luòchéng by night,
and the river bridge was cut in the morning.
With iron sword and golden tortoise,
his glory followed the jade cauldron.
He was a descendant of the Hàn lineage,
and his family carried the Wèi succession.
Both lineages were illustrious clans,
both were known as people of influence.
The husband and wife were a perfect match,
and their ages were both advanced.
The zither of Zhào and the sounds of Qín,
together they became a tomb.
A stone sarcophagus at Xiǎolíng,
a grave in Hóngyuán Township.
Two straw effigies lead the way,
a pair of pool willows go before.
The tunnel paths are joined,
and the city of pines is connected.
Frost follows the willow's white,
the moon follows the mound’s roundness.
How many generations of irises and orchids?
What year for the mounds and valleys?
— Wényuàn Yīnghuá, 947.
〈Epitaph for Yǔwén Xiǎn, Zhōu General of Chariots and Cavalry, Posthumously Granted the Title of Xiǎo Sīkōng〉
The Duke’s taboo name was Xiǎn,
his courtesy name was [omitted],
he was a man of Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng.
Since the heavy mist floated over the River
and the long rainbow reflected on the islet,
his source began at Ruòshuǐ
and his lineage was continued at Cānglín.
Shàngdǎng lies to the west of Hán,
Chángshān is to the north of Zhào;
taking the place name as his surname,
this can be briefly stated.
His grandfather was Qiúnán,
General of the Guards and Governor of Jìzhōu.
His father was Jīndiàn,
General who Conquers the South and Governor of Dìngzhōu.
Both commanded the crane troops,
both displayed the music of the army;
the abundance of their reputation and glory
followed in succession during their years.
〈Epitaph for Yǔwén Xiǎn, Zhōu General of Chariots and Cavalry, Posthumously Granted the Title of Xiǎo Sīkōng〉
The Duke was endowed with the spirit of the mountains,
and possessed the aura of the winds and clouds.
His bearing was dignified and solemn,
and his reputation was exceedingly great.
He could bend a strong bow,
and shoot while galloping to either side.
Thus his fame was high in Shànggǔ,
and his awe shook Lóufán.
He inherited the title of Marquis of Ānjí County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
In the third year of Yǒngxīng,
Yōu and Bìng revolted,
harboring disloyal hearts towards the sovereign.
The Emperor looked at the Duke and said:
"The world is in turmoil,
what shall be done about it?"
The Duke said:
"Choose the good and follow it."
He then recited from the Shī, saying:
"That beautiful person,
is a person of the West."
The Emperor said:
"This is my heart's desire."
Thereupon the strategy to enter the Pass was determined.
Because the Duke’s mother was old and his family large,
the Emperor ordered him to make plans in advance.
The Duke said:
"In the matters of today,
loyalty and filial piety cannot both be fulfilled.
If the ruler is not discreet, he loses his ministers;
if the minister is not discreet, he loses his life."
The Emperor was moved and changed expression, saying:
"You are my Wáng Líng."
He was promoted to Attendant of the Vermilion Clothing and Grand Commander of the Palace,
and his title was changed to Duke of Zhǎngguǎng County,
with a fief of one thousand five hundred households.
When Wǔdì first arrived at Tóngguān,
Tàizǔ personally welcomed him at the Zhēnshuǐ River.
Tàizǔ had long known the Duke's name but did not yet recognize him.
Scanning the crowd,
he was uncertain but did not ask,
and simply said:
"Order this man to shoot the small crow by the water."
He hit it as soon as he released the arrow.
Tàizǔ said happily:
"I know your name now."
He was immediately appointed as the Commander of the Tents, Commander of Military Affairs in Cāngzhōu, and Governor of Cāngzhōu,
with his fief increased to a total of two thousand five hundred households.
As Huáng Gōnghéng decided matters,
the Empress of Wèi thus placed her trust in him;
as Pān Chéngmíng was loyal and brave,
the King of Wú treated him with courtesy.
Such honor shared across different eras
is seen again today.
At the border of Dōngxià,
where the land meets the wild regions,
the Jǐngxíng pass was blocked,
and the Fēihú road was cut off.
Thereupon the Duke was made Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, General of the Guard, Commander of Military Affairs in Dōngxiàzhōu, and Governor of Dōngxiàzhōu.
The soldiers of Báibō and Qīngdú,
and the rebels of Tóngmǎ and Jīnshéng,
all folded their arms and knelt,
leading sheep and embracing horses in surrender.
While in the province, he fell ill,
and resigned his post to return to court.
His small horses were left in the stables,
and his remaining garments hung on the screen;
the officials and people clung to him in affection,
and carved stones at Jǐngshān.
Though it was not the city of Hànyáng,
it was like the road of Fúfēng.
He was granted the titles of Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Great General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Equal in Dignity to the Three Gentry,
with the added title of Attendant-in-Ordinary of Cavalier Attendants.
In the first year of the Latter Wèi, his illness became severe,
and he died in Tóngzhōu
at the age of fifty-seven.
The Son of Heaven stopped the music,
and the various dukes gathered for the funeral;
Tàizǔ personally attended to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and his grief moved those around him.
At that time, as warfare was constant,
all posthumous gifts and titles were suspended;
thus he was provisionally buried with the seals and ribbons of his current office
at the North Mountain of Tóngzhōu.
Now, on the twenty-third day of the second month of the second year of Jiàndé,
he was reburied at the Hóngdú Yuán of Cháng’ān County in Xiányáng.
Meeting the time of the transition of rites and music,
and belonging to an era of changing songs of praise,
though the state has a different administration,
it is sufficient for people to pursue posthumous honor for him.

Thus he was posthumously granted Envoy with Extraordinary Powers, Great General of Agile Cavalry, Opening Office and Equal in Dignity to the Three Gentry, Lesser Minister of Works, Commander of Military Affairs in the three provinces of Dān, Yán, and Suí, and Governor of Yánzhōu.
He was given the posthumous title of Duke Zhuāng,
in accordance with the rites.
His wife, Lady Gāo,
was a person of Bóhǎi.
She assisted in the administration of Jìn,
resisting the deviant schemes of Cáo Shuǎng;
rising in the Han court,
she was like the mother of Wáng Líng.
Moreover, her instructions and admonitions were orderly,
and her speech and appearance were virtuous;
she was solemn and respectful in managing the household,
a talented and virtuous model of inner regulations.
She did not merely refuse to listen to vulgar music,
to change the customs of the State of Qí;
or refuse to eat fresh game,
to stop the hunting of the King of Jīng.
Formerly, for a joint burial,
there was the Western Chamber of Jì Wǔzǐ;
now, for the same tomb,
there is the Northern Tomb of the Chángpíng Hóu.
His heir Shénjǔ and his brothers
were of the purest and most filial nature,
observing the funeral rites well;
they were faithful from beginning to end,
and their character remained unchanged.
Thus their careers were successful and their names established,
their filial piety manifest and their loyalty enduring.
The Inscription says:
The Northern Peak has two names,
and the Cōng River has two sources.
Its height is supreme,
and its source is far-reaching.
Customs are endowed by the mountains and rivers,
and the people are supported by the high ministers.
Righteous and fierce, majestic and grand,
talented and heroic, sincere and earnest.
The grandfather and the father
followed one another in majesty and might.
Striking the metal in the Northern Lands,
and sounding the jade in the Southern Palace.
Formidable like Wú Hàn,
and worthy like Dòu Róng.
The Guìshuāng relied on their virtue,
and the Wúléi turned toward their influence.
Manifesting this hidden beauty,
and born with this held virtue.
Filial piety is indeed a heavenly nature,
and loyalty is the rule for men.
Smooth chariots and carved harnesses,
south of Yān and north of Zhào.
If the Ruòshuǐ River is about to open,
the nine tribes can be inscribed.
Participating in strategy within the tents,
and managing duties within the palace gates.
Choosing good and loyal words,
and able to guard against changing expressions.
The Fánruò bow was already strong,
and the Qíyuán bamboo was straight.
Hitting the small branch of the halberd,
and piercing the left wing of the bird.
Setting up the banners in Chìgǔ,
and waving the spear in Wǔzhōu.
The Great Wall of ten thousand miles,
and the River flowing in two streams.
Yǐngchuán has many ailments,
and the Huái River is not yet healed.
Righteousness as heavy as piercing the wall,
and grace as deep as establishing post stations.
At the mouth of the valley,
and on the sunny side of the Wèi River.
The hills and mountains are falling away,
and the stele and gates are rising and falling.
The grass bites the autumn fire,
and the trees embrace the spring frost.
Books and swords have both vanished,
and the man and his zither are both gone.
Sorrowful is the heir,
with no place to entrust his pure heart.
The water of filial piety has not dried,
but the sorrowful pines fall first.
A wren nests in the room,
and a crane comes to the gate to mourn.
The meritorious official has died;
his portrait will meet in the Lín Gé.
Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 947.
Epitaph of Sīmǎ Yì, the Great General and Duke Zhuāng of Lángyá of Zhōu.
Epitaph of Sīmǎ Yì, the Great General and Duke Zhuāng of Lángyá of Zhōu.
The Duke’s taboo name was Yì,
his courtesy name was Zūnyìn,
and he was a native of Wēn in Hénèi.
The Nánzhèng oversaw the heavens,
and the Běizhèng oversaw the earth;
these were called the offices of Xī and Hé,
which inherited the governance of Zhòng and Lí.
When Áng returned to Chǔ,
he was enfeoffed alongside Zhāng Hán;
when Yù avoided the Qín,
he departed together with Máogōng.
His grandfather was Jīnlóng,
who remained in the Xuǎnbù,
serving as a "Water Mirror" for the Sāntái.
His father was Yuè,
who twice governed Jīng and Hé,
his majestic influence extending for a thousand li,
yet he encountered a disastrous turn of fate
and was ultimately mourned by Jì Bù;
that a descendant survived
was truly due to the loyalty of Chéng Yīng.
The State, in remembrance of its meritorious ministers,
again cared for the son of Shū’áo;
thinking of the official clans,
they sought out the descendant of Nǚ Qí.
The Duke first responded to a summons
to serve as the Gōngcáo of Hénèi,
and was appointed as a Yuánwàiláng Chángshì.
He trained troops in Jìjùn,
and his horses swam across the Huánghé;
