he broke the enemy's front in the victory at Zhǐguān,
and pursued the fleeing northern tribes at the battle of the Chángchéng.
He was appointed Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Amidst the dust of Liǔquán,
he swept through the Sānchéng;
amidst the arrows and bolts of Tángyīn,
a thousand households entered the Pass.
He was promoted to Chēqì Dàjiāngjūn, Yítóng Sānsī, and Kāiguó Lóngmén Xiànbó,
and was further appointed Bāzhōu Cìshǐ.
Although the Bāshuǐ wound three times
and the local songs played several tunes,
he merely encountered the crossbows of the Bǎizhú,
having already accomplished the feats of Qīngyī.
The court, believing that a meritorious official of Hàn
should open the office of a high general,
and that a descendant of Jìn
should succeed to the state of Lángyá,
promoted him to Piàoqì Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ,
and changed his title to Lángyá Gōng,
with a fief of one thousand five hundred households.
The inner palace being a place of intimacy,
it truly required loyalty and integrity;
a decree appointed him as Dàyùbó,
and he was further appointed as Dàyùzhèng.
His duties were those of a Chángbó,
and his responsibilities were as central as those of Kuí and Lóng;
the Kingly Way being pacified,
his silken words were ever appropriate.
Soon after, he was appointed Shǐzhōu Cìshǐ and Dūdū of Military Affairs of Shǐzhōu.
The barbarians relied on the mountain fastnesses,
looking back like wolves and spreading like owls.
High mountains reached for the clouds,
and deep valleys saw no sunlight;
the nine levels of earth were crisscrossed,
and the Sānmén rose and fell.
On perilous peaks, horses were reined in;
over dangerous waters, bridges flew.
Consequently, the valleys became quiet and the mountains empty,
as ice melted and mists dispersed.
He then became Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ and Dūdū of Military Affairs of Xìnzhōu.
Elite troops guarded Báidì,
sufficient to secure the city of Bāzhōu;
wood shavings from ship-building floated down to Jīngzhōu,
further unsettling the garrisons of Xīlíng.
He was then appointed Shǐchíjì, Dàjiāngjūn, Dūdū of Military Affairs of Xīníngzhōu, and Xīlíngzhōu Cìshǐ.
About to open the way for the people of the northern gates,
and connect to the southern lands of the clouds,
he received favor as if with alarm,
and suddenly passed away in the deep of night.
He died on the eighteenth day of the first month of the sixth year of Tiānhé,
at the age of sixty-five.
A decree posthumously granted him his original offices,
with the addition of Cìshǐ of the four prefectures of Huái, Shào, Fén, and Jìn,
and the posthumous title Zhuāng Gōng,
according to the rites.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of Jiàndé,
he was buried at Sānchóuyuán in Wǔgōng Jùn.
The Duke’s love and respect were pure and deep;
he was discreet and never offensive.
He was loyal, upright, and sincere,
doing everything he knew should be done.
He was in the military for forty-two years
and personally experienced sixty-nine battles.
Whether it was increasing the number of stoves or counting tallies,
he always achieved success;
even when flying sand enveloped stones,
he never strayed from military discipline.
Respectfully teaching righteousness,
he had the style of Wú Qǐ at Xīhé;
leisurely commanding drums and flags,
he had the governance of Lǐ Mù at Chángpíng.
On the day of his death,
his family had no surplus wealth;
the resources for his burial
were entirely provided by the imperial decree.
Having a beginning and an end,
he had glory in life and grief in death.
The inscription says:
Zhùróng received the mandate,
and Zhòng and Lí were able to fulfill it.
The official clan was thus established,
and the celestial offices were set in order.
Avoiding the world in Qín,
and continuing the family in Chǔ.
When the Jìn dynasty lost its reins,
and the jade mirror lost its luster.
My illustrious ancestor
recognized the changes and seized the opportunity.
The yellow flag vanished in the east,
and the blue canopy flew to the west.
Falling stars marked the path,
and Chángzhōu emerged from the siege.
When it came to my August Father,
he twice governed Jīng and Hé.
The age was one of death and disorder,
and he perished at the hands of a cunning scoundrel.
Alas for me, the remaining descendant,
as hard-pressed as Zhào Wǔ.
In the cold, covered by bird wings;
in hunger, swallowing the milk of beasts.
Returning to Hénèi,
and once again succeeding at Lángyá.
In the years of the bamboo horse,
resentment toward the long snake was formed.
Hiding troops in the nine levels of earth,
and placing swords in a thousand homes.
Snowy mountains buried the horses,
and icy rivers trapped the chariots.
Then, having distributed the governance,
he remained transcendent in his honorable post.
Red herons flew frequently,
and the golden tortoise seals turned.
Building fortifications at Chángyú,
and establishing camps at Gāoliǔ.
Jade tables offered food,
and at Hénjiáo, wine was encouraged.
Shímén's ice dissolved,
and Jīndī's lightning dispersed.
The gates of Lúshuǐ were closed,
and Máojīn became a watchtower.
Riding the wind with swift wings,
the long journey had only reached its half.
Among the meritorious officials of Jiànwǔ,
one first grieves for Wú Hàn.
Deep silence and falling leaves,
the field of play gradually fades.
The road to Jīnchéng is cut off,
and people in Méiwù are few.
Wind through the pines is a cloudy canopy,
and white waters are the mountain’s garment.
The worthy one has fallen like a star,
the man is gone and the orchids wither.
— Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 947.
〈Epitaph of the Zhōu Dàjiāngjūn, Huáidé Gōng, Wú Míngchè〉
〈Epitaph of the Zhōu Dàjiāngjūn, Huáidé Gōng, Wú Míngchè〉
The Duke’s taboo name was Míngchè,
his courtesy name was Tōngzhāo,
and he was a native of Qínjùn in Yǎnzhōu.
Among the states of the Western Capital,
the Chángshā Wáng’s merit covered the mountains and rivers;
among the noble officials of the Eastern Capital,
the Dà Sīmǎ’s name was higher than the heavens.
It was not only that Xīhé had a defender
whose wisdom was sufficient to resist Qín,
or that Jiànpíng had a city
whose might could move Jìn!
His grandfather, Shàng,
was the Nánqiáo Tàishǒu.
His father, Biāo,
was the Yòujūn Jiāngjūn.
Resisting at the Huái and Yí,
and pacifying the Jì and Luò,
they were famous generals for generations,
as seen herein.
The Duke’s spirit and ambition were expansive and unrestrained;
his manner was elegant and uninhibited.
At Yǐ Qiáo he retrieved the shoe,
early on manifesting knowledge of military strategy;
in the bamboo forest he met the ape,
gaining complete mastery of swordsmanship.
Thus he attained courageous peerages in court,
and was selected as a talented official.
He began his career as Sīzhí of the Dōnggōng,
and was later appointed to the Zuǒjūn.
Gē Zhān had just succeeded to military command
when he encountered the destruction of Shǔ;
Lù Jī had only just begun to discuss his achievements
when he faced the downfall of Wú.
The Duke’s service to the Liáng
was not yet considered reaching full prominence.
Since Liáng received its end
and the ministers of Qí held the government,
rites, music, and military expeditions
all returned to the descendants of Shùn.
Thus his prestige spread to the four seas,
and his virtuous teachings reached the feudal lords;
clearing away the desolate mist and clouds,
he shone like the sun and moon.
The Duke assisted the times with brilliant strategies,
and aided affairs with heroic plans;
like scales and wings spreading anew,
his wind and gale reached afar.
Guànjūn Hóu’s use of troops
did not necessarily follow the ancients;
Wǔ’ān Jūn’s nurturing of soldiers
could win people’s hearts.
Comparing him to their rank,
this describes the Duke.
He served as Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and soon was promoted to Zhènjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
As Běijūn Zhònghòu,
he oversaw the administration of the six armies;
as Hénán Jīngyǐn,
he was the leader of a hundred commanderies.
Civil and military matters were entrusted to him;
the Duke was without shame in this.
In the campaign of Xiāoxiāng,
he overran the islands.
With wind-driven boats and fire-ships,
Zhōu Yú had the troops of Chìbì;
with stem-to-stern canopies and decks,
Hè Qí had the battle of Héngjiāng.
He then became Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Dūdǔ and Cìshǐ of the four provinces of Xiāng, Héng, Guì, and Wǔ;
thus the gate of the left flank was turned back,
and the rumbling chariots returned smoothly.
The Chǔ iron of Chángshā
entered the weapon racks once more;
the rhinoceros hides hidden in Dòngpǔ
were returned to the armor treasury.
Although battle songs repeatedly celebrated victory,
the military tents were still pitched;
Huáinán looked at the prisoner of the Tíngwèi,
and Héfèi called him the general of the bandits.
None failed to lose their burrows or have their nests startled,
sinking into water or falling into fire.
He became Shǐchíjié, Shìzhōng, Sīkōng, Chēqì Dàjiāngjūn, Dūdǔ of the military affairs of the five provinces of Nán-Běi Yǎn, Qīng, and Qiáo, Cìshǐ of Nányǎn Zhōu, and Nánpíng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng,
with a household fief of eight thousand
and a set of drums and pipes.
The Zhōngtái was in the palace of Xuánwǔ,
the Shàngjiàng was ranked among the stars of Wénchāng;
high cicada-wing hats graced his temples,
singing egrets accompanied his carriage.
The town of Píngyáng had ten thousand households,
the horses of Línzī numbered a thousand teams.
Sitting, he was served food on jade tables;
traveling, the ranks under his banner were divided.
His life was thus;
such were his achievements.
Soon, the spirit of the metal element became strong,
and the army set out for a just cause;
the sound of the stone drums was loud,
and the engagement of troops could reach afar.
Thus, where the ships arrived,
they covered the Huái and Sì;
where the banners attacked,
they suddenly possessed Guī and Méng.
The Wèi generals had already fled,
yet names were still written on the tree of Mǎlíng;
the Qí army retreated,
looking in vain at the crows of Píngyīn.
Shortly after, Nánzhòng set out with his chariots,
and Fāngshū arrived;
with smooth hubs and patterned cushions,
hooked breastplates and leather reins.
However, because the Way of Heaven was in the north,
the southern wind did not prevail.
In the past, when the lieutenant general lost discipline,
the Wèijiāngjūn then awaited punishment;
when the central army struggled to cross,
Xún Huánzǐ was then executed.
The heart is grieved;
how can one serve the lord?
In the first year of Xuānzhèng,
he reached the pavilion of the Dōngdū;
an edict was issued to release his carriage bits
and pardon the ritual offenses.
He began by receiving the rites of the guesthouse
and immediately received the appointment at the altar.
He was appointed Shǐchíjié Dàjiāngjūn and Huáidé Jùn Kāiguó Gōng,
with a fief of two thousand households.
Returning to the manor of Píngjīn,
he occasionally heard the neighing of stable horses;
staying at the lodging of Guǎngchéng,
he barely saw the guests of the feudal lords.
Lián Pō was full of longing,
yet when would he hear of being used again?
Lǐ Guǎng lingered,
no longer having hope of being the vanguard.
The drunken lieutenant of Bàlíng,
his insult can be known;
the former Marquis of Dōnglíng,
his life was over.
On the twenty-eighth day of the seventh month in the second year of Dàxiàng,
his respiratory illness suddenly worsened,
and he passed away in the guesthouse
at the age of seventy-seven.
On the nineteenth day of the eighth month of that year, he was temporarily buried in the eastern suburbs of Wànnián Xiàn in Jīngzhào.
An edict posthumously granted him a certain office,
and the posthumous title of so-and-so,
according to ritual.
The eight thousand youths of Jiāngdōng
followed Xiàng Jí and did not return;
the five hundred soldiers on the sea island
died together for Tián Héng.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Máo Xiūzhī was buried beyond the frontier,
wandering and not remaining;
Lù Píngyuán was defeated at Héqiáo,
dying with shame and regret.
Returning the coffin of Gōngsūn
is yet far off;
returning the body of Liányǐn,
on what day will it finally be known?
A wandering soul in a foreign land
enough to wound the heart of Wēn Xù;
in the dark night thinking of return,
finally having the dream of Sū Sháo.
Thus, it makes the neighborhood of Guǎngpíng
forever hold the aggrieved soul;
at the pavilion of Rǔnán,
one long hears night crying.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, the inscription says:
The nine rivers are the dwelling land,
the three rivers offer tribute.
That beautiful Zhōngbāng,
the Lord cultivated and enriched it.
Possessing talent and priding himself on wisdom,
braving danger and relying on strength.
Like floating sounding-stones concealed and withdrawing scales,
like a solitary paulownia drooping its wings.
The five weapons were early exhausted,
the spirit of the first drum-beat previously declined.
Moving the camp and reducing the stoves,
birds fly over the empty tents.
Can a sheepskin robe ransom him?
How can the painted horse be pursued?
Xún Yīng has gone forever,
Suí Huì has no return.
Life and death in an instant,
time is mournful and sad.
The mountain crumbles at the Zhōngtái,
the star is empty at the Shàngjiàng's position.
Thinking of the wife and children,
distant at the pavilion and barrier.
The soul perhaps can be summoned,
but how can the funeral procession be hoped for?
Great ambitions have sunk,
heroic plans are buried.
The west of Lǒng is enough to reach,
yellow dust crushes the bones.
Where are the ponds and terraces?
Whose home is the wind and moon?
The tomb path is far and foreign,
the wandering soul stays abroad.
No mound on the banks of the Bà,
no trees at Pínglíng.
The mound of a brave man,
the tomb of a general.
In what age, in what year,
will it return to being an armory?
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 947.
Inscription for the Tomb of the Zhōu Dàjiāngjūn, Shàng Kāifǔ, Guǎngráo Gōng, Zhèng Cháng.
The Lord’s taboo name was Cháng,
his courtesy name was so-and-so,
and he was a man of Xíngyáng.
He was a descendant of the younger brother of Zhōu Xuān Wáng,
who was first enfeoffed with that state;
and a grandson of Zhèng Mù Gōng,
from whom his surname first began.
His grandfather was Sīqìng,
Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Shānyáng.
His father was Xù,
Yítóng Sānsī and Provincial Governor of Yùzhōu.
Whistling while seated in Nányáng,
he met with the lords of this land;
establishing the falcon-pennant in Xīhé,
he encountered those administrative duties.
Dukes and marquises followed in succession,
their caps and carriages rode side by side;
this can be spoken of
and is recorded in the historical archives.
The Lord knew the rites since his childhood
and galloped toward fame in his early years.
He studied the classics at the school
and gained a general view in the hall of books;
he practiced martial arts at the military barracks
and was especially skilled in swordsmanship.
Even though he was still of primary school age,
he was already praised by Confucian scholars;
while holding a junior officer's position,
he received the rewards of a general.
In the third year of Dàtǒng,
he raised righteous troops in Huáyáng
and was appointed the Founding Baron of Yǒng'ān Xiàn.
When Wén Huángdì first established the foundations of his hegemony,
heroes converged like spokes at a hub;
the Lord drew his sword at the camp gate,
following like the men of Yǐngchuān.
In the counterattack at Luòchéng,
he was braver than the troops of Báimǎ;
at the breaking of the siege at Héqiáo,
he was bolder than the strategy at Wūlín.
He was appointed Píngdōng Jiāngjūn and Shuàidūdū,
inheriting his father's title.
In the second year of the Later Wèi,
he was appointed Chíjié, Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn, and Yítóng Sānsī.
The Chēqí post utilized the merit of Guō Huái,
and the Yítóng rank took the nobility of Wáng Shěn;
regarding the Lord’s appointment,
everyone said that the right person had been found.
He was promoted to the peerage of Duke of Guǎngráo Xiàn,
with a fief of one thousand households.
In the third year of Bǎodìng, he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Commander of Military Affairs of Qiānzhōu, and Provincial Governor of Qiānzhōu.
He took general command of the troops of Jīnzhōu
to expand into the Běiróng territory.
High mountains touched the clouds,
and deep valleys saw no light;
they climbed using ropes and ladders,
and passed through only by floating on bamboo;
his influence reached Mǐnyuè,
and his prestige moved Gōuwú.
The Lord went out to fight with short weapons,
and all enemies fled in defeat;
they crumbled like tiles and shattered like ice,
leaving the mountains empty and the valleys silent.
He was appointed Chíjié and Kāifǔ Yítóng Dàjiāngjūn.
At the grand banquet of Báiliáng,
there was the poem of the Great General;
when the administration office was first opened,
there was the fief of the Marquis of Pínglíng.
Compared to today,
how could they be spoken of in the same breath!
From then on, his envoy carriage
was covered in embroidered robes;
folk songs were observed
and punishments and government were supervised.
The Lord displayed his tallies as he drove east,
and the bands of bandits fled like the wind;
he buried the wheels in the road,
and his majesty shook the Central Plains.
When Wǔ Huángdì led the army at Méngjīn,
he used the Lord as the strength of the central corps;
externally he followed to secure victory,
and internally he attended to military strategy.
Once the writing and ruts were unified,
and the banners were laid down,
the Ministry of Merit distributed rewards,
and military officials recorded achievements;
he was then appointed Shǐchíjié and Shàngkāifǔ,
with an increase of five hundred households to his fief.
He was bestowed the surname Yǔwén,
sharing the honor of riding with the imperial family;
as a member of the Zhōu dynastic alliance,
he was no longer a descendant of a different surname.
Entrusted as a protective screen,
and the recipient of great favor,
there was no distance from the imperial house;
this is what was meant.
The Commander of the Nine Provinces
must have such talent;
the feudal lords of a thousand lǐ
truly await such governance.
He was appointed Shǐchíjié, Commander of Military Affairs of Dōngxúzhōu, and Provincial Governor of Xúzhōu.
Soon he was moved to Commander of Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu and Provincial Governor of Nányǎnzhōu.
The Lord frequently managed the "six articles" of administration,
and twice toiled for the "ten regions";
customs changed and the atmosphere shifted,
as the people felt his care and the officials felt his awe.
Lingering stalks and abandoned sheaves
benefited the weary people;
mountain mulberries and wild silkworms
were sufficient to fulfill the tribute and taxes.
His transformation reached distant customs,
and his majesty spread to neighboring borders;
when reporting affairs to the capital,
he was the first among the four quarters.
To speak of a true Provincial Governor,
would it not be him?
Before his years were advanced,
he suddenly fell ill.
He died at his provincial post in the first year of Dàxiàng,
at the age of sixty-three.
Alas, how sorrowful! Officials and people clung to him in longing,
and even the birds and beasts changed color;
at the Hé and Jǐ rivers, the pounding of grain was halted;
at the Huái and Yí rivers, the markets were suspended.
In this year, he was returned for burial in the mountains of Xíngyáng.
An imperial decree posthumously granted him a certain office,
as is the ritual.
Lamenting the shifting of mounds and valleys,
and fearing that his fine legacy would fade into the distant future,
enduring as long as the earth and sky,
I venture to engrave this enduring stone.
The inscription says:
Jīng and Hé are the Yù province,
the foundation of the Luò capital.
Waters encircle the Xíngyáng waves,
and mountains slant toward Lùhún.
The stars of virtue still shine,
and the auspicious winds are not far.
Generations do not lack worthy men,
and their writings are never without the official robes.
When the Lord was born,
a heroic spirit truly descended.
Loyalty was the root of his virtue,
and filial piety was his heavenly constant.
He studied books in the Tiger Hall
and learned swordsmanship at the Dragon Pavilion.
His carved bow was like a waning moon,
and his galloping horse like a shooting star.
He set up battle lines at Líyáng
and directed troops at Guāndù.
Listening to the crows at Píngyīn,
and writing on the tree at Mǎlíng.
He observed the aura at the returning ford
and divined the stars for his swift steps.
Fire cut off the Qiāng camp,
and sands collapsed the bandits' road.
Then driving with his rhino-horn tally,
he governed the great provinces.
Officials did not startle the dogs,
and the people had no gasping oxen.
The western silkworms flourished in their season,
and the eastern crops met the autumn.
Grass rotted at the prison gates,
and the stars hung low over the market towers.
The five general stars have vanished,
and the Three Terraces of the mountains have split.
Alas, the Way of Heaven,
it had to take the wise and bright.
The pillars and beams have collapsed,
and the wind and clouds have been extinguished.
The northern outskirts are filled with long sorrow,
and the Eastern Capital bids an eternal farewell.
Deep and secluded is this place,
where the burial site rests.
The mountains encircle the tiger enclosure,
and the road passes by the fish mound.
The sorrowful wind is fierce at night,
and the bitter dew congeals in the morning.
Fragrant orchids and lush chrysanthemums
shall succeed one another through all eternity.
From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, volume 947.
〈Epitaph of the Great General of Zhōu, Duke of Wénxǐ, Liǔ Xiá〉
〈Epitaph of the Great General of Zhōu, Duke of Wénjiāxǐ, Liǔ Xiá〉
The lord’s name was Xiá,
and his courtesy name was Zǐshēng.
He was a man from Xiè District in Hédōng.
In the land where the Qín first conquered Jìn,
and the township where the Hàn first opened Píngyuè,
its pitch corresponds to Yízé,
and its star resides in Chuánshǒu.
Furthermore, like Zhuāng who plotted in Wèi,
he was already a minister of the state;
like Xǐ who served in Qí,
he did not neglect the duties of the feudal lords.
His grandfather was Shūzhēn,
who was the Sòng Yuánwài Sànjì Chángshì and Governor of Yìyáng.
He possessed the responsiveness of Xú Miǎo
while serving in the Department of the Sànjì;
he had the uprightness of Jì Àn
while governing the commandery of Huáiyáng.
His father was Jìyuǎn,
who was the Zīyì Cānjūn to the Prince of Línchuān and Governor of Yídū.
The Lántái and the Shíshì
were where he was extensively learned;
at Báimǎ and Fēihú,
his literary spirit was even loftier.
Wú Róng of the western capital
was famous south of the River;
when they met in conversation,
they were just like old friends.
The lord inherited the spirit of illustrious virtue
and was endowed with an aura that reached the heavens.
In his childhood with baby teeth and bunned hair,
his innate wisdom was early formed.
Love and respect came naturally from heaven;
reverence and humility were part of his nature.
He harbored benevolence and embraced righteousness;
he practiced faithfulness and dwelt in integrity.
His paternal uncle, the Duke Zhōnghuì of Yítóng, held him in exceptional regard
and thus said to him:
"In the past, when I served my uncle the Grand Marshal,
he told me:
'Last night I dreamed you climbed a tall tower;
the tower was utterly lofty and beautiful,
and I gave you my sitting mat.
You may attain wealth and honor,
but I regret that I will not live to see it.'
Just now, I took a short nap,
and I dreamed again of taking that old sitting mat
and giving it back to you.
Your rank and office will surely be seen by me again."
Like Wáng Xiáng’s sword,
they were a family of high officials for generations;
like Bào Yǒng’s dapple-grey horse,
their family heritage was that of the Sīlì.
Comparing him to such examples,
he truly had no reason for shame in his virtues.
When the Light Chariot General, the Marquis of Xīchāng, governed the Xiāng and Hàn regions,
the lord was twelve years old.
He paid his respects with the etiquette of a commoner;
his movements were composed, and his spirit was elegant and upright.
The Marquis watched him without ceasing
and tried sending his attendants
to step on the lord's robe
to observe his movements.
The lord slowly stepped forward
without ever looking back.
When the Marquis of Wèi saw Liú Yì,
he unconsciously straightened his expression;
when the Hàn sovereign observed Tián Fèng,
he consequently ordered him to write on a pillar.
Compared to today,
how could those even be worth mentioning?
When the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Prince of Lújiāng, a son of the Emperor, went out to govern a province,
he set high standards for selection.
Because of the lord’s illustrious reputation,
he summoned him to be his Master of Records.
Zhāng Tǎn’s direct remonstrances
were already praised like the fragrance of Lord Xún;
Zōu Zhàn’s insightful words
further manifested the virtue of Lord Yáng.
When the Zīyì passed away in the capital,
the lord hurried to the funeral,
reaching the capital in six days.
His body was so wasted and emaciated
that he was no longer recognizable.
While the coffin was being transported up the river,
it reached the middle of the stream at dusk;
the turbulent current was at its peak,
and a whirling wind reversed the sails.
The people on the boat
looked at each other and lost color.
He embraced the coffin and wailed in grief,
vowing not to seek survival.
In a short moment,
the wind and waves became calm;
everyone believed it was brought about by the lord’s sincere devotion.
The filial son of Chéngdū
threw himself into the river's flow;
the ancient worthy of Guìyáng
exposed his body to the wild fire.
Both preserved the coffins
and were equally worthy of sorrowful sighs.
The Great Lady developed a sore between her breasts;
the doctor said:
"Only if someone sucks out the pus and blood
can we hope she might recover."
The lord’s heart was already in turmoil;
responding to the call, he immediately sucked the wound.
Within ten days,
she finally attained a complete recovery.
The lord’s service to his parents
can truly be called the ultimate.
His older cousin, the General of the Right Guard,
held the banner in the Lǐngbiǎo region
and earnestly invited him to join him.
In the past, Mǎ Yóu’s ambition
was recognized by Mǎ Yuán;
Bān Sì’s talent and learning
were appreciated by Bān Biāo—
this was heard once again today.
He was then appointed as Magistrate of Yǒnghuà County.
He quietly cleared away the leaning desks,
sometimes chanting of the distance of Chángcén;
occasionally playing the sounding zither,
he did not consider Héyáng to be lowly.
The gold pillars of Rìnán
and the pearl springs of Hépǔ
never occupied his thoughts
and never caught his eye.
He left retirement to become Legal Officer Cānjūn for the Prince of Shàolíng, General of the West,
and subsequently transferred to become Shàngshū Gōngbù Shìláng.
He first entered the gates of ritual
and then ascended to the Orchid Gallery.
The Shàngshū Púshè Xiè Jǔ of Chén Commandery,
who was a man of prestige and the glory of the state,
drew the lord into conversation
and said to those sitting with them:
"The heroic spirit of the Jiāng and Hàn
is seen here!"
The Prince of Yuèyáng, General of the Middle West,
with the prestige of the green carriage,
oversaw the administration of Xīhé.
By decree, the lord was appointed as Zhìzhōng of his home province,
and soon after promoted to Biéjià.
Wáng Shǔlǐ gained fame through his classification of things;
Chén Zhòngjǔ spread his reputation by inscribing on the eaves;
as for the lord’s display of his talent,
he possessed both their qualities.
When the great bandit subverted the state
and the royal house was in turmoil,
the moon moved and the stars shook,
clouds leveled and rainbows straightened.
The Prince of Yuèyáng exercised imperial authority in Shǎnzǔo
and took charge in Hànnán.
Where the heavenly net was cast,
heroes and worthies all gathered.
He appointed the lord as Sànjì Shìláng, Yuánwàiláng of the Ministry of Personnel, and Sànjì Chángshì,
as well as Tutor to the Crown Prince.
Supervising the heir in the Jiǎguān,
his duties were as significant as those of Shǐ Dān;
lecturing in the Guì Palace,
his fame was as high as that of Zhāng Yǔ.
He was soon promoted to Great General of Chariots and Cavalry and Grand Commander,
granted the title of Duke of Wénxǐ County, Shìzhōng, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with the rest as before.
Comparing him to those who shared the carriage,
Huò Qùbìng was a Shìzhōng;
likening him to those leading troops,
Gōngsūn Áo was a General of Chariots and Cavalry.
This was sufficient to illuminate the Six Offices
and clarify the Nine Virtues.
Was he merely a match for the great generals
or an assistant to the central army?
Afterward, he followed the words of the State of Liáng
and administered governance in Fèngdū.
Like Guǎn Zhòng who had words,
he immediately received the rites of a lower minister;
like Zāngsūn whose virtue was seen,
he returned to be honored at the banquet for esteemed guests.

An imperial decree appointed him as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Great General of Chariots and Cavalry, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Commander of All Military Affairs in Huòzhōu, and Governor of Huòzhōu.
With rhinoceros-horn tallies, he left the pass;
in ceremonial robes, he hurried by courier carriage.
For the welcome in the suburbs, men of letters were his vanguard;
for his retinue, the lords of the land carried his crossbow.
But because the Five Creeks were far away,
he had Mǎ Fùbō’s desire to return;
because the Three Xiāng regions were low and damp,
he shared Jiǎ Chángshā’s reluctance.
Thus, as Governor of Yíchéng,
he directly met at Lùmén;
in the ancient land of Báishā,
the dragon's seed remained.
Pestilence was not avoided,
and he suddenly reached his end.
In a certain year of the Tiānhé era,
he was buried in the old family cemetery at Báishā in Xiāngyáng.
The Duke had an auspicious and upright bearing,
a profound and quick discernment.
He purified his character and bathed in virtue,
roamed in the arts and relied on benevolence.
He possessed the high reputation of Rǔnán,
and the seniority of an elder from Fúfēng.
He did not speak of wealth or profit,
embodying the virtue of Wáng Yīfǔ;
he did not discuss the faults of people,
following the character of Ruǎn Sìzōng.
Calmly navigating the opportunities amidst chaos and separation,
he preserved this fine name;
in the midst of rising and falling like wind and clouds,
it did not hinder his noble career.
After the armillary sphere of Zhāng Héng,
he immediately composed the "Rhapsody on Returning to the Fields";
since the submerged stone tablets of Dù Yù,
he then stayed in his home village.
Wáng Zhòngxuān had a tower for reading books,
Zhūgé Liàng had a residence for playing the qín;
he truly wished to use this as a reason to resign due to illness,
and live in leisure until the end.
With a sounding qín on his lap,
he sometimes faced old friends;
with a precious sword accompanying him,
he occasionally encountered young children.
A hundred years pass in an instant,
alas, how sorrowful!
Thus, it came to pass that the tomb of the gentleman
buried only a bronze sword;
the grave of the worthy official
was only inscribed on a stone casket.
The inscription says:
Having the qualities of Zhuāng and Huì,
dwelling in Lǔ and Wèi.
Righteousness followed the times,
talent was sufficient to save the world.
Minister of the Northern Department,
Retainer of the Eastern Capital.
He will surely return to his origins,
with the Lord Marquis succeeding him.
The Flowery Canopy is a peak,
the Literary Brilliance is a star.
In his youth, he distinguished his ambition;
as a child, he mastered the classics.
His sense of justice urged him not to be like the "non-horse,"
his study was as diligent as those who use the light of fireflies.
In past years, the coffin
drifted on the Jiāng and Tuó rivers.
Because of the gentleman's profound mourning,
the Lord of the River stopped the waves.
Spreading fame in Běihǎi,
gallop of reputation in Xīhé.
Who would ascend the nine bends,
and not enter Cháogē?
The brilliance of his patterns has changed,
the company he kept is now far away.
White deer followed the carriage,
red halos attached to the ceremonial cap.
His position ranked among the great generals,
his glory combined with his original selection.
The snake coiled and the ribbons tied,
the turtle turned and the seal revolved.
Coming to court at Pínglè,
returning governance to Xiányáng.
The regional defense was established,
the military curtain was stretched out.
Initiating these rituals and measures,
elevating these military regulations.
The long-departed phoenix gracefully
preened its feathers at the Língjiāng.
The world is like a rushing stream,
the years are urged by a startled falcon.
Vanishing, he halted the bridle;
at Fúsāng, the carriage crossbar shook.
The wise man is like a split rock,
the worthy man is a fallen star.
The Ganoderma of Xī’è has withered,
the chrysanthemums of Nányáng are gone.
Mournfully, he yielded his life,
his lifetime glory reached its end.
The pestles stopped pounding,
the sounding looms ceased weaving.
The lonely heir
watches the shadows with his remaining breath.
Stepping on frost and dew,
how sorrowful the state of mourning.
Looking north toward Lóngcháo,
viewing the Phoenix Gate in front.
Pines are tall and the wind is distant,
the earth is deep and the springs are cold.
Books are buried and bamboo slips fall,
the qín is covered and the strings are loose.
The tablets for the funeral procession
are written and placed in the coffin.
— Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 948.
Tomb Inscription of the Late Zhōu Grand General, Duke of Yìxīng, Lord Xiāo.
Tomb Inscription of the Late Zhōu Grand General, Duke of Yìxīng, Lord Xiāo.
Formerly, when the Sītú spread the Five Teachings,
it was at the beginning of Yáo’s abdication;
when the Prime Minister managed the myriad affairs,
it was after the fall of Qín.
If the people of Yīn received their surname,
it was inheriting the fief of Wēizǐ;
when the Liáng destiny followed the charts,
it truly opened the state of Yánlíng.
The Duke’s taboo name was Tài,
his courtesy name was Shìyí,
a man of Lánlíng,
grandson of Emperor Wén Huángdì, the Great Progenitor, and son of King Zhōngliè of Pōyáng.
His lineage branched from the Heavenly River,
his descent divided from the Ruò Tree;
the straight trunk was naturally high,
the clear source was already distant.
Flourishing relatives and bright virtue,
this is called the merit of Máo and Bì;
the clan sons were the wall of the city,
thus establishing the states of Xíng and Máo.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
at age sixteen,
he was enfeoffed as the Founding Marquis of Fèngchéng County,
with a fief of five hundred households.
The mountains approached the Crane Pass,
not without guests like Táo Kǎn;
his aura connected to the Dipper and the Ox,
like the sword of Zhāng Huá.
Removing his commoner's garb, he became a Gěishìzhōng,
and then the Crown Prince's Xǐmǎ.
As a scion of a noble family entering service,
though not a Court Gentleman, he held the same rank;
a Xǐmǎ of the Central Court,
different from the Shìdào who clears the way.
For the Duke to hold this position,
it was truly a high selection.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he entered to serve in the Palace Secretariat.
In that year,
he was transferred to be the Crown Prince's Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Guarding the Southern Palace,
in charge of the weapon racks;
following the ranks in the Northern Pavilion,
honorably participating in consultations.
With access to both palaces,
he was truly a man of talent.
In the third year of Dàtóng,
he was appointed as Commissioner with a Seal, General of Benevolent Might, and Governor of Qiáozhōu.
Raising the carriage curtain in a region of auspicious aura,
inspecting a place where worries were dispelled.
In the customs of Nányáng,
there were many more literary scholars;
at Měijì he was welcomed,
children came from even further away.
Soon after, there was the distress of war and separation,
the royal house was in turmoil,
officials felt the sorrow of military service,
and gentlemen felt the resentment of having no return date.
Leaving the passes and longing for Chǔ,
he traveled by a small boat;
at Jiānghàn he served the ruler who matched the jade,
at Zhānghuá he returned to the lord of the restoration.
In the first year of Chéngshèng,
he was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Peerless in responding to inquiries,
he truly followed in the footsteps of Dīng Hóng;
with great knowledge of old regulations,
he was equal to Wáng Càn.
In the second year,
he was appointed Commissioner with a Seal, General who Pacifies the West, and Interior Minister of Línchuān,
and then transferred to General who Pacifies the South and Interior Minister of Guìyáng.
The Imperial Workshop cast his sword,
twice he changed his golden turtle pouch;
as an official dividing the tallies,
he was twice enfeoffed with bronze tigers.
Not only was Dèng Yōu pure and honest,
praised in the song of the five drums;
Liú Chǒng was also incorruptible and capable,
famous for the "one-coin prefecture."
Consequently, because the Tiānbǎo era was not yet settled,
and the royal path was much obstructed,
returning to Wú was impossible,
and there was no road back to Shǔ.
Línzī sits by the sea;
he suddenly changed his course,
taking refuge at the Qīngzhāng River
and resting his wings at Bóhǎi.
He was granted the titles of Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn and Sǎnqì Chángshì,
and further served as Chíjié, Dūdū, and Yǒngzhōu Cìshǐ.
However, Qíntíng pressed upon the borders,
and the watchman's clappers of Zhū were heard in the city.
Drums and horns sounded from the earth;
the general descended from the heavens.
Although he used jars to listen for sounds,
it could not defend against the underground tunnels;
although he used tied ropes and bundled brushwood,
it did not repel the scaling ladders.
He requested terms and accepted surrender,
ultimately returning to the Protectorate.
The Zhōu court, using talent from Chǔ for the benefit of Jìn,
did not cease in its deliberations;
like the jade of Zhào sought by Qín,
regardless of his distance or displacement.
In the fifth year of Bǎodìng, he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and the Founding Duke of Yìxīng Commandery,
with a fief of one thousand three hundred households.
In the second year of Tiānhé,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of the various military affairs of Càizhōu, and Càizhōu Cìshǐ.
The beloved son of King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ
once wore commoner's clothes while guarding the valleys;
the younger brother of King Ānlí of Wèi
was also a traveler in Hándān.
As sorrow wounds a man,
his granted years were not long.
At the age of fifty-one,
he passed away at his post in Càizhōu.
Escorting the deceased into the Pass,
only the ceremonial robes remained;
the returning carriage was on the road,
with the curtains once again hanging down.
Alas, how sorrowful!
An edict was issued to grant posthumous titles,
and he was posthumously named [Name omitted],
as is the ritual.
In the eleventh month of the fifth year,
he was buried on the northern plains of Cháng'ān.
The tomb of Chūlǐ Zǐ
directly overlooks the armory;
the grave of Tàishǐ Gōng
faces the Gāomén Gate.
The inscription says:
The distant brilliance of the Dark Bird,
the grand plans of Xiāngtǔ.
In the east, enfeoffed at the Sòng altar;
in the west, gathering the maps of Qín.
His people assisted the Hàn;
his state succeeded in opening Wú.
Possessing beautiful and fine virtue,
he flourished in the princely residence of a close relative.
Establishing the state as an imperial branch,
inheriting the house as an emperor's brother.
Guided by mystical encounters,
his integrity was inspired by Heaven.
Yuán Gù heard the *Shī*,
Táng Dū studied the *Lǐ*.
The garden of Bówàng,
the palace of Jīnhuá.
In the Grove of Literature, he discussed virtue;
in the military tent, he participated in warfare.
His name was inscribed upon the pillars;
his strategies filled the inner curtains.
He sought refuge to the west of the Zī River
and governed to the east of the Huái River.
Qíntíng pressed from the west;
the marshes of Chǔ were exhausted to the south.
Sometimes startled by hunting fires,
sometimes fearing the autumn winds.
Entrusted with far-reaching strategies,
meeting with these changing circumstances.
The battle lines stretched ten lǐ;
the troops laid siege on one side.
A lunar halo over the isolated city;
dust rising at the false reinforcements.
Spring bamboo shoots were not grain;
autumn mugwort was not arrows.
Folding his wings like a reclining dragon,
the humble and the proud ceased fighting.
At the time of being conciliated and welcomed,
grace was added to his initial rewards.
His noble rank became more exalted;
his military honors rose even higher.
No sooner had the Red Heron music taken flight
than the Yú songs resounded.
Weeping for his children, leaving behind regrets;
concealing his books, he departed forever.
Heat and cold cycle in turn;
one withers away in the hills and mounds.
Frosty mists veil the moon;
the scent of pines overrides the autumn.
Alas, the prince of the Southern Land
has become the former Marquis of Dōnglíng.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Fascicle 948.
〈Epitaph of the late Grand General of Zhōu, the Duke of Zhào〉
〈Epitaph of the late Grand General of Zhōu, the Duke of Zhào〉
The Duke’s taboo name was Guǎng,
and his courtesy name was Qiānguī.
He was the great-grandson of Duke Huì of Shào
and the eldest son of Duke Xiào of Bīn.
The Ruòmù tree brushes the sun;
the long serpent reclines in the sky.
The Dragon Chart screens the light of the River;
the Divine Tripods connect the vapors of the clouds.
Six principles constructed the characters;
the Five Phases signaled auspiciousness.
Thus, the sacred peaks sent down a spirit,
and Heaven bestowed virtue.
With skin like congealed lard and eyes like dots of lacquer,
with a forehead like the sun and a pearly court,
as a son, his name was high in the Five Capitals;
as a minister, his light shone for a thousand lǐ.
The peak of Huágài in the midst of heaven
does not reach his height;
the waters of Yúyuān where the sun bathes
do not exhaust his source.
When the year star was in the carved carriage,
his years were those of playing with bamboo horses.
Like the cinnamon tree within the moon,
he could provide instruction when asked;
like a tree growing on a stone,
he attained sudden realization through contemplation.
At the age of eleven,
Duke Xiào passed away.
Solitary in his mourning,
his childlike longing exceeded ritual propriety.
The springs were startled by his filial water;
the bamboo stirred in the cold forest.
The three conducts were made known;
the eight wings were thus uplifted.
When the Great Zhōu established the state,
the royal sons served as the city walls.
Altars were established and men were enfeoffed;
duties were divided to oversee the mandates.
He was made the Founding Duke of Tiānshuǐ Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
In the first year,
he was appointed Shǐchíjié, Piàoqí Dàjiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
In the fourth month of that year,
he was appointed Dūdū and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ.
Duke Xiào had long governed Qiānlǒng,
and his lingering love remained among the people.
Now they are comforted, saying,
"This is the son of our lord."
Was it only in the terrace of the Sīlì
that Bào Xuān served for successive generations?
Or in the office of the Chancellor
that Wéi Xián served for multiple ages?
In the second year,
he was appointed Dàjiāngjūn.
Just as Wèi Qīng pitched his tent,
he was recorded as a great meritorious official;
just as Hán Xìn ascended the platform,
his honor was high in being uniquely appointed.
In the first year of Wǔchéng,
he was promoted to Dūdū of the military affairs of nineteen provinces including Xīng and Liáng, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
Mount Bōzhǒng guides the Yàng River,
which then crosses the eastward flow of the Hàn River;
the sacrifice at Cài and Méng is performed on the plains,
which is truly the western limit of Huáyáng.
In the ninth month of that year,
his title was changed to Duke of the State of Cài,
with a fief of ten thousand households.
His lands bordered Hánchéng,
and his passes were adjacent to the fortifications of Chǔ.
His fief covered eight counties,
with grace as deep as the merit of Kòu Xún;
his domain opened to ten thousand households,
with matters reaching the rewards of Cáo Shān.
In the first year of *Bǎodìng*,
he was appointed as *Shào Sī Kòu*.
Moss grew at the prison doors,
and the locks of the jails were rarely turned.
Carrying wine in the accompanying carriages,
he was fortunate to have no air of grievance;
observing the prisoners within the military command,
he would occasionally listen to the playing of the zither.
In the second year,
he was decreed to guard *Púchéng*
and serve as *Dūdǔ* of the various military affairs of the six defenses, including *Tóngguān*.
In the leap month of that year,
he was promoted to *Dūdǔ* of the various military affairs of the twelve prefectures, including *Qín* and *Wèi*, and as the *Cìshǐ* of *Qínzhōu*.
The Duke frequently governed *Jìchéng*
and often resided in *Lǒngdǐ*;
the powerful and unruly folded their hands in submission,
and the greedy and cruel resigned their seals of office.
Added to this were the elite troops of *Shànggǔ*
and the drums of *Yúyáng*;
to the north he faced *Gāoliǔ*,
and to the south he looked toward *Zhàngyú*.
From the mountain where the *Xiōngnú* dismounted
to the valley where the noble minister hid his wine,
all admired his majestic reputation from afar
and remotely received his civilizing influence.
In the same year,
he received an imperial decree to go to *Gānzhōu* to welcome the Empress.
With the patterns of text on his palm,
it was like the return of *Zhòngzǐ*;
as *Jì Lièyú* came,
the minister welcomed on behalf of the sovereign.
Were it not for a reputation that stands high in distant lands
and prestige that covers harmonious neighbors,
how could one be chosen from the clan to carry out the honored sovereign’s command?
In the fourth year,
he was appointed as *Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn*.
*Zhāoyáng* was employed for his high merit,
and *Xiàng Liáng* held office as a famous general;
comparing them to the present,
they would have felt a sense of shame regarding their virtue.
In the third year of *Tiānhé*,
he was appointed as *Dūdǔ* of the various military affairs of the eight prefectures and the *Gān* defense, including *Shǎn* and *Yú*, and as the *Cìshǐ* of *Shǎnzhōu*.
With the horses of *Qūchǎn* and the jades of *Chuíjí*,
there were already the troops that destroyed *Guó*;
with *Wángguān* and *Jīmǎ*,
there was no lack of a road to cut off *Qín*.
The Duke used orderly drums and banners
and calm carriage tracks;
he subdued the rebellious and awed the borders,
and not a single plan of his was misplaced.
But because he had long toiled at home and abroad,
this accumulated into a disastrous illness.
For him, prayers were offered to the various spirits of the mountains and rivers,
and for him, the guests and feudal lords gathered at his gate.
Therefore, he requested an audience at the *Chéngmíng* Palace
to return to his fief for recuperation.
He was just then inquiring about the sacrifices of the *Xià* suburbs
or discerning the misfortune of the *Sānglín*.
He was reappointed as *Cìshǐ* of *Qínzhōu*
and inherited his father's title as the *Bīnguó Gōng*.
Before he could climb the ridge where the waters divide,
he looked in vain toward the cities of the late frontier.
The Grand Lady, seeing the Duke’s emaciation,
stayed by his side in tearful sorrow.
As grief and illness collided in her chest,
she suddenly passed away in the lodge.
The Duke prostrated himself on a straw mat and slept on a clod,
and neither water nor broth entered his mouth.
Although the royal envoy urged him to moderate his mourning,
his great wound only increased.
The mother died because of the son,
and the son died because of the parent;
the ways of compassion and filial piety
were gathered together in a single morning.
At the hour of his passing,
his age was twenty-nine.
Markets in the four passes closed in mourning,
and the three armies wept as they marched.
Seeking where he once heard lawsuits,
one still sees the sweet pear tree;
looking back at the empty camp,
only the withering willows remain.
He was posthumously granted certain offices,
as is proper according to the rites.
In the sixth month of the sixth year,
he was returned for burial at a certain plain in *Qínzhōu*.
Black armor opened the way,
commemorating the merit of the *Piàoqì* General;
dragon banners were bestowed for the procession,
deeply mourning the distance of *Dōngpíng*.
The Duke was upright and loyal,
gentle, respectful, and filial.
He dwelled in benevolence and righteousness
and adorned himself with rites and music.
His spirit was alert and keen,
and his wisdom was brilliant and clear.
His virtue was as deep as the palace walls,
and no trace of joy or anger showed on his face.
Regarding the records of the *Jīnbǎn* and *Yùcè*,
he read them tirelessly even while resting;
regarding the illustrations of orchid leaves and fungus flowers,
he would surely lift the lamp to read them.
Like the autumn clouds over *Jiéshí*
or the setting moon over *Zhāoyáng*,
poetic thoughts filled his breast,
and a spring of words flowed from his lips.
In his elegant writings,
he was like *Ruǎn Yǔ* and *Chén Lín*;
in his refined bearing,
he was like *Wáng Měng* and *Xiè Tiǎo*.
Speaking of his archery,
his bow was more silent than an ape's cry;
discussing his precision,
his sword went deeper than the wild goose formation.
When *Méi Chéng* looked toward *Liángyuàn*,
he did not fear resigning his office;
when *Yuè Yì* sought the road to *Yān*,
he did not decline a journey of a thousand miles.
As for his generalship in responding to changes,
it was as instantaneous as thunder and lightning;
in his strategies within the command tent,
he secretly coincided with *Sūn* and *Wú*.
He had the ambition to evaluate human character
and the heart to bring peace to the world.
The path of the *péng* bird was suddenly cut short,
and the dragon's ford was then blocked.
Alas! How tragic!
The *Tàizǎi* flourished early like the three thorns of high office
and has long departed from all beginnings.
He nurtured the orphaned child,
as they were branches of the same breath.
Like *Mǎ Yuán*'s admonition to his nephews,
his intent lay in prudence and restraint;
like *Wáng Chén*'s service to his paternal uncle,
his feelings were deep in love and respect.
Sharing virtue and comparable in righteousness,
does this not describe him?
Thus, the inscription says:
Ruling according to the Qián order,
ascending the Lí position to become a sage.
The white ring signifies yielding virtue,
the dark Gui tablet signifies receiving the mandate.
Unifying the earth's nexus,
increasing the brilliance of the heavenly mirror.
Sheltering several states with his shade,
looking down upon the Seven Rectifiers.
The land belonged to those who first ascended,
the era encountered the martial legacy of Xià Wǔ.
The jade Huang pendant suppressed disorder,
the Golden Casket illuminated the assistance.
Wèi and Jìn inherited the houses,
Xíng and Máo were granted territories.
Waves branched from the Jiànmù tree,
streams flowed from the Xuánhù.
The great mandate was reverently ordered,
the glorious path was deep and vast.
Loyalty possessed excellent plans,
filial piety was the complete virtue.
With mountain-patterned beams he governed,
with the Huán Guī tablet he guarded the state.
About to approach the Hànhǎi,
about to carve inscriptions on Yànshān.
Grand banquets at Pínglè,
explaining the scriptures at Jīnhuá.
Discoursing on Confucianism at the Bìshuǐ,
personally performing rites in the Míngtíng.
The wind vane awaits a rhapsody,
the dew collector requires an inscription.
Sailing toward the sun,
galloping horses following the stars.
Virtue is upheld and clearly manifest,
talent and worthiness are truly excellent.
The supreme general is granted the sacrificial meat,
the chief commander is pushed forward by the chariot wheel.
Zhào lost its eastern fishing grounds,
the Hú ceased their southern grazing.
Arrows fell upon Liáochéng,
mud sealed the Hāngǔ Pass.
Ceremonial robes were frequently exposed,
red curtains were often rolled up.
Laws were simplified with empathy,
complex rhetoric was dismissed with reason.
Suspicions were clarified like the hanging crow,
doubts were immediately settled like the snake in the cup.
People shared the public garden,
families gathered the wild silk cocoons.
Treading on clouds to chase the sun,
following the wind to descend from the heights.
A star split from the Zhōngtái,
a mountain collapsed at the Zuǒzhèn.
At the Xià columns, cups were set aside,
on the Yīn steps, the wake was begun.
The mourning canopy moved in procession,
the bright funeral banner was led from the courtyard.
Looking directly toward the Qínchuān,
the Lǒng waters flew apart.
Mountains and rivers filled the eyes,
the ceremonial guard and the spirit returned.
Grave maps and stone horses,
carriages painted with ceremonial robes.
The small mountain shook and withered,
the long forest changed and decayed.
Mournful were the plains and marshes,
desolate was the tomb site.
Trees are thick and people are few,
mountains are many and paths are small.
Ten li of the pine-covered city,
a thousand years for the ornamental pillars.
The Night Terrace is now silent,
the deep springs know no dawn.
From Wényuàn Yīnghuá, chapter 948.
〈Epitaph of the Lady of Bùlùgū Clan, Wife of the Duke of Qiáoguó of Zhōu〉
The Lady’s taboo name was such-and-such,
her courtesy name was such-and-such,
her original surname was Lù,
and she was from Wújùn.
When the Son of Heaven expanded the borders,
the Bǎiyuè came to the court;
when the Chancellor led the troops,
the Sānjiāng was swept clean.
Her great-grandfather Zài
served as the Chief Administrator for Liú Yìzhēn,
remaining to guard Guānzhōng.
After it fell to Hèlián,
he consequently served the Wèi.
Near his death,
he exhorted his children and grandchildren, saying:
“Delight in practicing the local customs,
and do not forget your origins.
Always think of your ancestors,
and do not go against this heart.”
Her grandfather Zhèng
was a General of the Agile Cavalry, Grand Master of Equitable Three Offices, and Governor of Héngzhōu.
Her father Tōng
was a Pillar State General, Grand Minister of War, and Duke of Wén'ān.
He assisted in the foundation of the state
and consulted on the transitions of power.
His fame was higher than Guǎngwǔ,
and his merit was heavier than Chángpíng.
The Lady possessed the seven virtues and cherished brilliance,
like four stars shining in succession.
Respect and love were her natural disposition,
her words and appearance followed the ritual codes.
On the ninth day she would ascend the heights,
writing inscriptions for the autumn chrysanthemums;
at the start of the Three Origins,
she would offer odes to the spring pepper wine.
At the age of fourteen,
she was betrothed to the Duke of Qiáoguó.
Harmonious as the zither and lute,
she increased her heart of reverence and frugality;
pruning the branches,
she truly upheld the virtue of diligence and concern.
The brocade of ascending heights in the Yè region,
she personally washed in the river waves;
at the mulberry-picking ferry of Píngyáng,
she personally labored during the silkworm months.
In the first year of Tiānhé,
she was invested as the Lady of Qiáoguó.
The wife of the Dōngwǔ Pavilion officer
was already said to have a rank;
the wife of the Marquis of Nánchéng
was also known to receive a title.
His Highness the Pillar State, with his glorious name radiating,
expanded the lands of Zēngchéng,
raised banners on the thorny paths,
and administered politics in Qióngdū.
At the stream of the Báiláng,
the path was as difficult as the slope of the Huángniú;
at the mountains of Lìzhī,
the land was as dangerous as the country of Pútáo.
The Lady was separated from her relatives;
passes and rivers formed heavy obstacles.
A single song of the barbarians
was not enough to dispel her sorrow;
three cries of the gibbons
soaked her clothes with endless tears.
Thus, a pestilential illness from the heavens
consequently became a chronic ailment.
Jade drops were difficult to apply,
and golden ointments were truly far away.
On the ninth day of the seventh month of the first year of Jiàndé,
she passed away at her private residence in Chéngdū,
at the age of twenty-one.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of that year, she was returned for burial in the northern plain of Cháng'ān.
An edict posthumously granted her the title of Lady of Qiáoguó,
as was ritual.
The Lady served her superiors with total loyalty
and her parents with exhaustive filial piety.
She promoted the worthy in an orderly manner
and showed kindness to her subordinates.
When she was about to be covered by the mysterious springs,
her words followed the deep night.
Relatives by blood and marriage
all felt deep grief for this chaste woman;
the concubines
truly felt longing for her management of the household.
His Highness’s spirit was wounded by the autumn moon,
and he hid his tears among the tall pines.
The letters left by Zhōu Jìzhí
made the darkness even deeper;
the literary compositions of Pān Ānrén
merely increased the sorrowful resentment.
How can it be said that only the woman of Xīhé
alone saw the Silver Terrace,
or that the woman of the Dōnghǎi
first encountered the Golden Gate?
The inscription says:
Retreating from Shānlíng, the banners return;
at Jiāoshān, the weapons are stilled.
Golden essence occupies the ridges;
prosperous pavilions rise above the waves.
In the west, she traveled as the wife of ministers and chancellors;
in the east, her family held lands partitioned by mountains and rivers.
Like the nobility of Huàtíng,
and the music and songs of Gǔshuǐ.
The clan moved to the eastern region of Zhèn;
they served as officials at the border of Yàn.
Entering the pass at Fēihú;
connecting to the passes of Míngyàn.
Strategies were prepared for ascending the mounds;
merits were joined by the side of the streams.
Precious tripods leave behind inscriptions;
carved spears retain their praise.
Her virtue matched the auspicious signs of the charts;
holding to the rites, she has returned.
Leaning on the rail of the fish-skin carriage;
wearing the patterned robes of the marsh pheasant.
The bright moon shines upon the mirror;
immortal stones prop up the loom.
Passing clouds gently rise;
whirling snow lightly flies.
In the north, the imperial daughter descended;
in the south, she commanded the Prefect of Shǔ.
The Ruòshuǐ River has been opened;
the Spirit Mountain has been carved.
Gibbons wail at Moon Gorge;
river gods battle like oxen.
The star-loom turns to the north;
the sun's reins return to the west.
At Yángquán, the vital breath is hidden;
in the yin-laws, the ashes have sunk.
The crane bids farewell to the market of Wú;
the phoenix departs from the Terrace of Qín.
Divine light disperses and gathers;
lamp shadows linger and pace.
Following the two streams for burial;
a hundred carriages return the banners.
The Young Maiden leaves her position;
the Lady departs the city.
The curtained hall is set in the fields;
the tented palace is built in the suburbs.
Mountains and rivers hold strange events;
the wind and moon are heartless.
Withered and fallen upon the autumn mounds;
desolate and lonely is the sealed domain.
Every tree carries the sound of autumn;
every mountain wears a cold hue.
Short grass is flatter than ever;
long pines grow even straighter.
The tomb of integrity is now firm;
the garden mausoleum is planted forever.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
Epitaph of Lady Hédòulíng, Wife of the Duke of Zhào of the Zhōu Dynasty.
Epitaph of Lady Hédòulíng, Wife of the Duke of Zhào of the Zhōu Dynasty.
The Lady’s taboo name was Hánshēng;
her original surname was Dòu.
She was a native of Pínglíng in Fúfēng.
In the court discussions of the Marquis of Wèiqí,
among the marquises, none could rival the decorum;
in presenting the maps of the Marquis of Ānfēng,
among the meritorious ministers, all yielded the seat of honor.
Her clan’s biography among the imperial in-laws
is already known from the *Book of Jiànwǔ*;
the ancient tripod of Zhòngshān
perhaps marks the tribute of the Shányú.
Her grandfather, Lüè,
was Junior Protector and Duke of Jiànchāng Commandery.
Her father, Chì,
was Pillar of State Generalissimo, Grand Minister of Rites, and Duke of Dèng.
At the Great Oath of Mèngjīn,
he was always among the ministers of one heart;
regarding the broken oaths at Xiányáng,
he assisted the lord who was first to enter.
Both attained positions within the Six Offices
and had merits among the Eight Powers.
The Lady had auspicious lines upon her hand;
she had signs corresponding to the charts.
Her glory was manifested early;
her splendid virtue flourished young.
Respectful and reverent in accordance with ritual,
she received instruction in the Ducal Palace;
with virtue in her speech and appearance,
she was renowned among the preceptresses.
When she came to the virtuous gentleman,
she became the mistress of Hǎndān.
Zithers and harps were in the hall;
she rode in the covered carriages.
Long-lasting in her integrity,
she was worthy of the Inscription of the Autumn Chrysanthemum;
acting rightly from the beginning,
she was worthy of the Ode of the Pepper Flower.
Not only did Zhuāng Jī cover her mouth,
making the Chancellor of Chǔ feel ashamed;
Dìng Jiāng consulted the omens,
and the troops of Qí did not enter.
In the second year of Wǔchéng,
she was invested as the Lady of the Duke of Zhào.
The King of Hàn heard of the righteous woman
and enfeoffed her with Yánxiāng;
the Marquis of Qí saw the ritual-abiding wife
and enfeoffed her with Shíjiào.
Sharing the same glory in different eras,
she had no cause for shame in her virtue.
His Highness the Pillar of State resided on a branch of the Ruòmù tree,
within a branch of the Heavenly River.
Raising banners at Yùlěi;
driving the post-carriage at Tónglíng.
To the south, reaching the people who face the sun;
to the east, covering the land where no thunder strikes.
The Lady followed the administration at Yuèxiá
and assisted in virtue at Yúnmén.
Silks were washed in the river waves;
she returned to the weaving room.
The mountains brightened the stone mirror,
which she faced at her dressing tower.
Soon the jade pitch-pipes frequently shifted;
the golden brazier remained unchanged.
Four ounces of Hú incense—
lamenting that envoys from the Western Regions were rare;
one sprig of spirit herb—
regretting that the path to the Jasper Fields was cut off.
On the twenty-second day of the fourth month of the fifth year of Tiānhé,
she passed away in Jǐnchéng of Chéngdū,
at the age of twenty.
Sūn Zǐjīng’s grief over the passing
saw resentment rise with the autumn wind;
Pān Ānrén’s mourning for the deceased
saw sorrow deepen upon the long bamboo mat.
Furthermore, eternal parting from the Immortal Terrace,
the sound of the flute is heard no more;
the preceptress has returned forever,
leaving only the zither tunes.
On a day in the second month of the seventh year,
she was returned for burial at Hóngdú Plain in Cháng'ān.
An imperial decree posthumously granted her the title of Lady of the State of Zhào;
this was in accordance with the rites.
Clouds and rain come and go,
lingering for the King of Chǔ;
time separates and unites,
truly causing melancholy for the Prince of Chén.
The Inscription says:
West of the River, the land ends abruptly;
at Guānjīn, the terrain rises in isolation.
The worthy minister of Zhāngwǔ;
the worthy official of Ānfēng.
Wooden towers a thousand fathoms high;
golden mountains ten thousand miles long.
Continuing the blessings of the Aunt of Xíng;
building prosperity like the Lady of Sòng.
Tying the sash in the north of Zhào;
serving the mother in the south of Qín.
Ceremonial tassels and threads;
sated with the fine steeds of the Dí.
Her righteousness surpassed the *Jiāngsì*;
her benevolence spread like the *Gětán*.
A jade basket to welcome the swallows;
a golden cage to aid the silkworms.
Respect and love were pure and deep;
dignified, with a reputation for goodness.
Bringing light to the state history;
showing no sign of joy or anger.
Raising the tray with outward respect;
stopping the loom to give instruction.
More fragrant than the orchid;
her years were as fleeting as the hibiscus.
Wind and rain have dissipated;
the divine spirit is severed.
The weaving girl returns to the stars;
Héng'é returns to the moon.
The evening libation by the left pillar;
the morning departure from the high hall.
Vainly raising the "Treading the Waves";
no more "Whirling Snow."
The low ground is called a marsh;
the high ground is called a plain.
To the west, bordering the fire-wells;
to the north, looking toward the fortress gates.
Still wearing the pheasant robes;
still riding the fish-skin carriage.
The plain is suddenly gone;
what can the Way of Heaven say?
Mountains turn to the city of the earth;
the road is lost at Téngchéng.
Pines grieve as the crane departs;
grass is wild where fireflies are born.
New clouds rise separately;
the old moon shines alone.
The worthy tomb is an eternal model;
the mound of integrity is forever steadfast.
*Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
Epitaph of Lady Zhèng, Wife of the Duke of Ānchāng of the Zhōu Dynasty.
The Lady, whose taboo name was [omitted],
was a native of Yángwǔ in Xíngyáng.
A younger brother of King Xuān of Zhōu
was enfeoffed as a Marquis in Zhèng;
the many generations of descendants of Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng
served as High Officials in Zhōu.
Taking the name of the state as their clan name,
it began from this.
Her grandfather, Qióng,
was the Tàicháng and Marquis Gōng.
Her father, Mù,
was the Sīkōng and Duke Zhēn.
When composing poems in the Western Capital,
as the Tàicháng he attended the Bǎiliáng banquet;
when interpreting prophecies in the Eastern Capital,
as the Sīkōng he served as a Wǔwèi official.
Their lineage was linked to the imperial genealogy,
as solid as a massive rock;
their gate was called Tōngdé,
never failing to produce scholars.
The Lady practiced ritual and righteousness within the inner chambers,
being dignified and virtuous,
gathering plantains
and the luxuriant vines.
When she became the match for a gentleman,
she served her parents-in-law,
with a humble manner and pleasant voice,
performing her duties with towel and broom,
treating relatives with ritual propriety,
and bringing harmony to the inner quarters.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
she was formally appointed as the Commandery Lady of Xíngyáng.
Following the rank of her relatives to higher honors,
she received a stipend according to her husband's rank.
Was she merely a wife who established righteousness,
whose title was extended to a township?
Or a wife of ritual,
enfeoffed at Shíjiào?
While the Great General submerged his rhinoceros armor in the Two Rivers,
the Lady heard the cry of the monkeys in the Three Gorges.
Amidst the obstructions of Míngyuè and Língguān,
and the difficulty of the Shǔ road in the autumn wind,
she was covered like a jade flower,
and first followed the spring dew.
On the twentieth day of the fifth month in the eighteenth year of Tiānhé,
she passed away in Chéngdū,
at the age of thirty-six.
An imperial decree posthumously granted her the title of Lady of the State of Ānchāng,
in accordance with the rites.
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, she was returned for burial at Báiqǐ Plain in Xiányáng.
Thus causing the hills to turn and the earth to be moved,
they first sealed the tomb of the chaste wife;
as the sun set into the Yúyuān abyss,
it truly covered the tomb of the virtuous lady.
Alas, how sorrowful!
The inscription says:
The state was founded by the Heavenly River,
dividing the capital region and establishing government.
The land possessed ten cities,
and the people held the nine ranks.
The fiefdom of former times
has now become the clan name.
Discerning conduct and transmitting the legacy,
attending the carriage and leaving behind blessings.
Three stars were at the door,
as a hundred carriages returned.
Reverently managing internal affairs,
she brought glory to the inner quarters.
Serving the mother-in-law with water for washing,
instructing her children by stopping the loom.
Tending silkworms in the mulberry garden,
the luan bird flying in the brocade room.
Walking rhythmically with jade pendants,
wearing garments decorated with aquatic weeds and fire.
The waters of Bā sob mournfully,
the monkeys' cries are cut short.
The moon sets and the pearl is damaged,
spring withers and the cassia branch breaks.
The Zhào zither says a long farewell,
the Qín flute says an eternal goodbye.
The chaste lady is hidden in the tunnel,
the virtuous woman's tomb is sealed.
No moon shines on the banks of the Luò,
the Jīng Terrace has lost its clouds.
The birds' grief is painful to hear,
the sound of the pines is mournful.
A thousand years into antiquity,
a hundred generations of remaining fragrance.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 963.
〈Epitaph of Lady Dòu, Wife of the Northern Zhou Great General, Duke of Lóngdōng Commandery, Lord Houmòchén〉
The Lady, whose taboo name was [omitted],
was a native of Pínglíng in Fǔfēng.
When Zhāngwǔ founded the state,
her name was higher than the foremost imperial relatives;
when Ānfēng entered the court,
his position was above the meritorious officials.
Her grandfather, at the beginning of Xiàochāng,
governed Huáiyáng;
her father, at the start of Zhèngguāng,
held office in Hǎidài.
The Lady was born into a family of ritual and righteousness
and was rooted in the virtue of admonitions.
Reverently following ritual,
her virtue was her model.
When the hundred carriages returned home,
and the three stars were at the door,
she began her duties with water and admonitions,
taking the branches and stems as her rule.
Though her son was involved in government,
she still had no heart for leisure or ease;
though her husband went out on campaign,
she herself recognized the signs of the burial mounds.
In the sixteenth year of Dàtǒng,
she was formally granted the title of Commandery Lady of Yǒng'ān.
A wife’s honor is based on her husband's status,
and a mother's nobility comes from her son;
the court's regulations and the family's joy,
she possessed both.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
her title was changed to Lady of the State of Lóng.
The ritual numbers of her carriages and garments,
the classic rules of her robes and sashes,
as beautiful as the fish in the river,
were sufficient to illuminate the Red Records.
Then, when the wind and frost arrived,
and the gray pipe of time encroached,
what can be said of the virtuous?
She reached the Great Change.
On the seventh day of the fourth month in the sixth year of Tiānhé, she passed away,
at the age of sixty-six.
On the tenth day of the tenth month of that year, she was moved for burial at Dù Plain in Wànnián County, Xiányáng.
The rising and falling shapes of the mountain
match the auspicious sign of the white crane;
the wind and mist of the terrain
harmonize with the energy of the blue bird.
The inscription says:
The lineage of Guānjīn,
the prominent surname of Pínglíng.
Four marquises entered officialdom,
three lords participated in government.
Achievements established at Báiláng,
blessings inherited from the Red Snake.
The Hàn river is vast,
where her virtue was first heard.
Her husband at the head of the court,
talented men managing the house.
Hairpins and ornaments according to ritual,
carriages and horses according to decree.
Yielding indeed fosters integrity,
giving away pearls puts an end to competition.
A hundred years pass in a flash,
a thousand pieces of gold cannot be relied upon.
The chamber says farewell to the worthy husband,
the courtyard says goodbye to the noble son.
The returning saddle is left in the dew,
the gathering of mugwort for sacrifice has ceased.
The room is left with sleeping silkworms,
the clothes still bear the painted pheasants.
Clouds hang low over the marshes,
the sun is obscured at the late hour.
Empty curtains in the old hall,
vacant canopies at the new burial.
The mountain surrounds the funeral carriage,
the road is lost among deep pines.
How many times has the wandering soul changed?
Where has the great person gone?
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, Volume 963.
〈Epitaph of Lady Wūshílán, Wife of the Duke of Guànjūn of Zhōu〉
The Lady, whose taboo name was [omitted],
was a native of Lèlíng.
She was a descendant of Bāo, the Jìn Sītú and Duke of Lèlíng.
Her ancestors took the title as their fief,
and thus settled there.
In the old city of Fǔfēng,
the Iron Market still remains;
in the old villa of Hénán,
the Golden Valley still exists.
Some resided at the border of Yàn,
and served in Dài Commandery.
Her grandfather, Xíng,
was the Governor of Dài Commandery.
Her father was the Wèi Sīkōng and Duke of Lánlíng Commandery.
The Sīkōng assisted the imperial mandate,
was the Shǎofù of the Wèi court,
and a high official of the Zhōu house.
Both were great clans,
and both were bestowed with the surname.
A match like Qín and Jìn,
they are called families of common lineage.
The Lady was seventeen years old
when she married into the Yǔwén clan.
She was virtuous and dignified,
possessing inner beauty and chaste auspiciousness.
Her conduct in rituals and household duties was exemplary,
and she maintained order within the inner chambers.
In a certain year,
she was appointed Jīnxiāng Jùnjūn.
In another year,
she was reappointed as the Guàngjūn Guó Fūrén.
Possessing the four virtues of a noble wife,
she brought harmony to her household;
as the mistress within the home of a high official,
she humbly assisted in managing affairs.
In the fourth month of the fifth year of Bǎodìng, she fell ill and passed away,
at the age of forty-four.
On a certain day of a certain month in that year, she was returned for burial at a certain plateau in Jīngzhào.
The winds and mists of the human world
and the mountains and rivers pass by swiftly.
Amidst the green wheat on the burial mounds,
perhaps one will encounter the grave of this chaste woman;
by the white poplars at the head of the ridge,
one may find the tomb of this worthy lady.
Thus, the inscription says:
Three stars grace the heavens,
and the Five Peaks steady the earth.
Rituals have their order,
and people reside in their proper stations.
The regions of Yān and Zhào are full of the extraordinary,
and their mountains and rivers possess a heroic spirit.
From these was born this virtuous lady,
who possessed such inner beauty.
Like jade illuminating the courtyard,
or orchids filling the room with fragrance.
Dressed in the fine ritual garments like the aunts of Xíng,
or like the Sòng lady by the fish-filled rivers.
With a hundred carriages, she was married,
following the nine rituals of betrothal.
Dressed in the seven-colored ceremonial robes,
she rode in a carriage of the sixth rank.
From a noble house, she left her kin,
to assist in the governance of the high court.
Generations are like flowing water,
and human life is but a great dream.
Returning the curtains to the mountain gates,
moving the lamps into the spring caverns.
Golden dates are forever held,
and silver silkworms are sent eternally.
Fragrance fills the cypress coffin,
and the road to the pine city is closed.
A sorrowful phoenix with a solitary shadow,
a heroic sword with a lonely cry.
Lingering over the zither of Zhào,
grieving by the pipes of Qín.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 163.
<Tomb Inscription of Lady Zhèng, Wife of the Great Preceptor and Duke of Zhèng State of the Zhōu>
The Lady, whose taboo name was [blank],
was a native of Yuǎn Lǐ, Kāifēng Xiàn, Yíngyáng.
Seven sons composing poetry
was enough to bring glory to their guests;
three ministers engaging in governance
truly pacified the feudal lords.
When riding in the same carriage, the Jìn Empress would stop her palanquin;
when coming to court, the Hàn Emperor recognized the shoes.
Her noble lineage continued in succession,
never lacking in the historical records.
Her grandfather, Nà,
was the Biéjià of Qínzhōu.
Her father, Mòubó,
was the Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, and the Bóyáng Xiàn Hóu.
The Lady’s virtue and goodness were known early on,
like a lone orchid flourishing in its beauty.
Possessing both grace and virtue,
she was married with due ceremony.
Her fraternal respect was shown in her care for elders,
and she was diligent in her ritual duties.
The Tàifù assisted in harmonizing the Zhōu house,
serving as its most trusted support;
the Lady assisted her husband,
taking charge of the household labors.
Harmonious as the zither and lute,
they were as the trees and branches without conflict;
thus her influence was used in the state,
and she was perfected in filial piety and respect.
On a certain day of a certain month in a certain year,
she was enfeoffed as the Zhèng Guó Fūrén.
Having received the ceremonial robes,
she remained diligent in her ritual duties.
Though her husband possessed the nobility of an Ānshì,
she personally performed the washing of clothes;
though her son had the dignity of a Wénbó,
she never forgot the loom.
Inside and out, all was at peace,
and the inner chambers were upright.
When illness struck the family,
medical remedies were of no avail.
She passed away on the twentieth day of the third month in the third year of Tiānhé,
and was buried at Shí'ān Yuán in Cháng'ān.
Her eldest son, [blank],
and his brothers all followed her compassionate instructions,
all honoring her maternal example.
Their sorrow was as deep as the frost and dew,
and their grief was increased by the cold spring.
The inscription says:
Residing in virtue at Pǔtián,
serving in the offices of instruction.
Carriages were stationed for guests to arrive,
and schools were opened for scholars to gather.
She brought blessings to her household,
and worthy talents followed in her footsteps.
Like the flowers of the cherry tree,
or the wings of the locusts.
Possessing the seven virtues of human relations,
and the transformative influence of the "Two Nans."
Gathering the plantain,
and the thick-growing kudzu.
Her conduct and reputation were like resonant jade,
and she wore the hairpins and jewelry of her rank.
In the willow garden, she held the shuttle,
and at the mulberry ford, she bathed the silkworms.
The years passed swiftly by,
and the time of falling away came unexpectedly.
The family lost its virtuous lady,
and the state lost its worthy mistress.
Sending her off forever to the fragrant tomb,
as the dancing crane bids its long farewell.
The mountains are deep and the moon is dark,
the wind is sharp and the pines are sorrowful.
After a thousand years of opening and closing,
the spiritual tortoise will be proven true.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
<Tomb Inscription of Lady Yuán, Wife of the Later Wèi Piàojì Jiāngjūn and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Hèbá>
"On the islet in the river,"
one hears of the virtue of the gentleman's mate;
"gathering the ferns,"
one sees the propriety of the lady.
When applied to moral transformation,
human relations are enriched.
The Lady's taboo name was Ān,
and her style name was Dàluó.
She was a native of Luòyáng, Hénán.
Her grandfather was [blank],
the Kāng Wáng of Jīngzhào.
Her father was Zhāo,
the Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Lù Shàngshū, Sīzhōu Mù, and Rǔyáng Jùnwáng.
With a heroic lineage like petals on a calyx,
and a foundation laid for great deeds,
born into a house of lords and ministers,
they were the pillars of the state and the family.
The Lady was able to cultivate the laws and regulations,
never thinking to violate ritual propriety.
She was respectful, frugal, and economical,
and her concern lay in promoting the worthy.
In the fifth year of Dàtǒng,
she was enfeoffed as the Lè'ān Gōngzhǔ.
She married into the Hèbá family
at the age of thirteen.
She was thoughtful and diligent in her duties,
and her transformation into womanly virtue was complete.
