The red brush reflected her glory,
and the cherry trees flourished early.
When the songs of praise found their rightful place,
and her ceremonial robes were adjusted in rank,
she assisted her husband
and remained content in her home.
In the first year of Tiānhé of the Zhōu,
she was enfeoffed as the Zhāngwǔ Jùnjūn.
The frost and dew do not linger,
and the wind and smoke are fleeting.
After falling ill for several weeks,
she suddenly passed away.
She died on the twenty-sixth day of the second month in the fourth year of Tiānhé of the Zhōu in Wànnián Lǐ, Cháng'ān,
at the age of fifty-two.
A decree posthumously granted her the title of Dùnqiū Guó Fūrén,
as is the ritual.
On the twentieth day of the third month of that year, she was returned for burial at Shí'ān Yuán in Xiányáng.
Unlike the immortals riding on phoenixes,
she has departed forever;
though she is not the dancing crane,
the gates of the spring are now closed upon her.
Wishing to record the details of her fine tomb,
we thus make this inscription:
Far-reaching were the grand schemes,
how long-lasting the tracks of hegemony.
The fate of the nine regions shifted in secret,
and the Three Rivers were exhausted within.
High ministers rode side by side,
and virtuous talents ceased their dances.
Like fine wǎnyǎn jade in her grace and purity,
she tied the sash and knotted the tassels in marriage.
Comparable to the tángdì blossoms,
and likened to the prolific zhōngsī locusts.
Having fulfilled the virtues of a wife,
she was also praised as a model of motherhood.
The flowing waters surge on and on,
and the perilous path of life gradually passes.
Asking for medicine yielded no answer,
and the steaming of cinnabar proved ineffective.
Her dífú ceremonial robes are displayed in vain,
and the strings of her loom are silently covered.
The road turns at the city gate,
and the funeral dirges reach the end of the journey.
The deep grave is shrouded in mist,
and the tall pines gather the wind.
Like spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums,
everything has its beginning and its end.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 963.
<Epitaph of Lady Luó, Wife of Chángsūn Xiá, Great Commandant of Zhōu and Count of Yánglín>
<Epitaph of Lady Luó, Wife of Chángsūn Xiá, Great Commandant of Zhōu and Count of Yánglín>
The lady’s taboo name was [blank],
a native of Tàipíng County, Dài Commandery, Héngzhōu.
Her grandfather was [blank].
Her father was Xié,
Great General of Zhōu and Duke of Nányáng Commandery.
The lady was dedicated in serving her parents,
personally following their instructions and admonitions.
She taught within the clan,
and was well-versed in the *Shī* and the *Lǐ*.
When she was married,
she was as solemn and respectful as when serving her parents.
She maintained reverence through the offerings of duckweed and algae,
and was diligent with the weaving of cords and threads.
Within the household, she achieved harmony,
and in the inner chambers, there was peace.
Her lifespan did not endure,
as the frost and dew took her early.
There was no cup of Yánshòu to prolong her life,
and she lacked the pillow of longevity.
She passed away in Hónggù Village, Cháng’ān, on the eighth day of the second month in the fourth year of the Tiānhé era of Zhōu,
at the age of twenty-three.
On a certain day of a certain month in that year,
she was buried in Shòulǐ, Wànnián County.
Though the mountain was not in the State of Sòng,
it became the tomb of a virtuous woman;
though the land was different from Jīngtái,
it became the grave of an excellent consort.
The inscription says:
Bì and Láng established the state,
and the spiritual martial might founded the capital.
The land connects to the pillars of heaven,
and the mountains overlook the precious talismans.
The people are endowed with righteousness and fervor,
and generations have manifested grand designs.
The *Gétán* vines were lush,
and the tángdì blossoms flourished early.
Having settled in her virtuous character,
she followed her destined match.
The four teachings were widely proclaimed,
and the Three Stars were in their proper place.
Frost withers the cinnamon garden,
and the wind falls upon the fields of numinous fungi.
The Three Obediences failed her nature,
and the Five Blessings were marred by her early years.
Returning in peace is forever severed,
and her words are forever lost.
The outskirts and fields are mournful and desolate,
and the winding marshes and plains are lonely.
The wind is bitter and the clouds are sorrowful,
the pines are mournful and the dew weeps.
One sighs in vain at the bright moon,
for how can one reach the wounded spirit!
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 963.
<Epitaph of Lady Yùchí, Wife of Tuòbá Jìng, General of Equine Ceremonies of Zhōu and Duke of Sōngzī>
<Epitaph of Lady Yùchí, Wife of Tuòbá Jìng, General of Equine Ceremonies of Zhōu and Duke of Sōngzī>
The lady’s taboo name was [blank],
a native of Luòyáng, Hénán.
Her grandfather was [blank].
Her father was the Grand Preceptor and Duke of the State of Zhù.
During the chaos of the Wèi house,
he managed the state through peace and adversity;
when the Zhōu dynasty founded the state,
he assisted in the peaceful transition of power.
Recording the imperial genealogy,
there was kinship both within and without;
dividing the mountains and rivers,
it remained a state of uncles and nephews.
The lady’s appearance and demeanor were dignified,
her example was virtuous and fine.
Observing her virtue through the Six Meanings,
she was like the Lady in the poems of the *Nánfēng*;
with the eight trigrams forming their shapes,
she held the position of the Youngest Daughter in the East.
She learned the proper speech from her governess,
and received her education in the lord’s palace.
Diligent with the needle, basin, thread, and silk,
she wore the sash and the fragrant herbs.
At the age of twelve,
she was married to the General of Equine Ceremonies Tuòbá Jìng.
Wearing her ceremonial robes,
she attained the decorum of a primary wife;
riding in her fish-skin carriage,
she followed the rites of the various states.
The *Biāoméi* plums bore fruit three times,
never missing their season;
the *Yāotáo* peach blossoms bloomed nine-fold,
and she was able to cultivate her household governance.
In a certain month of a certain year,
she was invested as the Lady of Huíluò County.
Her mother,
Princess Jīnmíng,
was the eldest daughter of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
In spring, the emperor’s daughter would gather mulberry leaves;
in autumn, the royal lady would build her residence.
The lady frequented the princess’s house
and wandered among the relatives’ quarters,
in the Zhuólóng gardens
and the Chángmén palaces.
Soon, however, her noble and pampered life met with misfortune,
and her flourishing beauty was marred by her early years.
She became bedridden with a chronic illness,
passing through the changes of summer and winter.
The techniques of three generations
did not reach the physician’s gate;
the origins of the hundred herbs
were exhausted in vain in their medicinal properties.
She died on the seventh day of the fifth month in the third year of the Jiàndé era,
at the age of thirty.
Formerly, a woman of Xīhé
encountered the nine-sectioned sweet flag;
a woman of the Eastern Sea
obtained the numinous fungi of the three mountains.
But there was no way to meet such fortune again,
how tragic it is!
She was buried on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of that year on the Běilíng Plain of Jīngzhào.
The turtle shell and milfoil announced the hour,
and the mound was opened for the offerings.
To the west, it faces the temple of the Weaver Girl;
to the south, it looks toward the tomb of the Lady Xiāng.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus the inscription says:
Her father was called the Imperial Preceptor,
her mother was called the Royal Princess.
Her carriage and robes were not bound by ordinary things,
and her thoughts were as vast as the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Thus was born this fine and virtuous lady,
who observed the *Lǐ* and was devoted to the *Shī*.
Her reputation surpassed Sòngzǐ,
and her virtue was as flourishing as Xíngyí.
Inheriting generations of great virtue,
she was chosen as a worthy match.
The ritual goose was offered at the gate,
and the soaked duckweed filled the sacrificial vessels.
She performed the ritual washing as required,
and moved her mat according to order.
In spring, she bathed the silkworms in ice,
and in autumn, she held the shuttle at the loom.
A close relative to the emperor’s hometown,
a near minister in the imperial city.
A kinswoman of the Zhuólóng garden,
a hostess like those of Píngyáng.
The golden waves reflect the moon,
and the jade trees face the spring.
Like Lòngyù and the Phoenix,
or Chāngróng and the purple herb.
From this point for a thousand years,
no one shall attain the Way.
The hibiscus flower was radiant and glorious,
how early did it wither and fall.
On the northern plain of the Wèishuǐ river,
at the old garden of Pínglíng.
Just past the entrance of the valley,
one looks toward the gate of the grave.
Alas, in this place,
the returning soul departs.
In the tenth month of early winter,
the tall pines will stand for long years.
Relatives and guests cover their tears,
what can be said in such sorrow!
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Scroll 963.
<Epitaph of Lady Lǐ, Wife of Chái Liè, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand General, Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Equine Ceremonies, and Count of Guànjūn of Zhōu>
<Epitaph of Lady Lǐ, Wife of Chái Liè, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Grand General, Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General of Equine Ceremonies, and Count of Guànjūn of Zhōu>
The Lady, with the taboo name [Mǒu],
was a native of Dídào in Lóngxī.
The Zhōu dynasty had its Archivist,
whom the Master likened to a dragon;
the Hàn dynasty had its general,
for whose sake Yuànchéng surrendered horses.
There was also one who traveled west to submit a memorial,
remaining as the Chancellor of the State of Qín;
and one who turned east to offer strategies,
being the teacher of the King of Hán.
Her father, Yí,
was the Commissioner with a Cordon, Great General, Regional Inspector of Northern and Southern Huá Provinces, and Duke of Shùnyáng Commandery,
being the eldest uncle of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi.
Like the Marquis of Ráng, Wèi Rǎn,
who resided in the palace of Xiányáng;
or the King of Qǔyáng, Wáng Gēn,
who borrowed the Míngguāng Hall.
Speaking of her noble relatives,
they are quite comparable;
but discussing her humility and modesty,
those others would have much to feel ashamed of.
The Lady was intelligent and sensitive since childhood,
and her fine reputation for virtue was heard early on.
The red brush recorded her beauty,
and her worthy talents were highly praised.
When playing with her paper and brush,
she feared misinterpreting the intentions of her elder brothers;
cutting her hair at a young age,
she feared hurting the heart of her grandmother.
At the age of eleven,
she was married to the General of the Flying Cavalry and Opener of Office with Equal Honor to the Three Dignitaries, Chái Liè.
Liè, as a supreme general, promulgated the calendar
and held office in the Central Tower;
he was loyal and diligent in military and state affairs,
with a vast and complex scope of responsibility.
The Lady assisted her husband;
her speech and appearance provided support,
adding brilliance to the Three Stars,
and reverently manifesting the Four Virtues.
Handing the towel and pouring the water,
she was diligent in serving her mother-in-law;
cutting the silk and stopping the loom,
she never forgot the instruction of her son.
In the second year of Bǎodìng,
she was invested as the Lady of Dàxià District.
Since she was honored by her husband's status
and also ennobled by her son's rank,
she was then moved to Shùnyáng
and her title changed to Lady of the Commandery.
The fief of a lady
may sometimes use a township name;
the title of a wife
mostly follows the husband's rank.
The official documents arrived with glory,
truly worthy of being called an honor and favor.
She originally suffered from a wind-qi ailment,
which worsened frequently over the years,
leaving her mostly bedridden.
The powder of the flying turtle
showed no sign of dispelling the illness;
the charm of the painted dragon
proved ineffective in prolonging her years.
She passed away at her residence on a day in the third month of the fourth year of Jiàndé,
at the age of forty-nine.
She was buried on a day in the eighth month of that year at Hóngdù Plain in Cháng'ān.
Divine light separates and merges,
still remaining by the river bank;
cloud qi wanders,
still returning below the tower.
Alas, how sad!
Thus the inscription says:
Submitting memorials as the Qín Chancellor,
establishing merit as the Hàn general.
The Lóng River's waters flow apart,
gazing toward Qínchuān from afar.
In the land of Qiū, the customs are brave,
in the realm of Metal, the earth is strong.
Amidst the Guǎngwǔ army,
upon the Ānpíng River.
A wife is one who is equal,
marriage is called "returning."
The Three Stars shine at night,
a hundred carriages fly in the morning.
There are protocols for the ceremonial robes,
no conflict in appearance or etiquette.
Rank equal to the Terrace Court,
robes identical to those of a Marquis.
The son follows the mother's model,
the husband listens to the household governance.
The seven clans maintain harmony,
the nine chambers continue the celebrations.
Sashes and towels are handled with reverence,
warmth and coolness are provided with filial respect.
Holding the shuttle as autumn yields its harvest,
silkworms follow the commands of spring.
The beauty of her years had not yet faded,
but the flash of lightning passed first.
Vainly consuming the daily qi,
idly drinking from the Heavenly River.
A star withers in the Jade Well,
the moon sheds its golden waves.
The setting sun at Yúyuān,
the mournful song of "Xiè Lù."
Lonely and empty offerings,
desolate ritual settings.
The ghostly mound sealed like a tortoise,
the deep springs where ants gather.
The autumn colors are sorrowful,
the sound of pines is cut off.
How many are the years in a century?
Returning to this parting.
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, volume 963.
<Epitaph of Lady Ěrzhū, Wife of the Duke of Péngchéng>
<Epitaph of Lady Ěrzhū, Wife of the Duke of Péngchéng>
The Lady, of the Ěrzhū clan,
was a native of Luòyáng in Hénán.
Spanning the north and south of Yǐnshān,
she was aligned with the pivot of the Big Dipper;
the Hàn Sea encompasses all,
directly facing the constellations Bì and Mǎo.
The four seasons hold fire,
as the Torch Dragon opens the light that illuminates the earth;
the sixth month rides the wind,
as the great Péng bird spreads wings that cover the sky.
Thus possessing the capital districts,
they eventually ruled the central lands.
In chariots, books, rites, and music,
the changes of the Three Kings can be known;
for generals, ministers, dukes, and marquises,
the mountains and rivers of a hundred generations shall not perish.
Her grandfather, Chǎng,

was the Suí dynasty's Opener of Office with Equal Honor to the Three Dignitaries, Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, General Manager of the seven provinces of Qí, Tóng, Jīn, Shēn, Xìn, Lín, and Xú, Minister of War, and Foundation Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
In heaven are the stars of the Ministry,
on earth is the distinction of the Palace Grand Master.
Emerging from ten thousand miles away,
he was known for great merit like Lǚ Dài;
commanding a region on his own,
he was entrusted with heavy responsibility like Liú Hóng.
Her father, Xiūzuì,
was the Suí dynasty's Attendant of the Thousand Bulls of the Left, Grand Master of Court Audiences, and Marshal of the Prince of Qí's Mansion,
inheriting the title of Duke of Jīnchéng.
The grand master boasts of his achievements,
and the feudal lords are granted land.
The Huái immortal brings rain,
still climbing the mountain of cassia trees;
the guest of Chǔ faces the wind,
further entering the lotus waters.
The Lady possessed the virtuous spirit of the Jade Terrace
and the immortal essence of the Golden River.
Like the daughter of Cài Zhōngláng,
she early on listened to the colored silk;
within the household of Grand Tutor Xiè,
she first extolled beautiful rules.
The Duke of Péngchéng originated from Yīn Bó
and inherited the house of the Hàn Chancellor.
The climate of mountains and rivers
manifested the White Warrior at Gāoyáo;
the auspicious signs of the stars
brought down the Azure Dragon at Mànqiàn.
Three stars shine at night,
awaiting the appointed time of the crowing goose;
seven days holding autumn,
observing the omen of the flying Phoenix.
The Lady was just eighteen years old
when she was married to me.
Gazing south toward Wūshān,
she met the evening rain like Yáojī;
facing west toward Huàshān,
the Bright Star descended like the Jade Maiden.
Her every movement aligned with the *Shī* and *Lǐ*,
and her words became a standard of conduct.
Showing respect morning and evening,
her service was as extreme as "shifting the heavens";
offering duckweed and algae with sincerity,
her righteousness was expressed in domestic management.
The young lady's washing stone
sounds in the moonlight while she thinks of the autumn wind;
the weaving woman's loom
hears the cold crickets and urges the silk-reeling.
She followed the bequeathed teachings of Cáo Dàjiā
and maintained the chastity of Sòng Bójī.
Furthermore, her heart relied on the Eight Realizations,
and her understanding met the Three Emptinesses;
she wielded the blade of wisdom in the Sandalwood Forest
and sailed the immortal boat in the Sea of Dharma.
Her divine spirit shone alone,
silent beyond words and images;
forgetting both emptiness and existence,
she cast aside the trap and snare as of no use.
Humans are born between Heaven and Earth;
their longevity is not like that of gold or stone.
Stealing the medicine from the Yíntái,
one wonders for how many years she has fled to the Moon;
burning incense in the Golden Palace,
one thinks of the Soul-Returning Incense but there is no day for her return.
She died at her private residence in Píngkāng Lǐ on a certain year, month, and day.
On the twentieth day of the tenth month in the third year of the Shàngyuán era,
she was buried together at Bìyuán south of the city;
this is according to the rites.
Beside the bed of the Prince of Qí,
before the steps of the Dù family;
facing the Bìyuán of Wén Wáng,
following the joint burial of Zhōu Gōng.
Beneath the reclining pines of a thousand ages,
forever free from the sorrow of a lonely crane;
among the catalpa trees of a hundred fathoms,
once again seeing the gathering of a pair of mandarin ducks.
The inscription says:
Joint burial was not an ancient custom,
but was what Zhōu Gōng preserved.
Death and life for a thousand years,
inner and outer coffins for the two souls.
The wilderness is vast and the wind is sharp,
the sky is cold and the sun is dim.
Smoke and haze over the distant peaks,
fog obscures the remote villages.
Recording on the tablet of "yellow silk,"
facing the grave gates of green pines.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 964.
<Epitaph of my Paternal Aunt, Lady Lǐ of Dōngpíng Commandery>
The Lady’s surname was Lǐ,
a person from Dídào of Lǒngxī.
Since the time of Liáng Wǔzhāo Wáng,
one family produced three dukes;
they were a prominent clan within the four seas,
detailed in the national histories and family genealogies.
Her grandfather was Chōngyǐng,
Great General of Latter Zhōu, Prefect of Huázhōu, and Duke of Liújiāng Commandery.
Her father was Xuánmíng,
Shàng Yítóng of the imperial dynasty, Prefect of ◇, Jì, and three other prefectures, and Baron of Chéngjì County.
He served through three reigns,
holding the split tallies of authority;
in the lands of Qín, Lǒng, Hé, and Jì,
people praise him to this day.
Scholars and officials throughout the world, whether they knew him or not,
all looked up to his character.
The Lady was born with a pure and profound nature;
she was reverent in childhood,
harmonious in youth,
and kind and gracious in maturity.
When she had just reached the age of fifteen,
she was married to my elder relative.
Handling the broom and dustpan,
serving her parents-in-law,
people never heard any complaints among the wives and concubines;
within the inner gates,
all was harmonious.
Therefore, the clan promoted her good reputation,
and the neighborhood regarded it as a beautiful story.
The Duke of Dōngpíng maintained a foundation of integrity,
encountering days of great peace;
summons for office arrived in succession,
and his fame was heard in the heavens.
He was decreed as Shàngshū Láng,
promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and went out to serve as Prefect of Dì, Cáo, Héng, and Cháng prefectures.
The Lady assisted her husband
and diligently cultivated the internal governance.
At dawn, she arranged her hair and pins,
having the solemnity of ruler and minister;
washing hands and serving meals,
having the respect of father and son;
reporting her actions upon returning,
having the way of brothers;
being certain and cautious with promises,
having the trust of friends.
Her womanly virtues were like this.
Throughout his service in and out of the capital,
his reputation was exceedingly great.
Harmonizing the zither and lute,
and correcting the state and family,
the Lady truly contributed her strength.
She once sighed and said:
"In ancient times, the wives of high officials
were noblewomen with large sashes;
they prepared sacrificial robes and performed the silk offering;
how can one not be diligent!
How can one not be diligent!"
Because of this, she wore washed garments
and personally engaged in spinning and weaving.
Baskets, pans, and cooking pots
were the objects of her labor;
duckweed and hornwort
were used to manifest her virtue.
Unless one were extensively learned and reached in ritual,
chaste, gentle, and obedient,
who could achieve this!
When the Duke requested to retire due to old age,
he returned to his former humble attire.
The Lady was over sixty years of age,
yet her sight and hearing were undiminished.
Every New Year’s season
and at the Winter Solstice,
the younger relatives of the clan who came to offer toasts and wish her long life
often numbered dozens or hundreds;
she never failed to guide them with cheerful words,
welcoming them with a warm countenance.
She was resolute
and respectful;
she had the style of Mèngmǔ
and the instructions of Jìngjiāng.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Yǒngchún era,
her illness lingered on her bed;
she died in Wàngxiān Lǐ of Huáyīn,
at the age of eighty-one.
On the Bǐngchén day, the first day of the eleventh month,
she was buried on the plain of Yǒngfēng Township,
following the ancestral site.
The Duke of Dōngpíng mourned the living and cherished the past,
feeling painful grief in his heart.
Those from near and far gathered,
and the clan relatives all met;
glory in life and sorrow in death,
this is exactly what it means.
On that day,
the Crown Prince was overseeing Cháng'ān;
I, Jiǒng, being the Zhānshì Sīzhí,
could not go to the funeral site
to accompany the hearse.
I venture to present the writing of Lǐ Yóng,
hoping it might match the eulogy of Pān Yuè.
Alas, how sorrowful!
Thus the inscription says:
Upon the high peaks,
floating clouds soar;
outside Hángǔ Pass,
righteous breath rises.
Establishing merit against the northern Dí,
quelling the Róng and Qiāng;
enfeoffed in Nánzhèng,
the family has always been prosperous.
The illustrious ancestors and father
had dragon-like brilliance;
governing prefectures and commanderies,
they wore silver and gold.
Born with a virtuous nature,
bearing auspicious omens;
like the blooming of flowers and the richness of chrysanthemums,
like the fragrance of orchids and sweet flags.
Possessing beautiful virtue,
like jade tablets and scepters;
seeking her by divination,
like the crying of phoenixes.
When the gentleman arrived,
jade rings tinkled;
the household lived in harmony,
zithers and lutes were played.
Handling the hemp and ramie,
providing clothes;
serving the food,
clarifying the wines and broths.
Aunts and sisters-in-law
were harmonious, warm, and kind;
cousins and sisters,
their joy was unending.
When the Duke went out to govern,
protecting the four quarters;
the Lady’s influence
was vast and wide in virtue.
When the Duke retired,
returning to his hometown;
within the inner gates,
her way became even more manifest.
On the first day of the first month,
and the long Winter Solstice,
descendants celebrated,
each offering toasts.
Like Sòng Gōng, Mèngmǔ, and Lǔ Jìjiāng,
teaching without anger,
following the old regulations.
Just when we expected her to soar high,
to enter the Purple Chamber;
who would have thought it inappropriate,
that she would be covered in the dark hall.
Solemn pines and catalpas,
formed in dense rows;
in the deep and heavy night,
it will never turn to dawn.
○ Wényuàn Yīnghuá, scroll 964.
〈The Seventh Night〉
The Oxherd reflects from afar in the water,
The Weaver Girl is just mounting her carriage.
The bridge of stars connects to the envoy of the Hàn,
The loom stone follows the immortal raft.
Looking at each other across the river, they are near,
Having passed through autumn, their separation is long.
Sorrow takes the regret of tonight
And adds it to the flowers of next year.
○ *Yùtái Xīnyǒng*, Vol. 8.
*Gǔjīn Suìshí Záyǒng*, Vol. 25.
〈Untitled〉
Not worrying about the wind blowing gently,
Truly helpless against the snow falling heavily.
Courage relies only on wine,
Judging and discussing requires poetry.
○ *Quánfāng Bèizǔ*, Former Collection, Vol. 1, Plum Blossom Section.
White clouds emerge from the cliff edge,
The clear moon rises from within the waves.

〈The Cuckoo〉
〈The Cuckoo〉
Missing text.
○ *Cànghǎi Shīhuà*.
〈Untitled〉
Books have been stored for how many generations?
Watching games has already lasted a thousand years.
○ *Shēng'ān Shīhuà*, Vol. 1, quotes a poem by Yǔ Zǐshān.
〈Poem on Passing the Tomb of Prince Chénsī〉
〈Poem on Passing the Tomb of Prince Chénsī〉
The noble son alone worried about his life,
The tomb mound holds his remaining fame.
Woodcutters have taken all the dead trees,
Plowing fields has leveled the wild tomb paths.
How could he pursue the banquets at Pínglè?
How could he think of an audience at Chéngmíng?
This morning I came to receive the mandate,
Also saying the matters are concluded.
Drifting far to Héshuò,
The wind whirls and the hurricane howls.
Wild geese and clouds form ranks together.
Sand and mugwort are startled at once.
Withered mulberry leaves fall at the ancient shrine.
Cold birds return to the solitary city.
The waters of Lǒng mourn to the tune of the reed pipe.
At Yúyáng, the sound of drums is dismal.
A guest from afar leaves his home.
How can he not feel heartbroken?
○ *Wényuàn Yīnghuá*, Vol. 306, attributes this to Yǔ Jiānwú.
〈Rhapsody on Sorrow〉
Attacking the City of Sorrow, yet it never falls,
Battering the Gate of Sorrow, yet it never opens.
What can boil sorrow until it is cooked?
What can burn sorrow until it catches fire?
Closing the door to drive away sorrow,
Sorrow refuses to leave.
Hiding deep to avoid sorrow,
Sorrow already knows one's whereabouts.
○ *Hǎilù Suìshì*, Vol. 9.
Also *Mànsǒu Shīhuà* quotes the rhyme for "place."
Who knew that a one-inch heart
Could hold ten thousand bushels of sorrow?
○ *Hǎilù Suìshì*, Vol. 9.

Wind blows across Yúnmèng,
Ice freezes over the boat official's office.

〈Rhapsody on Mandarin Ducks〉
Once there was a pair of phoenixes,
That flew into the Wèi palace.
Now they have become two trees;
Which one is Hán Féng?

Wearing pearls and kingfisher ornaments,
The bridge of the hairpin is filled with gold grains.
